--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page contains the Royal Privilege, a formal license granting exclusive printing rights to the publishers of Isaac Newton's third edition of the "Principia." It follows the title page, serving as a legal protection against piracy—an early form of copyright.</meta>

# GEORGE R. <note>George Rex; King George I of Great Britain.</note>

WHEREAS Our Trusty and well beloved *William Innys* and *John Innys* of Our City of *London*, Booksellers, have by their Petition represented unto Us, that they have at great Charge and Expence printed a new and correct Edition of a Book entitled, *Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy; by the author Isaac Newton, Knight. Third edition, enlarged and corrected:* <note>original: "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica; Auctore Isaaco Newtono Eq. Aur. Editio tertia aucta & emendata." The title "Eq. Aur." stands for "Eques Auratus," or "Golden Knight," a term for a Knight Bachelor.</note> And the sole Right and Title of the Copy of the same, being vested in the said *William Innys* and *John Innys*, they have humbly besought Us to grant them Our Royal Privilege and Licence, for the sole printing and publishing thereof for the Term of fourteen Years: We being willing to give all due Encouragement to Works of this Nature, which tend to the Advancement of Learning, are graciously pleased to gratify them in their Request, and do, by these Presents, agreeable to the Statutes in that Behalf made and provided, for Us, Our Heirs and Successors, give and grant unto them the said *William Innys* and *John Innys*, their Executors, Administrators and Assigns, Our Royal License for the sole printing and publishing the said Book entitled, *Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy; by the author Isaac Newton, Knight* <note>original: "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica; Auctore Isaaco Newtono Eq. Aur."</note> for the Term of fourteen Years from the Date hereof, strictly forbidding all Our Subjects within Our Kingdoms and Dominions to reprint the same, either in the like or in any other Volume or Volumes whatsoever, or to Import, Buy, Vend, Utter <note>In this legal context, "utter" means to put into circulation or distribute unauthorized copies.</note> or Distribute any Copies thereof reprinted beyond the Seas, during the aforesaid term of fourteen Years, without the Consent or Approbation of the said *William Innys* and *John Innys*, their Heirs, Executors, and Assigns under their Hands and Seals first had and obtained, as they shall answer the contrary at their Peril: Whereof Our Commissioners and other Officers of Our Customs, the Master Wardens and Company of Stationers <note>The Stationers' Company was the London guild responsible for regulating the printing trade and enforcing publishing rights.</note>, are to take Notice that due Obedience be rendered thereunto. Given at Our Court at *St. James’s* the twenty fifth Day of *March*, 1726. in the twelfth Year of Our Reign.

->*By his Majesty’s Command,*<-

->TOWNSHEND.<- <note>Charles Townshend, 2nd Viscount Townshend, serving as the Secretary of State for the Northern Department.</note>

<summary>This document is a formal Royal License granted by King George I to booksellers William and John Innys, granting them exclusive 14-year copyright for the third edition of Isaac Newton's "Principia."</summary>
<keywords>Royal Privilege, copyright, William Innys, John Innys, Isaac Newton, Principia Mathematica, George I, Townshend, Stationers' Company, 1726, history of publishing</keywords>

# GEORGE

In this third edition of the books *The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy* <term>original: "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica," Newton’s seminal work on motion and gravitation.</term>, the care of which **Henry Pemberton**, M.D., <note>Henry Pemberton (1694–1771) was a physician and mathematician invited by Newton to edit this final edition, as Newton was then in his eighties.</note> a man most highly skilled in these matters, has undertaken, Newton has corrected several things and made additions to the mechanics and illustrated them with geometric demonstrations; this brevity renders the understanding easier <unclear>...</unclear>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page follows the third edition's introductory material and contains the opening lines of a famous celebratory poem by the astronomer Edmond Halley. This poem, traditionally included in the "Principia," extols Newton's achievement in uncovering the mathematical laws governing the universe. Catchword "Quæ" indicates the first word of the next page.</meta>

## ON
## THE MOST EXCELLENT MAN
# ISAAC NEWTON’S
### THIS WORK
## OF MATHEMATICAL PHYSICS
### the outstanding glory of our age and nation.

Behold for yourself the pattern of the heavens, and the balances of the divine mass,
Behold the calculation of Jupiter; and those laws which, while the beginnings of things
He was composing, the all-parenting Creator refused to violate,
And the foundations on which He placed His works.
The innermost sanctuaries of the conquered sky are laid open,
Nor does the force remain hidden which rotates the furthest spheres.
The Sun, sitting on his throne, <note>original: "folio residens." Halley uses regal imagery for the Sun to describe its gravitational dominance over the solar system.</note> commands all things to tend toward him
In a downward descent, nor does he allow the starry chariots
To be moved in a straight path through the vast void;
But he pulls each thing into fixed circles, with himself as the center.
Now it is clear what the curved path is for the terrifying comets;
Now we no longer wonder at the phenomena of the "bearded star." <term>original: "barbati astri," a traditional name for a comet, referring to its visible tail or coma.</term>
We learn from this at last by what cause the silvery Moon <note>original: "argentea Phœbe." Phoebe is a poetic name for the Moon, sister to the Sun-god Apollo.</note>
Walks with unequal steps; why, subject to no
Astronomer until now, she refused the reins of calculation:
Why the nodes return, and why the orbit's points advance. <term>The "nodes" are the points where the Moon's path crosses the Earth's orbital plane; the "auges" or apsides are the points where the orbit is closest to or furthest from the center.</term>
We learn also with what forces the wandering Moon <note>original: "vaga Cynthia." Cynthia is another name for the goddess of the Moon, referring to her birthplace on Mount Cynthus.</note> drives the ebbing sea,
While with weary waves it leaves the seaweed
And lays bare the sands feared by sailors;
Beating against the highest shores in alternating turns.

<summary>This page features the beginning of Edmond Halley’s introductory poem, which praises Newton for solving the mysteries of planetary motion, comets, and the tides through the law of universal gravitation.</summary>
<keywords>Edmond Halley, Isaac Newton, gravitation, planetary motion, comets, lunar theory, tides, celestial mechanics</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the celebratory poem by Edmond Halley begun on the previous page. Having described Newton's specific astronomical discoveries (the orbits of planets and comets, and the tides), Halley now shifts to the philosophical and historical significance of Newton's work, comparing him to the great lawgivers and inventors of antiquity. The catchword from the previous page was "Quæ."</meta>

The things that so often tormented the minds of ancient sages,
And which vex the schools in vain with loud disputes,
We now see clearly, as mathematics <note>original: "mathesi." Halley emphasizes that mathematical rigor, rather than just philosophical speculation, is what finally solved these ancient mysteries.</note> dispels the mist.
No longer does error weigh down the doubtful with darkness;
For those who possess the sharp insight of a sublime genius,
It is now granted to penetrate the dwellings of the gods and scale the heights of heaven.
      Arise, mortals! Cast aside your earthly cares;
And from these pages, learn to recognize the powers of a heaven-born mind,
Far removed from the lowly life of beasts.
The lawgiver who commanded that murder, theft, and adultery,
And the crimes of treacherous fraud be restrained by written laws;
Or he who first inspired wandering tribes to encircle cities with walls;
Or he who blessed nations with the gift of grain <note>original: "Cererisve... munere." Ceres was the Roman goddess of agriculture; her "gift" is the knowledge of farming.</note>;
Or he who pressed from the grape a solace for our cares;
Or he who showed how to join painted sounds with a reed from the Nile <note>original: "Niliaca... arundine." A poetic reference to the papyrus reeds used by the Egyptians to create paper, and thus the invention of writing.</note>,
And to set voices before our eyes—
All these improved the human condition less than this, for they provided 
Only meager comforts for our miserable lives.
But now, indeed, we are admitted as guests at the table of the gods;
We are permitted to handle the laws of the high heavens. Now the hidden
Gates of the dark earth stand open, as does the unchanging order of things,
And the secrets that lay concealed through all the past ages of the world.
      Celebrate with me in song the man who reveals such wonders!
You who delight in the nectar of the gods, 
Join me in praising **NEWTON**, who unlocks the treasury of hidden truth.
**NEWTON**, dear to the Muses, within whose pure heart
Apollo <note>original: "Phœbus." The god of the sun, light, and truth.</note> is present, filling his mind with his entire divine power.
No mortal may ever approach more closely to the gods.

->***EDM. HALLEY***<-

<summary>This concluding section of Halley’s poem argues that Newton’s mathematical breakthroughs are superior to all previous human inventions, such as law, agriculture, and writing, because they grant humanity access to the divine laws of the cosmos. It ends with the famous tribute that Newton has approached the divine more closely than any other mortal.</summary>
<keywords>Isaac Newton, Edmond Halley, Mathematics, Scientific Revolution, Human Progress, Classical Allusions, Laws of Nature, Poetry</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page marks the beginning of Isaac Newton's own preface to the first edition of the *Principia* (1687). It follows the celebratory poem by Edmond Halley. While Halley’s poem was a lyrical tribute, Newton now begins his formal technical introduction, shifting the tone from poetic praise to philosophical and mathematical definitions. The catchword "ca" from the previous transcription (though the snippet shows "Quæ") would have led into the first word of the preface in some editions, but here we begin the Author's Preface directly.</meta>

## THE AUTHOR’S
# PREFACE
### TO THE
# R E A D E R

Since the ancients (according to Pappus <note>Pappus of Alexandria was a Greek mathematician of the 4th century AD whose *Collection* is a major source for ancient geometry.</note>) held mechanics in the highest esteem for the investigation of natural things; and since more recent thinkers, having set aside "substantial forms" and "hidden qualities" <note>Newton is rejecting the Aristotelian tradition, which explained the world through internal "essences" rather than external, measurable forces.</note>, have attempted to bring the phenomena of nature under mathematical laws: it seemed appropriate in this treatise to cultivate mathematics <note>original: "mathesin."</note> insofar as it relates to philosophy <note>original: "philosophiam." In the 17th century, "natural philosophy" was the term for what we now call science.</note>.

The ancients established a twofold mechanics: rational mechanics, which proceeds accurately through demonstrations, and practical mechanics. To practical mechanics belong all the manual arts, from which the name "mechanics" was originally borrowed. However, since craftsmen usually work with little accuracy, it has come to pass that all mechanics is distinguished from geometry in such a way that whatever is accurate is referred to geometry, and whatever is less accurate to mechanics. 

Yet the errors are not in the art, but in the craftsmen. He who works less accurately is a more imperfect mechanic, and if anyone could work with perfect accuracy, he would be the most perfect mechanic of all. For the descriptions of straight lines and circles, upon which geometry is founded, belong to mechanics. Geometry does not teach how to draw these lines, but requires it <note>original: "postulat." In mathematics, a postulate is a starting assumption or required action.</note>. It requires that the student <note>original: "tyro." A beginner or apprentice.</note> learn to describe these accurately before he reaches the threshold of geometry; then, geometry teaches how problems may be solved through these operations. To draw straight lines and circles are indeed "problems," but they are not geometric problems. The solution to these is required from mechanics; the use of those solutions is taught in geometry. 

And geometry glories in the fact that, from so few principles borrowed from elsewhere, it can accomplish so many things. Geometry is therefore founded upon mechanical practice, and is nothing other than that part of universal mechanics which accurately proposes and demonstrates the art of measuring. However, since the manual arts are chiefly concerned with the moving of bodies, it follows that geometry relates to magnitude, and mechanics [to motion]... <note>The text ends mid-word at "mechani-", which will continue as "mechanica" on the next page.</note>

<summary>Newton introduces his work by redefining the relationship between geometry and mechanics, arguing that geometry is a precise branch of "universal mechanics" and that his "natural philosophy" will be based on mathematical laws rather than abstract qualities.</summary>

<keywords>rational mechanics, geometry, natural philosophy, mathematical laws, Pappus, manual arts, measurement, precision</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Isaac Newton’s preface to the first edition of the *Principia*. -> AUTHOR’S <-

*is ordinarily referred to motion. In this sense, rational mechanics will be the science of motions that result from any forces, and of the forces required for any motions, accurately proposed and demonstrated. This part of mechanics was cultivated by the ancients in the five powers* <note>These are the "simple machines" of classical antiquity: the lever, pulley, wheel and axle, wedge, and screw.</note> *relating to the manual arts, who considered gravity (since it is not a manual power) hardly otherwise than in the moving of weights by those powers. But we, considering not the arts but philosophy* <note>original: "philosophiae." In Newton's time, "natural philosophy" was the study of the physical world, what we now call science.</note>, *and writing not about manual but natural powers, treat those things primarily which relate to gravity, levity* <note>original: "levitatem." In older physics, levity was the supposed inherent quality of "lightness" that caused things like smoke to rise, the opposite of gravity.</note>, *elastic force, the resistance of fluids, and suchlike forces, whether attractive or impulsive: And for that reason, we propose these as our **Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy**. For the whole difficulty of philosophy seems to consist in this: that from the phenomena of motions we investigate the forces of nature, and then from these forces we demonstrate the remaining phenomena. And to this end relate the general propositions which we have treated in the first and second books. In the third book, however, we have proposed an example of this matter through the explanation of the system of the world. For there, from celestial phenomena, through the propositions mathematically demonstrated in the prior books, the forces of gravity are derived by which bodies tend toward the sun and the individual planets. Then from these forces, also through mathematical propositions, the motions of the planets, comets, the moon, and the sea are deduced. I wish it were possible to derive the rest of the phenomena of nature from mechanical principles by the same kind of reasoning. For many things move me to suspect somewhat that they may all depend upon certain forces by which the particles of bodies, through causes not yet known, are either mutually impelled toward one another and cohere according to regular figures, or are repelled and recede from one another; being ignorant of these forces, philosophers have hitherto attempted to understand nature in vain. I hope, however, that either to this mode of philosophizing, or to some truer one, the principles set down here will afford some light.*

*In publishing these things, the most keen and, in every branch of literature, most learned man Edmond Halley* <note>Halley was a renowned astronomer who not only encouraged Newton to write the Principia but also paid for its publication.</note> *has labored with great diligence; he not only corrected the errors of the typesetters and saw to the engraving of the diagrams, but he was also the primary mover behind my undertaking this edition. Indeed, when he had obtained from me the demonstration of the figure of the celestial orbits, he did not cease to request that I communicate the same to the Royal Society, which thereafter, by its encouragements and kind auspices, caused me to begin thinking about publishing the same. But after I had entered upon the inequalities of the lunar motions,*

I preferred to insert some things discovered late in less suitable places rather than change the numbering of the propositions and the citations. I earnestly request that everything be read with an open mind, and that defects in such a difficult subject be not so much criticized as investigated by the new efforts of my readers and kindly corrected.

# AUTHOR’S PREFACE

->TO<-

## THE SECOND EDITION.

*In this second edition of the **Principia** <note>original: "Principiorum"; shorthand for the "Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy"</note>, many things are corrected in various places, and several things are added. In Section 2 of the first book, the method of finding the **forces** <term>vires: the physical influences that cause bodies to move or change motion</term> by which bodies can revolve in given orbits is made easier and more extensive. In Section 7 of the second book, the theory of the **resistance of fluids** <note>Newton studied how air and water slow down moving objects, a field now called fluid dynamics.</note> is investigated more accurately and confirmed by new experiments. In the third book, the **theory of the moon** <term>theory of the moon: the mathematical calculation of the Moon's path, which is difficult because it is pulled by both the Earth and the Sun</term> and the **precession of the equinoxes** <term>precession of the equinoxes: the slow change in the orientation of Earth's rotational axis</term> are more fully derived from their own principles, and the theory of **comets** is confirmed by more numerous and more accurately computed examples of their orbits.*

Given at *London*,
March 28, 1713.

->ISAAC NEWTON.<-

# THE EDITOR’S PREFACE

->TO THE<-

# SECOND EDITION.

Kind reader, we present to you a new and long-desired edition of Newton’s philosophy, now greatly corrected and enlarged. What is chiefly contained in this most famous work, you may understand from the added indexes; as for what has been added or changed, the author’s own preface will mostly inform you. It remains for some things to be added regarding the method of this philosophy.

Those who have undertaken the study of physics <note>original: "physicam"; in this period, "physics" or "natural philosophy" referred to the general study of nature and the physical world.</note> can be grouped into roughly three classes. For there have been those who attributed specific and **occult** <term>occult: from the Latin 'occultus' meaning hidden; refers to properties that were claimed to exist but could not be observed or explained by mechanical laws</term> qualities to each kind of thing, upon which they claimed the operations of individual bodies depended in some unknown way. In this lies the essence of the **Scholastic doctrine** <term>Scholastic doctrine: the system of philosophy and theology taught in medieval European universities, largely based on the works of Aristotle</term>, derived from **Aristotle** and the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, named after the covered walkways (peripatoi) of the Lyceum where they met</term>. They assert that every effect arises from the particular natures of bodies; but they do not teach where those natures come from, and therefore they teach nothing. Since they are entirely concerned with the names of things rather than the things themselves, they should be considered to have invented a certain philosophical jargon, but not to have handed down a philosophy.

Others, therefore, hoped to achieve the praise of better diligence by rejecting this useless jumble of words. They established that all matter is **homogeneous** <term>homogeneous: uniform in substance; the idea that all matter is essentially the same at its most basic level</term>, and that all the variety of forms seen in bodies arises from certain very simple and easily understood **affections** <note>original: "affectionibus"; here referring to the basic properties of particles such as shape, size, and motion.</note> of the component particles. And indeed, a progression is rightly established from simpler things to more complex ones, provided they do not attribute any modes to those primary properties of particles other than those which

<summary>In this preface to the second edition, editor Roger Cotes begins a critique of previous scientific methods, specifically attacking the "Scholastic" tradition for using empty jargon and "occult" qualities to explain nature.</summary>
<keywords>Roger Cotes, Newtonian philosophy, second edition, Scholasticism, Aristotle, Peripatetics, physics, homogeneous matter, mechanical philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues Roger Cotes's preface to the second edition of Newton’s "Principia." In the preceding text, Cotes dismissed the Scholastic "occult qualities." Here, he critiques the second group—the mechanical philosophers (like Descartes) who rely on unproven hypotheses—before introducing the third and superior group: experimental philosophers like Newton.</meta>

->EDITOR'S<-

...which nature herself bestows. But when they take the liberty to assume whatever unknown shapes and sizes of parts they please, along with uncertain positions and motions; and when they even invent certain **occult fluids** <term>occult fluids: subtle, invisible substances (like the "ether") that many 17th-century thinkers imagined filled the universe to explain how forces moved through space</term> that freely permeate the pores of bodies, possessed of an all-powerful subtlety and agitated by hidden motions; they then slide into dreams, neglecting the true constitution of things. This truth is sought in vain from deceptive conjectures, when it can scarcely be tracked down even through the most certain observations. Those who take the foundation of their speculations from **hypotheses** <term>hypotheses: in Newton's era, this term specifically referred to assumptions or "guesses" not yet proven by observation</term>—even if they proceed thereafter with the utmost accuracy according to mechanical laws—may be said to compose an elegant and beautiful **fable** <note>original: "fabulam"; Cotes is likely taking a jab at René Descartes, whose "vortex theory" Newton sought to replace</note>, but it is a fable nonetheless.

There remains, therefore, a third class: those who profess **experimental philosophy** <term>experimental philosophy: the scientific method based on observation and repeatable experiments rather than pure logic or "armchair" reasoning</term>. These thinkers indeed wish to derive the causes of all things from the simplest possible principles; however, they assume nothing as a principle that has not yet been proven by phenomena. They do not devise hypotheses, nor do they admit them into physics, except perhaps as questions whose truth may be debated. They proceed by a double method: **analysis** and **synthesis**. They deduce the forces of nature and the simpler laws of those forces from certain selected phenomena through analysis; from these, they then provide the constitution of the remaining things through synthesis. This is that far superior way of philosophizing which our most celebrated author deemed worthy to be embraced above all others. This alone he judged worthy of his effort to cultivate and adorn. Of this method, he gave the most illustrious example: namely, the explanation of the **system of the world** <note>original: "mundani systematis"; this refers to the structure and mechanics of the solar system</note> most successfully deduced from the theory of gravity. Others had suspected or imagined that the power of gravity existed in all bodies; he was the first and only one who could demonstrate it from appearances and place it upon a firm foundation by his excellent speculations.

I am well aware, indeed, that some men of great name, being more occupied by certain prejudices than is fair, have found it difficult to agree with this new principle and have repeatedly preferred uncertainties to certainties. It is not my intention to pick at their reputation; rather, kind reader, I wish to set before you in a few words the facts from which you may bear a fair judgment yourself.

Therefore, to begin the argument from the simplest and nearest things, let us look for a moment at what the nature of gravity is in earthly objects, so that we may then proceed more safely to the celestial bodies, which are located at a very great distance from—

<summary>Roger Cotes distinguishes Newton’s experimental method from the "fables" of speculative philosophers who invent hidden fluids and unproven hypotheses. He argues that Newton’s theory of gravity is unique because it is demonstrated through observation rather than mere guesswork.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Roger Cotes's preface to the second edition of Isaac Newton’s "Principia." On the previous page, Cotes defined "experimental philosophy" as the pursuit of causes through observation. Here, he begins to apply this method to the phenomenon of gravity, arguing against the existence of "innate lightness" and demonstrating that gravity is a mutual force between all bodies.</meta>

->### PREFACE.<-

...removed from our [senses], it has been reached. It is now agreed among all philosophers that all bodies near the Earth gravitate toward the Earth. Multiplex experience has long since confirmed that no truly light bodies exist. What is called **relative levity** <term>relative levity: the ancient idea that some objects, like smoke, possess an inherent quality of "lightness" that makes them rise; Cotes argues they only rise because heavier air pushes them up</term> is not true lightness, but only apparent; it arises from the more powerful gravity of adjacent bodies.

Furthermore, just as all bodies gravitate toward the Earth, so the Earth in turn gravitates equally toward those bodies. That the action of gravity is mutual and equal on both sides is demonstrated as follows: Let the mass of the whole Earth be divided into any two parts, whether equal or unequal in any way. Now, if the weights of these parts were not mutually equal to one another, the lesser weight would yield to the greater, and the parts joined together would continue to move in a straight line to infinity toward the direction in which the greater weight tends—which is entirely contrary to experience. Therefore, it must be said that the weights of the parts are established in equilibrium; that is, the action of gravity is mutual and equal on both sides.

The weights of bodies, at equal distances from the center of the Earth, are proportional to the quantities of matter within those bodies. This is gathered from the equal acceleration of all bodies falling from rest through the forces of their weights; for the forces by which unequal bodies are equally accelerated must be proportional to the quantities of matter to be moved. Now, that all falling bodies are indeed accelerated equally is clear from the fact that in a **Boylean vacuum** <term>Boylean vacuum: a space from which air has been removed using an air pump, named after the scientist Robert Boyle</term>, they describe equal spaces in falling during equal times—once, of course, the resistance of the air has been removed. However, this is even more accurately proven by experiments with **pendulums** <note>Newton conducted experiments with pendulums made of different materials (gold, silver, glass, etc.) to show that gravity acts on all matter identically, regardless of its composition.</note>.

The attractive forces of bodies, at equal distances, are proportional to the quantities of matter in those bodies. For since bodies gravitate toward the Earth and the Earth in turn toward those bodies with equal momentum, the weight of the Earth toward each body—or the force by which the body attracts the Earth—will be equal to the weight of that same body toward the Earth. Moreover, this weight was proportional to the quantity of matter in the body; therefore, the force by which each body attracts the Earth (or the body’s "absolute force") will be proportional to that same quantity of matter.

Therefore, the attractive force of whole bodies arises and is composed from the attractive forces of their parts; since it has been shown that if the mass of matter is increased or diminished, its power is proportionally increased or diminished. Thus, the action of the Earth is composed of the combined actions of its parts...

<meta>catchword: ...posed (original: flari)</meta>

<summary>In this section of the preface, Cotes argues that gravity is a universal, mutual force proportional to the amount of matter in an object, using Robert Boyle’s vacuum experiments and pendulum tests as evidence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Roger Cotes's preface to the second edition of Isaac Newton’s "Principia." ->## OF THE EDITOR<-

...must be considered <note>original: "flari cenſenda erit"</note>; and so it follows that all terrestrial bodies must attract each other with absolute forces that are in proportion to the quantity of matter attracting. This is the nature of gravity near the Earth; let us now see what its nature is in the heavens.

That every body perseveres in its state of either resting or moving uniformly in a straight line, except insofar as it is compelled to change 그 state by impressed forces, is a law of nature received by all philosophers. From this it follows that bodies moving in curved lines, and which therefore constantly depart from the straight lines tangent to their orbits, are kept in their curvilinear path by some continuously acting force. Therefore, for the planets revolving in curved orbits, there will necessarily be some force by whose repeated actions they are deflected indefinitely from the tangents.

Now it is right to grant what is gathered and most certainly demonstrated by mathematical reasoning: namely, that all bodies moving in some curved line described in a plane, and which—by a radius drawn to a point that is either resting or moving in any way—describe areas around 그 point proportional to the times, are urged by forces tending toward that same point. Since, therefore, it is agreed among astronomers that the **primary planets** <note>The "primary planets" refers to the planets we know today (Mercury, Venus, Mars, etc.) orbiting the Sun.</note> describe areas proportional to the times around the sun, and the **secondary planets** <note>The "secondary planets" refers to moons orbiting their respective planets.</note> around their primaries, it follows that the force by which they are perpetually turned aside from rectilinear tangents and compelled to revolve in curvilinear orbits is directed toward the bodies located at the centers of those orbits. This force, therefore, may not be inaptly called **centripetal** <term>centripetal: from the Latin 'centrum' (center) and 'petere' (to seek); a force that pulls an object toward a center point</term> with respect to the revolving body, and **attractive** with respect to the central body, from whatever cause it may be imagined to arise.

Furthermore, these things must also be granted and are mathematically demonstrated: If several bodies revolve with uniform motion in concentric circles, and the squares of the periodic times are as the cubes of the distances from the common center, the centripetal forces of the revolving bodies will be inversely as the squares of the distances. Or, if bodies revolve in orbits that are close to circles and the **apsides** <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where the planet is either closest to or farthest from the body it orbits</term> of the orbits remain at rest, the centripetal forces of the revolving bodies will be inversely as the squares of the distances. Astronomers agree that one or the other of these cases holds for all the planets. Therefore, the centripetal forces of all planets are inversely as the squares of the distances from the centers of their orbits. If anyone should object that the apsides of the planets, and especially the moon, do not remain entirely at rest, but with a certain [slow] motion...

# PREFACE
<meta>catchword: in time</meta>

...to be carried slowly forward: it can be answered that, even if we grant that this very slow motion results from the proportion of the **centripetal force** <term>centripetal force: a "center-seeking" force that pulls an object toward a center, such as gravity pulling a planet toward the Sun</term> deviating slightly from the **duplicate ratio** <note>original: "a duplicata," referring to the inverse-square law where force decreases as the square of the distance increases</note>, that deviation can be found by mathematical calculation to be entirely imperceptible. For the very ratio of the lunar centripetal force, which ought to be the most disturbed of all, will indeed slightly exceed the duplicate ratio; but it will approach this ratio nearly sixty times more closely than it does the triplicate ratio <note>original: "triplicatam," or an inverse-cube law</note>. But the truer answer will be to say that this **progression of the apsides** <term>progression of the apsides: the slow rotation of the major axis of an elliptical orbit, such as the point where a planet is closest to the sun shifting over time</term> arises not from a deviation from the duplicate proportion, but from an entirely different cause, as is excellently demonstrated in this philosophy. It remains, therefore, that the centripetal forces, by which the **primary planets** tend toward the sun and the **secondary planets** toward their primaries, are accurately as the squares of the distances inversely.

From what has been said so far, it is established that the planets are retained in their orbits by some force constantly acting upon them: it is established that this force is always directed toward the centers of the orbits: it is established that its efficacy increases as they approach the center and decreases as they recede from it: and indeed, it increases in the same proportion as the square of the distance decreases, and decreases in the same proportion as the square of the distance increases. Let us now see, by making a comparison between the centripetal forces of the planets and the force of gravity, whether they might perhaps be of the same kind. They will indeed be of the same kind if the same laws and the same properties are found on both sides. First, therefore, let us weigh the centripetal force of the **Moon**, which is nearest to us.

The straight-line distances which are described in a given time by bodies released from rest at the very beginning of their motion, when urged by any forces whatever, are proportional to those forces: this follows certainly from mathematical reasoning. Therefore, the centripetal force of the Moon revolving in its orbit will be to the force of gravity on the surface of the earth, as the distance which the Moon would describe in the shortest possible time by descending toward the earth by its centripetal force (if it were imagined to be deprived of all circular motion), is to the distance which a heavy body describes in the same shortest possible time in the vicinity of the earth, by falling through the force of its own gravity. The first of these distances is equal to the **versed sine** <note>original: "sinui verso," a geometric measurement representing the distance between the arc of the Moon's path and the straight line it would have traveled if no force were pulling it; this measures how much the Moon "falls" toward Earth to stay in orbit</note> of the arc described by the Moon in the same time, because that measures the Moon's translation from the tangent, caused by the centripetal force; and thus it can be computed from the data of the Moon's...

<summary>Roger Cotes argues that planetary orbits are governed by a centripetal force that follows the inverse-square law, dismissing minor orbital shifts as irrelevant to this fundamental rule. He then proposes that this celestial force is identical to the gravity observed on Earth by comparing the Moon's motion to falling bodies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Roger Cotes's preface to the second edition of Isaac Newton’s "Principia." On the previous page, Cotes discussed how planetary orbits suggest an inverse-square law of force. Here, he connects the force holding the Moon in its orbit to the familiar force of gravity on Earth, eventually extending this principle to the entire solar system.</meta>

# FROM THE EDITOR

...periodic time, as well as its distance from the center of the earth. The latter distance <note>Referring to the distance an object falls on Earth in a given time</note> is found through pendulum experiments, just as *Huygens* <note>Christiaan Huygens (1629–1695), a Dutch mathematician and physicist who first calculated centrifugal force and improved the pendulum clock</note> taught. Thus, having begun the calculation, the ratio of the former distance to the latter—or rather, the ratio of the **centripetal force** <term>centripetal force: a "center-seeking" force that pulls an object toward a center, such as gravity pulling a planet toward the Sun</term> of the moon revolving in its orbit to the force of gravity on the earth's surface—will be as the square of the earth's **radius** <note>original: "semidiametri"</note> to the square of the orbit's radius. By what has been shown above, the centripetal force of the moon revolving in its orbit has this same ratio to the moon's centripetal force near the earth's surface. Therefore, the centripetal force near the earth's surface is equal to the force of gravity. These forces are not different, therefore, but one and the same; for if they were different, bodies would fall toward the earth twice as fast by the combined forces as they do by the force of gravity alone. It is established, then, that this centripetal force, by which the moon is perpetually drawn or driven away from its **tangent line** <note>the straight path an object would take if no force were pulling it toward a center</note> and kept in its orbit, is the very force of terrestrial gravity reaching all the way to the moon. And it is indeed consistent with reason that this power should extend to immense distances, since no perceptible decrease in it can be observed even on the highest mountain peaks. Thus the moon gravitates toward the earth; moreover, by a mutual action, the earth in turn gravitates equally toward the moon—a fact which is abundantly confirmed in this philosophy where it treats the **tides of the sea** <note>original: "maris æstu"</note> and the **precession of the equinoxes** <term>precession of the equinoxes: the slow change in the orientation of Earth's axis, which affects the timing of the seasons</term>, arising from the action of both the moon and the sun upon the earth. From this we are finally taught the law by which the force of gravity decreases at greater distances from the earth. For since gravity is no different from the lunar centripetal force, and the latter is **inversely proportional to the square of the distance** <note>original: "reciproce proportionalis quadrato distantiæ"</note>, gravity will also decrease in the same ratio.

Let us now proceed to the remaining planets. Since the revolutions of the **primary planets** <term>primary planets: the major planets orbiting the Sun, such as Mars or Venus</term> around the sun and the **secondary planets** <term>secondary planets: moons or satellites orbiting a larger planet</term> around Jupiter and Saturn are phenomena of the same kind as the moon's revolution around the earth; and since it has further been demonstrated that the centripetal forces of the primary planets are directed toward the center of the sun, and those of the secondary planets toward the centers of Jupiter and Saturn, just as the moon's centripetal force is directed toward the center of the earth; and furthermore, since all these forces are inversely as the squares of the distances from their centers, just as the moon's force is as the square of its distance from the earth; we must conclude that their nature is the same for all. Therefore, as the moon gravitates toward the earth, and the earth in turn toward the moon, so too will all the secondary planets gravitate toward their primaries, and the primaries in turn...

Therefore, by the same argument, planets of both kinds gravitate toward the sun, and the sun toward them. Moreover, it is abundantly clear that the secondary planets gravitate toward the sun from the **lunar inequalities** <note>original: "inæqualitatibus lunaribus"; these are irregularities in the Moon's orbit caused by the Sun's gravitational pull</note>; the most accurate theory of these, revealed with admirable sagacity, we have set forth in the third book of this work.

These, coming from immense distances, are carried into the vicinity of the sun, and sometimes approach so near to it that, when passing through their **perihelia** <term>perihelion: the point in the orbit of a planet or comet where it is nearest to the sun</term>, they seem almost to touch its globe. The theory of these bodies—sought in vain by astronomers before this—has finally been successfully discovered in our own century and most certainly demonstrated through observations, a feat we owe to our most excellent author <note>Referring to Isaac Newton</note>. It is clear, then, that comets move in **conic sections** <term>conic sections: the shapes (circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas) created by intersecting a cone with a plane; Newton proved orbits follow these paths</term> having their focal points in the center of the sun, and by drawing lines to the sun, they describe areas proportional to the times of their travel. From these phenomena, it is manifest and mathematically proven that those forces by which comets are held in their orbits look toward the sun and are **inversely as the squares of the distances** <note>original: "reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum"; this is the Inverse Square Law, meaning the force of gravity gets four times weaker if the distance is doubled</note> from its center. Thus, comets gravitate toward the sun; and so the sun's attractive power reaches not only to the bodies of the planets placed at given distances and in nearly the same plane, but even to the comets located in the most diverse regions of the heavens and at the most diverse distances. This, therefore, is the nature of gravitating bodies: they exert their forces at all distances upon all other gravitating bodies. From this it follows that all planets and comets attract one another and gravitate toward each other. This is also confirmed by the **perturbation** <note>original: "perturbatione"; slight changes in a planet's orbit caused by the gravitational pull of another nearby planet</note> of Jupiter and Saturn, which is not unknown to astronomers and arises from the actions of these planets upon each other; and indeed from that very slow motion of the **apsides** <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where the planet is either closest to or farthest from the body it orbits</term>, which was mentioned above and proceeds from a similar cause.

# THE EDITOR'S PREFACE

...of each, therefore, the smallest particles will have their own attractive forces, prevailing in proportion to the quantity of matter; just as was shown above concerning terrestrial bodies. At different distances, these forces will also be in the reciprocal duplicate ratio of the distances <note>original: "duplicata ratione distantiarum reciproce"; this is the inverse-square law, which states that the strength of gravity decreases in proportion to the square of the distance from the source</note>: for it is mathematically demonstrated that spheres attracting according to this law must be composed of particles attracting by that same law.

The preceding conclusions rest upon this Axiom, which is accepted by all philosophers <note>In the 18th century, "philosophy" or "natural philosophy" referred to what we now call science.</note>; namely, that for effects of the same kind—those whose known properties are the same—the causes are the same, and the properties not yet known are also the same. For who doubts that if gravity is the cause of a stone's descent in *Europe*, the same is the cause of its descent in *America*? If there is mutual gravity between a stone and the earth in *Europe*, who will deny it is mutual in *America*? If the attractive force of the stone and the earth in *Europe* is composed of the attractive forces of their parts, who will deny a similar composition in *America*? If the attraction of the earth to all kinds of bodies and at all distances is propagated in *Europe*, why should we not say it is likewise propagated in *America*? All philosophy is founded upon this rule: for if it were removed, we could affirm nothing about universals. The constitution of individual things becomes known through observations and experiments; but from there, we judge the nature of universal things only by this rule.

Now, since all bodies found near the earth or in the heavens upon which we can perform experiments or observations are heavy, it must be said entirely that gravity belongs to all bodies universally. And just as no bodies ought to be conceived which are not **extended**, **movable**, and **impenetrable**; so none ought to be conceived which are not **heavy**. The extension, mobility, and impenetrability of bodies are known only through experiments: in exactly the same way gravity is known. All bodies of which we have observations are extended, movable, and impenetrable; and from this we conclude that all bodies universally, even those of which we have no observations, are extended, movable, and impenetrable. Likewise, all bodies of which we have observations are heavy: and from this we conclude that all bodies universally, even those of which we have no observations, are heavy. If anyone should say that the bodies of the **fixed stars** <term>fixed stars: stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, as opposed to "wandering" planets</term> are not heavy, because their gravity has not yet been observed, it would be permitted by the same argument to say...

# PREFACE

...[it would be proper to say they] are neither extended, nor movable, nor impenetrable, since these attributes of the fixed stars have not yet been observed. Why use many words? Either **gravity** will have its place among the primary qualities of all bodies; or extension, mobility, and impenetrability will not. And the nature of things will either be correctly explained through the gravity of bodies, or it will not be correctly explained through their extension, mobility, and impenetrability.

I hear some people disapprove of this conclusion, and mutter something about **occult qualities** <note>In the 17th and 18th centuries, an "occult quality" was a "hidden" property that could not be explained by mechanical contact, often dismissed as magical or unscientific by Newton's rivals.</note>. They are constantly arguing that gravity is something "occult"; and they claim that occult causes should be banished far from **philosophy** <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to "natural philosophy," what we today call "science."</note>. To these people, the answer is easy: "occult" causes are not those whose existence is very clearly demonstrated by observations, but only those whose existence is hidden, imagined, and not yet proven. Therefore, gravity will not be an occult cause of the movements of the heavens, since it has been shown from the phenomena <note>i.e., observable evidence</note> that this power truly exists. Rather, those people flee to occult causes who appoint certain **vortices** <note>original: "vortices"; This refers to René Descartes' theory that planets were carried around the sun by giant whirlpools of invisible matter. Newton's work proved this theory was mathematically impossible.</note>—made of a matter entirely fictional and completely unknown to the senses—to govern those same motions.

Shall gravity therefore be called an occult cause, and on that account be rejected from philosophy, because the cause of gravity itself is hidden and not yet found? Those who decide this should take care that they do not decide something absurd, which would eventually tear up the foundations of all philosophy. For causes usually proceed in a continuous chain from the complex to the simpler: when you reach the **simplest cause**, you can no longer go further. Therefore, no mechanical explanation can be given for the simplest cause; for if it were given, the cause would not yet be the simplest. Will you then call these simplest causes "occult" and order them into exile? If so, those things that depend immediately on them, and those that further depend on those, will go into exile at the same time, until philosophy is emptied and thoroughly purged of all causes.

There are those who say that gravity is "against nature" and call it a **perpetual miracle**. They want it rejected because preternatural causes <note>Causes that exist outside the laws of nature.</note> have no place in physics. It is hardly worth the effort to dismantle this completely foolish objection, which itself undermines all philosophy. Either they will deny that gravity is implanted in all bodies (which cannot be said), or...

There are some who dislike this entire **celestial physics** <note>The study of the physical laws governing the stars and planets.</note> simply because it seems to clash with the dogmas of **Descartes** <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), a French philosopher who proposed that planets were carried by "vortices" of invisible matter. Newton's work proved this model mathematically impossible.</note> and can hardly be reconciled with them. These people are welcome to enjoy their own opinion, but they ought to act fairly: they should not deny to others the same liberty they demand for themselves. Therefore, we are free to keep and embrace the **NEWTONIAN** philosophy, which we hold to be truer, and to follow causes proven by the **phenomena** <note>Observable facts and data.</note> rather than those that are merely imagined and not yet proven. 

It belongs to true philosophy to derive the nature of things from causes that truly exist. We must seek those laws by which the **Great Architect** <note>original: "summus opifex"; Cotes refers to God as the craftsman of the universe.</note> willed to establish this most beautiful order of the world, not those laws He *could* have used, had He so chosen. For it is consistent with reason that the same effect could arise from several different causes; however, the true cause will be the one from which the effect actually and truly proceeds. The other possible causes have no place in true philosophy. In **automated clocks**, the same motion of the hour hand can arise either from a hanging weight or from a **spring** <note>original: "elater"</note> hidden inside. But if a clock is actually equipped with a weight, we would laugh at anyone who imagines a spring and attempts to explain the movement of the hand based on such a hastily concocted hypothesis. It would have been necessary to examine the internal works of the machine more deeply to gain a certain knowledge of the true principle behind the movement.

A similar judgment may be passed on those philosophers who hold that the heavens are filled with a **subtle matter** <note>An invisible, fluid-like substance that many of Newton's contemporaries believed filled all of space.</note> and that this matter is driven in never-ending **vortices**. For even if they could satisfy the phenomena perfectly with their hypotheses, they still cannot be said to have produced a true philosophy or found the true causes of celestial motions—not until they demonstrate either that these vortices actually exist, or at least that no other causes exist. Therefore, if it is shown that the **attraction of all bodies** <note>i.e., universal gravitation.</note> has a real place in the nature of things, and if it is further shown how all celestial movements are explained by it, then [any objection] would be vain and rightly mocked—

If the bodies of the planets and comets are carried around the sun by vortices, then the bodies being carried and the parts of the vortices immediately surrounding them must move with the same velocity and in the same direction, and they must have the same density or the same **force of inertia** <term>vis inertiæ: the inherent property of matter to resist changes in its state of motion.</term> relative to the mass of their matter. For if the planets are carried around the sun by vortices <note>The "vortex theory" proposed by René Descartes, suggesting space is filled with a fluid matter that swirls like a whirlpool to move the planets.</note>; the parts of the vortices that most closely surround each planet will be of the same density as the planet, as was said above. For in order for the constitution of a vortex to remain stable, the less dense parts must occupy the center, and the more dense parts must move further from the center. Since the periodic times of the planets are in the <term>sesquiplicate</term> <note>original: "sesquiplicata"; the ratio of the square root of the cube, or the 3/2 power. From this it follows, indeed, that the <term>centrifugal forces</term> <note>original: "vires centrifugas"; the outward force acting on a body moving in a circle.</note> of these parts will be reciprocally as the squares of the distances. Those parts, therefore, which are at a greater interval from the center, strive to recede from it with less force: whence if they were less dense, it would be necessary for them to yield to the greater force with which the parts nearer the center attempt to ascend. Thus the denser parts will ascend, the less dense will descend, and an exchange of places will occur; until the fluid matter of the entire vortex is so arranged and ordered that it can finally rest in equilibrium. If two fluids of different density are contained in the same vessel, it will certainly happen that the fluid with the greater density seeks the lowest place with a greater force of gravity: and by a reasoning not at all dissimilar, it must be said that the denser parts of the vortex seek the highest place with a greater <term>centrifugal force</term>. Therefore, that entire and by far largest part of the vortex which lies outside the Earth's orbit will have a density, and thus a <term>force of inertia</term> <note>original: "vim inertiae"; the inherent property of matter to resist changes in its state of motion.</note> proportional to the mass of the matter, which will be no less than the density and force of inertia of the Earth: from this, a huge and very sensible resistance would arise for passing comets; I might even say a resistance which might rightly seem capable of entirely stopping and absorbing their motion. ### THE EDITOR’S PREFACE

...were sticky like oil and honey. The resistance which is felt in air, water, mercury, and similar fluids that are not viscous is almost entirely of the former kind <note>The "former kind" refers to resistance arising from the inertia of the matter, rather than its stickiness or friction.</note>; and it cannot be diminished by any further degree of <term>subtlety</term> <note>original: "subtilitatis"; referring to the fineness or smallness of the fluid's particles.</note>, so long as the density of the fluid or its <term>force of inertia</term> <note>original: "vis inertiæ"; the inherent power of matter to resist a change in its state of rest or motion.</note> remains, for this resistance is always proportional to that density. This has been most clearly demonstrated by our author <note>Sir Isaac Newton.</note> in his excellent theory of resistances, which is now explained a little more accurately in this second edition, and is more fully confirmed by experiments on falling bodies.

Bodies, in moving forward, gradually communicate their motion to the surrounding fluid; by communicating it they lose it, and by losing it they are slowed down. Therefore, the deceleration is proportional to the motion communicated. However, when the velocity of the moving body is given, the motion communicated is proportional to the density of the fluid; therefore, the deceleration or resistance will be proportional to that same fluid density. Nor can it be removed in any way, unless the motion lost is restored by the fluid flowing back to the rear parts of the body. 

But this cannot be claimed unless the pressure of the fluid against the body at its rear parts were equal to the pressure of the body against the fluid at its front parts; that is, unless the relative velocity with which the fluid rushes into the body from behind were equal to the velocity with which the body rushes into the fluid; that is, unless the absolute velocity of the returning fluid were twice as great as the absolute velocity of the propelled fluid; which is impossible. Therefore, the resistance of fluids which arises from their density and <term>force of inertia</term> can in no way be removed. 

We must therefore conclude that the celestial fluid has no force of inertia, since it has no force of resistance; it has no force by which motion can be communicated, since it has no force of inertia; it has no force by which any change can be induced in either single or multiple bodies, since it has no force by which motion is communicated; it has no efficacy at all, since it has no capacity to induce any change. Why, then, should we not be permitted to call this hypothesis—which is clearly destitute of foundation and does not serve in the slightest to explain the nature of things—most absurd and utterly unworthy of a philosopher? 

Those who wish the heavens to be filled with fluid matter, yet maintain that this matter is not inert, remove the <term>vacuum</term> <note>A space entirely empty of matter.</note> in words, but restore it in reality. For since fluid matter of this kind can be distinguished from empty space by no reasoning, the entire dispute is about the names of things, and not their natures. But if there are some who are so devoted to matter that they will by no means [admit] a space empty of bodies...

...should wish to admit it; let us see, then, where that line of reasoning must finally lead.

For they will either say that this constitution of a world full in every part <note>A reference to the "Plenum," the theory held by René Descartes that space contains no vacuum and is entirely filled with matter.</note>, which they have dreamed up, proceeded from the will of God for the end that a ready aid might be provided for the operations of nature by a most <term>subtle ether</term> <note>original: "æthere subtilissimo"; a hypothetical, extremely fine substance thought to permeate all space.</note> pervading and filling everything; which, however, cannot be said, since it has already been shown from the phenomena of comets that this ether has no effect. Or they will say it proceeded from the will of God for some unknown end; which also ought not to be said, since a different constitution of the world could be established just as easily by the same argument. Or, finally, they will not say it proceeded from the will of God, but from a certain <term>necessity of nature</term> <note>original: "necessitate naturæ"; the idea that the universe must be the way it is by its own inherent nature, rather than by choice.</note>. At length, therefore, they must sink into the filthy dregs of that most impure herd. These are the ones who dream that all things are ruled by fate, not providence; and that matter has existed by its own necessity always and everywhere, being infinite and eternal. Given these assumptions, matter would also be uniform everywhere, for variety of forms is entirely incompatible with necessity. It would also be motionless; for if it were moved by necessity in any certain direction with a certain velocity, it would, by a like necessity, be moved in a different direction with a different velocity; but it cannot be moved in different directions with different velocities at the same time; therefore, it must be motionless. Certainly, the world, distinguished by such a beautiful variety of forms and motions, could not have arisen except from the perfectly free will of God, who provides for and governs all things.

From this source, therefore, have flowed all those which we call the laws of nature: in which many traces of the wisest counsel certainly appear, but none of necessity. Accordingly, we must not seek these laws from uncertain conjectures, but learn them by observation and experiment. He who confides that he can find the principles of physics and the laws of things relying solely on the force of his own mind and the internal light of his reason, must either maintain that the world existed by necessity and that the proposed laws follow from that same necessity; or, if the order of nature was established by the will of God, that he, a <note>original: "homuncionem misellum"</note> pitiful little man, has a clear perspective of what is best to be done. All sound and true philosophy is founded on the phenomena of things; if these lead us, even against our will and reluctance, to principles of this kind, in which the best counsel and supreme dominion of the most wise and powerful Being are most clearly perceived, these principles are not to be rejected simply because they might be unpleasant to certain men.

# THE AUTHOR'S
# PREFACE
### TO THE
## THIRD EDITION.

In this third edition, which Henry Pemberton, M.D. <note>original: "M. D. vir harum rerum peritissimus" — a man most skilled in these matters. Pemberton (1694–1771) was a physician and mathematician who oversaw the final revisions of Newton's work.</note> supervised, several points in the second book concerning the **resistance of mediums** <note>This refers to the study of fluid dynamics—how air, water, or other fluids resist the movement of objects passing through them.</note> are explained a bit more fully than before, and new experiments are added regarding the resistance of heavy bodies falling through the air. In the third book, the argument by which it is proven that the moon is held in its orbit by **gravity** <note>Newton uses "gravitas" to describe the universal force that governs both terrestrial falling objects and celestial bodies.</note> is set out more extensively; and new observations are added concerning the ratio of the diameters of **Jupiter** to one another <note>Newton is referencing the "oblate" shape of Jupiter—the fact that it is wider at the equator than at the poles due to its rotation.</note>, made by Mr. Pound <note>James Pound (1669–1724), an astronomer and clergyman who provided Newton with high-quality telescopic data.</note>.

There are also added several observations of that comet which appeared in the year 1680, made by Mr. Kirch <note>Gottfried Kirch (1639–1710), a German astronomer.</note> in Germany during the month of November, which have recently come into our hands; with their help, it is established how closely **parabolic orbits** <note>A parabola is an open curve; Newton was demonstrating that comet paths could be modeled as geometric curves governed by gravity.</note> correspond to the motions of comets. Furthermore, the orbit of that same comet is determined more accurately than before through the calculations of **Halley** <note>Edmond Halley (1656–1742), who used Newtonian physics to prove that comets were periodic visitors to our solar system.</note>, and indeed as an **ellipse** <note>An oval path. Confirming a comet's orbit was an ellipse proved it would eventually return.</note>. It is demonstrated that the comet, in this elliptical orbit, completed its course through nine signs of the heavens <note>The "signs" refer to the constellations of the Zodiac; tracking a comet through nine signs means it was observed across three-quarters of the sky.</note> with no less accuracy than the planets are accustomed to move in the elliptical orbits defined by astronomy. Finally, the orbit of the comet that appeared in the year 1723, computed by Mr. Bradley <note>James Bradley (1693–1762), an Oxford professor who later discovered the aberration of light.</note>, professor of astronomy at Oxford, is also included.

IS. NEWTON

Given at London
Jan. 12, 1725–6. <note>In the 18th-century English calendar, the year officially began in March; "1725–6" indicates the year was 1725 by the old legal style but 1726 by the modern calendar.</note>

## Mathematical Principles of
# NATURAL PHILOSOPHY
<note>In the 17th century, "Natural Philosophy" was the term used for the study of nature and the physical universe—what we now call science or physics.</note>

---
### DEFINITIONS.
---

#### DEFINITION I.

*The quantity of matter is the measure of the same, arising from its density and magnitude conjointly.*
<note>original: "Quantitas materiæ" — This is Newton's formal definition of **mass**. He defines it as the product of density and "magnitude" (volume).</note>

Air of a double density, in a double space, becomes quadruple; in a triple space, sextuple. Understand the same for snow and powders condensed by compression or liquefaction. And the same reasoning applies to all bodies that are condensed in various ways by any causes whatsoever. Meanwhile, I have no regard here for any medium, if there be such, that freely pervades the interstices between the parts. <note>Newton is clarifying that his definition of mass refers to the "solid" parts of a body, excluding any "ether" or fluid that might flow through the gaps in a porous object.</note> Moreover, I understand this quantity everywhere in the following pages under the name of "body" or "mass." It becomes known through the weight of each body: for I found it to be proportional to the weight by experiments with pendulums most accurately performed, as shall be shown hereafter. <note>This is a crucial scientific observation: Newton discovered that "inertial mass" (resistance to change in motion) is proportional to "gravitational mass" (weight).</note>

#### DEFINITION II.

*The quantity of motion is the measure of the same, arising from the velocity and quantity of matter conjointly.*
<note>original: "Quantitas motus" — This is the modern definition of **momentum** ($p = mv$).</note>

The motion of the whole is the sum of the motions in the individual parts; and therefore in a body twice as large, with equal velocity, the motion is double, and with a double velocity, it is quadruple.

<summary>This page introduces the foundational definitions of Isaac Newton's physics, specifically defining mass (quantity of matter) and momentum (quantity of motion).</summary>
<keywords>mass, momentum, density, volume, weight, pendulums, natural philosophy, Isaac Newton</keywords>

# NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>
DEFINITIONS.

### DEFINITION III.

*The inherent force of matter is a power of resisting, by which every body, as much as in it lies, perseveres in its state either of resting or of moving uniformly forward in a straight line.*
<note>original: "Materiæ vis inſita" — Newton is defining what we now call **inertia**. He views it as an internal "force" or "power" that keeps an object doing whatever it is currently doing.</note>

This force is always proportional to the body it resides in, and does not differ at all from the inertia of the mass, except in the way we think about it. It is due to the inertia of matter that every body is only with difficulty disturbed from its state of resting or moving. Hence, this inherent force may be called by the very significant name "force of inertia" <note>original: "vis inertiæ"</note>. A body exerts this force only when its state is being changed by another force impressed upon it; and this exertion is, under different respects, both resistance and impulse. It is resistance insofar as the body struggles against the impressed force to preserve its own state; it is impulse insofar as the same body, by not easily yielding to the force of a resisting obstacle, endeavors to change the state of that obstacle. The common people attribute resistance to things at rest and impulse to things in motion; but motion and rest, as they are commonly conceived, are distinguished from each other only by point of view; nor are those things always truly at rest which are commonly looked upon as resting. <note>Newton is hinting at his concept of "relative" versus "absolute" motion here: an object might look still to us, but it is moving along with the Earth.</note>

---

### DEFINITION IV.

*An impressed force is an action exerted upon a body, in order to change its state, either of resting or of moving uniformly forward in a straight line.*
<note>original: "Vis impreſſa" — This is Newton’s definition of an external force. Unlike inertia, which is "inside" the object, this force comes from the outside.</note>

This force consists in the action alone, and does not remain in the body after the action has ceased. For a body perseveres in every new state it acquires by the force of inertia alone. Moreover, an impressed force has various origins, such as from a strike <note>original: "ictu"</note>, from pressure <note>original: "preſſione"</note>, or from centripetal force <note>original: "vi centripeta"</note>.

<meta>catchword: Force (Vis)</meta>

<summary>In these definitions, Newton establishes the concepts of inertia (the internal resistance of matter) and impressed force (the external action that changes an object's motion).</summary>

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES

DEFINITIONS.

## DEFINITION V.

*Centripetal force is that by which bodies are drawn or impelled, or tend in any manner, toward some point as to a center from every direction.*
<note>original: "Vis centripeta" — literally "center-seeking force." Newton created this term to contrast with "centrifugal" (center-fleeing) force.</note>

Gravity is of this kind, by which bodies tend toward the center of the earth; so is magnetic force, by which iron seeks a magnet; and that force, whatever it may be, by which the planets are perpetually drawn back from straight-line motions and compelled to revolve in curved lines. A stone whirled in a sling endeavors to fly away from the hand that whirls it, and by its endeavor it stretches the sling, doing so more strongly the more quickly it revolves; and as soon as it is let go, it flies off. The force contrary to that endeavor, by which the sling perpetually draws the stone back toward the hand and retains it in its orbit, I call "centripetal," because it is directed toward the hand as the center of the orbit. The same reasoning applies to all bodies that are moved in a circle. They all endeavor to recede from the centers of their orbits; and unless there is some force contrary to that endeavor, by which they are restrained and kept in their orbits—and which I therefore call centripetal—they will go off in straight lines with uniform motion. 

A projectile, if it were deprived of the force of gravity, would not be deflected toward the earth, but would go off into the heavens in a straight line, and that with a uniform motion, provided the resistance of the air were removed. Through its gravity, it is drawn back from its straight course and is perpetually bent toward the earth, and that more or less according to its gravity and the velocity of its motion. The less its gravity is in proportion to its quantity of matter, or the greater the velocity with which it is projected, the less it will deviate from a straight course and the farther it will go. 

If a lead ball, fired with a given velocity along a horizontal line from the summit of some mountain by the force of gunpowder <note>original: "pulveris tormentarii" — literally "the powder of engines," referring to cannons</note>, were to proceed in a curved line to a distance of two miles before it fell to the earth: this same ball, with double the velocity, would proceed roughly twice as far, and with ten times the velocity, roughly ten times as far; provided the resistance of the air were removed. And by increasing the velocity, the distance to which it might be projected could be increased at will, and the curvature of the line it describes could be decreased, so that it might finally fall at a distance of ten or thirty or ninety degrees; or even so that it might circle the entire earth, or finally

<meta>catchword: nique (the start of the word "denique," meaning "finally")</meta>

<summary>Newton introduces the concept of centripetal force, using the examples of a stone in a sling and a cannonball to explain how gravity acts as a center-seeking force that keeps objects in orbit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction of "Definitions" from Page 3. It completes the discussion on centripetal force (Definition V) by introducing the famous thought experiment of the orbital cannonball—linking earthly gravity to celestial mechanics—and moves into the specific ways to measure these forces (Definitions VI and VII).</meta>

-> 4 NATURAL PHILOSOPHY <-

<margin>
DEFINITIONS.
</margin>
...finally, it would depart into the heavens and proceed to infinity in its motion of departure. By the same reasoning that a projectile could be bent into an orbit by the force of gravity and travel around the whole earth, so too the moon—either by the force of gravity (if indeed it has weight) or by any other force urging it toward the earth—can always be drawn back from a straight-line course toward the earth and bent into its orbit: and without such a force, the moon cannot be retained in its orbit. 

This force, if it were less than what is required, would not bend the moon enough from its straight-line course; if it were greater than required, it would bend it more than enough and lead it down from its orbit toward the earth. Indeed, it is required that it be of the right magnitude: and it is the task of mathematicians to find the force by which a body can be accurately retained in any given orbit with a given velocity; and conversely to find the curved path into which a body, departing from any given place with a given velocity, is bent by a given force. <note>This marks a revolutionary shift: Newton is stating that the same math applies to a stone and the Moon.</note> Moreover, there are three kinds of quantities of this centripetal force: absolute, accelerative, and motive.

# DEFINITION VI.

*The absolute quantity of a centripetal force is its measure, greater or lesser according to the efficacy of the cause propagating it from the center through the surrounding regions.*
<note>original: "Vis centripetæ quantitas abſoluta"</note>

As the magnetic force is greater in one magnet and lesser in another, according to the size of the magnet or the intensity of its power.

# DEFINITION VII.

*The accelerative quantity of a centripetal force is its measure proportional to the velocity it generates in a given time.*
<note>original: "Vis centripetæ quantitas acceleratrix" — this refers to what we now call "acceleration due to gravity" ($g$).</note>

Just as the power of the same magnet is greater at a smaller distance and lesser at a greater distance: or the force of gravity is greater in valleys, lesser on the peaks of high mountains, and still lesser (as will be shown hereafter) at greater distances from the globe of the earth; but at equal distances it is the same everywhere, because it accelerates all falling bodies (heavy or light, large or small) equally, once the resistance of the air is removed.
