This section is crucial as it establishes the mathematical framework Newton uses to describe gravity without having to explain its "hidden" physical cause.</meta>

-> MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. <-

<margin>DEFINITIONS.</margin>

## DEFINITION VIII.

*The motive quantity of a centripetal force is its measure proportional to the motion which it generates in a given time.*
<note>original: "Vis centripetæ quantitas motrix"</note>

Just as a greater weight acts on a larger body and a smaller weight on a smaller body; and on the same body, the weight is greater near the earth and smaller in the heavens. This quantity is the "centripetency" <note>Newton uses the term "centripetentia" to describe the total tendency or propensity of a whole body to move toward a center.</note> or propensity of the whole body toward the center, and (so to speak) its weight; and it is always identified by the force equal and opposite to it, by which the descent of the body can be prevented.

For the sake of brevity, we may call these quantities of forces motive, accelerative, and absolute forces; and for the sake of distinction, we refer them to the bodies seeking the center, to the locations of those bodies, and to the center of the forces respectively. Specifically:
*   **Motive force** refers to the body, as the endeavor of the whole toward the center composed of the endeavors of all its parts; 
*   **Accelerative force** refers to the location of the body, as a certain efficacy diffused from the center through each of the surrounding locations to move the bodies that are in them; 
*   **Absolute force** refers to the center, as if it were endowed with some cause without which motive forces are not propagated through the surrounding regions; whether that cause be some central body (such as a magnet in the center of a magnetic force, or the earth in the center of a gravitating force) or something else that is not visible. This concept is purely mathematical: for I am not yet considering the physical causes and seats of these forces.
<note>This is a famous "agnostic" stance by Newton; he is saying that he can describe how gravity works with math even if he doesn't know what gravity actually *is* or what causes it.</note>

Therefore, accelerative force is to motive force as velocity is to motion. <note>In Newton's terminology, "motion" refers to momentum (mass × velocity). Therefore, he is saying that if Force = Mass × Acceleration, then Acceleration is the force divided by the mass.</note> For the quantity of motion arises from the velocity and the quantity of matter together, and the motive force arises from the accelerative force and the quantity of the same matter together. For the sum of the actions of the accelerative force upon each individual particle of the body is the motive force of the whole. Hence near the surface of the earth, where the accelerative gravity or gravitating force is the same in all bodies, the motive gravity or weight is proportional to the body: but if one ascends to regions where the accelerative gravity becomes less, the weight will likewise be diminished, and will always be proportional to the body and the accelerative gravity together. Thus, in regions where the accelerative gravity is half as much, the weight of a body that is half or a third as large will be four or six times less.

He emphasizes that these definitions are mathematical tools rather than physical explanations of the "nature" of gravity.</summary>

<margin>DEFINITIONS.</margin>
Furthermore, I use the terms attraction, impulse, or any kind of propensity toward a center indifferently and interchangeably. I consider these forces not physically, but only mathematically. <note>Newton is being very careful here to tell his readers that he is describing *how* gravity behaves through math, not *what* gravity actually is or what causes it—a point of great controversy in his time.</note> Hence, let the reader beware: do not think that by words of this kind I am defining a species or a mode of action, or a physical cause or reason. Nor should the reader think I am attributing true and physical powers to centers (which are merely mathematical points) if I happen to say that centers attract or that centers have forces.

### Scholium.
<note>In academic writing of this period, a "Scholium" is an explanatory note or a commentary added to clarify the preceding definitions or propositions.</note>

Up to this point, it has seemed appropriate to explain the senses in which less familiar words are to be understood in the following pages. Time, space, place, and motion are very well known to everyone. It must be noted, however, that the common people <note>original: "vulgus." Newton refers to everyday observers who rely on their senses rather than mathematical rigor.</note> do not conceive of these quantities except in relation to sensible objects. From this, certain prejudices arise; to remove these, it is convenient to distinguish these quantities into absolute and relative, true and apparent, and mathematical and common.

I. Absolute, true, and mathematical **time**, in itself and by its own nature without relation to anything external, flows equably <note>meaning: at a constant, unchanging rate</note>, and by another name is called **duration**. Relative, apparent, and common time is any sensible and external measure of duration (whether accurate or unequal) made by means of motion, which the common people use instead of true time; such as an hour, a day, a month, or a year.

II. Absolute **space**, by its own nature without relation to anything external, always remains similar and immovable. Relative space is any movable measure or dimension of this absolute space, which is defined by our senses through its position relative to bodies, and is used by the common people instead of immovable space. For example, the dimension of a space underground, in the air, or in the heavens is defined by its position relative to the Earth. Absolute and relative space are the same in form and magnitude, but they do not always remain the same in numerical identity. <note>Newton means that while the "amount" of space is the same, the relative space moves through the absolute space.</note> For if the Earth moves, for instance, the space of our air—which relatively and with respect to the Earth always remains the same—will now be one part of absolute space into which the air passes, and now another part of it; and thus, in an absolute sense, it will be changing perpetually.

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

<margin>
DEFINITIONS.
</margin>

III. Place is the part of space which a body occupies, and according to the nature of the space, it is either absolute or relative. I say a *part* of space; not the *position* <note>original: "situs"</note> of the body, nor the surrounding surface. For the places of equal solids are always equal; yet their surfaces are often unequal because of the differences in their shapes. Position, properly speaking, does not have quantity, nor are positions so much "places" as they are qualities or attributes of places. The motion of a whole is the same as the sum of the motions of its parts; that is, the displacement of the whole from its place is the same as the sum of the displacements of the parts from their own places. Therefore, the place of the whole is the same as the sum of the places of the parts, and is thus internal and within the whole body.

IV. Absolute motion is the movement of a body from one absolute place to another absolute place; relative motion is the movement from one relative place to another. For example, in a ship sailing with its sails spread, the relative place of a body is that region of the ship in which the body is located, or that part of the interior which the body fills, which moves along with the ship. Relative rest is the remaining of the body in that same region of the ship or part of the interior. But true rest is the remaining of the body in the same part of that *immovable space* in which the ship itself, along with its interior and everything it contains, moves.

From this, it follows that if the Earth were truly at rest, a body that is relatively at rest in the ship would move truly and absolutely with the same velocity as the ship moves across the Earth. But if the Earth also moves, the true and absolute motion of the body will arise partly from the true motion of the Earth in immovable space, and partly from the relative motion of the ship on the Earth. Furthermore, if the body also moves relatively within the ship, its true motion will arise partly from the true motion of the Earth in immovable space, and partly from the relative motions of both the ship on the Earth and the body within the ship; and from these relative motions, the relative motion of the body on the Earth will arise.

For example, if that part of the Earth where the ship is located moves truly toward the east with a velocity of 10,010 parts; and the ship is carried by wind and sails toward the west with a velocity of 10 parts; but a sailor walks on the ship toward the east with 1 part of velocity: then the sailor will move truly and absolutely in immovable space toward the east with 10,001 parts of velocity, and relatively on the Earth toward the west with 9 parts of velocity. <note>Newton is demonstrating how we calculate "true" motion by adding or subtracting various relative movements. In this case: 10,010 (Earth East) minus 10 (Ship West) plus 1 (Sailor East) equals 10,001 East. Relative to the ground, the sailor moves 9 parts West because the ship's 10 parts West outweighs his 1 part East.</note>

Absolute time is distinguished from relative time in Astronomy by the equation of common time. <note>The "equation of time" is the mathematical correction needed to account for the fact that a "solar day"—the time between one noon and the next—actually changes slightly in length throughout the year due to the Earth's elliptical orbit.</note> For natural days are unequal, though they are commonly held to be equal for the purpose of measuring time. # NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>
DEFINITIONS.
</margin>

...astronomers correct this inequality <note>original: "inæqualitatem"; Newton is referring to the "Equation of Time," the difference between time measured by a sundial and time measured by a perfect clock</note> so that they may measure celestial motions by a truer time. It is possible that there is no truly uniform motion by which time may be accurately measured. All motions can be accelerated or slowed, but the flow of absolute time cannot be changed. The duration or perseverance of the existence of things remains the same, whether motions are fast, slow, or nonexistent; therefore, this duration is rightly distinguished from its sensible measures, and is gathered from them by means of an astronomical equation. The necessity of this equation for determining phenomena is proven both by experiments with the pendulum clock <note>original: "horologii oscillatorii"; Christiaan Huygens had recently patented the pendulum clock, the first truly precise timekeeper</note> and by the eclipses of the moons of Jupiter.

Just as the order of the parts of time is immutable, so also is the order of the parts of space. If these parts were moved from their places, they would be moved (so to speak) out of themselves. For times and spaces are, as it were, the "places" of themselves and of all things. All things are placed in time according to the order of succession, and in space according to the order of position. It is of their very essence to be places; and it is absurd for primary places to move. These are, therefore, absolute places; and only translations <note>displacements from one point to another</note> from these places are absolute motions.

However, because these parts of space cannot be seen and cannot be distinguished from one another by our senses, we use sensible measures in their stead. From the positions and distances of things from some body which we regard as immobile, we define all places; then we also estimate all motions with respect to these aforementioned places, insofar as we conceive of bodies being transferred from them. Thus, instead of absolute places and motions, we use relative ones; this is not inconvenient in human affairs, but in philosophical matters <note>In the 17th century, "natural philosophy" was the term for what we now call science</note> we must abstract from the senses. For it may be that no body is truly at rest, to which places and motions might be referred.

Absolute and relative rest and motion are distinguished from each other by their properties, causes, and effects. It is a property of rest that bodies truly at rest stay at rest relative to one another. Therefore, while it is possible that some body in the regions of the fixed stars <note>original: "fixarum"; the distant stars which were then believed to be completely stationary</note>, or far beyond, is absolutely at rest, it cannot be known from the position of bodies relative to each other in our own regions whether any of these maintain a given position to that distant body or not; thus, true rest cannot be defined by the position of these bodies relative to one another.

<meta>This page continues Newton’s "Scholium" on space, time, and motion. Having previously established that absolute space and time exist independently of our senses, he now explains how to distinguish "true" (absolute) motion from "relative" motion. He argues that the motion of a part is tied to the motion of the whole and introduces the role of "force" as the ultimate test for whether an object is truly moving.</meta>

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES

<margin>
DEFINITIONS.
</margin>

It is a property of motion that parts, which maintain fixed positions relative to their wholes, share in the motions of those same wholes. For all the parts of rotating bodies <note>original: "gyrantium"; Newton is describing centrifugal force, where parts of a spinning object try to fly outward from the center</note> strive to recede from the axis of motion, and the momentum of things moving forward arises from the combined momentum of their individual parts. Therefore, when surrounding bodies move, those objects that are at rest relative to their surroundings move as well. For this reason, true and absolute motion cannot be defined simply by an object's shift away from neighboring bodies that are merely *seen* as if they were at rest. External bodies must not only be viewed as resting, but must truly be at rest. Otherwise, all things contained within—besides shifting away from their immediate surroundings—will also share in the true motions of those surroundings; and if that shift is removed, they will not truly be at rest, but will only be seen as if they were at rest. For surroundings are to the things they contain as the outer shell of a whole is to the inner part, or like a husk to a kernel <note>original: "cortex ad nucleum"</note>. When the husk moves, the kernel also moves as part of the whole, even without shifting its position relative to the husk.

Related to the previous property is the fact that when a place moves, the object located there moves along with it; therefore, a body moving out of a place that is itself in motion also shares in the motion of its place. All motions that occur from moving places are, therefore, only parts of entire and absolute motions. Every whole motion is composed of the motion of the body from its first place, and the motion of that place from its own place, and so on, until one reaches an **immovable place**, as in the example of the sailor mentioned above <note>Newton refers to a previous example where a sailor walks on a ship: his "true" motion is a sum of his walking, the ship's speed across the sea, and the Earth's rotation/orbit</note>. Thus, whole and absolute motions can only be defined through immovable places; for this reason, I referred to these earlier as "absolute" in relation to immovable places, and "relative" in relation to movable ones. Immovable places are only those that, from infinity to infinity, maintain fixed positions relative to one another; they always remain unmoved and constitute what I call **immobile space**.

The causes that distinguish true and relative motions from each other are the **forces** impressed upon bodies to generate motion. True motion is neither created nor changed except by forces applied directly to the moving body itself; however, relative motion can be created or changed without any forces being applied to that specific body. It is enough for forces to be applied only to the *other* bodies to which it is related; as they give way, that relationship—which constitutes the body's relative rest or motion—is altered. Conversely, true motion is always changed by forces applied to the moving body;

# PHILOSOPHY OF NATURE

<margin>
DEFINITIONS.
</margin>

...moved; yet relative motion is not necessarily changed by these forces. For if the same forces are applied to the other bodies used for reference, such that their relative positions are maintained, the relationship defining the relative motion will be preserved. Thus, all relative motion can change while the true motion remains the same, and it can remain the same while the true motion changes. Therefore, true motion does not consist in such relationships at all.

The effects that distinguish absolute and relative motion from one another are the forces of receding from the axis of circular motion <note>Newton is describing what we now call centrifugal force—the outward "push" felt in a spinning system</note>. In merely relative circular motion, these forces are non-existent; in true and absolute motion, they are greater or smaller according to the quantity of the motion. 

If a bucket <note>original: "situla"</note> is suspended by a very long cord and is spun around repeatedly until the cord becomes quite stiff with twisting, then is filled with water and kept still alongside the water; then, if by some sudden force it is spun in the opposite direction and continues in this motion as the cord untwists; the surface of the water will initially be flat, just as it was before the vessel moved. But after the vessel, by a force gradually impressed upon the water, causes the water also to begin rotating noticeably, the water will gradually recede from the middle and climb up the sides of the vessel, taking on a concave shape (as I have experienced myself). With increasingly rapid motion, it will climb more and more until, completing its revolutions in the same time as the vessel, it rests relative to the vessel. 

This ascent indicates the striving <note>original: "conatus"; in 17th-century physics, this refers to the "endeavor" or internal force of an object to move in a certain way</note> to recede from the axis of motion, and through such a striving, the true and absolute circular motion of the water becomes known and measured, showing itself to be entirely contrary to the relative motion here. At the start, where the relative motion of the water in the vessel was greatest <note>i.e., when the bucket was spinning fast but the water was still</note>, that motion produced no striving to recede from the axis: the water did not seek the edges by climbing the sides of the vessel but remained flat, and therefore its true circular motion had not yet begun. Later, however, when the relative motion of the water decreased, its ascent to the sides of the vessel indicated its striving to recede from the axis; and this striving showed its true circular motion to be constantly increasing, finally becoming greatest when the water was at rest relative to the vessel <note>i.e., when both bucket and water spin at the same speed, their relative motion is zero, yet the "true" motion is at its peak</note>. Therefore, that striving does not depend on the movement of the water with respect to surrounding bodies, and consequently true circular motion cannot be defined by such movements. There is only one truly circular motion for any revolving body, corresponding to a single striving as its own proper and adequate effect. Relative motions, however, are countless, depending on various relationships to external things; and like

...like [relative motions], they are completely devoid of true effects, except insofar as they participate in that true and unique motion. Hence, in the system of those who claim that our heavens revolve in an orbit below the heavens of the fixed stars <note>Newton refers to the Tychonic or Geocentric models where the celestial spheres rotate around the Earth</note> and carry the planets with them, the individual parts of the heavens, and the planets which are relatively at rest in their own immediate heavens, are in truth moved. For they change their positions relative to one another (otherwise than occurs in things truly at rest) and, being carried along with the heavens, they participate in their motions and, as parts of revolving wholes, they strive to recede from their axes <note>Newton is arguing that even if a planet looks "still" relative to the sky around it, it is still experiencing the physical "outward pull" of rotation</note>.

Relative quantities, therefore, are not those very quantities whose names they bear, but are those sensible measures <note>perceptible by the senses</note> of them (whether true or errant) which the common people use in place of the measured quantities. But if the meanings of words are to be defined by usage, then by those names of "time," "space," "place," and "motion," these sensible measures are properly to be understood; and the language will be unusual and purely mathematical if the measured quantities are understood here. Therefore, they do violence to the Holy Scriptures <note>original: "sacris literis." Newton is defending himself against theological critics who argued that the Bible describes the Earth as still and the Sun as moving</note> who interpret these words there as referring to absolute, measured quantities. Nor do they any less defile mathematics and philosophy who confuse true quantities with their relative relations and common measures.

Indeed, to recognize the true motions of individual bodies and to distinguish them in practice from apparent ones is very difficult, because the parts of that immobile space in which bodies truly move do not strike our senses. Yet the cause is not entirely hopeless. For arguments can be drawn, partly from apparent motions which are the differences of true motions, and partly from the forces which are the causes and effects of true motions. As if two globes, connected to each other at a given distance by an intervening thread, were rotated around a common center of gravity; the endeavor of the globes to recede from the axis of motion would become known from the tension of the thread, and from this the quantity of circular motion could be computed. Then, if any equal forces were simultaneously impressed upon opposite faces of the globes to increase or decrease the circular motion, the increase or decrease of the motion would become known from the increased or decreased tension of the thread; and from this, at last, it could be discovered which faces of the globes the forces should be applied to in order to increase the motion the most; that is, the rear faces, or those which follow in the circular motion. Once the faces that follow are known,

<meta>This page follows the introductory sections of the Principia, moving from definitions of terms like mass and momentum into the core "Axioms" or Laws of Motion that form the foundation of classical mechanics.</meta>

# AXIOMS,

->OR<-

## LAWS OF MOTION.

---

### LAW I.

*Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of moving uniformly forward in a straight line, unless it is compelled to change its state by forces impressed upon it.* <note>original: "Corpus omne perseverare in statu suo quiescendi vel movendi uniformiter in directum..." This is the foundational definition of inertia—the resistance of an object to any change in its motion.</note>

Projectiles <term>Projectiles: objects thrown or propelled into space, like an arrow or a cannonball</term> continue in their motions, except insofar as they are slowed by the resistance of the air and driven downward by the force of gravity. A top <term>Trochus: a spinning top or hoop</term>, whose parts by cohering constantly pull themselves away from straight-line motions, does not stop rotating except insofar as it is slowed by the air. The larger bodies of planets and comets, however, preserve their motions—both their forward progress and their orbits—for a much longer time, as they move in spaces offering less resistance.

### LAW II.

*The change of motion is proportional to the motive force impressed; and is made along the straight line in which that force is impressed.* <note>original: "Mutationem motus proportionalem esse vi motrici impressæ..." Newton here establishes that the more force you apply, the more the motion changes (the origin of the famous F=ma formula).</note>

If any force generates a certain motion, a double force will generate double the motion, and a triple force triple the motion, whether that force is applied all at once or gradually and successively. And this motion (since it is always directed toward the same region as the generating force) is handled differently depending on the body's prior state: if the body was already moving, this new motion is either added to the previous motion (if they are in the same direction), subtracted from it (if they are opposite), or added obliquely (if they meet at an angle). In the case of an oblique force, it is combined with the original motion according to the specific direction of each.

<summary>This page introduces the first two of Newton's three fundamental laws of motion, defining the concept of inertia and the proportional relationship between force and the resulting change in a body's motion.</summary>
<keywords>Laws of Motion, Newton, inertia, force, projectiles, gravity, planetary motion, motive force, physics axioms</keywords>

OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>LAWS OF MOTION.</margin>

### LAW III.

> *To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction: or the mutual actions of two bodies upon each other are always equal and directed to contrary parts.* <note>original: "Actioni contrariam semper & æqualem esse reactionem..." This is Newton’s famous third law, often summarized as "for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction."</note>

Whatever presses or pulls another is pressed or pulled just as much by it. If anyone presses a stone with their finger, their finger is also pressed by the stone. If a horse pulls a stone tied to a rope, the horse will also be drawn back (so to speak) equally toward the stone; for the rope, being stretched at both ends, will by the same endeavor to relax itself urge the horse toward the stone and the stone toward the horse; and it will impede the progress of one as much as it promotes the progress of the other. If a body, striking another body, changes its motion in any way by its force, that same body will in turn undergo the same change in its own motion in the opposite direction by the force of the other (because of the equality of the mutual pressure). By these actions, equal changes are made, not of the velocities, but of the motions <term>Motus: Newton uses "motion" to mean momentum (mass multiplied by velocity), not just speed</term>; specifically in bodies not otherwise hindered. For the changes of velocities, likewise made in opposite directions, because the motions are changed equally, are inversely proportional to the bodies <note>This means that if a heavy object and a light object interact, the light one will experience a much greater change in speed, even though the total "quantity of motion" (momentum) changed for both is the same.</note>. This law also holds in attractions, as will be proved in the next scholium <term>Scholium: an explanatory note or scholarly commentary</term>.

## COROLLARY III.

*The quantity of motion, which is calculated by taking the sum of the motions directed the same way, and the difference of those directed opposite ways, is not changed by the action of bodies upon each other.* <note>Newton is describing the Law of Conservation of Momentum. In a closed system, the total momentum remains constant regardless of how the objects inside collide or interact.</note>

For action and its opposite reaction are equal by Law III, and therefore by Law II they produce equal changes in motion toward opposite directions. Therefore, if the motions are in the same direction, whatever is added to the motion of the leading body will be subtracted from the motion of the following body so that the sum remains the same as before. But if the bodies meet head-on, the subtraction from the motion of each will be equal, and therefore the difference of the motions made in opposite directions will remain the same.

For example, if a spherical body *A* is three times larger than spherical body *B*, and has two parts of velocity; and *B* follows in the same straight line with ten parts of velocity, then the motion of *A* is to the motion of *B* as six is to ten. <note>Newton defines "motion" (what we call momentum) as mass multiplied by velocity. For A: 3 (size) x 2 (velocity) = 6. For B: 1 (size) x 10 (velocity) = 10.</note> Let us suppose the motions they have are of six parts and ten parts, and the sum will be sixteen parts. Therefore, in the collision of the bodies, if body *A* gains three or four or five parts of motion, body *B* will lose exactly as many parts. Consequently, after the impact, body *A* will continue with nine or ten or eleven parts, and *B* with seven or six or five parts, the sum always remaining sixteen parts as before. If body *A* gains nine or ten or eleven or twelve parts, and therefore moves forward after the collision with fifteen or sixteen or seventeen or eighteen parts; body *B*, by losing as many parts as *A* gains,

### COROLLARY IV.

*The common <term>center of gravity|original: "centrum gravitatis"; in modern physics, we usually call this the "center of mass."</term> of two or more bodies does not change its state of motion or rest by the actions of the bodies upon each other; and therefore the common center of gravity of all bodies acting mutually upon each other (excluding external actions and impediments) either remains at rest or moves uniformly forward in a straight line.*

For if two points proceed with uniform motion in straight lines, and the distance between them is divided in a <term>given ratio|original: "ratione data"; a fixed proportion based on the masses of the objects</term>, the dividing point either remains at rest or proceeds uniformly in a straight line. This is demonstrated later in Lemma XXIII and its corollary, if the motions of the points occur in the same plane; and by the same reasoning it can be demonstrated if those motions do not occur in the same plane. Therefore, if any number of bodies move uniformly in straight lines, the common center of gravity of any two of them either remains at rest or proceeds uniformly in a straight line; because the line joining the centers of these bodies, which are proceeding uniformly in straight lines, is divided by this common center in a given ratio. Similarly, the common center of these two and of any third body either remains at rest or proceeds uniformly in a straight line; because the distance between the common center of the first two bodies and the center of the third body is divided by it in a given ratio. In the same way, the common center of these three and of any fourth body either remains at rest or proceeds uniformly in a straight line; because the distance between the common center of the three and the center of the fourth is divided by it in a given ratio, and so on to infinity. Therefore, in a system of bodies which are entirely free from actions upon each other and from all other actions impressed upon them from the outside, and which therefore move individually and uniformly in individual straight lines, the common center of gravity either remains at rest or moves uniformly forward.

Furthermore, in a system of two bodies acting upon each other, since the distances of the centers of both from the common center of gravity are <term>reciprocal|original: "reciproce"; meaning inversely proportional</term> to the bodies <note>In Newton's era, "bodies" was often used to mean "masses."</note>; the relative motions of those same bodies—whether of approaching that center or of receding from it—will be equal to each other.

<summary>Newton demonstrates that the center of mass of a system remains unaffected by the internal forces (like collisions or gravity) between the objects within that system. This establishes that a group of objects behaves as a single unit relative to its shared balance point.</summary>

Wherefore, since that center—where bodies do not act upon each other—either rests or progresses uniformly in some straight line; it will continue the same, notwithstanding the actions of the bodies among themselves, to either always rest or always progress uniformly in a straight line; unless it is disturbed from this state by <term>forces impressed|original: "viribus... impressis"; external pushes or pulls</term> upon the system from the outside. Therefore, the law for a system of several bodies is the same as that for a solitary body, regarding perseverance in a state of motion or rest. For the progressive motion, whether of a solitary body or of a system of bodies, must always be <note>Newton is arguing that the "true" motion of a collection of objects is best understood by looking at the movement of its balance point (the center of mass).</note> estimated from the motion of the center of gravity.

## COROLLARY VI.

*If bodies are moving in any way among themselves, and are urged by equal accelerating forces along parallel lines; they will all continue to move among themselves in the same way as if they had not been acted upon by those forces.*

For those forces, by acting equally (in proportion to the quantities of the bodies to be moved) and along parallel lines, will move all the bodies equally (in terms of velocity) according to the second law; and therefore they will never change the positions and motions of those bodies relative to each other.

### *Scholium.*

Hitherto I have presented principles accepted by mathematicians and confirmed by manifold experience. By means of the first two laws and the first two corollaries, Galileo discovered that the descent of heavy bodies is in the <term>duplicate ratio|original: "duplicata ratione"; a mathematical term meaning the ratio of the squares</term> of the time, and that the motion of projectiles occurs in a parabola; experience agreeing with this, except insofar as those motions are somewhat retarded by the resistance of the air. When a body falls, uniform gravity, by acting equally in each equal particle of time, impresses equal forces on that body and generates equal velocities: and in the total time it impresses the total force and generates a total velocity proportional to the time. And the spaces described in proportional times are as the velocities and times combined; that is, in the <term>duplicate ratio of the times|meaning that if you double the time, the distance fallen increases fourfold (t squared)</term>. And when a body is projected upward, uniform gravity impresses forces and takes away velocities proportional to the times; and the times of ascending to the highest altitudes are as the velocities to be taken away, and those altitudes are as the velocities and times combined, or in the duplicate ratio of the <insert>initial</insert> velocities.

For it is a proposition very well known to mathematicians <note>original: "geometris" — literally geometers, as geometry was the primary language of physics in this era.</note> that the velocity of a pendulum at its lowest point is proportional to the chord of the arc which it described in falling. And so body *B* must be multiplied into the chord of the arc *Bl*, so that we may have its motion immediately after reflection. And by a similar method, where two bodies are let go at the same time from different locations, the motions of both are to be found both before and after reflection; and then at last the motions are to be compared among themselves and the effects of reflection gathered. By trying the experiment in this way with ten-foot pendulums, and that with bodies both unequal and equal, and by making it so that the bodies would collide from very large intervals, say of eight or twelve or sixteen feet; I always found, within an error of less than three inches <note>original: "trium digitorum" — literally three fingers, a traditional unit of measurement approximately equal to an inch.</note> in the measurements, where the bodies encountered each other directly, that the changes of motion imparted to the bodies in opposite directions were equal, and therefore that action and reaction were always equal. For example, if body *A* fell upon body *B* which was at rest with nine parts of motion, and having lost seven parts, it continued after reflection with two; the body *B* would leap back with those seven parts. If the bodies went to meet each other, *A* with twelve parts and *B* with six, and *A* returned with two; *B* would return with eight, a deduction of fourteen parts being made on both sides. For from the motion of *A*, subtract twelve parts...

I tested this using tightly packed and strongly bound wool in the following way. In the case of attractions, I demonstrate the matter briefly as follows. Imagine any two bodies, *A* and *B*, pulling each other, and conceive of an obstacle placed between them to prevent them from coming together. If one body *A* is pulled more toward body *B* than that other body *B* is pulled toward the first body *A*, the obstacle will be urged more by the pressure of body *A* than by the pressure of body *B*; and therefore, it will not remain in equilibrium. The stronger pressure will prevail and cause the system of the two bodies and the obstacle to move in a straight line toward *B*, and, with a motion always accelerated in free space, to go off to infinity. This is absurd and contrary to the first law <note>The First Law of Motion states that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by an outside force. Newton argues that a system cannot "pull itself" into motion without an external force.</note>. For by the first law, the system ought to persist in its state of resting or moving uniformly in a straight line; therefore, the bodies will urge the obstacle equally, and for that reason, they are equally attracted toward each other. I tested this with a magnet and iron. If these are placed in their own separate vessels touching each other and float side by side in still water, neither will propel the other; instead, through the equality of attraction on both sides, they will sustain their mutual efforts against each other, and at last, established in equilibrium, they will come to rest.

And unless those weights were equal, the entire earth floating in the free ether <note>Newton refers to "ether" here as the subtle medium then thought to fill all space, though his point is simply that the Earth would move through space if its internal forces were unbalanced.</note> would yield to the greater weight, and by fleeing from it, would go off into infinity.

->[Image: A circle representing the Earth divided into three segments by two vertical lines. The left segment is labeled E, F, G; the right segment is labeled H, I, K.]<-

Just as bodies in collision and reflection have equal power when their velocities are inversely proportional to their <term>inherent forces</term> <note>original: *vires insitæ*. This refers to what we now call "momentum" or "inertia," depending on the context of the interaction.</note>: so too in the operation of mechanical instruments, the "agents" <note>The source of the power or force, like a hand or a weight.</note> have equal power and sustain each other by opposing efforts when their velocities, estimated according to the direction of the forces, are inversely proportional to those forces. Thus, weights are of equal power for moving the arms of a balance <note>original: *libra*</note> when, as the balance oscillates, the weights are inversely proportional to their velocities upward and downward; that is, the weights (if they ascend and descend vertically) are of equal power when they are inversely proportional to the distances of the points from which they are suspended to the axis of the balance. But if they ascend or descend obliquely because of slanted planes or other obstacles, they are of equal power when they are inversely proportional to the ascent and descent, insofar as those movements are made vertically: and this is due to the downward determination of gravity.

Similarly, in a <term>pulley</term> <note>original: *trochlea*</note> or <term>hoist</term> <note>original: *polyspasto* — a system of many pulleys or a "tackle" used for lifting heavy loads.</note>, the force of a hand pulling a rope directly, which is to the weight (ascending either directly or obliquely) as the velocity of the vertical ascent is to the velocity of the hand pulling the rope, will sustain the weight. In clocks and similar instruments, which are constructed from joined gears, opposing forces for promoting and impeding the motion of the gears will sustain each other if they are inversely proportional to the velocities of the parts of the gears upon which they are impressed. The force of a <term>screw</term> <note>original: *cochleæ*</note> for pressing a body is to the force of the hand turning the handle, as the circular velocity of the handle (at the point where it is pushed by the hand) is to the progressive velocity of the screw toward the pressed body. The forces with which a <term>Wedge</term> <note>original: *Cuneus*</note> presses the two parts of a split log are to the force of the hammer upon the wedge, as the progress of the wedge in the direction of the force from the hammer...

The efficiency and use of these [machines] consist solely in this: that by decreasing velocity, we may increase the force, and vice-versa. From this is solved, in every kind of fit instrument, the problem: *To move a given weight with a given force*, or to overcome any other given resistance with a given force. For if machines are so constructed that the velocities of the agent <note>The "agent" is the source of the power or force, such as a person pushing a lever or a falling weight.</note> and the resistant <note>The object or load being moved.</note> are inversely proportional to their forces, the agent will sustain the resistance; and with a greater disparity of velocities, it will overcome it. Certainly, if the disparity of velocities is so great that all resistance is overcome—which usually arises from the friction <term>attrition</term> <note>original: *attritio*. Newton recognizes that real-world machines lose energy to friction between sliding parts.</note> of bodies touching and sliding against each other, as well as from the cohesion of parts that must be separated and the weights of those to be lifted—once all that resistance is overcome, the redundant <note>Extra or leftover force beyond what is needed to balance the load.</note> force will produce an acceleration of motion proportional to itself, partly in the parts of the machine and partly in the resisting body. 

However, to treat mechanics is not the purpose of this undertaking. By these examples, I intended only to show how widely the third law of motion extends and how certain it is. For if the action of the agent is estimated from its force and velocity together <note>Newton is essentially describing what modern physics calls "Power" (Force × Velocity) or the rate of doing work.</note>; and similarly, the reaction of the resistant is estimated together from the velocities of its individual parts and the forces of resistance arising from their friction, cohesion, weight, and acceleration; then action and reaction, in every use of instruments, will always be equal to each other. And insofar as the action is propagated through the instrument and finally impressed upon every resisting body, its final direction <note>original: *determinatio*</note> will always be contrary to the direction of the reaction.

### LEMMA I.

*Quantities, as well as the ratios of quantities, which throughout any finite time tend constantly toward equality, and before the end of that time approach closer to each other than by any given difference, become ultimately equal.*

If you deny this; let them be ultimately unequal, and let their ultimate difference be *D*. ## LEMMA VI.

*If any arc ACB given in position is subtended by a chord AB, and at any point A, in the middle of a continuous curvature, it is touched by a straight line AD produced on both sides; then if points A and B approach each other and coincide; I say that the angle BAD, contained between the chord and the tangent, will be diminished to infinity and ultimately vanish.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating Lemma VI. It shows a curve labeled ACB with a chord AB and a tangent line AD at point A. For if that angle does not vanish, the arc *ACB* would form with the tangent *AD* an angle equal to a <term>rectilinear angle</term> <note>An angle formed by two straight lines. Newton is arguing that if the angle didn't vanish, the curve would essentially have a "sharp corner" at point A.</note>, and therefore the curvature at point *A* would not be continuous, which is contrary to the hypothesis.

## LEMMA VII.

*The same things being supposed; I say that the ultimate ratio of the arc, the chord, and the tangent to each other is the ratio of equality.* <note>original: "ratio æqualitatis". This refers to the limit where the values become identical as they approach zero.</note>

For while point *B* approaches point *A*, let *AB* and *AD* always be understood to be extended to the distant points *b* and *d*, and let the line *bd* be drawn parallel to the <term>secant</term> <note>A line that cuts through a curve at two points; in this case, the line segment BD.</note> *BD*. And let the arc *Acb* always be similar to the arc *ACB*. And as points *A* and *B* meet, the angle *dAb*, by the previous lemma, will vanish; and therefore the straight lines *Ab* and *Ad*, which are always finite, and the intermediate arc *Acb* will coincide, and therefore will be equal. From this, the straight lines *AB* and *AD*, and the intermediate arc *ACB*, which are always proportional to these larger segments, will vanish and will have the <term>ultimate ratio</term> <note>Newton’s term for the limit of a ratio as the quantities themselves disappear.</note> of equality. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

*Corollary 1.* Hence, if through *B* a line *BF* is drawn parallel to the tangent, perpetually cutting any straight line *AF* passing through *A* at the point *F*, then this *BF* will ultimately have a ratio of equality to the vanishing arc *ACB*, because once the parallelogram *AFBD* is completed, *BF* always has a ratio of equality to *AD*.

### LEMMA VIII.

*If given straight lines AR, BR together with the arc ACB, chord AB, and tangent AD, constitute three triangles RAB, RACB, and RAD, and then points A and B approach each other: I say that the ultimate form of the vanishing triangles is of similarity, and the ultimate ratio is of equality.*

For while point *B* approaches point *A*, let *AB*, *AD*, and *AR* always be understood to be extended to the distant points *b*, *d*, and *r*, and let *rbd* be drawn parallel to *RD*, and let the arc *Acb* always be <term>similar</term> <note>In geometry, "similar" means having the same shape regardless of size.</note> to arc *ACB*. And as points *A* and *B* coincide, the angle *bAd* will vanish, and therefore the three triangles—which always remain finite—*rAb*, *rAcb*, and *rAd* will coincide, and for that reason they are similar and equal. From this, the triangles *RAB*, *RACB*, and *RAD*, which are always similar and proportional to these, will ultimately become similar and equal to each other. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

### LEMMA X.

> *The spaces which a body describes when urged by any finite force, whether that force is fixed and unchanging, or is continually increased or continually decreased, are at the very beginning of the motion in the <term>duplicate ratio</term> of the times.*

*Corollary 1.* And from this it is easily concluded that the <term>errors</term> <note>original: "errores". In this context, Newton is not referring to mistakes, but to "deviations"—the distance a body is pulled away from its straight-line inertial path by a force.</note> of bodies describing similar parts of similar figures in proportional times—which are generated by any equal forces applied similarly to the bodies, and are measured by the distances of the bodies from those places of the similar figures to which the same bodies would have arrived in those same proportional times without those forces—are as the squares of the times in which they are generated, very nearly.

*Corollary 4.* And therefore the forces are as the spaces described at the very beginning of the motion directly, and the squares of the times inversely.

*Corollary 5.* And the squares of the times are as the spaces described directly, and the forces inversely.

### Scholium.

If <term>indeterminate quantities</term> <note>Variables or unknown values.</note> of different kinds are compared among themselves, and any one of them is said to be as any other is, either directly or inversely: the meaning is, that the former increases or decreases in the same ratio as the latter, or as its reciprocal. And if any one of them is said to be as two or more others, directly or inversely: the meaning is, that the first increases or decreases in a ratio <term>compounded</term> <note>Resulting from the multiplication of ratios.</note> of the ratios in which the others (or the reciprocals of the others) increase or decrease. For example, if *A* is said to be as *B* directly and *C* directly and *D* inversely: the meaning is, that *A* increases or decreases in the same ratio as *B* x *C* x 1/*D*; that is, that *A* and *BC/D* are to each other in a given ratio.

*Case 1.* Let *AB* be that arc, *AD* its tangent, *BD* the <term>subtense</term> <note>A line segment connecting the tangent and the arc, here perpendicular to the tangent.</note> of the angle of contact perpendicular to the tangent, and *AB* the chord of the arc. It is manifest that the distance *Gj* can be less than any assigned length. However (from the nature of circles passing through the points *A, B, G* and *A, b, g*), the **square of AB** is equal to *AG* multiplied by *BD*, and the **square of Ab** is equal to *Ag* multiplied by *bd*; and therefore the ratio of the **square of AB** to the **square of Ab** is composed of the ratios of *AG* to *Ag* and *BD* to *bd*. But since *Gj* can be assumed smaller than any assigned length, it can happen that the ratio of *AG* to *Ag* differs from the ratio of equality <note>A ratio of 1:1.</note> by less than any assigned difference, and therefore that the ratio of the **square of AB** to the **square of Ab** differs from the ratio of *BD* to *bd* by less than any assigned difference. Therefore, by Lemma 1, the ultimate ratio of the **square of AB** to the **square of Ab** is the same as the ultimate ratio of *BD* to *bd*. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

Furthermore, in all these cases we assume that the <term>angle of contact</term> <note>The infinitesimal opening between a curve and its tangent line.</note> is neither infinitely greater than the angles of contact which circles make with their tangents, nor infinitely smaller than them; that is, that the <term>curvature</term> at point *A* is neither infinitely small nor infinitely large, or that the distance *AJ* <note>Referring to the diameter of curvature at that point.</note> is of a finite magnitude. For *DB* can be taken as proportional to $AD^3$: in which case no circle can be drawn through point *A* between the tangent *AD* and the curve *AB*, and therefore the angle of contact will be infinitely smaller than circular ones. And by a similar argument, if *DB* is made successively proportional to $AD^4, AD^5, AD^6, AD^7,$ etc., there will be a series of angles of contact proceeding to infinity, of which every subsequent one is infinitely smaller than the preceding. And if *DB* is made successively proportional to $AD^2, AD^{3/2}, AD^{4/3}, AD^{5/4}, AD^{6/5}, AD^{7/6},$ etc., there will be another infinite series of angles of contact, of which the first is of the same kind as circular ones, the second is infinitely larger, and every subsequent one is infinitely larger than the preceding. But also between any two of these angles, a series of intermediate angles proceeding to infinity on both sides can be inserted, of which every subsequent one will be infinitely larger or smaller than the preceding. As if between the terms $AD^2$ and $AD^3$ there is inserted the series $AD^{13/6}, AD^{11/5}, AD^{9/4},$ ...

<margin>BOOK ONE</margin>

Those things demonstrated about curved lines and the surfaces they enclose are easily applied to the curved surfaces and volumes of solids. I have put these <term>lemmas</term> <note>Preliminary propositions used to prove following theorems.</note> first so that I might avoid the tediousness of conducting long proofs by "reduction to absurdity" <note>original: *ad absurdum*; a method of proof that shows a statement is true by showing the impossibility of its opposite.</note> in the manner of the ancient geometers. For demonstrations are made more concise by the <term>method of indivisibles</term> <note>original: *methodum indivisibilium*; an early mathematical method that treated lines as composed of infinitely many points and areas as made of infinitely many lines.</note>. But because the hypothesis of indivisibles is somewhat harsh, and for that reason that method is considered less "geometrical," I preferred to derive the proofs of the following things from the **ultimate sums and ratios of vanishing quantities**, and the **first sums and ratios of nascent quantities**—that is, to the **limits** of sums and ratios. Therefore, I have presented the proofs of those limits as briefly as I could. For by these, the same thing is achieved as by the method of indivisibles; and since these principles have now been proven, we may use them with more confidence. 

Therefore, in the following pages, whenever I consider quantities as if they consist of small particles, or if I use small curved lines instead of straight ones, I do not wish them to be understood as <term>indivisibles</term> <note>Newton is distancing himself from the idea that matter or space is made of "atoms" that cannot be divided further.</note>, but as **vanishing divisibles**; not as the sums and ratios of fixed parts, but as the **limits of sums and ratios**, always keeping in mind that the force of such proofs rests on the method of the preceding lemmas.

There is an objection that there is no "ultimate proportion" of vanishing quantities; for, before they have vanished, the proportion is not the ultimate one, and once they have vanished, there is no proportion at all. But by the same argument, it could just as well be contended that there is no "ultimate velocity" of a body reaching a certain place where its motion ends: for before the body reaches that place, the velocity is not the ultimate one, and when it reaches it, the velocity is nothing. But the answer is easy: By "ultimate velocity" is understood that velocity with which the body moves, neither before it reaches its final place and the motion ceases, nor after, but at the very moment it reaches it; that is, that very velocity with which the body reaches its final place and with which the motion ceases. And similarly, by the **ultimate ratio of vanishing quantities**, we must understand the ratio of the quantities not before they vanish, nor after, but the ratio with which they vanish. Likewise, the **first ratio of nascent quantities** is the ratio with which they begin to exist. And the first and last sum

...is that with which they begin (or increase or decrease) and cease to be. There exists a limit which the velocity can reach at the end of the motion, but not exceed. This is the **ultimate velocity** <note>original: *velocitas ultima*; Newton is describing the concept of a "limit" in calculus—the value a changing quantity approaches as it gets closer and closer to its end point.</note>. And the same reasoning applies to the limit of all quantities and proportions as they begin or cease. And since this limit is certain and definite, the problem of determining it is truly geometrical. Indeed, all geometrical principles are legitimately used in determining and demonstrating other geometrical things.

It can also be argued that if ultimate ratios of vanishing quantities are given, then ultimate magnitudes will also be given: and thus every quantity would consist of <term>indivisibles</term> <note>Tiny, atomic parts of a line or shape. Newton rejects this because it leads to mathematical paradoxes.</note>, contrary to what **Euclid** <note>The famous Greek "Father of Geometry."</note> demonstrated concerning <term>incommensurables</term> <note>Numbers that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction, like the square root of 2.</note> in the tenth book of his *Elements*. But this objection rests upon a false hypothesis. Those **ultimate ratios** with which quantities vanish are not truly ratios of ultimate quantities <note>i.e., they aren't the ratio of two "last" tiny pieces.</note>, but limits to which the ratios of quantities decreasing without limit always approach; and which they can reach closer than any given difference, but never exceed, nor reach before the quantities are diminished to infinity. 

The matter will be understood more clearly in the case of infinitely large quantities. If two quantities, whose difference is given, are increased to infinity, their ultimate ratio will be given—namely, the **ratio of equality** <note>As two things grow toward infinity, their original small difference becomes so insignificant that they effectively become equal.</note>—and yet for that reason, ultimate or maximum quantities of which that is the ratio will not be given. In the following pages, therefore, if ever I speak of "smallest possible" or "vanishing" or "ultimate" quantities for the sake of an easy conception of things, take care not to understand quantities determined in magnitude, but think of them as always to be diminished without limit.

The areas swept out are represented by the triangles SAB, SBC, SCD, etc. These triangles are shown to have equal areas even though their shapes change.</image-desc>

<columns/>

By a similar argument, if the centripetal force acts successively at points $C, D, E$, and so on, causing the body to describe the individual straight lines $CD, DE, EF$, etc., in individual tiny particles of time, all these points will lie in the same flat plane; and triangle $SCD$ will be equal in area to triangle $SBC$, and $SDE$ will be equal to $SCD$, and $SEF$ to $SDE$. Therefore, in equal times, equal areas are described in an unmoving plane: and by adding these together, any sums of the areas, such as $SADS$ and $SAFS$, are to each other exactly as the lengths of the times it took to describe them. Now, let the number of triangles be increased and their width be diminished to infinity <note>This is the core of Newton's "calculus" method: turning a jagged, stepped path into a smooth curve by making the steps infinitely small.</note>; their ultimate perimeter $ADF$ (by Corollary 4 of Lemma 3) will become a curved line. Therefore, the centripetal force, by which the body is perpetually drawn back from the tangent <note>The straight-line path the body "wants" to take.</note> of this curve, will now act without interruption; and any described areas $SADS, SAFS$, which are always proportional to the times of description, will remain proportional to those same times in this case. **Q. E. D.** <note>original: *Quod Erat Demonstrandum*; a Latin phrase meaning "Which was to be demonstrated," traditionally used at the end of a mathematical proof.</note>

<meta>catchword: Corol. (indicates the next page begins with a Corollary)</meta>

<summary>Newton provides a geometric proof for Kepler's Second Law, demonstrating that a body moving under the influence of a central force (like gravity) will sweep out equal areas in equal times. He achieves this by first modeling the force as discrete impulses and then using a limit to describe a continuous force.</summary>

*Corollary 1.* The velocity of a body attracted toward an immobile center in a vacuum <note>original: *spatiis non resistentibus*; literally "non-resisting spaces." For the motions of the body *BC* and *EF* are composed (according to Corollary 1 of the Laws of Motion) from the motions *Bc, BV* and *Ef, EZ:* but *BV* and *EZ,* being equal to *Cc* and *Ff,* were generated in the proof of this proposition by the impulses of centripetal force <term>centripetal force</term><note>original: *vis centripeta*; Newton coined this term from the Latin words for "center" and "seeking." ## PROPOSITION 2. THEOREM 2.

*Every body that moves in some curved line described in a plane, and by a radius drawn to a point that is either immobile or moving uniformly forward in a straight line, describes areas about that point proportional to the times, is urged by a centripetal force tending toward that same point.*

*Case 1.* For every body that moves in a curved line is turned aside from a straight path by some force acting upon it (by Law 1). And that force, by which the body is turned from its straight path and is compelled to describe the smallest possible triangles $SAB, SBC, SCD$, etc., about the immobile point $S$ equal in equal times, acts at position $B$ along a line parallel to $cC$ (by Proposition 40, Book 1 of the *Elements* <note>original: *prop. xl. lib. 1. elem.*; referring to Euclid’s geometry, where triangles of equal area on the same base have the same height</note>, and Law 2); that is, along the line $BS$; and at position $C$ along a line parallel to $dD$, that is, along the line $SC$, and so on. Therefore, it always acts along lines tending toward that immobile point $S$. Which was to be demonstrated <note>original: *Q. E. D.* or *Quod Erat Demonstrandum*</note>.

*Case 2.* And, by the fifth corollary of the Laws, it is all the same whether the surface in which the body describes the curvilinear figure is at rest, or whether it moves uniformly forward in a straight line together with the body, the figure described, and its point $S$.

*Corollary 1.* In spaces or media that do not offer resistance, if the areas are not proportional to the times, the forces do not tend toward the meeting point of the radii; but they deviate from there in the direction of the motion <note>original: *in consequentia*; a term from astronomy meaning moving in the same direction as the planet's usual orbit</note>, or toward the region in which the motion occurs, if the description of the areas is accelerated; but if it is retarded, they deviate in the opposite direction <note>original: *in antecedentia*; moving "backwards" against the usual direction of orbit</note>.

### Scholium <note>A "Scholium" is an explanatory note or commentary added to a text to clarify a proof or provide further context.</note>

A body can be urged by a centripetal force composed of several forces. In this case, the meaning of the proposition is that the force which is composed of all of them <term>composed force: today we call this the "resultant force," or the sum of all individual forces acting on an object.</term> tends toward the point *S*. Furthermore, if any force acts perpetually perpendicular to the line of the described surface, it will cause the body to deflect from the plane of its motion; but it will neither increase nor decrease the quantity of the described surface, and therefore, in the composition of forces, it is to be neglected.

## PROPOSITION 3. THEOREM 3.

*Every body which, by a radius drawn to the center of another body moving in any way, describes areas about that center proportional to the times, is urged by a force composed of the centripetal force tending toward that other body, and of all the accelerative force by which that other body is urged.*

Let the first body be *L*, and the second body *T*: and (by the sixth corollary of the laws <note>Newton refers to the "Axioms, or Laws of Motion" established at the beginning of the *Principia*.</note>) if both bodies are urged along parallel lines by a new force, equal and contrary to that by which the second body *T* is urged; the first body *L* will continue to describe about the second body *T* the same areas as before. However, the force by which the second body *T* was urged will now be destroyed by the force equal and contrary to it; and therefore (by Law 1) that second body *T*, now left to itself, will either rest or move uniformly forward in a straight line: and the first body *L*, under the urging of the difference of the forces—that is, the remaining force—will continue to describe areas proportional to the times about the second body *T*. Therefore (by Theorem 2), the difference of the forces tends toward that second body *T* as a center. *Which was to be demonstrated.* <note>original: "Q. E. D."</note>

*Corollary 1.* Hence, if one body *L*, by a radius drawn to another body *T*, describes areas proportional to the times; and from the total force (whether simple or composed of several forces according to the second corollary of the laws...

[the arcs] described, the <term>versed sines: the distance from the center of an arc to its chord, representing the displacement toward the center caused by a force.</term> are (by Corollary 4, Proposition 1) proportional to the squares of those same arcs divided by the diameters of the circles (by Lemma 7). Therefore, since these arcs are proportional to the arcs described in any equal times, and the diameters are proportional to their radii, the forces will be as the squares of any arcs described simultaneously divided by the radii of the circles. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Corollary 1.* Since those arcs are proportional to the velocities of the bodies, the centripetal forces will be in a ratio compounded of the square of the velocities directly, and the simple ratio of the radii inversely. <note>In modern terms: $F$ is proportional to $v^2/r$.</note>

*Corollary 2.* And, since the periodic times are in a ratio compounded of the ratio of the radii directly and the ratio of the velocities inversely, the centripetal forces are in a ratio compounded of the ratio of the radii directly and the square of the periodic times inversely. <note>In modern terms: $F$ is proportional to $r/T^2$.</note>

*Corollary 3.* Hence, if the periodic times are equal (and therefore the velocities are proportional to the radii), the centripetal forces will also be proportional to the radii; and vice versa.

*Corollary 4.* If both the periodic times and the velocities are in the <term>subduplicate ratio: the ratio of the square roots.</term> of the radii, the centripetal forces will be equal to each other; and vice versa.

*Corollary 5.* If the periodic times are proportional to the radii (and therefore the velocities are equal), the centripetal forces will be inversely proportional to the radii; and vice versa.

*Corollary 6.* If the periodic times are in the <term>sesquiplicate ratio: the ratio of the square roots of the cubes, or the 3/2 power.</term> of the radii (and therefore the velocities are inversely as the square roots of the radii), the centripetal forces will be inversely as the squares of the radii; and vice versa. <note>This specific case is the foundation for Kepler's Third Law of planetary motion.</note>

*Corollary 7.* And universally, if the periodic time is as any power $R^n$ of the radius $R$, and therefore the velocity is inversely as the power $R^{n-1}$ of the radius, the centripetal force will be inversely as the power $R^{2n-1}$ of the radius; and vice versa.

*Corollary 8.* All these same conclusions regarding times, velocities, and forces—by which bodies describe similar parts of any similar figures having centers similarly positioned within those figures—follow from the demonstration of the preceding points when applied to these cases. This is applied by substituting the uniform description of areas for uniform motion, and using the distances of the bodies from the centers instead of radii.

### Scholium

The case of the sixth corollary <note>referring to the rule where force decreases as the square of the distance increases</note> applies to the celestial bodies (as our own countrymen **Wren**, **Hooke**, and **Halley** have also independently concluded), and for that reason, I have decided to explain more extensively in the following pages those matters which relate to a centripetal force decreasing in a <term>duplicate ratio: the square of the ratio, specifically the inverse-square law.</term> of the distances from the centers.

Furthermore, by means of the preceding proposition and its corollaries, we can also determine the proportion of centripetal force to any known force, such as gravity. For if a body revolves in a circle sharing a center with the Earth by the force of its own gravity, this gravity is its very centripetal force. Moreover, from the observed fall of heavy bodies, we are given both the time of one revolution and the arc described in any given time, through the ninth corollary of this proposition. By using propositions of this kind, **Huygens**, in his outstanding treatise *On the Oscillatory Clock* <note>original: *de Horologio Oscillatorio* (1673), a foundational work on the physics of pendulums and circular motion.</note>, compared the force of gravity with the centrifugal forces of revolving bodies.

The preceding points can also be demonstrated in this manner. Let us imagine a polygon with any number of sides described inside a circle. If a body, moving at a given speed along the sides of the polygon, is reflected by the circle at each of its corners, the force with which it strikes the circle at each reflection will be proportional to its velocity. Therefore, the sum of the forces in a given time will be proportional to that velocity multiplied by the number of reflections. That is (if the shape of the polygon is fixed), proportional to the length described in that given time, increased or diminished in the ratio of that same length to the radius of the circle; that is, as the square of that length <term>applied to: an early mathematical term for 'divided by'.</term> the radius. Therefore, if the sides of the polygon are decreased infinitely so that it coincides with the circle, the force will be as the square of the arc described in a given time divided by the radius. This is the **centrifugal force** by which the body presses against the circle; and equal to this is the opposite force by which the circle continually repels the body toward the center <note>the centripetal force</note>.

<summary>Newton connects his mathematical proofs to the "inverse-square law" observed in the heavens, acknowledging colleagues like Hooke and Halley, and provides a geometric demonstration of centrifugal force using polygons.</summary>

## PROPOSITION 5. PROBLEM 1.

*Given the velocity in any number of locations where a body describes a given shape under the influence of forces tending toward a common center, to find that center.*

Let three straight lines *PT, TQV,* and *VR* touch the described shape <note>tangent lines representing the body's instantaneous direction</note> at three points *P, Q,* and *R*, meeting at *T* and *V*. From these tangents, let perpendicular lines *PA, QB,* and *RC* be erected, which are inversely proportional to the velocities of the body at those points *P, Q,* and *R* from which they are erected. That is, let *PA* be to *QB* as the velocity at *Q* is to the velocity at *P*, and let *QB* be to *RC* as the velocity at *R* is to the velocity at *Q*. Through the ends of these perpendiculars, *A, B,* and *C*, let the lines *AD, DBE,* and *EC* be drawn at right angles, meeting at *D* and *E*. Then, the lines *TD* and *VE*, when drawn, will intersect at the required center *S*.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a curved line with three points labeled P, Q, and R. Tangent lines PT, TQV, and VR are drawn at these points, meeting at T and V. Perpendiculars PA, QB, and RC are erected from the tangents. Lines AD, DBE, and EC connect the ends of these perpendiculars, meeting at points D and E. From the intersections of the tangents (T and V), lines are drawn through D and E, converging at a single point labeled S, representing the center of force.</image-desc>

For the perpendiculars dropped from the center *S* to the tangents *PT* and *QT* (by the first corollary of Proposition 1) are inversely proportional to the velocities of the body at points *P* and *Q*; and therefore, by this construction, they are directly proportional to the perpendiculars *AP* and *BQ*—that is, the same as the perpendiculars dropped from point *D* to the tangents. From this, it is easily gathered that points *S, D,* and *T* lie on a single straight line. By a similar argument, points *S, E,* and *V* are also on a single straight line; and therefore, the center *S* is located at the intersection of the straight lines *TD* and *VE*. <note>original: *Q. E. D.* (Quod Erat Demonstrandum) — Which was to be demonstrated.</note>

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. 47 BOOK ONE.

...through the center of forces: the centripetal force in the middle of an arc will be as the *sagitta directly and the square of the time inversely.* <note>The "sagitta" (Latin for "arrow") is the distance between the midpoint of an arc and the midpoint of its chord; Newton uses it here to represent the displacement caused by gravity or a central force.</note>

For the sagitta in a given time is as the force (by corollary 4 of proposition 1); and by increasing the time in any ratio, because the arc increases in the same ratio, the sagitta is increased in the square of that ratio (by corollaries 2 and 3 of lemma 11). Therefore, the sagitta is as the force once and the time twice. Subtract the doubled ratio <note>the square</note> of the time from both sides, and it becomes: the force is as the sagitta directly and the square of the time inversely. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

The same is easily demonstrated also by corollary 4 of lemma 10.

*Corollary* 1. If a body *P*, revolving around a center *S*, describes a curved line *APQ*; and the straight line *ZPR* touches that curve at any point *P*, and from any other point *Q* of the curve, *QR* is drawn parallel to the distance *SP*, and *QT* is dropped perpendicular to that distance *SP*: the centripetal force will be inversely as the solid <note>A "solid" in this context refers to a three-dimensional product of geometric lengths.</note> 
$\frac{SP^2 \times QT^2}{QR}$
; provided that for that solid, the quantity is always taken which it ultimately becomes where the points *P* and *Q* coincide. For *QR* is equal to the sagitta of the double arc *QP*, in the middle of which is *P*; and double the triangle *SQP* (or *SP* x *QT*) is proportional to the time in which that double arc is described; and therefore it can be written as the representative of the time.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a curve APQ. A center point S is located to the bottom left. A tangent line ZPR touches the curve at point P. Point Q lies on the curve further from P. A line QR is drawn from Q parallel to the radius SP. A line QT is dropped from Q perpendicular to SP. Another line SY is drawn from S perpendicular to the tangent at point Y. A line segment PV lies along the radius through S. Dashed lines connect S to P, S to Q, and S to R.</image-desc>

*Corollary* 2. By the same argument, the centripetal force is inversely as the solid 
$\frac{SY^2 \times QP^2}{QR}$
, if *SY* is the perpendicular dropped from the center of forces to the tangent *PR* of the orbit. For the rectangles *SY* x *QP* and *SP* x *QT* are equal. <note>original: "rectangula SY x QP & SP x QT æquantur"</note>

*Corollary* 3. If the orbit is either a circle, or touches a circle concentrically, or cuts it concentrically—that is, contains the smallest possible angle of contact or section with the circle, having the same curvature and the same radius of curvature at point *P*; and if *PV* is the chord of this circle drawn from the body through the center of forces: the centripetal force will be inversely as the solid $SY^2 \times PV$. For *PV* is $\frac{QP^2}{QR}$.

Newton means the velocity squared. The "chord" refers to the chord of the circle of curvature passing through the center of force.</note> For velocity is inversely as the perpendicular $SY$, by corollary 1 of proposition 1.

Corollary 5. Hence, if any curved figure $APQ$ is given, and a point $S$ is also given within it, toward which a centripetal force is perpetually directed, the law of centripetal force can be found, by which any body $P$, drawn back perpetually from a straight-line course, will be kept within the perimeter of that figure and will describe it by revolving. Namely, one must compute either the solid <note>A "solid" in this context is a geometric product of three dimensions, used here as a denominator in the force ratio.</note> $(SP^2 \times QT^2) / QR$ or the solid $SY^2 \times PV$ as being inversely proportional to this force. We shall provide examples of this in the following problems.

->The same thing another way.<-

Let the perpendicular $SY$ be dropped to the tangent $PR$ produced; and because of the similar triangles $SYP$ and $VPA$, $AV$ will be to $PV$ as $SP$ is to $SY$: and therefore $\frac{SP \times PV}{AV}$ is equal to $SY$, and $\frac{SP^2 \times PV^3}{AV^2}$ is equal to $SY^2 \times PV$. And therefore (by corollaries 3 and 5 of proposition 6) the centripetal force is inversely as $\frac{SP^2 \times PV^3}{AV^2}$, that is, because $AV$ is given, inversely as $SP^2 \times PV^3$. *Which was to be found.*

*Corollary* 1. Hence if the given point $S$, toward which the centripetal force always tends, is located on the circumference of this circle, say at $V$; the centripetal force will be inversely as the fifth power <note>original: "quadrato-cubus," literally a "square-cube." In the mathematics of this era, this refers to the fifth power ($x^2 \times x^3 = x^5$).</note> of the height $SP$.

*Corollary* 2. The force by which a body $P$ in the circle $APTV$ revolves around a center of forces $S$ is to the force by which the same body $P$ in the same circle and in the same periodic time could revolve around any other center of forces $R$, as $RP^2 \times SP$ is to the cube of the straight line $SG$, which is drawn from the first center of forces $S$ to the tangent of the orbit $PG$, and is parallel to the distance of the body from the second center of forces. For by the construction of this proposition, the first force is to the second force as $RP^2 \times PT^3$ to $SP^2 \times PV^3$.
