### PROPOSITION VIII. PROBLEM III.

> *Let a body move in a semicircle PQA: for this effect, the law of centripetal force is required tending to a point S so distant that all lines PS, RS drawn to it may be considered parallel.*

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of a semicircle PQA with center C. Point P is on the arc, and a perpendicular PM is dropped to the diameter. A neighboring point Q is also on the arc. Lines PS and RS are shown extending vertically downwards, indicating they are parallel and directed towards an infinitely distant center of force S. A tangent is drawn at P with point Z. Segments QT and RN are marked as part of the geometric proof.</image-desc>

From the center of the semicircle *C*, let the radius <term>semidiameter|The distance from the center of a circle to its edge; a radius.</term> *CA* be drawn, cutting those parallel lines perpendicularly at *M* and *N*, and let *CP* be joined. Because of the similar triangles *CPM*, *PZT*, and *RZQ*, $CP^2$ is to $PM^2$ as $PR^2$ is to $QT^2$; and from the nature of the circle, $PR^2$ is equal to the rectangle <note>In geometry of this period, "the rectangle" refers to the product of two line segments.</note> $QR \times (RN + QN)$, or, as points *P* and *Q* coincide <note>Newton is applying the "method of first and last ratios," an early form of calculus. He imagines point Q moving closer and closer to point P until they essentially overlap.</note>, the rectangle $QR \times 2 PM$. Therefore, $CP^2$ is to $PM^2$ as $QR \times 2 PM$ is to $QT^2$; and therefore $\frac{QT^2}{QR}$ is equal to $\frac{2 PM^3}{CP^2}$, and $\frac{QT^2 \times SP^2}{QR}$ is equal to $\frac{2 PM^3 \times SP^2}{CP^2}$.

### Scholium.
<note>A "Scholium" is an explanatory note or commentary following a proof.</note>

And by a not much dissimilar argument, a body will be found to move in an ellipse, or even in a hyperbola or parabola, by a centripetal force which is inversely as the cube of the ordinate <term>ordinate: a line segment used to define the position of a point on a curve relative to an axis</term> tending toward a very distant center of forces.

### PROPOSITION IX. PROBLEM IV.

Let a body revolve in a spiral *PQS* cutting all the radii *SP, SQ*, etc., at a given angle: the law of centripetal force tending toward the center of the spiral is required.

Let an infinitely small angle *PSQ* be given, and because all the angles are given, the shape of the figure *SPRQT* will be fixed. <note>original: "dabitur specie," meaning the proportions of the shape remain constant even as its size changes.</note> Therefore, the ratio *QT / QR* is fixed, and $\frac{QT^2}{QR}$ is as *QT*, that is (because the shape is fixed) as *SP*.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a spiral curve winding toward a central point S. A radial line SP connects the center to a point P on the spiral. A tangent line is drawn through P. A second nearby point Q is shown on the spiral, with a perpendicular line QT dropped to the radius SP. A line QR represents the displacement from the tangent toward the center, used to calculate the force.</image-desc>

Now let the angle *PSQ* be changed in any way, and the straight line *QR* subtending the angle of contact *QPR* will change (by Lemma 11) in the duplicate ratio <note>"duplicate ratio" is a classical mathematical term for the square of a ratio.</note> of *PR* or *QT*. Therefore, $\frac{QT^2}{QR}$ will remain the same as before, that is, as *SP*. Wherefore $\frac{QT^2 \times SP^2}{QR}$ is as ***the cube of SP*** <note>original: "SP cub."</note> and therefore (by Corollaries 1 and 5 of Proposition 6) the centripetal force is inversely as the cube of the distance *SP*.
***Which was to be found.***

   $2 DC^2$
   --------

*Corollary 1.* The force is therefore proportional to the distance of the body from the center of the ellipse: and conversely, if the force is as the distance, the body will move in an ellipse having its center at the center of forces, or perhaps in a circle, into which an ellipse can certainly transform.

*Corollary 2.* And the periodic times <note>The time taken to complete one full orbit.</note> of revolutions made in all ellipses around the same center will be equal. For those times in similar ellipses are equal (by Corollaries 3 and 8 of Proposition 4); however, in ellipses having a common major axis, the times are to one another directly as the total areas of the ellipses, and inversely as the particles of areas described in the same time; that is, directly as the minor axes, and inversely as the velocities of the bodies at the principal vertices; that is, as those minor axes...

### Scholium.

If the center of an ellipse recedes to infinity, the ellipse turns into a parabola, and a body will move in this parabola; the force now tending toward a center infinitely distant will become uniform. This is the theorem of *Galileo*. <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642). Newton is acknowledging that Galileo’s discovery of constant gravity for terrestrial projectiles is a "limit case" of his own orbital laws.</note> And if a parabolic conic section (by changing the inclination of the plane cutting the cone) is turned into a hyperbola, the body will move on the perimeter of this hyperbola with the centripetal force turned into a centrifugal <note>Latin: "centrifuga," literally "fleeing the center."</note> force. And just as in a circle or an ellipse, if the forces tend toward the center of the figure located on the abscissa <note>The horizontal coordinate (x-axis) along which the figure is centered.</note>; these forces—by increasing or decreasing the ordinates in any given ratio, or even by changing the angle of inclination of the ordinates to the abscissa—are always increased or decreased in the ratio of the distances from the center, provided that the periodic times remain equal; so also in all figures, if the ordinates are increased or decreased in any given ratio, or if the angle of the ordinates is changed in any way, while the periodic time remains the same, the forces tending toward any center located on the abscissa are increased or decreased in the ratio of the distances from the center in each ordinate.

## PROPOSITION XII. PROBLEM VII.

### *A body is moved in a hyperbola: the law of centripetal force tending toward the focus of the figure is required.*

Let $CA$ and $CB$ be the semi-axes of the hyperbola; $PG$ and $KD$ other conjugate diameters; $PF$ the perpendicular to diameter $KD$; and $Qv$ an <term>ordinate<gloss>A line segment drawn from a point on the curve to a diameter, parallel to the tangent at the vertex of that diameter.</gloss></term> applied to the diameter $GP$. It is evident that $EP$ is equal to the transverse semi-axis $AC$, because, a line $HI$ being drawn from the other focus $H$ of the hyperbola parallel to $EC$, then on account of the equals $CS$ and $CH$, the lines $ES$ and $EI$ are equal; so that $EP$ is the half-difference of $PS$ and $PI$, which is to say (on account of the parallel lines $IH$ and $PR$ and the equal angles $IPR$ and $HPZ$ <note>These equal angles are a fundamental property of the tangent to a hyperbola relative to the foci.</note>) it is the half-difference of $PS$ and $PH$, the difference of which equals the entire axis $2 AC$. Let the perpendicular $QT$ be dropped to $SP$. And with the principal <term>latus rectum<gloss>Literally "straight side." A constant chord of a conic section through the focus, used here as a proportionality constant.</gloss></term> (or $\frac{2 BC^2}{AC}$) called $L$, then $L \times QR$ will be to $L \times Pv$ as $QR$ is to $Pv$, or $Px$ to $Pv$, that is (on account of the similar triangles $Pxv$ and $PEC$) as $PE$ is to $PC$, or $AC$ to $PC$. There will also be $L \times Pv$ to $Gv \times Pv$ as $L$ to $Gv$; and (from the nature of conic sections) the rectangle $GvP$ to $Qv^2$ as $PC^2$ to $CD^2$; and (by corollary 2 of lemma VII) as the points $Q$ and $P$ coincide, the ratio of $Qv^2$ to $Qx^2$ becomes equality; and $Qx^2$ or $Qv^2$ is to $QT^2$ as $EP^2$ to $PF^2$, that is, as $CA^2$ to $PF^2$, or (by lemma XII) as $CD^2$ to $CB^2$: and by joining all these ratios together, $L \times QR$ is to $QT^2$ as $AC \times L \times PC^2 \times CD^2$, or $2 CB^2 \times PC^2 \times CD^2$ to $PC \times Gv \times CD^2 \times CB^2$, or as $2 PC$ to $Gv$. ## LEMMA XIII.

*The <term>latus rectum<gloss>Literally "the right side"; a line segment through the focus, perpendicular to the axis, that defines the "width" of the parabola.</gloss></term> of a parabola belonging to any vertex is four times the distance of that vertex from the <term>focus<gloss>A fixed point used to define the curve's shape; Newton uses the Latin "umbilicus" (navel).</gloss></term> of the figure. This is evident from the study of conic sections.*

## LEMMA XIV.

*The perpendicular line dropped from the focus of a parabola to its tangent is a <term>mean proportional<gloss>In a sequence of three numbers, the middle term when the ratio of the first to the second is the same as the second to the third.</gloss></term> between the distances of the focus from the point of contact and from the principal vertex of the figure.*

### Corollary 1.
From the three most recent propositions, it follows that if any body *P* departs from place *P* along any straight line *PR* with any velocity, and is simultaneously acted upon by a centripetal force that is inversely proportional to the square of the distance of the places from the center, this body will move in one of the conic sections having a <term>focus</term><note>original: "umbilicum"; literally "navel," the geometric center-point of a conic section.</note> at the center of forces; and vice versa. For given the focus, the point of contact, and the position of the tangent, a conic section can be described which will have a given curvature at that point. Moreover, the curvature is given from the given centripetal force and the velocity of the body: and two orbits touching each other cannot be described with the same centripetal force and the same velocity.

### PROPOSITION XIV. THEOREM VI.
*If several bodies revolve around a common center, and the centripetal force is inversely as the square of the distance of the places from the center; I say that the principal latera recta of the orbits are in the duplicate ratio <note>The square of the ratio.</note> of the areas which the bodies describe in the same time by radii drawn to the center.*

For (by Corollary 2, Proposition XIII) the *latus rectum* *L* is equal to the quantity *2Tq / 2R*, which it ultimately becomes where the points *P* and *Q* coincide. But the smallest line *QR* in a given time is as the generating centripetal force, that is (by hypothesis) inversely as *SP²* <note>original: "SPq", where q stands for quadratum or squared.</note>.
Therefore *2Tq / 2R* is as *2Tq x SP²*, that is, the *latus rectum* *L* is in the duplicate ratio of the area *2T x SP*. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

For the total area is as the area *2T x SP*, which is described in a given time, multiplied by the periodic time.

*Corollary 2.* The velocities of bodies, at their greatest and least distances from the common focus <note>original: "umbilico"; literally "navel," the term used in geometry for the focus of an ellipse or parabola</note>, are in a ratio compounded of the inverse ratio of the distances and the direct square root ratio <note>original: "subduplicata ratione"; the ratio of the square roots</note> of the principal latus recta <note>term: latus rectum (plural: latera recta). The "upright side," a chord passing through the focus of a conic section perpendicular to its major axis, used to define its width.</note>. For at these points, the perpendiculars are the distances themselves.

*Corollary 3.* And therefore the velocity in a conic section, at the greatest or least distance from the focus, is to the velocity in a circle at the same distance from the center in the square root ratio of the principal latus rectum to twice that distance.

*Corollary 4.* The velocities of bodies revolving in ellipses at their mean distances <note>The distance equal to the semi-major axis</note> from the common focus are the same as the velocities of bodies revolving in circles at those same distances; that is (by Corollary 6, Proposition 15) inversely in the square root ratio of the distances. For the perpendiculars are now the semi-minor axes, and these are as the mean proportionals between the distances and the latera recta. Combine this ratio inversely with the direct square root ratio of the latera recta, and it becomes the inverse square root ratio of the distances.

*Corollary 5.* In the same figure, or even in different figures whose principal latera recta are equal, the velocity of a body is inversely as the perpendicular dropped from the focus to the tangent line.

*Corollary 6.* In a parabola, the velocity is inversely in the square root ratio of the distance of the body from the focus of the figure; in an ellipse it varies more, and in a hyperbola less than in this ratio. For (by Corollary 2, Lemma 14) the perpendicular dropped from the focus to the tangent of a parabola is in the square root ratio of the distance. In a hyperbola the perpendicular varies less, and in an ellipse more.

*Corollary 7.* In a parabola, the velocity of a body at any distance from the focus is to the velocity of a body revolving in a circle at the same distance from the center in the square root ratio of the number two to one <note>The ratio of $\sqrt{2}:1$</note>; in an ellipse it is less, and in a hyperbola greater than this ratio. For by the second corollary of this section, the velocity at the vertex of a parabola is in this ratio, and by the sixth corollaries of this and the fourth proposition, the same proportion is preserved at all distances. Hence also in a parabola the velocity is everywhere equal to the velocity of a body revolving in a circle at half the distance; in an ellipse it is less, and in a hyperbola greater.

*Corollary 8.* The velocity of a body revolving in any conic section is to the velocity of a body revolving in a circle at a distance of half the principal latus rectum...

### PROPOSITION XVII. PROBLEM IX.
*Assuming that the centripetal force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance of places from the center, and that the absolute quantity of that force is known; it is required to find the line which a body describes, starting from a given place with a given velocity along a given straight line.*

Let the angle *RPH* be made equal to the two right angles <note>original: "duos rectos"; this refers to the supplementary angle of the tangent</note>; and the line *PH* will be given in position, in which the other focus *H* is located. Having dropped the perpendicular *SK* to *PH*, let the semi-conjugate axis *BC* <term>semi-conjugate axis: the shorter radius of an ellipse, perpendicular to the main axis</term> be understood to be raised, and it will be:
*SP² - 2KPH + PH² = SH² = 4CH² = 4BH² - 4BC² = (SP + PH)² - L × (SP + PH) = SP² + 2SPH + PH² - L × (SP + PH)*.
Add to both sides *2KPH - SP² - PH² + L × (SP + PH)*, and it becomes *L × (SP + PH) = 2SPH + 2KPH*, or *SP + PH* is to *PH* as *2SP + 2KP* is to *L* <note>L represents the latus rectum, a constant characterizing the width of the curve at the focus</note>. From this, *PH* is given both in length and in position.

Indeed, if the velocity of the body at *P* is such that the latus rectum *L* is less than *2SP + 2KP*, then *PH* will lie on the same side of the tangent *PR* as the line *PS*; and therefore the figure will be an **ellipse**, and it will be given from the known foci *S, H*, and the principal axis *SP + PH* <note>The text reads AH, likely a typo for PH or the major axis length</note>. But if the velocity of the body is so great that the latus rectum *L* is equal to *2SP + 2KP*, the length *PH* will be infinite; and therefore the figure will be a **parabola** having its axis *SH* parallel to the line *PK*, and it will be given from there.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a point P on a curve with a tangent line PR. A central axis contains points S (the sun or primary focus), C (center), and H (secondary focus). Various lines connect these points to P and to each other, forming the triangles used in the geometric proof. A perpendicular line SK meets the line PH.</image-desc>

But if the body departs from its place *P* with an even greater velocity, the length *PH* must be taken on the other side of the tangent; and therefore, with the tangent passing between the foci, the figure will be a **hyperbola** having a principal axis equal to the difference of the lines *SP* and *PH*, and it will be given from there. For if a body in these cases revolves in a conic section so discovered, it has been demonstrated in Propositions 11, 12, and 13 that the centripetal force will be inversely as the square of the distance of the body from the center of forces *S*; and therefore the line *PQ* is correctly shown, which a body will describe by such a force, departing from a given place *P*, with a given velocity, according to the line *PR* given in position. **Which was to be done.** <note>original: "Q. E. F." (Quod erat faciendum)</note>

**Corollary I.** Hence, in every conic section, from a given principal vertex *D*, latus rectum *L*, and focus *S*, the other focus *H* is given by taking *DH* to *DS* as the latus rectum is to the difference between the latus rectum and *4DS*. For the proportion of *SP + PH* to *PH* as *2SP + 2KP* to *L*...

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

In the case of this corollary, let *DS* + *DH* be to *DH* as 4 *DS* is to *L*, and by division <note>A geometric method of ratio manipulation</note> *DS* is to *DH* as 4 *DS* - *L* is to *L*.

### Corollary 2.
Hence, if the velocity of a body is given at the principal vertex *D*, the orbit will be found expeditiously; namely, by taking its *latus rectum* <note>The "straight side"—a chord passing through the focus of a conic section, perpendicular to its major axis</note> to be to twice the distance *DS* in the duplicate ratio <note>The ratio of the squares</note> of this given velocity to the velocity of a body revolving in a circle at the distance *DS* (by Corollary 3, Proposition 16); then *DH* is to *DS* as the *latus rectum* is to the difference between the *latus rectum* and 4 *DS*.

### Corollary 3.
From this, if a body is moving in any conic section and is driven out of its orbit by any impulse, the orbit can be known in which it thereafter completes its course. For by combining the body's own motion with that motion which the impulse alone would generate, the motion will be obtained with which the body will depart from the given location of the impulse, along a straight line given in position.

### Corollary 4.
And if that body is continuously disturbed by some force impressed from without, its course will be known very nearly, by collecting the changes which that force induces at certain points, and by estimating the continuous changes in the intermediate places from the analogy of the series.

->Scholium.<-
<note>A "Scholium" is an explanatory note or remark added to a text to clarify a point of theory.</note>

If a body *P* moves by a centripetal force <note>original: "vi centripeta" — a force directed toward a center</note> tending toward any given point *R* in the perimeter of any given conic section whose center is *C*; and the law of centripetal force is required: let *CG* be drawn parallel to the radius *RP*, and meeting the tangent of the orbit *PG* at *G*; and that force (by Corollary 1 and the Scholium of Proposition 10, and Corollary 3, Proposition 7) will be as $\frac{CG^{3}}{RP^{2}}$ <note>The cube of CG divided by the square of RP</note>.

## SECTION IV.
### *On the finding of elliptical, parabolic, and hyperbolic orbits from a given focus.* <note>original: "umbilico". In this context, Newton uses the term "umbilicus" (navel) to refer to the focus of a conic section.</note>

### LEMMA XV.
*If from the two foci S and H of any ellipse or hyperbola, two straight lines SV and HV are bent toward any third point V, of which one line HV is equal to the principal axis of the figure (that is, the axis on which the foci lie), and the other line SV is bisected at T by a perpendicular TR let down upon it; that perpendicular TR will touch the conic section somewhere: and conversely, if it touches the section, HV will be equal to the principal axis of the figure.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a triangle SVH. A line TR is drawn from T on SV, perpendicular to SV, and extending to R. R is also on HV. Another line SR is drawn. The points are labeled S, V, H, T, R.</image-desc>

For let the perpendicular TR cut the straight line HV (produced, if necessary) at R; and let SR be joined. Because TS and TV are equal, the straight lines SR and VR will also be equal, as will the angles TRS and TRV. From this, point R will be on the conic section, and the perpendicular TR will touch the same: and conversely. Which was to be demonstrated.

## PROPOSITION XIX. PROBLEM XI.

*To describe a parabolic trajectory about a given focus, which shall pass through given points and touch straight lines given in position.*

Let *S* be the focus, *P* a point, and *TR* a tangent of the trajectory to be described. With center *P* and distance *PS*, describe a circle *FG*. From the focus to the tangent, let fall the perpendicular *ST*, and extend it to *V*, so that *TV* is equal to *ST*. In the same way, another circle *fg* is to be described if another point *p* is given; or another point *v* is to be found if another tangent *tr* is given; then a straight line *IF* is to be drawn which touches the two circles *FG, fg* if two points *P, p* are given, or passes through two points *V, v* if two tangents *TR, tr* are given, or touches the circle *FG* and passes through the point *V* if a point *P* and tangent *TR* are given. To *FI* let fall the perpendicular *SI*, and bisect it at *K*; and with the axis *SK* and the principal vertex *K*, let the parabola be described. I say the task is done. For the parabola—on account of the equal lengths *SK* and *IK*, and *SP* and *FP*—will pass through the point *P*; and (by the 3rd corollary of the 14th lemma) on account of the equal lengths *ST* and *TV* and the right angle *STR*, it will touch the line *TR*. Which was to be done.

## PROPOSITION XX. PROBLEM XII.

*To describe a trajectory of a given kind about a given focus, which shall pass through given points and touch straight lines given in position.*

Case 1. Given the focus S, let a trajectory ABC be described passing through two points B and C. Since the trajectory is given in kind <note>original: "specie datam"; this means the shape or eccentricity of the curve (ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola) is already known</note>, the ratio of the principal axis to the distance between the foci will be given. In that ratio, take the distance KB relative to BS, and LC relative to CS. With centers B and C, and intervals BK and CL, describe two circles; and upon the straight line KL, which touches these same circles at K and L, let fall the perpendicular SG. Divide this perpendicular at points A and a, such that the ratio of GA to AS and Ga to aS is the same as the ratio of KB to BS. Then, with the axis Aa and vertices A and a, let the trajectory be described. I say the task is done.

For let H be the other focus of the described figure. Since the ratio of GA to AS is the same as Ga to aS, it will follow by division <note>a geometric method of comparing ratios</note> that the ratio of GA minus Ga (or the axis Aa) to aS minus AS (or the distance between the foci SH) is in that same ratio. Therefore, it is in the ratio which the principal axis of the figure to be described has to the distance between its foci.

The point *Z* will be located on a hyperbola whose foci <note>original: "umbilici"</note> are *A* and *B*, and whose principal axis is that given difference. Let that axis be *MN*. Where the trajectory is a hyperbola, I do not include the opposite hyperbola under the name of this trajectory. For a body, by proceeding in its motion, cannot pass over into the opposite hyperbola.

Therefore, the points *B, C, D* lie in a conic section described around the focus <note>original: "umbilicum"</note> *S* in such a way that all straight lines drawn from the focus *S* to the individual points of the section are in that same given ratio to the perpendiculars dropped from those same points to the straight line *GF*.
The most renowned geometer De la Hire <note>Philippe de La Hire (1640–1718), a French mathematician famous for his work on conic sections</note> provides a solution to this problem by a method not much different in his *Conics*, Book VIII, Proposition XXV.

### S E C T I O N V.
->*The discovery of orbits where neither focus is given.*<-

### LEMMA XVII.
If from any point *P* of a given <term>conic section</term> <note>A curve obtained by intersecting a cone with a plane, such as a circle, ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola</note> four straight lines *PQ, PR, PS, PT* are drawn at given angles to the four infinitely extended sides *AB, CD, AC, DB* of any quadrilateral <note>original: "trapezii"</note> inscribed in that conic section, each line to each side: the <term>rectangle</term> <note>In this context, the product of the lengths of the lines</note> of those drawn to two opposite sides, *PQ* × *PR*, will be in a given ratio to the <term>rectangle</term> of those drawn to the other two opposite sides, *PS* × *PT*.

Case I. Let us first suppose that the lines drawn to the opposite sides are parallel to one or the other of the remaining sides, for instance, *PQ* and *PR* to side *AC*, and *PS* and *PT* to side *AB*. Furthermore, let two of the opposite sides, for instance *AC* and *BD*, be parallel to each other. Then the straight line which bisects those parallel sides will be one of the <term>diameters</term> <note>A line passing through the center of a conic section that bisects all chords parallel to a specific direction</note> of the conic section, and it will also bisect *RQ*. Let *O* be the point in which *RQ* is bisected, and *PO* will be an <term>ordinate</term> <note>original: "ordinatim applicata"; a line segment from a point on the curve to a diameter, parallel to the tangent at the diameter's endpoint</note> to that diameter. Extend *PO* to *K*, so that *OK* is equal to *PO*, and *OK* will be an ordinate to the opposite side of the diameter. Since, therefore, the points *A, B, P*, and *K* are on the conic section, and *PK* cuts *AB* at a given angle, it will be (by Propositions 17, 19, 21, and 23 of Book III of the Conics... <note>Referring to Apollonius of Perga’s "Conics," the foundational Greek text on the subject</note>

### Case 2.
Let us now suppose that the opposite sides of the trapezium *A C* and *B D* are not parallel. Draw *B d* parallel to *A C* and meeting both the straight line *S T* at *t*, and the conic section at *d*. Join *C d* cutting *P Q* at *r*, and draw *D M* parallel to *P Q* itself, cutting *C d* at *M* and *A B* at *N*. Now, on account of the similar triangles *B T t* and *D B N*; *B t* (or *P Q*) is to *T t* as *D N* is to *N B*. So also *R r* is to *A Q* (or *P S*) as *D M* is to *A N*. Therefore, by multiplying the <term>antecedents</term><note>The first terms in a mathematical ratio.</note> by the antecedents and the <term>consequents</term><note>The second terms in a mathematical ratio.</note> by the consequents, as the rectangle *P Q* by *R r* is to the rectangle *P S* by *T t*, so the rectangle *N D M* is to the rectangle *A N B*, and (by Case 1) so the rectangle *P Q* by *P r* is to the rectangle *P S* by *P t*, and by division so the rectangle *P Q x P R* is to the rectangle *P S x P T*. Which was to be demonstrated.

### Case 3.

## LEMMA XVIII.

*The same things being supposed <note>Referring to the conditions established in the previous Lemma XVII regarding lines drawn at given angles to the sides of a quadrilateral</note>, if the rectangle of the lines drawn to two opposite sides of a trapezium <note>term: trapezium (a quadrilateral or four-sided shape)</note> PQ × PR is to the rectangle of the lines drawn to the other two sides PS × PT in a given ratio; the point P, from which the lines are drawn, will touch a conic section described around the trapezium.*

Through points A, B, C, D and any one of the infinite points P, let us say p, conceive a conic section to be described: I say that the point P always touches this. If you deny this, join AP cutting this conic section elsewhere than in P, if possible, say in b. Therefore, if from these points P and b there are drawn at given angles to the sides of the trapezium the straight lines *pq, pr, ps, pt* and *bk, bn, bf, bd*; it will be as *bk × bn* is to *bf × bd* so (by Lemma XVII) *pq × pr* is to *ps × pt*, and so (by hypothesis) *PQ × PR* is to *PS × PT*. Also, on account of the similarity of the trapeziums *bkAf* and *PQAS*, as *bk* is to *bf* so *PQ* is to *PS*. Wherefore, by dividing the terms of the former proportion by the corresponding terms of this one, *bn* will be to *bd* as *PR* is to *PT*. Therefore the equiangular trapeziums *Dnbd* and *DRPT* are similar, and their diagonals *Db* and *DP* therefore coincide. Thus *b* falls upon the intersection of the straight lines *AP* and *DP* and therefore coincides with point *P*. Wherefore the point *P*, wherever it is taken, falls on the assigned conic section. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

From these points, various lines are drawn to the vertices of the quadrilateral and to points on its sides. Key points labeled include A, B, C, D, P, p, R, S, T, f, g, k, n, r, s, t, d, b. The lines form several triangles and quadrilaterals, demonstrating the relationships described in the text.</image-desc>

->*Scholium* <note>original: "Scholium" — an explanatory note or commentary following a proof.</note><-

The name "conic section" is used broadly in this lemma, so that it includes both a rectilinear section passing through the vertex of the cone and a circular section parallel to the base. For if the point *p* falls upon the straight line by which points *A* and *D* or *C* and *B* are joined, the conic section will turn into two straight lines, one of which is that line upon which point *p* falls, and the other is the line by which the other two of the four points are joined. If two opposite angles of a trapezium <note>A four-sided plane figure with no sides parallel; in modern geometry, this often refers to a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides.</note> added together equal two right angles, and the four lines *PQ, PR, PS, PT* are drawn to its sides either perpendicularly or at any equal angles, and the rectangle formed by the two drawn lines *PQ x PR* is equal to the rectangle formed by the other two *PS x PT*, the conic section will become a circle. The same will happen if the four lines are drawn at any angles, and the rectangle of the two drawn lines *PQ x PR* is to the rectangle of the other two *PS x PT* as the rectangle of the sines of the angles *S* and *T* (in which the last two *PS* and *PT* are drawn) is to the rectangle of the sines of the angles *Q* and *R* (in which the first two *PQ* and *PR* are drawn). In all other cases, the locus <note>The set of all points whose coordinates satisfy a given equation or condition.</note> of point *P* will be one of the three figures commonly called conic sections <note>The ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.</note>. Moreover, in place of the trapezium *ABCD*, a quadrilateral can be substituted whose two opposite sides cross each other like diagonals. But also, one or two of the four points *A, B, C, D* can recede to infinity, and in that way the sides of the figure which converge at those points become parallel: in which case the conic section will pass through the remaining points and extend to infinity in the direction of the parallel lines.

### LEMMA XIX.

*To find a point P, from which if four straight lines PQ, PR, PS, PT are drawn to as many other lines given in position AB, CD, AC, BD, each to each, at given angles, the rectangle contained by two of the lines, PQ x PR, shall be to the rectangle contained by the other two, PS x PT, in a given ratio.*

<note>This problem is a variation of the "Pappus's hexagon theorem" or the "problem of four lines," which was a foundational challenge in classical geometry. Newton uses it here to establish the properties of curves.</note>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating Lemma XIX. It shows a quadrilateral ABCD. From an internal point P, lines PQ, PR, PS, PT are drawn to the sides AB, CD, AC, BD respectively. Additional construction lines are present: a line from C to F, a line from A to H, a line from D to E, and a line from B to F. Points E, F, H, I, R are marked at various intersections. The overall shape suggests a complex geometric construction involving ratios of areas.</image-desc>

Let the lines *AB, CD*, to which the two lines *PQ, PR* containing one of the rectangles are drawn, meet with the other two lines given in position at points *A, B, C, D*. From any one of them, *A*, draw any straight line *AH*, in which you wish the point *P* to be found. Let it cut the opposite lines *BD, CD*, namely *BD* in *H* and *CD* in *I*; and because all the angles of the figure are given, the ratios of *PQ* to *PA* and *PA* to *PS* will be given, and therefore the ratio of *PQ* to *PS*. By taking this away from the given ratio of *PQ x PR* to *PS x PT*, the ratio of *PR* to *PT* will be given; and by adding the given ratios of *PI* to *PR*, and *PT* to *PH*, the ratio of *PI* to *PH* will be given, and therefore the point *P*. <term>Q. E. I.</term> <note>original: "Quod Erat Inveniendum" — Which was to be found.</note>

Corollary 1. From this, a tangent can also be drawn to any point *D* of the locus of infinite points *P*. For the chord *PD*, where the points *P* and *D* coincide—that is, where *AH* is drawn through point *D*—becomes a tangent. In that case, the ultimate ratio of the vanishing lines *IP* and *PH* will be found as above. Therefore, draw *CF* parallel to *AD*, meeting *BD* in *F*, and cut in that ultimate ratio at *E*; and *DE* will be the tangent, because *CF* and the vanishing line *IH* are parallel, and are similarly cut at *E* and *P*.

Corollary 2. From this, the locus of all points *P* can also be defined. Through any of the points *A, B, C, D*, for instance *A*, draw the tangent *AE* of the locus, and through any other point *B* draw *BF* parallel to the tangent, meeting

### LEMMA XX.

If any parallelogram ASPQ touches any conic section at two opposite angles A and P at points A and P; and the sides of one of those angles, AQ and AS, being infinitely produced, meet the same conic section at B and C; and from the points of meeting B and C to any fifth point D of the conic section two straight lines BD and CD are drawn, meeting the other two infinitely produced sides of the parallelogram PS and PQ at T and R: the abscissas <note>term: abscissas (the segments cut off on the sides of the parallelogram)</note> of the sides PR and PT will always be to each other in a given ratio. And conversely, if those abscissa parts are to each other in a given ratio, the point D will touch a conic section passing through the four points A, B, C, and P.

## LEMMA XXI.

*If two mobile and infinite lines BM and CM, drawn through given points B and C as poles, describe by their intersection M a third line MN given in position; and two other infinite lines BD and CD are drawn through those given points B and C, forming given angles MBD and MCD with the first two lines: I say that these two lines BD and CD will, by their intersection D, describe a conic section passing through the points B and C. And conversely, if the lines BD and CD by their intersection D describe a conic section passing through the given points B, C, and A, and the angle DBM is always equal to the given angle ABC, and the angle DCM is always equal to the given angle ACB: the point M will touch a line given in position.*

For let the point N be given on the line MN, and where the mobile point M falls upon the fixed point N, let the mobile point D fall upon the fixed point P.

## PROPOSITION XXIV. PROBLEM XVI.
*To describe a trajectory <note>In this context, a trajectory refers to a conic section, such as an ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola, representing the path of a body.</note> which shall pass through three given points, and shall touch two straight lines given in position.*

Let the tangents *HI, KL* and the points *B, C, D* be given. Through any two of the points, *B, D*, draw the infinite line *BD* meeting the tangents in points *H* and *K*. Then also through any other two points, *C, D*, draw the infinite line *CD* meeting the tangents in points *I* and *L*. Cut the lines thus drawn in *R* and *S*, such that *HR* is to *KR* as the mean proportional <note>The mean proportional between two numbers $a$ and $b$ is the square root of their product ($\sqrt{ab}$).</note> between *BH* and *HD* is to the mean proportional between *BK* and *KD*; and *IS* is to *LS* as the mean proportional between *CI* and *ID* is to the mean proportional between *CL* and *LD*. Moreover, perform this cutting at your pleasure either between the points *K* and *H*, *I* and *L*, or outside of them; then draw *RS* cutting the tangents in *A* and *P*, and *A* and *P* will be the points of contact. For if *A* and *P* are assumed to be the points of contact located anywhere on the tangents; and through any of the points *H, I, K, L*—say *I*—located on either tangent *HI*, a straight line *IT* is drawn parallel to the other tangent *KL*, which meets the curve in *X* and *Y*, and on it is taken *IZ* as the mean proportional between *IX* and *IY*: then, from the properties of conics, the rectangle <note>In geometric language, "the rectangle" refers to the product of two line segments.</note> *XIY* or *IZ* squared is to *LP* squared as the rectangle *CID* is to the rectangle *CLD*, that is (by construction) as *SI* squared is to *SL* squared; and therefore *IZ* is to *LP* as *SI* is to *SL*. Therefore the points *S, P, Z* lie in one straight line. Furthermore, with the tangents meeting at *G*, it will be (from the properties of conics) that the rectangle *XIY* or *IZ* squared is to *IA* squared as *GP* squared is to *GA* squared, and therefore *IZ* is to *IA* as *GP* is to *GA*. Therefore the points *P, Z* and *A* lie in one straight line, and therefore the points *S, P* and *A* are in one straight line. And by the same argument it will be proved that the points *R, P* and *A* are in one straight line. Therefore the points of contact *A* and *P* lie on the line *RS*. These being found, the trajectory may be described as in the first case of the preceding problem.

### LEMMA XXII.
*To transform figures into other figures of the same kind.*

Suppose any figure *HGI* is to be transformed. Let there be drawn at will two parallel straight lines *AO* and *BL* cutting a third line *AB*, given in position, at points *A* and *B*. From any point *G* of the figure, let there be drawn any line *GD* to the line *AB*, parallel to *OA*. Then, from some point *O* given on the line *OA*, let a straight line *OD* be drawn to the point *D*, meeting the line *BL* at *d*. From that point of meeting, let a straight line *dg* be erected, containing any given angle with the line *BL*, and having the same ratio to *Od* as *DG* has to *OD*; then *g* will be the point in the new figure *hgi* corresponding to point *G*. By the same reasoning, the individual points of the first figure will give as many points of the new figure. Conceive, therefore, the point *G* to run through all points of the first figure in a continuous motion, and the point *g* will likewise run through all points of the new figure in a continuous motion and describe the same. For the sake of distinction, let us call *DG* the first <term>ordinate</term><note>In geometry, an ordinate is a coordinate representing the vertical distance from a point to a horizontal axis.</note>, and *dg* the new ordinate; *AD* the first <term>abscissa</term><note>The horizontal coordinate representing the distance along the axis.</note>, and *ad* the new abscissa; *O* the pole, *OD* the cutting radius, *OA* the first ordinate radius, and *Oa* (by which the parallelogram *OABa* is completed) the new ordinate radius.

<note>The following diagram illustrates Newton's method for "stretching" or "projecting" one geometric shape into another while maintaining its fundamental algebraic degree.</note>

I say now that if the point *G* touches a straight line given in position, the point *g* will also touch a straight line given in position. If the point *G* touches a conic section, the point *g* will also touch a conic section. Here I include the circle among the conic sections. Furthermore...

<margin>ON THE MOTION OF BODIES</margin> Therefore, if point G touches a line of the third analytical order <note>In modern terms, a cubic curve or a polynomial of degree three.</note>, point g will likewise touch a line of the third order; and so it is for curved lines of higher orders. Two lines will always be of the same analytical order if they are touched by points G and g. For as *ad* is to *OA*, so are *Od* to *OD*, *dg* to *DG*, and *AB* to *AD*; and therefore *AD* is equal to $\frac{OA \times AB}{ad}$ and *DG* is equal to $\frac{OA \times dg}{ad}$. Now, if point G touches a straight line, and therefore in any equation by which the relation between the abscissa <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate, usually denoted as x</term> *AD* and the ordinate <term>ordinate: the vertical coordinate, usually denoted as y</term> *DG* is maintained, those unknowns *AD* and *DG* rise to only a single dimension <note>i.e., a first-degree or linear equation</note>; by writing $\frac{OA \times AB}{ad}$ for *AD* and $\frac{OA \times dg}{ad}$ for *DG* in this equation, a new equation will be produced, in which the new abscissa *ad* and the new ordinate *dg* will rise to only a single dimension, and therefore it designates a straight line. But if *AD* and *DG*, or either one of them, rose to two dimensions in the first equation, *ad* and *dg* likewise rise to two in the second equation. And so it is for three or more dimensions. The unknowns *ad*, *dg* in the second equation, and *AD*, *DG* in the first, always rise to the same number of dimensions, and for that reason the lines which points G and g touch are of the same analytical order.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating a coordinate transformation. An origin O is shown. A horizontal line extends to the right with points A, B, D, I. From d, a vertical line extends upwards to g. From O, a line extends upwards and to the right, passing through H and L. Dotted lines connect O to G, O to g, O to d, O to D, and b to d. The diagram shows two sets of coordinates (AD, DG) and (ad, dg) related by a transformation.</image-desc>

I say further, that if any straight line touches a curved line in the first figure; this straight line, transferred in the same manner with the curve into the new figure, will touch that curved line in the new figure; and vice versa. For if any two points of a curve approach each other and join together in the first figure, the same transferred points will approach each other and join in the new figure; and therefore the straight lines by which these points are joined will simultaneously become tangents of the curves in both figures.

Demonstrations of these assertions could be composed in a more geometric manner. But I consult brevity <note>original: "brevitati consulo" — a common phrase used by Newton to indicate he is skipping a lengthy proof for the sake of conciseness.</note>.

<header>MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.</header>

*Therefore, if a rectilinear figure <note>A shape made of straight lines, like a polygon.</note> is to be transformed into another, it is sufficient to transfer the intersections of the straight lines of which it is composed, and to draw straight lines through those same points in the new figure. But if it is necessary to transform a curvilinear figure, one must transfer the points, tangents, and other straight lines by which the curved line is defined. Moreover, this lemma <note>A preliminary proposition used to prove a later theorem.</note> serves the solution of more difficult problems by transforming the proposed figures into simpler ones. For any converging straight lines are transformed into parallels by using, as the first ordinate radius <note>A reference line used in the transformation process.</note>, any straight line that passes through the meeting point of the converging lines; and this is because that meeting point, by this method, recedes to infinity; and parallel lines are those which never meet. After the problem is solved in the new figure, if this figure is transformed back into the original figure by inverse operations, the desired solution will be obtained.*

*This lemma is also useful in the solution of solid problems <note>Problems involving conic sections like parabolas or hyperbolas.</note>. For whenever two conic sections occur whose intersection can solve the problem, one may transform either of them—if it be a hyperbola or a parabola—into an ellipse; then an ellipse is easily changed into a circle. Likewise, a straight line and a conic section, in the construction of plane problems, are turned into a straight line and a circle.*

For, from the properties of conics, the square of *h c* to the rectangle *a h b*, and the square of *i c* to the square of *i d*, and the square of *k e* to the square of *k d*, and the square of *e l* to the rectangle *a l b* are in the same ratio; and therefore *h c* to the square root of *a h b*, *i c* to *i d*, *k e* to *k d*, and *e l* to the square root of *a l b* are in that subduplicate ratio <note>The square root of the ratio</note>, and by composition, in the given ratio of all the antecedents *h i* and *k l* to all the consequents, which are the square root of the rectangle *a h b*, the line *i k*, and the square root of the rectangle *a l b*. Therefore, from that given ratio, the points of contact *c, d, e* are obtained in the new figure. By the inverse operations of the most recent lemma, let these points be transferred into the first figure, and there (by Problem 14) the trajectory will be described. Which was to be done. <note>Q.E.F. - Quod erat faciendum</note> Furthermore, according as the points *a, b* lie either between the points *h, l* or outside them, the points *c, d, e* must be taken either between the points *h, i, k, l* or outside. If either one of the points *a, b* falls between points *h, l* and the other falls outside, the problem is impossible.

Furthermore, let these segments be described on those sides of the lines *DE, DF, EF* so that the letters *DRED* follow the same circular order as the letters *BACB*, the letters *DGFD* the same as *ABCA*, and the letters *EMFE* the same as *ACBA*; then let these segments be completed into full circles. And now the figure *ABC* may be constructed similar and equal to the figure *abc DEF*. Which being done, the problem is completed.

## LEMMA XXVIII.

*There exists no oval figure whose area, cut off by straight lines at will, can be found generally by means of equations finite in the number of their terms and dimensions.*
<note>original: "Nulla extat figura ovalis..." This is Newton’s famous "no-go" theorem regarding the impossibility of algebraically squaring the circle or any oval.</note>

Within the oval, let any point be given, around which, as a pole, a straight line revolves perpetually with a uniform motion; and meanwhile, let a moving point go out from the pole along that straight line, proceeding always with a velocity that is as the square of that straight line within the oval. By this motion, that point will describe a spiral with infinite turns. Now, if the portion of the area of the oval cut off by that straight line can be found by a finite equation, the distance of the point from the pole—which is proportional to this area—will also be found by the same equation; and therefore all points of the spiral can be found by a finite equation. Consequently, the intersection of any straight line given in position with the spiral can also be found by a finite equation. And yet, every straight line produced infinitely intersects the spiral in an infinite number of points; and an equation by which any intersection of two lines is found exhibits all their intersections by as many roots, and therefore rises to as many dimensions as there are intersections.

Since two circles intersect each other in two points, one intersection will not be found except by an equation of two dimensions <note>a quadratic equation</note>, by which the other intersection may also be found. Since there can be four intersections of two conic sections <note>curves like ellipses, parabolas, or hyperbolas</note>, any one of them cannot generally be found except by an equation of four dimensions, by which all may be found together. For if those intersections were sought separately, since the law and condition of all are the same, the calculation would be the same in every case, and therefore the conclusion always the same, which must therefore embrace all intersections at once and exhibit them indifferently.

Hence also the intersections of conic sections and curves of the third power <note>cubic curves</note>, because there can be six, come out together by equations of six dimensions; and the intersections of two curves of the third power, because there can be nine, come out together by equations of nine dimensions. Unless this happened by necessity, it would be possible to reduce all <term>solid problems</term> <note>problems solvable by conic sections</note> to <term>plane problems</term> <note>problems solvable by ruler and compass</note>, and problems more than solid to solid ones. I speak here of curves irre-
<meta>catchword: irre-</meta>

<summary>Newton argues that the area of an oval cannot be determined by finite algebraic equations because a spiral related to that area would intersect a straight line at infinite points, requiring an equation of infinite degree.</summary>
<keywords>oval, area, finite equations, dimensions, spiral, intersections, conic sections, cubic curves, solid problems, plane problems</keywords>

<margin>BOOK ONE.</margin>
irreducible. For if the equation by which a curve is defined can be reduced to a lower power, the curve will not be a single entity, but composed of two or more, whose intersections can be found separately through different calculations. In the same manner, the two intersections of straight lines and conic sections always arise through equations of two dimensions <note>original: "duarum dimensionum"; referring to quadratic equations</note>; the three intersections of straight lines and irreducible curves of the third power through equations of three dimensions; the four intersections of straight lines and irreducible curves of the fourth power through equations of four dimensions, and so on to infinity. Therefore, the intersections of a straight line and a spiral, which are infinite in number—since this curve is simple and irreducible into multiple curves—require equations with an infinite number of dimensions and roots, by which all intersections can be shown simultaneously. For the law and the calculation for all of them is the same. For if a perpendicular is dropped from the pole <note>The fixed central point of a coordinate system</note> to that secant line, and that perpendicular, together with the secant, is rotated around the pole, the intersections of the spiral will pass into one another; that which was first or nearest, after one revolution will be the second, after two the third, and so on: nor meanwhile will the equation change except for the changed magnitude of the quantities by which the position of the secant is determined. Since those quantities return to their original magnitudes after individual revolutions, the equation will return to its original form, and therefore one and the same equation will exhibit all intersections, and consequently will have an infinite number of roots by which all can be shown. Therefore, the intersection of a straight line and a spiral cannot generally be found by a finite equation, and for that reason, there exists no oval whose area, cut off by commanded straight lines <note>Lines defined by specific geometric constraints</note>, can be generally exhibited by such an equation.

By the same argument, if the interval between the pole and the point by which the spiral is described is taken as proportional to the perimeter of the cut-off Oval, it can be proven that the length of the perimeter cannot be generally exhibited by a finite equation. However, I am speaking here of ovals which are not touched by conjugate figures <note>Related geometric shapes or branches of a curve</note> extending to infinity.

By a not dissimilar calculation, the problem is resolved for the **hyperbola**. Let its center be **O**, the vertex **A**, the focus <note>original: "umbilicus"</note> **S**, and the asymptote **OK**. Let the quantity of the area to be cut off, which is proportional to the time, be known. Let that area be **A**, and let a conjecture be made regarding the position of the straight line **SP**, which cuts off an area **APS** very near to the true one. Let **OP** be joined, and from **A** and **P** let **AI** and **PK** be drawn to the asymptote, parallel to the other asymptote; then, by a table of logarithms, the area **AIKP** will be given, and equal to it the area **OPA**, which, when subtracted from the triangle **OPS**, will leave the cut-off area **APS**. By applying the double difference between the area to be cut off **A** and the cut-off area **APS**—that is, **2 APS — 2 A** or **2 A — 2 APS**—to the line **SN**, which is perpendicular from the focus **S** to the tangent **TP**, the length of the chord **PQ** will arise. Moreover, let that chord **PQ** be inscribed between **A** and **P** if the cut-off area **APS** is greater than the area to be cut off **A**, otherwise on the opposite side of point **P**; and point **Q** will be the more accurate location of the body. And by repeating the computation, the same will be found more accurately forever.

But it is also accurate enough for the theory of the planets. For even in the orbit of Mars itself, whose maximum equation of the center is ten degrees, the error will hardly exceed one second. Moreover, once the angle of the equated mean motion *BHP* is found, the angle of the true motion *BSP* and the distance *SP* are readily available through the most well-known method.

*Corollary* 2. A body revolving in any circle at a given distance from the center, if its motion is turned upwards, will ascend to twice its distance from the center.

## PROPOSITION 36. PROBLEM 25.
*To determine the times of descent of a body falling from a given place A.*

Upon the diameter AS (the distance of the body from the center at the beginning), describe a semicircle ADS, and also an equal semicircle OKH around the center S. From any position of the body C, erect the ordinate <note>a vertical line perpendicular to the axis</note> CD. Join SD, and make the sector OSK equal to the area ASD. It is evident by Proposition 35 that the body, in falling, will describe the space AC in the same time that another body, revolving uniformly around the center S, can describe the arc OK. Which was to be done.

### PROPOSITION XXXIX. PROBLEM XXVII.

*Given a <term>centripetal force</term><note>A force that pulls a body toward a center, such as gravity.</note> of any kind, and granted the <term>quadratures</term><note>The process of finding the area under a curve, an early form of integration.</note> of curvilinear figures, it is required to find both the velocity of a body ascending or descending in a straight line at any given place, and the time in which the body will reach any given place: And vice versa.*

Let *BFG* be the curved line which the point *G* continually touches. At the very beginning of the motion, let *EG* coincide with the perpendicular *AB*, and the velocity of the body in any place *E* will be as the straight line whose square is equal to the curvilinear area *ABGE*. **Which was to be found.**

For, having completed the rectangle *DRSE*, since the area *ABFD* is to the area *DFGE* as $VV$ to $2VI$, and therefore as $\frac{1}{2}V$ to *I*, that is, as half of the total velocity to the increment of velocity of the body falling by the unequal force; and similarly the area *PQRD* is to the area *DRSE* as half of the total velocity to the increment of velocity of the body falling by the uniform force; and since those increments (on account of the equality of the nascent times) are as the generating forces, that is, as the ordinates <note>ordinates: the vertical lines or y-coordinates in the diagram</note> *DF* and *DR*, and therefore as the nascent areas *DFGE* and *DRSE*; the total areas *ABFD* and *PQRD* will be to each other as the halves of the total velocities, and therefore, on account of the equality of the velocities, they are equal.

## PROPOSITION XL. THEOREM XIII.

*If a body, driven by any centripetal force <note>A force directed toward a center, such as gravity.</note>, moves in any manner, and another body ascends or descends in a straight line, and if their velocities are equal at any one point of equal altitude, their velocities will be equal at all equal altitudes.*

Let a certain body descend from *A* through *D* and *E* toward the center *C*, and let another body move from *V* along the curved line *VIKk*. From the center *C*, with any intervals, let concentric circles *DI* and *EK* be described, meeting the straight line *AC* at *D* and *E*, and the curve *VIK* at *I* and *K*. Let *IC* be joined, meeting *KE* at *N*; and let the perpendicular *NT* be dropped onto *IK*; and let the interval between the circumferences of the circles, *DE* or *IN*, be as small as possible, and let the bodies have equal velocities at *D* and *I*. Since the distances *CD* and *CI* are equal, the centripetal forces at *D* and *I* will be equal. Let these forces be represented by the equal small lines *DE* and *IN*; and if one force *IN* (by Corollary 2 of the Laws <note>Referring to the laws of motion established earlier in the work.</note>) is resolved into two, *NT* and *IT*, the force *NT*, acting along the line *NT* perpendicular to the body's path *ITK*, will not change the velocity of the body in that path, but will only pull the body back from a straight-line course, making it deflect perpetually from the tangent of the orbit and proceed along the curvilinear path *ITKk*. In producing this effect, that entire force will be consumed; however, the other force *IT*, acting along the body's course, will entirely accelerate it, and in a given minimal time will generate an acceleration proportional to itself. Accordingly, the accelerations of the bodies at *D* and *I* made in equal times (if...

**Corollary 1.** Hence, if a body either oscillates hanging from a thread, or is compelled to move in a curved line by any very smooth and perfectly slippery impediment <note>Newton is describing an idealized frictionless surface.</note>, and another body ascends or descends in a straight line, and their velocities are equal at any same altitude: then their velocities will be equal at any other equal altitudes. The body is not retarded by it, nor accelerated, but is only compelled to depart from its rectilinear course.

**Corollary 2.** Hence also, if the quantity *P* is the maximum distance from the center to which a body—either oscillating or revolving in any trajectory, and projected upward from any point of the trajectory with the velocity it has there—is able to ascend; and let the quantity *A* be the distance of the body from the center at any other point of the orbit; and let the centripetal force <term>centripetal force: the "center-seeking" force, like gravity, that pulls an object toward a central point</term> always be as any power of *A*, *A*ⁿ⁻¹, where the index *n*−1 is any number *n* diminished by one; the velocity of the body at every altitude *A* will be as the square root of *P*ⁿ−*A*ⁿ, and therefore it is given. For the velocity of a body ascending and descending in a straight line (by Proposition 39) is in this very ratio.

**Corollary 1.** From this, the maximum and minimum altitudes of bodies, that is, the apsides <term>apsides: the points in an orbit closest to or farthest from the center of force</term> of the trajectories, can be found expeditiously. **Corollary 2.** But also the angle *KIN*, in which the trajectory cuts that line *IC* anywhere, is found expeditiously from the given altitude of the body *IC*; namely, by taking its sine to the radius as *KN* is to *IK*, that is, as *Z* to the square root of the area *ABFD*.

**Corollary 3.** If with center *C* and principal vertex *V* any conic section *VRS* is described, and from any point *R* of it a tangent *RT* is drawn meeting the axis *CV* produced to infinity at point *T*; then, with *CR* joined, a straight line *CP* is drawn which is equal to the abscissa <term>abscissa: the horizontal coordinate or distance along the axis</term> *CT*, and constitutes an angle *VCP* proportional to the sector *VCR*; and if a centripetal force tends toward the center *C* inversely proportional to the cube of the distance of the places from the center, and the body departs from place *V* with the correct velocity along a line perpendicular to the straight line *CV*: that body will proceed in the trajectory *VPQ* which the point *P* perpetually touches; and therefore if the conic section *VRS* be a hyperbola, the same will descend to the center: but if it be an ellipse, it will ascend perpetually and go away

### PROPOSITION XLV. PROBLEM XXXI.
*To find the motion of the apsides <note>The points of greatest or least distance from the center of force, such as perihelion or aphelion.</note> for orbits that are very nearly circular.*

The problem is solved arithmetically by making the orbit—which a body describes in an immobile plane while revolving in a moving ellipse (as in Corollary 2 or 3 of the preceding Proposition)—approach the form of the orbit whose apsides are required, and by seeking the apsides of the orbit which that body describes in the immobile plane. Moreover, the orbits will acquire the same form if the centripetal forces by which they are described, when compared with one another, are made proportional at equal altitudes. Let point *V* be the highest apse, and let *T* be written for the maximum altitude *CV*, *A* for any other altitude *CP* or *Cp*, and *X* for the difference in altitudes *CV*—*CP*; and the force, by which a body is moved in an ellipse revolving about its focus *C* (as in Corollary 2), and which in Corollary 2 was as $FF / AA$, that is, as $(FFA + RGG - RFF) / A^3$ <note>original: "A cub."</note>, by substituting $T - X$ for $A$, will be as $(RGG - RFF + TFF - FFX) / A^3$. Any other centripetal force is likewise to be reduced to a fraction whose denominator is $A^3$, and the numerators, after a comparison of the corresponding terms is made, are to be set as analogous. The matter will be made clear by examples.

Example 1. Let us suppose the centripetal force to be uniform, and therefore as $A^3 / A^3$, or (by writing $T - X$ for $A$ in the numerator) as $(T^3 - 3T^2X + 3TX^2 - X^3) / A^3$; and by comparing the corresponding terms of the numerators—namely, the given terms with the given and the non-given with the non-given—it follows that $RGG - RFF + TFF$ is to $T^3$ as $-FFX$ is to $-3T^2X + 3TX^2 - X^3$, or as $-FF$ is to $-3T^2 + 3TX - X^2$. Now, since the orbit is assumed to be very nearly circular, let the orbit coincide with a circle; and because $R$ and $T$ are made equal, and $X$ is diminished infinitely, the ultimate ratios will be $RGG$ to $T^3$ as $-FF$ to $-3T^2$, or $GG$ to $3T^2$ as $FF$ to $3T^2$, and conversely $GG$ to $FF$ as $T^2$ to $3T^2$, that is, as

Therefore, since a body in a stationary ellipse, descending from the upper <term>apsis</term><note>The highest point in an orbit, furthest from the center of force.</note> to the lower apsis, completes an angle *VCP* (so to speak) of 180 degrees; another body in a moving ellipse, and therefore in the stationary orbit of which we are treating, descending from the upper apsis to the lower apsis, will complete an angle *VCp* of 180/√3 degrees. This is due to the similarity between this orbit, which a body describes under the action of a uniform centripetal force, and that orbit which a body performing revolutions in a rotating ellipse describes in a stationary plane. By the preceding comparison of terms, these orbits are rendered similar, not universally, but at the time when they approach most closely to a circular form. Therefore, a body revolving with a uniform centripetal force in a nearly circular orbit will always complete an angle of 180/√3 degrees, or 103 *deg*. 55 *min*. 23 *sec*. at the center, between the upper apsis and the lower apsis; arriving from the upper apsis to the lower apsis when it has once completed this angle, and returning from there to the upper apsis when it has again completed the same angle; and so on indefinitely.

*Example 2.* Let us suppose the centripetal force to be as any power of the altitude A, namely Aⁿ⁻³ or Aⁿ/A³; where *n*-3 and *n* signify any indices of powers, whether whole or fractional, rational or irrational, positive or negative. That numerator Aⁿ, or (T-X)ⁿ, being reduced into an indeterminate series by our method of converging series, becomes Tⁿ - *n*XTⁿ⁻¹ + (*nn-n*)/2 XXTⁿ⁻² etc. And by comparing the terms of this with the terms of the other numerator RGG - RFF + TFF - FFX, RGG - RFF + TFF becomes to Tⁿ as -FF is to -*n*Tⁿ⁻¹ + (*nn-n*)/2 XXTⁿ⁻² etc. And by taking the ultimate ratios where the orbits approach a circular form, RGG becomes to Tⁿ as -FF to -*n*Tⁿ⁻¹, or GG to Tⁿ as FF to *n*Tⁿ⁻¹, and conversely GG to FF as Tⁿ to *n*Tⁿ⁻¹, that is, as 1 to *n*; and therefore G to F, that is the angle *VCp* to the angle *VCP*, as 1 to √*n*. Wherefore, since the angle *VCP*, completed in the descent of a body from the upper apsis to the lower apsis in an ellipse, is 180 degrees; the angle *VCp*, in the descent of the body from...

<margin>On the Motion of BODIES</margin>
Regarding the motion from the highest <term>apsis</term><note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of attraction.</note> to the lowest <term>apsis</term><note>The point in an orbit closest to the center of attraction.</note>, in an orbit that is nearly circular which any body describes by a centripetal force proportional to the power A⁻³; this motion is equal to an angle of 180/√n degrees; and by repeating this angle, the body will return from the lowest apsis to the highest, and so on indefinitely. For example, if the centripetal force is as the distance of the body from the center, that is, as A or `A⁴/A³`, then *n* will be equal to 4 and `√n` will be equal to 2. Therefore, the angle between the highest apsis and the lowest apsis is equal to `180/2` degrees, or 90 degrees. Thus, having completed a fourth part of one revolution, the body will reach the lowest apsis, and having completed another fourth part, it reaches the highest apsis, and so on by turns indefinitely. This is also evident from Proposition 10. For a body urged by this centripetal force will revolve in an immovable ellipse, the center of which is at the center of forces. But if the centripetal force is reciprocally as the distance, that is, directly as `1/A` or `A²/A³`, *n* will be equal to 2, and therefore the angle between the highest and lowest apsis will be `180/√2` degrees, or 127 degrees, 16 minutes, and 45 seconds; and therefore a body revolving with such a force will, by the perpetual repetition of this angle, arrive by alternating turns from the highest apsis to the lowest and from the lowest to the highest forever. Furthermore, if the centripetal force is reciprocally as the <term>quadrato-quadrate side</term><note>The fourth root.</note> of the eleventh power of the altitude, that is, reciprocally as `A^(11/4)`, and therefore directly as `1/A^(11/4)` or as `A^(1/4)/A³`, *n* will be equal to 1/4. <note>The original text notes n as 11/4, but the calculation follows the fractional power logic.</note>

And `180/√n` degrees is equal to 360 degrees; and therefore a body departing from the highest apsis and thereafter perpetually descending, will reach the lowest apsis when it has completed an entire revolution; then, by a perpetual ascent completing another entire revolution, it will return to the highest apsis: and so by turns forever.

Example 3. Assuming *m* and *n* for any indices of the powers of the altitude, and *b*, *c* for any given numbers, let us suppose the centripetal force to be as `(bAᵐ + cAⁿ) / A cubed`, that is, as `(b * (T-X)ᵐ + c * (T-X)ⁿ) / A cubed`.

So also where the force, in receding from the center, decreases in a ratio greater than the cubed ratio of the altitude, a body departing from the apsis, according to whether it begins to descend or ascend, will either descend all the way to the center or ascend to infinity. But if the force, in receding from the center, either decreases in a ratio less than the cubed ratio of the altitude, or increases in any ratio of the altitude whatever; the body will never descend all the way to the center, but will eventually reach the lowest apsis: and conversely, if a body descending and ascending by turns from apsis to apsis never reaches the center; the force in receding from the center will either be increased, or will decrease in a ratio less than the cubed ratio of the altitude: and the more quickly the body returns from apsis to apsis, the further the ratio of the forces will recede from that cubed ratio. **Corollary 2.** From this, if a body—driven by a centripetal force that is inversely as the square of the altitude—revolves in an <term>ellipse</term> having a <term>focus</term><note>original: "umbilicum"</note> at the center of forces, and to this centripetal force is added or subtracted any other extraneous force; the motion of the apsides arising from that extraneous force can be known (by the third examples): and vice versa. As if the force by which the body revolves in an ellipse is as 1/AA, and the subtracted extraneous force is as *cA*, and therefore the remaining force is as (A-cA^4)/A^3; then (in the third examples) *b* will be equal to 1, *m* equal to 1, and *n* equal to 4, and therefore the angle of revolution between the apsides will be equal to an angle of 180 √( (1-c)/(1-4c) ) degrees. Let us suppose that extraneous force to be 357.45 parts smaller than the other force by which the body revolves in the ellipse, that is, *c* is 1/357.45, with A or T being equal to 1, and 180 √( (1-c)/(1-4c) ) will become 180 √( (356.45)/(353.45) ), or 180.7623, that is, 180 degrees, 45 minutes, 44 seconds. Therefore, the body departing from the upper apsis, with an angular motion of 180 degrees, 45 minutes, 44 seconds, will arrive at the lower apsis, and by doubling this motion will return to the upper apsis: and therefore the upper apsis, by progressing in each revolution, will complete 1 degree, 31 minutes, 28 seconds. The apsis of the Moon is about twice as swift.

<margin>On the Motion of Bodies</margin> on eccentric planes. For writers who treat the motion of heavy bodies are accustomed to consider the ascents and descents of weights, both oblique on any given planes and perpendicular; and by the same right, the motion of bodies acted upon by any forces tending toward centers and resting upon eccentric planes comes to be considered here. Furthermore, we suppose the planes to be highly polished and absolutely slippery so that they do not retard the bodies. Nay, rather, in these demonstrations, instead of the planes upon which the bodies rest and which they touch in resting, we employ planes parallel to these, in which the centers of the bodies move and describe orbits by their motion. And by the same law, we shall hereafter determine the motions of bodies performed on curved surfaces.

### Scholium <note>A "Scholium" is an explanatory note or commentary added to a mathematical proof to provide further context or applications.</note>
Related to these are the ascents and descents of bodies on curved surfaces. Imagine curved lines described in a plane, then revolved around any given axes passing through the center of forces, and by that revolution they describe curved surfaces; then suppose bodies move in such a way that their centers are perpetually found on these surfaces. If those bodies, by ascending and descending obliquely, move back and forth; their motions will be carried out in planes passing through the axis, and therefore in the curved lines by whose revolution those curved surfaces were generated. Therefore, in those cases, it is sufficient to consider the motion in these curved lines.

## PROPOSITION 48. THEOREM 16.

*If a wheel stands at right angles upon the outside of a globe, and by revolving in the manner of wheels progresses along a great circle; the length of the curvilinear path which any given point on the perimeter of the wheel has completed since it first touched the globe (which path may be called a <term>cycloid</term> <note>A curve traced by a point on the rim of a circular wheel as it rolls along a straight line.</note> or an <term>epicycloid</term> <note>A curve traced by a point on the circumference of a circle as it rolls around the outside of another fixed circle.</note>) will be to twice the versed sine <note>The versed sine (versin) is 1 minus the cosine of an angle; it measures the "height" of a circular arc.</note> of half the arc which has touched the globe during that motion, as the sum of the diameters of the globe and the wheel is to the semi-diameter of the globe.*

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

<margin>BOOK ONE.</margin>
Because of the similarity of the vanishing figure *Pnomq* and the figure *PFGVI*, the ultimate ratio of the vanishing lines *Pm, Pn, Po, Pq*—that is, the ratio of the momentary changes of the curve *AP*, the straight line *CP*, the circular arc *BP*, and the straight line *VP*—will be the same as the ratio of the lines *PV, PF, PG, PI* respectively. Moreover, since *VF* is perpendicular to *CF* and *VH* to *CV*, and the angles *HVG* and *VCF* are therefore equal; and the angle *VHO* (because the angles of the quadrilateral *HVEP* at *V* and *P* are right angles) is equal to the angle *CEP*, the triangles *VHG* and *CEP* will be similar; and from this it follows that as *EP* is to *CE*, so is *HG* to *HV* or *HP*, and so is *KI* to *KP*; and by composition or division, as *CB* is to *CE*, so is *PI* to *PK*; and by doubling the consequents, as *CB* is to 2 *CE*, so is *PI* to *PV*, and thus *Pq* to *Pm*. Therefore, the decrease of the line *VP*—that is, the increase of the line *BV—VP*—is to the increase of the curved line *AP* in the given ratio of *CB* to 2 *CE*; and therefore (by the corollary to Lemma 4) the lengths *BV—VP* and *AP*, generated by those increments, are in the same ratio. But, with *BV* being the radius, *VP* is the cosine of the angle *BVP* or ½ *BEP*, and therefore *BV—VP* is the versed sine <note>The versed sine, or versine, is a trigonometric function equal to 1 minus the cosine.</note> of that same angle; and therefore in this wheel, whose radius is ½ *BV*, *BV—VP* will be double the versed sine of the arc ½ *BP*. Therefore *AP* is to double the versed sine of the arc ½ *BP* as 2 *CE* is to *CB*. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

For the sake of distinction, we shall call the line *AP* in the former proposition the cycloid outside the globe, and the other in the latter proposition the cycloid inside the globe.

Corollary 1. Hence, if a complete cycloid *ASL* is described and bisected at *S*, the length of the part *PS* will be to the length *VP* (which is double the sine of the angle *VBP*, with *EB* being the radius) as 2 *CE* is to *CB*, and thus in a given ratio.

Corollary 2. And the length of the semi-perimeter of the cycloid *AS* will be equal to a straight line which is to the diameter of the wheel *BV* as 2 *CE* is to *CB*.
