If pendulum bodies are now made to oscillate in different cycloids <note>A cycloid is the curve traced by a point on the rim of a circular wheel as it rolls along a straight line; here, Newton applies it to motion within a sphere.</note> described within different spheres, the absolute forces of which are also different: and, if the absolute force of any sphere *2QS* is called *V*, the accelerating force by which the pendulum is urged along the circumference of this sphere, where it begins to move directly toward its center, will be as the distance of the pendulum body from that center and the absolute force of the sphere combined, that is, as *CO x V*. Therefore, the small line *HY*, which is as this accelerating force *CO x V*, will be described in a given time; and, if a perpendicular *TZ* is erected meeting the circumference at *Z*, the nascent arc <note>The "nascent arc" refers to an infinitesimally small segment of the curve at its beginning.</note> *HZ* will denote that given time. Moreover, this nascent arc *HZ* is in the subduplicate ratio <note>The square root.</note> of the rectangle *GHT*, and therefore as `√GH x CO x V`. From this, the time of a complete oscillation in the cycloid *QRS* (since it is as the semi-periphery *HKM*, which denotes that complete oscillation, directly; and as the arc *HZ*, which similarly denotes the given time, inversely) will be as *GH* directly and `√GH x CO x V` inversely, that is, because *GH* and *SR* are equal, as `SR / CO x V` or (by the corollary of proposition 50) as `AR / AC x V`. Therefore, the oscillations in all spheres and cycloids, performed with any absolute forces whatever, are in a ratio which is compounded of the subduplicate ratio of the length of the string directly, and the subduplicate ratio of the distance between the point of suspension and the center of the sphere inversely, and the subduplicate ratio of the absolute force of the sphere also inversely. *Which was to be found.*

**Corollary 1.** From this, the times of oscillating, falling, and revolving bodies can also be compared among themselves. For if the diameter of the wheel by which the cycloid is described within the sphere is made equal to the semi-diameter of the sphere, the cycloid becomes a straight line passing through the center of the sphere, and the oscillation will now be a descent and subsequent ascent in this straight line. From which is given both the time of descent from any place to the center, and the time equal to this by which a body, revolving uniformly around the center of the sphere at any distance, describes a quadrant arc. For this time is (by the second case) to the time of a semi-oscillation in any cycloid *QRS* as 1 to `√AR / AC`.

**Corollary 2.** From this also follow those things which *Wren* <note>Sir Christopher Wren, the architect and mathematician.</note> and *Huygens* <note>Christiaan Huygens, who first patented the pendulum clock.</note> discovered concerning the common cycloid. For if the diameter of the sphere is increased to infinity: its spherical surface will be changed into a plane, and the centripetal force will act uniformly according to lines perpendicular to this plane,

## PROPOSITION LV. THEOREM XIX.
*If a body moves on any curved surface whose axis passes through the center of forces, and from the body a perpendicular is let fall to the axis, and a line parallel and equal to it is drawn from any given point of the axis: I say that this parallel line will describe an area proportional to the time.*

## SECTION XI.
### *On the motion of bodies seeking each other through centripetal forces.*

Up to this point, I have set forth the motions of bodies attracted to a fixed center, though such a thing hardly exists in the nature of things. For attractions are usually made toward bodies; and the actions of the attracting and attracted bodies are always mutual and equal, by the Third Law of Motion: so much so that neither the attractor nor the attracted can remain still if there are two bodies, but both (by the fourth corollary of the laws) must revolve around a common center of gravity as if by mutual attraction. And if there are many bodies, which are either attracted by a single one that they also attract, or all attract each other mutually; these must move among themselves in such a way that their common center of gravity either remains still or moves uniformly forward in a straight line. For this reason, I now proceed to set forth the motion of bodies attracting each other, considering centripetal forces <term>centripetal forces: "center-seeking" forces, like gravity, that pull objects toward a point</term> as "attractions," although perhaps, if we were to speak in the language of physics, they might more truly be called "impulses." <note>Newton is making a famous distinction here: he is providing a mathematical description of how gravity behaves ("attraction") without claiming to know the underlying physical cause of how it works (which might be a "push" or "impulse").</note> For we are now occupied with mathematics; and therefore, putting aside physical disputes, we use a familiar language so that we may be more easily understood by mathematical readers.

# PROPOSITION LIX. THEOREM XXII.

*For two bodies, S and P, revolving around a common center of gravity C, the periodic time is to the periodic time of either body P, revolving around the other body S as if it were immobile, and describing a figure similar and equal to the figures which the bodies describe around each other, in the <term>square root ratio</term> <note>original: "subduplicata ratione"; this means the ratio of the square roots of the values.</note> of the other body S to the sum of the bodies S + P.*

And by compounding these, the sums of the times in which all the similar arcs *PQ* and *pq* are described—that is, the total times in which the whole similar figures are described—are in that same square root ratio. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

## PROPOSITION 60. THEOREM 23.

*If two bodies, S and P, attracting each other with forces inversely proportional to the square of their distance, revolve around their common center of gravity: I say that the principal axis <note>The "principal axis" or major axis is the longest diameter of an ellipse.</note> of the ellipse which either body P describes in this motion around the other body S, will be to the principal axis of the ellipse which the same body P could describe around the other body S (if S were at rest) in the same periodic time, as the sum of the two bodies (S + P) is to the first of two <term>mean proportionals</term> <note>In classical geometry, if you have two numbers A and B, two "mean proportionals" x and y satisfy the ratio A:x = x:y = y:B. Here, Newton uses this to express a specific ratio involving the cube root of the masses.</note> between this sum and that other body S.*

For if the described ellipses were equal to each other, the periodic times <note>The time taken to complete one full orbit.</note> (by the previous theorem) would be in the <term>subduplicate ratio</term> <note>The ratio of the square roots.</note> of the body S to the sum of the bodies S + P. If the periodic time in the latter ellipse is diminished in this ratio, the periodic times will become equal; then the principal axis of the ellipse (by Proposition 15) will be diminished in a ratio of which this is the <term>sesquiplicate</term> <note>The 3/2 power (the square root of the cube). This refers to Kepler’s Third Law, where the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the axis.</note>, that is, in a ratio of which the ratio S to S + P is the <term>triplicate</term> <note>The ratio of the cubes.</note>; and therefore it will be to the principal axis of the other ellipse as the first of two mean proportionals between S + P and S is to S + P. And inversely, the principal axis of the ellipse described around the moving body will be to the principal axis of the ellipse described around the immobile body, as S + P is to the first of two mean proportionals between S + P and S. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

## PROPOSITION 61. THEOREM 24.

*If two bodies attracting each other by any forces, and not otherwise agitated or impeded, are moved in any manner whatever; their motions will be the same as if they did not attract each other, but were both attracted by a third body situated in the common center of gravity by those same forces: And the law of the attracting forces will be the same with respect to the distance of the bodies from that common center, as it is with respect to the total distance between the bodies.*

<meta>This page continues the logical progression from Proposition 61, concluding the demonstration that forces in a two-body system can be treated as if they originate from a single central point (the common center of gravity). # MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK ONE.

For those forces with which bodies attract each other, by aiming toward the bodies themselves, aim toward the common center of gravity <term>center of gravity</term> <note>The "center of gravity" (or center of mass) is the unique point where the weighted relative position of the distributed mass sums to zero; essentially the balance point of the system.</note> lying between them; and therefore, these forces are the same as if they originated from a body located at that center. <note>original: "Q.E.D." (Quod Erat Demonstrandum) — Which was to be demonstrated.</note>

And since the ratio of the distance of either body from that common center to the total distance between the bodies is constant, the ratio of any power <note>For example, if the distance is squared or cubed.</note> of the distance of one to the same power of the distance of the other will also be fixed. Likewise, the ratio of any quantity derived from one distance and given values to another quantity derived from the other distance and similar values will be fixed. Therefore, if the force with which one body is attracted by the other is directly or inversely proportional to the distance between the bodies—or to any power of that distance, or finally to any quantity derived in any way from that distance and given values—then the same force with which the body is attracted toward the common center of gravity will likewise be directly or inversely proportional to the distance of the attracted body from that common center, or to the same power of this distance, or finally to a quantity similarly derived from this distance and analogous given values. That is, the law of the attracting force will be the same with respect to both distances. <note>original: "Q.E.D." — Which was to be demonstrated.</note>

# PROPOSITION 62. PROBLEM 38.

*To determine the motions of two bodies that attract each other with forces inversely proportional to the square <note>The "inverse square law" means the force gets four times weaker if the distance doubles.</note> of their distance, when they are released from given positions.*

The bodies (according to the most recent theorem) will move just as if they were being attracted by a third body placed at the common center of gravity. That center, by our initial assumption, will be at rest at the start of the motion; and therefore (according to the fourth corollary of the Laws of Motion) it will remain at rest forever. We must therefore determine the motions of the bodies (using Problem 25) <note>Problem 25, found earlier in the book, describes the motion of a single body attracted to a fixed center.</note> just as if they were driven by forces tending toward that center, and we will thereby obtain the motions of the bodies attracting each other. <note>original: "Q.E.I." (Quod Erat Inveniendum) — Which was to be found.</note>

### PROPOSITION LXIII. PROBLEM XXXIX.

*To determine the motions of two bodies that attract each other with forces inversely proportional to the square of their distance, and which start from given positions, along given straight lines, and with given velocities.*

From the initial motions of the bodies, we can determine the uniform <term>uniform motion</term> <note>Motion at a constant speed in a straight line.</note> of their common center of gravity. We also know the motion of the "space" or frame of reference that moves along with this center in a straight line, as well as the bodies' initial motions relative to this space. 

According to the fifth corollary of the laws <note>Newton refers back to the foundational Laws of Motion established at the start of the book.</note> and the most recent theorem, the subsequent motions within this relative space occur exactly as if the space itself and the center of gravity were at rest, and as if the bodies did not attract each other, but were instead both attracted by a third body located at that center. Therefore, the motion of either body—starting from a given place, in a given direction, at a given speed, and governed by a centripetal force <note>A "center-seeking" force, like gravity pulling a planet toward the sun.</note> tending toward that center—must be determined by Problem 9 and Problem 26. This will simultaneously reveal the motion of the second body around the same center. Finally, by combining this orbital motion with the uniform forward motion of the whole system (which we found earlier), we obtain the absolute motion of the bodies in unmoving space. <note>original: "Q. E. I." (Quod Erat Inveniendum) — Which was to be found.</note>

## PROPOSITION LXV. THEOREM XXV.

*Several bodies, whose forces decrease in the inverse square ratio <note>original: "duplicata ratione"; this is the famous inverse-square law where gravity weakens as the square of the distance increases.</note> of the distances from their centers, can move among themselves in ellipses; and by radii drawn to the foci <note>original: "umbilicos"; literally "navels," the geometric points around which an ellipse is formed.</note> describe areas proportional to the times, very nearly.*

In the preceding proposition, a case was demonstrated where several motions are performed in ellipses accurately. The more the law of forces deviates from the law established there, the more the bodies will disturb each other's motions; nor can it happen that bodies, attracting each other according to the law established here <note>Referring to the inverse-square law of universal gravitation.</note>, move in ellipses accurately, except by maintaining a certain proportion of distances from each other. However, in the following cases, the motion will not wander far from ellipses.

*Case 1.* Suppose several smaller bodies revolve around a single very large one at various distances from it, and let absolute forces tend toward each body proportional to their masses. And since the common center of gravity of them all (by the fourth corollary of the Laws) either rests or moves uniformly forward in a straight line, let us imagine the smaller bodies to be so small that the largest body is never sensibly distant from this center. Thus, that largest body will either rest or move uniformly in a straight line without any sensible error; while the smaller bodies will revolve around this largest one in ellipses, and by radii drawn to it, they will describe areas proportional to the times; except insofar as errors are introduced, either by the deviation of the largest body from that common center of gravity, or by the actions of the smaller bodies upon one another. Furthermore, the smaller bodies can be diminished in size until this error and the mutual actions are smaller than any given limit; and therefore until the orbits match with ellipses, and the areas correspond to the times, without an error that is not smaller than any given amount. *Which was to be demonstrated.* <note>original: "Q. E. O." (Quod Erat Ostendendum).</note>

<summary>Newton explains that while perfect elliptical orbits require specific force laws, the inverse-square law of gravity allows for nearly perfect ellipses when small planets orbit a much larger central sun.</summary>

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK ONE.

*Case 2.* Let us now imagine a system of smaller bodies revolving in the manner just described around a very large one, or any other system of two bodies revolving around each other, moving forward uniformly in a straight line, while in the meantime being urged to the side by the force of another body, by far the largest and situated at a great distance. And since equal accelerative forces <note>original: "vires acceleratrices"; these are forces that cause acceleration regardless of the mass of the object being moved, much like gravity on Earth makes all objects fall at the same rate.</note>, by which bodies are urged along parallel lines, do not change the positions of the bodies relative to each other, but instead cause the whole system to be moved together as one (preserving the motions of the parts among themselves): **it is manifest that from the attractions toward the largest body, no change at all will arise in the motion of the attracted bodies relative to each other, unless from either the inequality of the accelerative attractions, or from the inclination of the lines toward each other along which the attractions occur.** Suppose, therefore, that all accelerative attractions toward the largest body are inversely as the squares of the distances <note>This is the famous inverse-square law: if you double the distance, the gravity becomes four times weaker.</note>; and by increasing the distance of the largest body until the differences of the straight lines drawn from it to the rest (relative to their length) and their inclinations toward each other are smaller than any given amount; the motions of the parts of the system among themselves will persist without errors that are not smaller than any given amount. And since, because of the small distance of those parts from each other, the whole system is attracted in the manner of a single body, it will move by this attraction in the manner of a single body; that is, it will describe with its center of gravity <term>center of gravity: the point at which the entire weight of a system may be considered to be concentrated</term> some conic section around the largest body (*namely, a hyperbola or parabola if the attraction is weak, or an ellipse if it is stronger*) and by a radius drawn to the largest body it will describe areas proportional to the times, without any errors except those which the distances of the parts—certainly very small and able to be diminished at will—are capable of producing. *Which was to be shown.* <note>original: "Q. E. O." (Quod Erat Ostendendum).</note>

By a similar argument, one may proceed to cases more complex without end.

*Corollary 1.* In the second case, the closer the largest body of all approaches the system of two or more, the more the motions of the parts of the system among themselves will be disturbed; because the inclination of the lines drawn from the largest body to these is now greater, and the inequality of the proportion is greater.

*Corollary 2.* But they will be most disturbed if we assume that the accelerative attractions of the parts of the system toward the largest body of all are not inversely as the squares of the distances from that largest body; especially if the inequality of this proportion is greater

## PROPOSITION LXVI. THEOREMA XXVI.

Their motions relative to one another would then be the same (by Corollary 6 of the Laws) as if these attractions were removed altogether. And by the same reasoning, if the attraction $SN$ were less than the attraction $SM$, it would cancel out the part $SN$ of the attraction $SM$, and only the part $MN$ would remain, by which the proportionality of the times and areas and that elliptical shape of the orbit would be disturbed. And similarly, if the attraction $SN$ were greater than the attraction $SM$, the disturbance of the proportionality and of the orbit would arise from the difference $MN$ alone. Thus, by the attraction $SN$, the superior third attraction $SM$ is always reduced to the attraction $MN$, while the first and second forces remain entirely unchanged; and therefore the areas and times [approach] proportionality, and the orbit $PAB$ [approaches] the aforementioned <insert>shape</insert> <note>original: "præfatam"; the text ends with the prefix "præ-" and the catchword "fatam," meaning "aforementioned."</note>

**Case 2.** Now let the smaller bodies $P, S$ revolve around the greatest body $T$ in different planes; and the force $LM$, acting along the line $PT$ situated in the plane of the orbit $PAB$, will have the same effect as before, nor will it disturb the body $P$ from the plane of its orbit. **Corollary 1.** From these things it is easily gathered that, if several smaller bodies $P, S, R$, etc., revolve around the greatest body $T$, the motion of the innermost body $P$ will be least disturbed by the attractions of the outer ones when the greatest body $T$ is attracted and agitated by the others in the same way, in proportion to the accelerating forces, as the others are by each other.

**Corollary 2.** In a system of three bodies $T, P, S$, if the accelerating attractions of any two toward a third are inversely to each other as the squares of the distances; the body $P$, with radius $PT$, will describe an area around the body $T$ more quickly near conjunction $A$ <note>Conjunction occurs when the three bodies are in a straight line, with P between T and S (like a New Moon).</note> and opposition $B$ <note>Opposition occurs when T is between P and S (like a Full Moon).</note>, than near the quadratures $C, D$ <note>Quadratures occur when the bodies form a right angle relative to one another (First or Last Quarter Moon).</note>. For every force by which body $P$ is urged and body $T$ is not urged, and which does not act along the line $PT$, accelerates or retards the description of the area, depending on whether it is directed in the direction of motion <note>original: "in consequentia"</note> or against the motion <note>original: "in antecedentia"</note>. Such is the force $NM$. This, in the passage of body $P$ from $C$ to $A$, tends in the direction of motion, and accelerates the motion; then up to $D$ against the motion, and retards the motion; then in the direction of motion up to $B$, and finally against the motion passing from $B$ to $C$.

### OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>ON THE MOTION OF BODIES</margin> *Corollary 3.* And by the same argument it is evident that body *P*, all else being equal, moves more swiftly in conjunction and opposition <note>These points of alignment are collectively called "syzygy." In conjunction, the Moon is between the Earth and Sun (New Moon); in opposition, the Earth is between the Moon and Sun (Full Moon).</note> than in the quadratures <note>The points in the orbit where the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun as seen from Earth (First and Third Quarters).</note>.

*Corollary 4.* The orbit of body *P*, all else being equal, is more curved in the quadratures than in conjunction and opposition. For swifter bodies deflect less from a straight path. And furthermore, the force *K L*, or *N M*, in conjunction and opposition is contrary to the force by which body *T* pulls body *P*; and therefore it diminishes that force; but body *P* will deflect less from a straight path where it is less urged toward body *T*.

*Corollary 5.* Hence body *P*, all else being equal, will recede further from body *T* in the quadratures than in conjunction and opposition. This is how things stand if the motion of eccentricity <note>Eccentricity refers to how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> is excluded. For if the orbit of body *P* is eccentric, its eccentricity (as will soon be shown in corollary 9 of this proposition) will become greatest when the apsides <note>The points in an orbit where the body is either closest (perigee) or farthest (apogee) from the center.</note> are in the syzygies; and from this it can happen that body *P*, approaching the higher apsis <note>The point of maximum distance from the central body.</note>, is further away from body *T* in the syzygies than in the quadratures.

*Corollary 6.* Since the centripetal force <term>centripetal force: literally "center-seeking" force; the gravitational pull of Earth that keeps the Moon in orbit</term> of the central body *T*, by which body *P* is retained in its orbit, is increased in the quadratures by the addition of the force *L M*, and is diminished in the syzygies by the subtraction of the force *K L*, and on account of the magnitude of the force *K L*, it is diminished more than it is increased; and furthermore, since that centripetal force (by corollary 2 of proposition 4) is in a ratio compounded of the simple ratio of the radius *T P* directly and the duplicate ratio <note>original: "ratione duplicata"; meaning the square of the value.</note> of the periodic time inversely: it is clear that this compounded ratio is diminished by the action of the force *K L*; and therefore the periodic time, if the radius of the orbit *T P* remains the same, is increased, and that in the subduplicate ratio <note>original: "ratione subduplicata"; meaning the square root of the ratio.</note> in which that centripetal force is diminished: and therefore, with this radius being increased or diminished, the periodic time is increased more, or diminished less, than in the ratio of this radius

<summary>Newton describes how the Sun's gravity causes the Moon to move faster and closer to Earth at the New and Full Moon phases (syzygy) while slowing down and curving more at the Quarter Moon phases (quadrature). He also introduces how these perturbations increase the time it takes the Moon to complete a full orbit.</summary>

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

<margin>
BOOK
FIRST.

<meta>catchword: Corol.</meta>

...the <term>sesquiplicate ratio</term><note>A ratio of 3/2, or the square root of the cube. Newton uses this to describe the relationship between orbital distance and time, following Kepler's Third Law.</note> (by Corollary 6, Proposition 4). If that force of the central body were to gradually weaken, body *P*, being less and less attracted, would perpetually recede further from the center *T*; and conversely, if that force were increased, it would approach nearer. Therefore, if the action of the distant body *S*, by which that force is diminished, is increased and decreased in turn: the radius *TP* will increase and decrease in turn; and the <term>periodic time</term><note>The time required to complete one full orbit.</note> will increase and decrease in a ratio compounded of the sesquiplicate ratio of the radius and the <term>subduplicate ratio</term><note>The square root ratio.</note> by which that centripetal force of the central body *T* is diminished or increased by the increase or decrease of the action of the distant body *S*.

*Corollary 7.* From the premises, it also follows that the axis of the ellipse described by body *P*—or the line of <term>apsides</term><note>The line connecting the points where the orbiting body is closest (perigee) and farthest (apogee).</note>—with respect to its angular motion, advances and recedes in turn, but yet it advances more, and by the excess of that advancement is carried <insert>forward</insert> <note>original: "in consequentia," meaning in the direction of the orbital motion.</note>. For the force by which body *P* is urged toward body *T* in the <term>quadratures</term><note>When the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun as seen from Earth.</note>, where the force *MN* has vanished, is composed of the force *LM* and the centripetal force by which body *T* pulls body *P*. The former force *LM*, if the distance *PT* is increased, increases in nearly the same ratio as this distance, and the latter force decreases in that <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>The square ratio (inverse-square law).</note>; therefore, the sum of these forces decreases in a ratio less than the duplicate ratio of the distance *PT*, and for that reason (by Corollary 1, Proposition 45), it causes the <term>aux</term><note>Also known as the apogee; the highest or furthest point of the orbit.</note>, or highest apsis, to recede. But in conjunction and opposition, the force by which body *P* is urged toward body *T* is the difference between the force by which body *T* pulls body *P* and the force *KL*; and that difference—because the force *KL* increases very nearly in the ratio of the distance *PT*—decreases in a ratio greater than the duplicate ratio of the distance *PT*, and therefore (by Corollary 1, Proposition 45) causes the *aux* to advance. In locations between the <term>syzygies</term><note>The points of alignment (New and Full Moon).</note> and quadratures, the motion of the *aux* depends on both causes together, so that it advances or recedes according to the excess of one or the other. Hence, since the force *KL* in the syzygies is about twice as great as the force *LM* in the quadratures, the excess will lie with the force *KL*, and it will shift the *aux* forward. The truth of this and the preceding corollary will be more easily understood by conceiving the system of two bodies *T, P* to be surrounded on all sides by several bodies *S, S, S, etc.* situated in an orbit *ESE*. For by their actions, the action of body *T* itself will be diminished on all sides, and will decrease in a ratio greater than the duplicate ratio of the distance.

*Corollary 8.* Since, however, the advancement or retreat of the <term>apsides</term><note>The points in an orbit where the satellite is closest to (perigee) or farthest from (apogee) the central body.</note> depends on the decrease of the centripetal force being in a ratio greater or less than the <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>The "square" of the distance (inverse-square law). Newton is explaining that if gravity doesn't follow a perfect $1/r^2$ pattern, the orbit's orientation shifts.</note> of the distance *TP*, during the body's passage from the lowest apsis to the highest; as well as on a similar increase during the return to the lowest apsis; and therefore the movement is greatest where the proportion of the force at the highest apsis to the force at the lowest apsis deviates most from the inverse duplicate ratio of the distances: it is manifest that the apsides, in their <term>syzygies</term><note>From the Greek word for "yoked together." This refers to when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a straight line (New Moon or Full Moon).</note>, will advance more swiftly due to the <term>ablative force</term><note>original: "vim ablatitiam." A force that "takes away" from the Earth's pull, effectively weakening gravity.</note> *KL* or *NM — LM*, and in their <term>quadratures</term><note>When the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun (the Quarter Moons).</note> they will retreat more slowly due to the <term>additive force</term><note>original: "vim addititiam." A force that "adds" to the Earth's pull, effectively strengthening gravity.</note> *LM*. On account of the long duration of time in which the speed of the advancement or the slowness of the retreat is continued, this inequality becomes by far the greatest.

*Corollary 9.* If some body were revolving around a center in an ellipse, driven by a force inversely proportional to the square of its distance from that center; and then, in its descent from the <term>highest apsis</term><note>original: "apside summa seu auge." The point of greatest distance in an orbit.</note> to the lowest apsis, that force were increased by the constant addition of a new force in a ratio greater than the duplicate ratio of the diminished distance: it is manifest that the body, always pushed toward the center by the constant addition of that new force, would incline more toward this center than if it were urged by the lone force increasing in the duplicate ratio of the diminished distance; and therefore it would describe an orbit interior to the elliptical orbit, and at the lowest apsis it would approach closer to the center than before. The orbit, therefore, by the addition of this new force, will become more <term>eccentric</term><note>A measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle. A "more eccentric" orbit is more elongated or oval-shaped.</note>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram representing orbital mechanics. On the left is an arc labeled E S E (representing the distant Sun). Dotted arcs and lines labeled K, L, and M extend from point P toward the right side of the diagram, illustrating the different components of gravitational or perturbing forces exerted by body S. Points C and D mark the vertical extremities (quadratures) of the orbit.</image-desc>

If now the force, in the retreat of the body from the lowest apsis to the highest, should decrease by the same degrees by which it had previously increased, the body would return to its former distance; and therefore if the force decreases in a greater ratio, the body—now less attracted—will ascend to a greater distance, and thus the eccentricity of the orbit will be increased even more. Wherefore, if the ratio of the increase and decrease of the centripetal force is increased in each individual revolution, the eccentricity will always increase; and conversely,

Therefore, the ratio of the total decrease and increase, in the passage between the apsides, is minimal in the quadratures and maximal in the syzygies: and for that reason, in the passage of the apsides from the quadratures to the syzygies, it is perpetually increased, and increases the <term>eccentricity</term><note>The degree to which the Moon's orbit is elongated rather than circular.</note> of the ellipse; and in the passage from the syzygies to the quadratures, it is perpetually diminished, and diminishes the eccentricity.

*Corol.* 12. *Corol.* 13. *Corol.* 16. From this, if the shapes of the orbits and their inclination to one another are given, and if the sizes of the bodies, the forces, and the distances are changed in any way; from the given errors and the times of those errors in one case, the errors and the times of those errors in any other case can be gathered, very nearly: but more briefly by this method. These are the linear <term>errors</term><note>Newton uses "errors" to describe "perturbations"—the deviations from a perfect elliptical path caused by the pull of a third body like the Sun.</note> of body *P*; and from this, the angular errors viewed from the center *T* (that is, both the motion of the <term>apsis</term><note>original: "augis"—the point in an orbit where the body is closest to or farthest from the center.</note> and the <term>nodes</term><note>The two points where the orbit of a satellite crosses the plane of the larger body's orbit.</note>, as well as all the apparent errors in longitude and latitude) are, in any revolution of body *P*, as the square of the time of revolution very nearly. ![A geometric diagram illustrating orbital mechanics and perturbations. A central circle represents the orbit of body P around center T, with points A, N, B, and J marked on or near the circle. And from this, the mean motion of the apsis will be in a given ratio to the mean motion of the nodes; and both motions will be directly as the periodic time of body *P* and inversely as the square of the periodic time of body *T*. By increasing or decreasing the <term>eccentricity</term><note>A measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> and the inclination of the orbit *PAB*, the motions of the apsis and nodes are not significantly changed, except where these same values are too great.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation of the forces acting on a satellite (body P) as it orbits a larger body (T), while both are influenced by a distant third body (S, usually the Sun). Newton is moving from abstract points to physical models, specifically preparing the reader to understand the tides and the precession of the equinoxes.</meta>

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

<margin>BOOK ONE.</margin>

->*Corol.* 17.<- However, since the line $LM$ is sometimes greater and sometimes smaller than the radius $PT$, let the <term>mean force</term><note>Newton is looking for an average or "mean" value for the perturbing force over the course of an orbit.</note> $LM$ be represented by that radius $PT$; and this will be to the mean force $SK$ or $SN$ (which may be represented by $ST$) as the length $PT$ is to the length $ST$. Moreover, the mean force $SN$ or $ST$, by which body $T$ is held in its orbit around $S$, is to the force by which body $P$ is held in its orbit around $T$, in a ratio compounded of the ratio of the radius $ST$ to the radius $PT$, and the squared ratio of the periodic time of body $P$ around $T$ to the periodic time of body $T$ around $S$. And by equality, the mean force $LN$ to the force by which body $P$ is held in its orbit around $T$ (or by which the same body $P$, in the same periodic time, could be revolved around any stationary point $T$ at the distance $PT$) is in that squared ratio of the periodic times. Therefore, given the periodic times along with the distance $PT$, the mean force $LM$ is given; and with that given, the force $MN$ is also given very nearly by the analogy of the lines $PT, MN$.

*Corol.* 18. By the same laws under which body $P$ revolves around body $T$, let us imagine several fluid bodies moving around the same $T$ at equal distances from it; then, having made these bodies touch, let them be joined into a <term>fluid ring</term><note>This is a brilliant conceptual leap: Newton models the Moon's orbit as a solid ring of water to explain how "tugs" from the Sun affect the whole system at once.</note>, circular and concentric with body $T$; and the individual parts of the ring, performing all their motions according to the law of body $P$, will approach closer to body $T$ and move faster in <term>conjunction and opposition</term><note>original: "syzygiis"—when the bodies are in a straight line, as in a New or Full Moon.</note> relative to body $S$, than in the <term>quadratures</term><note>The points in the orbit at a 90-degree angle from the Sun, like the Half Moon.</note>. And the <term>nodes</term> of this ring, or its intersections with the plane of the orbit of body $S$ or $T$, will be at rest in the syzygies; but outside the syzygies, they will move backward <note>original: "in antecedentia"—moving in the opposite direction to the body's primary orbital motion.</note>, and indeed most rapidly in the quadratures, and more slowly in other places. The inclination of the ring will also vary, and its axis will oscillate during each revolution, and once a revolution is completed, it will return to its original position, except insofar as it is carried around by the <term>precession of the nodes</term>.

*Corol.* 19. Now imagine the globe of body $T$, consisting of non-fluid matter, to be enlarged and extended out to this ring, and that it contains water in a channel excavated around its circumference, and revolves uniformly around its own axis with the same periodic motion. This liquid, being alternately accelerated and retarded (as in the previous corollary), will be faster in the syzygies and slower in the quadratures than the surface of the globe, and thus it will flow and ebb in the channel in the manner of the sea. If the attraction of body $S$ is removed, the water revolving around the stationary center of the globe will acquire no motion...

The reasoning is the same for a sphere stripped of its ring, which in the equatorial regions is either a little higher than near the poles, or consists of somewhat denser material. For that excess of matter in the equatorial regions takes the place of the ring. And although, however much the <term>centripetal force</term><note>The force pulling an object toward a center; here, gravity.</note> of this sphere is increased, all its parts are supposed to tend downward (in the manner of the gravitating parts of the Earth), nevertheless the phenomena of this and the preceding corollary will hardly be changed; except that the locations of the maximum and minimum heights of the water will be different. For the water is now held and remains in its orbit, not by its own centrifugal force, but by the channel in which it flows. And furthermore, force *LM* pulls the water downward most in the <term>quadratures</term><note>Points in the orbit at a 90-degree angle from the Sun.</note>, and force *KL* or *NM—LM* pulls the same water upward most in the <term>syzygies</term><note>Points where the bodies are in a straight line, such as New or Full Moon.</note>. And these forces combined stop pulling the water downward and begin pulling it upward in the <term>octants</term><note>The points halfway between a syzygy and a quadrature (45, 135, 225, and 315 degrees).</note> before the syzygies; and they stop pulling the water upward and begin pulling it downward in the octants after the syzygies. And from this, the maximum height of the water can occur in the octants after the syzygies, and the minimum height around the octants after the quadratures; except insofar as the motion of ascending or descending impressed by these forces either continues a little longer by the water's <term>inherent force</term><note>original: "vis insita"; Newton’s term for what we now call inertia—the tendency of an object to remain in motion.</note>, or is stopped a little sooner by the obstacles of the channel.

*Corol. 21.* By the same reasoning by which the redundant matter of the sphere near the equator causes the nodes to <term>regress</term><note>original: "regredi"; to move backward, or opposite to the direction of the orbit.</note>—and therefore this regression is increased by the growth of that matter, diminished by its reduction, and removed by its withdrawal—if more than the redundant matter is removed (that is, if the sphere is made flatter near the equator, or rarer than near the poles), a motion of the nodes <term>forward</term><note>original: "in consequentia"; moving in the same direction as the orbiting body.</note> will arise.

*Corol. 22.* And conversely from this, the composition of the sphere is known from the motion of the nodes. Specifically, if the sphere constantly maintains the same poles and the motion is <term>backward</term><note>original: "in antecedentia"; synonymous with regression.</note>, the matter is redundant near the equator; if it is forward, it is deficient. Suppose a uniform and perfectly round sphere first to be at rest in free spaces; then to be propelled by any impulse made obliquely against its surface, and from there to conceive a motion partly circular and partly in a straight line. Since this sphere is indifferent to all axes passing through its center, and is no more inclined toward one axis or one position of an axis than toward any other, it is clear that it will never change its axis, nor the inclination of its axis, by its own force. and, in that same part of the surface as before, by any new impulse; and since it makes no difference whether an impulse occurs earlier or later, it is evident that these two impulses, applied successively, will produce the same motion as if they had been applied at the same time. That is, the result is the same as if the globe had been struck by a single force composed of both (by <term>Corollary 2 of the Laws</term><note>original: "per legum corol. 2." Newton refers to his previously established laws of motion regarding the composition of forces.</note>), and therefore the motion is simple, around an axis given by its inclination. The reasoning is the same for a second impulse made in any other place on the <term>equator</term><note>The great circle around the sphere's middle, perpendicular to its axis.</note> of the first motion; as it is for a first impulse made in any place on the equator of the motion which the second impulse would have generated without the first; and therefore, this applies to both impulses made in any places whatsoever. These will generate the same circular motion as if they had been applied simultaneously and at once to the place where the equators of those motions (which they would have generated separately) intersect. Therefore, a <term>homogeneous</term><note>Uniform in structure or composition throughout.</note> and perfect globe does not retain multiple distinct motions, but combines all those impressed upon it and reduces them to one. As far as it is able, it always rotates with a simple and uniform motion around a single axis, given by an always unchanging inclination.

Furthermore, <term>centripetal force</term><note>The force that draws a body toward a center, such as gravity.</note> can change neither the inclination of the axis nor the speed of the rotation. If a globe is understood to be divided into two hemispheres by any plane passing through its own center and the center toward which the force is directed, that force will always urge both hemispheres equally; and therefore, it will not incline the globe in any direction regarding its rotational motion. 

But suppose that somewhere between the pole and the equator, a new mass of matter is added, piled up in the form of a mountain. This mass, by its perpetual effort to recede from the center of its motion <note>Newton is referring to what we now call centrifugal force.</note>, will disturb the motion of the globe. It will cause its poles to wander across its surface, describing circles around themselves and the point opposite to them. This irregularity of "wandering" will not be corrected unless that mountain is placed either at one of the poles—in which case (by Corollary 21) the <term>nodes</term><note>The points where the plane of the equator intersects the plane of the orbit.</note> of the equator will move forward; or on the equator itself, by which means (by Corollary 20) the nodes will move backward; or finally, by adding new matter on the other side of the axis so that the mountain is balanced as it moves. In this way, the nodes will either move forward or backward, depending on whether the mountain and this new matter are closer to the pole or the equator.

For the <term>accelerative attractions</term><note>original: "attractiones acceleratrices." This is the measure of the force that causes a specific acceleration at a given distance, similar to what we now call the "gravitational field strength" (g).</note> of all bodies *B, C, D* towards *A*, at equal distances, are equal to each other by hypothesis; and similarly, the accelerative attractions of all bodies towards *B*, at equal distances, are equal to each other. Now, the absolute attractive force of body *A* is to the absolute attractive force of body *B* as the accelerative attraction of all bodies towards *A* is to the accelerative attraction of all bodies towards *B*, at equal distances; and so is the accelerative attraction of body *B* towards *A* to the accelerative attraction of body *A* versus *B*. But the accelerative attraction of body *B* towards *A* is to the accelerative attraction of body *A* towards *B* as the mass of body *A* is to the mass of body *B*; because the <term>motive forces</term><note>original: "vires motrices." These are the total forces acting on a body (F = ma), as opposed to just the acceleration.</note>—which (by Definition 2, 7, and 8) are as the accelerative forces and the attracted bodies jointly—are here (by the <term>Third Law of Motion</term><note>The law stating that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.</note>) equal to each other. Therefore, the absolute attractive force of body *A* is to the absolute attractive force of body *B* as the mass of body *A* is to the mass of body *B*. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

**Corollary 1.** Hence, if each individual body of a system *A, B, C, D,* etc., considered separately, attracts all the others with accelerative forces that are inversely as the squares of the distances from the attractor; the absolute forces of all those bodies will be to each other as the bodies themselves.

**Corollary 2.** By the same argument, if each individual body of a system *A, B, C, D,* etc., considered separately, attracts all the others with accelerative forces that are either inversely or directly in the ratio of any power of the distances from the attractor, or which are defined according to any common law based on the distances from each attractor; it is established that the absolute forces of those bodies are as the bodies.

### *Scholium.*

By these propositions, we are led by the hand to an analogy between <term>centripetal forces</term><note>Forces that pull an object toward a center point, such as gravity.</note> and the central bodies toward which those forces are usually directed. For it is consistent with reason that forces directed toward bodies should depend on the nature and quantity of those bodies, as occurs in magnets. And whenever such cases occur, the attractions of bodies are to be estimated by assigning to each of their particles their own proper forces and by gathering the sums of those forces. 

I use the word <term>attraction</term> here in a general sense for any endeavor of bodies to approach each other: whether that endeavor arises from the action of the bodies themselves (either seeking each other out or agitating each other through <term>emitted spirits</term><note>original: "spiritus emissos." Newton is referencing older theories that matter "breathed out" invisible substances to pull things in; he mentions it to show his math works regardless of the physical mechanism.</note>), or whether it arises from the action of the <term>ether</term><note>A hypothesized invisible fluid filling space.</note>, or of air, or of any medium—whether corporeal or incorporeal—impelling the bodies floating within it toward one another in any way. In the same general sense, I use the word <term>impulse</term>, considering in this treatise not the types of forces or physical qualities, but the mathematical quantities and proportions, as I explained in the definitions. 

In mathematics, we must investigate the quantities and ratios of forces that follow from any given conditions. Then, when we descend into physics, these ratios are to be compared with <term>phenomena</term><note>Observed events in the natural world.</note>, so that it may become known which conditions of force correspond to each type of attractive body. And only then will it be safer to dispute about the types, causes, and physical explanations of forces. Let us see, therefore, with what forces spherical bodies, composed of particles that attract in the manner just explained, ought to act upon one another; and what motions follow from there.

# SECTION XII.

### *On the attractive forces of spherical bodies.*

## PROPOSITION 70. THEOREM 30.

*If equal <term>centripetal forces</term><note>Forces pulling toward a center.</note> tend toward the individual points of a spherical surface, decreasing in the <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>original: "duplicata ratione." This is the historical term for the "inverse square law," meaning if the distance doubles, the force becomes four times weaker (2 squared).</note> of the distances from those points: I say that a small body placed inside the surface is attracted by these forces in no direction.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle representing a spherical surface labeled HIKL. A point P is located inside the circle, to the left of the center. Two straight lines, HK and IL, intersect at point P and extend to the circle's circumference, defining two small arcs HI on the left and KL on the right.</image-desc>

Let *HIKL* be that spherical surface, and *P* the small body placed within. Through *P*, let two lines *HK* and *IL* be drawn to this surface, intercepting very small arcs *HI* and *KL*; and, because the triangles *HPI* and *LPK* are similar (by Corollary 3, Lemma 7), those arcs will be proportional to the distances *HP* and *LP*; and any particles of the spherical surface at *HI* and *KL*, bounded on all sides by lines passing through point *P*, will be in that duplicate ratio. Therefore, the forces of these particles exerted on body *P* are equal to each other. For they are as the particles directly, and the squares of the distances inversely. And these two ratios combine to form a ratio of equality. Therefore, the attractions, being made equally in opposite directions, destroy each other. And by a similar argument, all attractions throughout the entire spherical surface are destroyed by contrary attractions. Consequently, the body *P* is impelled in no direction by these attractions. <term>Q. E. D.</term><note>Abbreviation for "Quod Erat Demonstrandum," Latin for "which was to be demonstrated." It marks the end of a mathematical proof.</note>

Let the perpendiculars *SD*, *sd*; *SE*, *se*; and *IR*, *ir* be dropped to these lines; of these, let *SD* and *sd* cut *PL* and *pl* at *F* and *f*. This refers to Newton’s method of limits, where the angles are made infinitesimally small to perform calculus-like calculations using geometry.</note>; and because *DS* and *ds* are equal, as are *ES* and *es*, let the lines *PE*, *PF* and *pe*, *pf*, and the small lines *DF*, *df* be considered equal; for their <term>ultimate ratio</term><note>The ratio they reach as they both approach zero.</note>, as the angles *DPE* and *dpe* vanish together, is a ratio of equality.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two spheres represented by circles and arcs. On the left, a point P is outside a large circle with center S and diameter AB. Lines PHK and PIL are drawn from P to the circle, with various perpendiculars and intersections labeled D, E, F, H, I, K, L, Q, R. On the right, a smaller, identical construction is shown with point p, center s, diameter ab, and corresponding points labeled with lowercase letters: d, e, f, h, i, k, l, q, r.</image-desc>

These things being established, *PI* will be to *PF* as *RI* is to *DF*, and *pf* will be to *pi* as *df* (or *DF*) is to *ri*; and by compounding the ratios, *PI times pf* is to *PF times pi* as *RI* is to *ri*, which is (by Corollary 3, Lemma 7) as arc *IH* is to arc *ih*. Again, *PI* is to *PS* as *IQ* is to *SE*, and *ps* is to *pi* as *se* (or *SE*) is to *iq*; and by compounding, *PI times ps* is to *PS times pi* as *IQ* is to *iq*. And by combining these ratios, *PI squared times pf times ps* is to *pi squared times PF times PS* as *IH times IQ* is to *ih times iq*; that is, as the <term>circular surface</term><note>A ring-shaped area on the sphere.</note> which the arc *IH* describes by the <term>revolution of the semicircle</term><note>original: "convolutione semicirculi." This describes the process of generating a 3D surface (a sphere or a zone of a sphere) by rotating a 2D curve around an axis.</note> *AKB* around the diameter *AB*, is to the circular surface which the arc *ih* describes by the revolution of the semicircle *akb* around the diameter *ab*. And the forces with which these surfaces attract the small bodies *P* and *p* along lines tending toward themselves are (by hypothesis) directly as the surfaces themselves, and inversely as the squares of the distances of the surfaces from the bodies, that is, as *pf times ps* to *PF times PS*. ## PROPOSITION LXXII. THEOREM XXXII.

*If equal centripetal forces tend toward the individual points of any sphere, decreasing in the <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>The inverse square law ($1/d^2$).</note> of the distances from those points; and both the density of the sphere and the ratio of the sphere’s diameter to the distance of the small body from its center are given: I say that the force by which the small body is attracted will be proportional to the <term>semidiameter</term><note>The radius of the sphere.</note> of the sphere.*

For conceive two small bodies to be attracted separately by two spheres, one by one sphere and the second by the other, and let their distances from the centers of the spheres be proportional to the diameters of the spheres respectively, and let the spheres be resolved into particles that are similar and similarly placed in relation to the small bodies. Then the attractions of one small body, directed toward the individual particles of the first sphere, will be to the attractions of the other body toward the many analogous particles of the second sphere, in a ratio compounded of the ratio of the particles directly and the duplicate ratio of the distances inversely. But the particles are as the spheres, that is, in the <term>triplicate ratio</term><note>The ratio of the cubes ($d^3$); Newton is noting that volume/mass scales with the cube of the size.</note> of the diameters, and the distances are as the diameters; and the former ratio directly, combined with the latter ratio twice inversely, is the ratio of diameter to diameter. <term>Which was to be demonstrated.</term><note>original: "Q.E.D."</note>

*Corollary 1.* From this, if <term>little bodies</term><note>original: "corpuscula." Newton uses this term to refer to point-masses or infinitesimal particles of matter.</note> revolve in circles around spheres composed of matter that is equally attractive, and the distances from the centers of the spheres are proportional to their respective diameters: then the periodic times will be equal.

*Corollary 2.* And conversely, if the periodic times are equal, the distances will be proportional to the diameters. These two points are established by Corollary 3 of Proposition 4.

*Corollary 3.* If toward every individual point of any two similar and equally dense solids there tend equal centripetal forces decreasing in the <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>The "duplicate ratio" refers to the inverse square law ($1/d^2$), where the force of gravity weakens according to the square of the distance.</note> of the distances from those points; the forces with which little bodies, situated similarly in relation to those two solids, are attracted by them, will be to each other as the diameters of the solids.

# PROPOSITION LXXIII. THEOREM XXXIII.

*If toward the individual points of any given sphere there tend equal centripetal forces decreasing in the duplicate ratio of the distances from the points: I say that a little body placed inside the sphere is attracted by a force proportional to its distance from the sphere's center.*

## PROPOSITION LXXIV. THEOREM XXXIV.

*The same things being granted, I say that a <term>little body</term><note>original: "corpusculum." Newton uses this term to refer to an idealized point-mass or a particle of matter.</note> situated outside a sphere is attracted by a force inversely proportional to the square of its distance from the sphere’s center.*

For let the sphere be divided into innumerable concentric spherical surfaces, and the attractions of the little body arising from the individual surfaces will be inversely proportional to the square of the distance of the little body from the center (by Proposition 71). And by combining them, the sum of the attractions—that is, the attraction of the little body toward the whole sphere—will be in the same ratio.
*Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Corollary 1.* Hence, at equal distances from the centers of uniform spheres, the attractions are as the spheres <note>That is, the force is proportional to the volume (and thus the mass) of the spheres.</note>. For (by Proposition 72) if the distances are proportional to the diameters of the spheres, the forces will be as the diameters. Let the greater distance be diminished in that ratio; and, with the distances now made equal, the attraction will be increased in that <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>The "duplicate ratio" refers to the square of the ratio (inverse square law).</note>; and therefore it will be to the other attraction in that <term>triplicate ratio</term><note>The "triplicate ratio" refers to the cube of the ratio ($x^3$). In geometry, volumes of similar solids are in the triplicate ratio of their diameters.</note>, that is, in the ratio of the spheres.

*Corollary 2.* At any distances, the attractions are as the spheres <term>applied to</term><note>In early modern mathematics, "applied to" often means divided by ($Sphere / distance^2$).</note> the squares of the distances.

*Corollary 3.* If a little body, placed outside a uniform sphere, is attracted by a force inversely proportional to the square of its distance from the center, and the sphere consists of attractive particles, the force of each individual particle will decrease in the duplicate ratio of the distance from that particle.

*...points; I say that any other similar sphere is attracted by that same sphere with a force inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centers.*

For the attraction of any particle is inversely as the square of its distance from the center of the attracting sphere (by Proposition 74); and therefore the attraction is the same as if the entire attracting force emanated from a single <term>little body</term><note>original: "corpusculo." Newton uses this to describe an idealized point-mass.</note> situated in the center of this sphere. Moreover, this attraction is as great as the attraction of that same little body would be in turn, if it were attracted by the individual particles of the attracted sphere with the same force by which it attracts them. And that attraction of the little body would be (by Proposition 74) inversely proportional to the square of its distance from the center of the sphere; and therefore the attraction of the sphere, which is equal to this, is in the same ratio. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Corollary 1.* The attractions of spheres toward other <term>homogeneous</term><note>spheres made of the same uniform material throughout.</note> spheres are as the attracting spheres <note>meaning their masses or volumes</note> divided by the squares of the distances of their centers from the centers of those which they attract.

*Corollary 2.* The same holds true when the attracted sphere also attracts. For each individual point of the one will attract each individual point of the other with the same force by which they are in turn attracted; and therefore, since in every attraction (by the 3rd Law of Motion) both the attracting point and the attracted point are urged toward each other, the force of mutual attraction will be doubled, while the proportions are preserved.

*Corollary 3.* All the same things that were demonstrated above concerning the motion of bodies about the <term>focus</term><note>original: "umbilicum." In geometry, the focus of an ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola.</note> of <term>conic sections</term><note>The curves—circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas—formed by intersecting a cone with a plane. This refers to planetary orbits.</note> hold true when the attracting sphere is located at the focus and the bodies move outside the sphere.

*Corollary 4.* However, those things which are demonstrated concerning the motion of bodies about the center of conic sections hold true when the motions are performed inside the sphere.

### PROPOSITION 78. THEOREM 38.

*If spheres are in any way dissimilar and unequal as one moves from the center to the circumference, but are everywhere similar at any given distance from the center as one moves around it; and the attractive force of each point is as the distance of the attracted body: I say that the total force with which two such spheres attract each other is proportional to the distance between the centers of the spheres.*

This is demonstrated from the preceding proposition in the same way that Proposition 76 was demonstrated from Proposition 75. <note>Newton is applying the logic of "layering"—even if the sphere's density changes like the layers of an onion, as long as each layer is uniform, the math holds.</note>

### L E M M A  XXIX.

*If, with center S, any circle AEB is described, and with center P, two circles EF and ef are described, intersecting the former at E and e, and the line PS at F and f; and perpendiculars ED and ed are dropped to PS: I say that, if the distance of the arcs EF and ef is understood to be diminished to infinity, the ultimate ratio of the <term>evanescent line</term><note>A "vanishing" line that is becoming infinitely small as it approaches zero; this is Newton's way of describing a differential or a "limit" in calculus.</note> Dd to the evanescent line Ff is the same as that of the line PE to the line PS.*

For if the line *Pe* cuts the arc *EF* at *q*; and the straight line *Ee*, which coincides with the <term>evanescent arc</term><note>An arc so small that it effectively behaves like a straight line.</note> *Ee*, meets the line *PS* at *T* when extended; and from *S*, a <term>perpendicular</term><note>A line meeting another at a 90-degree angle.</note> *SG* is dropped to *PE*: on account of the <term>similar triangles</term><note>Triangles that have the same shape but different sizes; their corresponding angles are equal and their sides are proportional.</note> *DTE*, *dTe*, and *DES*; *Dd* will be to *Ee* as *DT* is to *TE*, or as *DE* is to *ES*;

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating a lemma concerning evanescent lines and ratios. A large circle AEB is centered at point S on a horizontal line. Point P lies on the same horizontal line to the left of the circle. Two concentric circular arcs EF and ef, centered at P, are drawn very close together, intersecting the circle AEB at points E and e respectively. Perpendicular lines ED and ed are dropped from these intersection points to the horizontal line PS at points D and d. Points F and f are where the arcs EF and ef cross the horizontal line PS. A chord Ee is extended to intersect the horizontal line at point T. A line SG is drawn from center S perpendicular to the line PE at point G. A point q is marked on the arc EF where the line Pe intersects it.</image-desc>

and on account of the triangles *Eeq* and *ESG* being similar (by Lemma 8 and Corollary 3 of Lemma 7), *Ee* will be to *eq* (which is the same as *Ff*) as *ES* is to *SG*; and by equality of ratios, *Dd* will be to *Ff* as *DE* is to *SG*; that is (on account of the similar triangles *PDE* and *PGS*) as *PE* is to *PS*. <note>original: "Q.E.D." (Quod Erat Demonstrandum)</note> *Which was to be demonstrated.*

### PROPOSITION 79. THEOREM 39.

*If a surface, just about to vanish because its width is infinitely diminished, E F f e, by its rotation around the axis P S, describes a spherical concavo-convex solid <note>This refers to a thin spherical shell or layer.</note>, toward each of whose equal particles equal <term>centripetal forces</term><note>A force that pulls an object toward a center point; here, it acts like gravity.</note> tend: I say that the force with which that solid attracts a <term>corpuscle</term><note>A "corpuscle" is Newton's term for a tiny, point-like particle of matter.</note> situated at P, is in a ratio composed of the ratio of the solid D E squared × F f, and the ratio of the force with which a given particle in location F f would attract the same corpuscle.*

For if we first consider the force of the spherical surface *F E*, which is generated by the rotation of the arc *F E*, and is cut anywhere by the line *d e* at *r*; the <term>annular</term><note>Ring-shaped.</note> part of the surface, generated by the rotation of the arc *r E*, will be as the small line *D d*, while the radius of the sphere *P E* remains constant (as Archimedes demonstrated in his book <note>original: "de Sphæra & Cylindro"</note> *On the Sphere and Cylinder*). And the force of this part—exerted along the lines *P E* or *P r* situated everywhere on a conical surface—is as this very annular part of the surface; that is, as the small line *D d*, or, what is the same, as the rectangle formed by the given radius of the sphere *P E* and that small line *D d*. 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle with a horizontal axis passing through points P, A, S, D, d, F, f, and B. Point P is outside the circle to the left. S is the center of the circle. Points E and e are located on the upper circumference. Lines connect point P to E and e. Vertical lines drop from E to D and from e to d on the axis. The arc segment between E and e contains points F and f.</image-desc>

But along the line *P S* tending toward the center *S*, the force is smaller in the ratio of *P D* to *P E*, and therefore is as *P D x D d*. Now, let the line *D F* be understood to be divided into innumerable equal particles, each of which may be called *D d*; and the surface *F E* will be divided into just as many equal rings, whose forces will be as the sum of all the products *P D x D d*, that is, as 1/2 *P F squared* — 1/2 *P D squared*, and therefore as *D E squared*. Now let the surface *F E* be multiplied into the height *F f*; and the force of the solid *E F f e* exerted on the corpuscle *P* will become as *D E squared x F f*: assuming the force is given which any given particle *F f* at the distance *P F* exerts on the corpuscle *P*. But if that force is not given, the force of the solid *E F f e* will be as the solid *D E squared x F f* and that non-given force combined. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

## PROPOSITION 80. THEOREM 40.

*If, toward each of the equal particles of some sphere* **ABE**, *described with center* **S**, *equal <term>centripetal forces</term><note>A center-seeking force, such as gravity.</note> tend; and to the axis of the sphere* **AB**, *in which some <term>corpuscle</term><note>A tiny, point-like particle of matter.</note>* **P** *is located, perpendiculars* **DE** *are erected from each point* **D**, *meeting the sphere at* **E**, *and on these [perpendiculars] lengths* **DN** *are taken, which are as the quantity* $\frac{DE^2 \times PS}{PE}$ *and the force which a particle of the sphere situated on the axis at the distance* **PE** *exerts on the corpuscle* **P**, *jointly: I say that the total force with which the corpuscle* **P** *is drawn toward the sphere is as the area* **ANB** *contained by the axis of the sphere* **AB**, *and the curved line* **ANB**, *which the point* **N** *continually touches.*

*Corollary* 1. From this, if the <term>centripetal force</term> tending toward each individual particle remains always the same at all distances, and *D N* is made to be as (*DE squared* $\times$ *P S$) / *P E*; then the total force by which the small body is attracted by the sphere will be as the area *A N B*.

*Corollary* 2. If the centripetal force of the particles is <term>inversely</term><note>meaning the force gets weaker as the distance increases.</note> as the distance of the small body attracted by them, and *D N* is made to be as (*DE squared* $\times$ *P S*) / *PE squared*; the force by which the small body *P* is attracted by the whole sphere will be as the area *A N B*.

*Corollary* 3. If the centripetal force of the particles is inversely as the <term>cube of the distance</term><note>A force that weakens very rapidly, specifically $1/r^3$.</note> of the small body attracted by them, and *D N* is made to be as (*DE squared* $\times$ *P S*) / *PE to the fourth power*<note>original: "PE q q," meaning the square of the square ($PE^2 \times PE^2$).</note>; the force by which the small body is attracted by the whole sphere will be as the area *A N B*.

## PROPOSITION 82. THEOREM 41.

*In a sphere described with center S and radius SA, if SI, SA, and SP are taken as continuous proportionals <note>This means the segments are in a geometric progression where the ratio of the first to the second is the same as the second to the third: SI/SA = SA/SP.</note>: I say that the attraction of a small body inside the sphere, at any place I, is to the attraction of the same body outside the sphere, at place P, in a ratio compounded of the square root <note>original: "subduplicata ratione"</note> of the distances from the center IS and PS, and the square root of the centripetal forces in those places P and I, tending toward the center.*

For instance, if the centripetal forces <term>centripetal forces</term> <note>Forces directed toward a center, like gravity pulling an object toward the middle of a planet.</note> of the particles of a sphere are inversely as the distances of the small body attracted to them; the force with which a small body situated at *I* is attracted by the whole sphere, will be to the force with which it is attracted at *P*, in a ratio compounded of the square root ratio <note>original: *subduplicata ratione*; this refers to the ratio of the square roots of the values.</note> of the distance *SI* to the distance *SP*, and the square root ratio of the centripetal force in place *I*, originating from some particle in the center, to the centripetal force in place *P* originating from the same particle in the center; that is, in the square root ratio of the distances *SI* and *SP* to each other reciprocally. # OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>
On the Motion of BODIES
</margin>

->Scholium<-

Having explained the attractions of spherical bodies, it would now be appropriate to proceed to the laws of attraction for certain other bodies likewise composed of attractive particles; however, treating these in detail is not strictly necessary for our purpose. It will suffice to subjoin certain more general propositions concerning the forces of bodies of this kind, and the motions arising from them, on account of their occasional use in philosophical matters.

## SECTION XIII.

->On the attractive forces of non-spherical bodies.<-

### PROPOSITION LXXXV. THEOREMA XLII.

*If the attraction of an attracted body becomes far stronger when it is contiguous to the attracting body than when they are separated by even the smallest interval, the forces of the particles of the attractor, as the attracted body recedes, decrease in a ratio greater than the <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>original: "plusquam duplicata distantiarum"; the "duplicate ratio" refers to the square of the distance ($1/d^2$). Newton is saying the force must fall off faster than gravity, perhaps as $1/d^3$ or $1/d^4$.</note> of the distances from the particles.*

For if the forces decrease in the duplicate ratio of the distances from the particles, the attraction toward a spherical body—because (by Prop. <term>LXXIV</term> <note>Proposition 74 proved that for a sphere, the force on an external point acts as if all mass were concentrated at the center.</note>) it is inversely as the square of the distance of the attracted body from the center of the sphere—will not be sensibly increased by contact. The increase at contact would be even less significant if the attraction, as the attracted body recedes, were to decrease in a smaller ratio. The proposition is therefore evident regarding <term>attractive spheres</term>. The same reasoning applies to concave spherical shells attracting external bodies. And the point is even more established in the case of shells attracting bodies placed within them, since the attractions are everywhere canceled throughout the cavities of the shells by contrary attractions (by Prop. <term>LXX</term> <note>Proposition 70 proved that a point inside a hollow shell feels no net gravitational force because the forces from all sides balance out.</note>), and therefore there are no such forces even in the moment of contact. If, from these spheres and spherical shells, any parts remote from the point of contact are removed, and new parts are added anywhere else, the shapes of these attractive bodies can be changed at will; yet the added or removed parts, being distant from the place of contact, will not notably increase the excess of attraction that arises from contact. Therefore, the proposition holds for bodies of all shapes. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

<meta>catchword: PROPO.</meta>

<summary>Newton explains that if an attractive force (like magnetism or cohesion) is significantly stronger at the point of contact than at a tiny distance away, that force must diminish much faster than the standard inverse-square law of gravity. This marks a transition from studying perfect spheres to studying how shape and proximity affect attraction.</summary>

<keywords>attraction, non-spherical bodies, inverse square law, duplicate ratio, contact force, Newton's Principia, Section 13</keywords>

MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK ONE.

## PROPOSITION 86. THEOREM 43.

*If the forces of the particles of which an attracting body is composed decrease, as the attracted body recedes, in a <term>triplicate ratio</term> <note>original: "triplicata ratione"; this refers to the inverse cube of the distance, or $1/d^3$.</note> or more than a triplicate ratio of the distances from the particles: the attraction will be far stronger at the point of contact than when the attractor and the attracted body are separated from each other by even the smallest interval.*

For it is established by the solution to Problem 41, as shown in the second and third examples, that the attraction increases toward infinity as the attracted <term>corpuscle</term> <note>A tiny particle of particle or "little body."</note> approaches such an attracting sphere. The same can be easily inferred, by comparing those examples with Theorem 41, regarding the attractions of bodies toward <term>concavo-convex shells</term> <note>original: "orbes concavo-convexos"; essentially hollowed-out spherical shells.</note>, whether the attracted bodies are placed outside the shells or inside their cavities. Moreover, by adding or subtracting any attractive matter anywhere outside the point of contact from these spheres and shells, so that the attracting bodies take on any assigned shape, the proposition will hold for all bodies in general. Which was to be demonstrated. <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod erat demonstrandum).</note>

## PROPOSITION 87. THEOREM 44.

*If two bodies similar to each other, and made of equally attractive matter, separately attract small corpuscles that are proportional to themselves and positioned similarly with respect to them: the <term>accelerating attractions</term> <note>original: "attractiones acceleratrices"; this refers to the gravitational field strength or the acceleration produced by the force, rather than the total force itself.</note> of the corpuscles toward the whole bodies will be as the accelerating attractions of the corpuscles toward their particles, which are proportional to the whole and similarly situated within the whole.*

For if the bodies are divided into particles that are proportional to the whole and situated similarly within the whole; then, as the attraction toward any particle of one body is to the attraction toward the corresponding particle in the other body, so are the attractions toward the individual particles of the first body to the attractions toward the individual corresponding particles of the second; and by combining them, so is the attraction toward the first whole body to the attraction toward the second whole body. Which was to be demonstrated.

<summary>Newton demonstrates that if attraction decreases at an inverse-cube rate (or faster), the force becomes infinitely strong at contact. He also establishes a scaling law: similarly shaped bodies of the same material exert proportional accelerative forces on similarly placed particles.</summary>
