*Corollary 1.* Therefore, if the attractive forces of the particles decrease, as the distances of the attracted <term>corpuscles</term> <note>Tiny particles or "little bodies."</note> increase, in the ratio of any power <note>original: "dignitatis"; in this context, it refers to a mathematical power or degree, such as squared or cubed.</note> of the distances; the accelerative attractions toward the whole bodies will be directly as the bodies themselves, and inversely as those powers of the distances. For example, if the forces of the particles decrease in a <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>The square of the distance ($1/d^2$).</note> of the distances from the attracted corpuscles, and the bodies are as $A$ cubed and $B$ cubed (and thus both the cubic sides of the bodies and the distances of the attracted corpuscles from the bodies are as $A$ and $B$): then the accelerative attractions toward the bodies will be as $\frac{A\ cubed}{A\ squared}$ and $\frac{B\ cubed}{B\ squared}$, which is to say, as those cubic sides $A$ and $B$. If the forces of the particles decrease in a <term>triplicate ratio</term> <note>The cube of the distance ($1/d^3$).</note> of the distances from the attracted corpuscles; the accelerative attractions toward the whole bodies will be as $\frac{A\ cubed}{A\ cubed}$ and $\frac{B\ cubed}{B\ cubed}$, which is to say, they will be equal. If the forces decrease in a <term>quadruplicate ratio</term> <note>The fourth power of the distance ($1/d^4$).</note>; the attractions toward the bodies will be as $\frac{A\ cubed}{A\ to\ the\ 4th}$ and $\frac{B\ cubed}{B\ to\ the\ 4th}$, which is to say, inversely as the cubic sides $A$ and $B$. And so on for the rest.

*Corollary 2.* From this, conversely, from the forces by which similar bodies attract corpuscles situated similarly to themselves, one can infer the ratio of the decrease of the particular attractive forces as the attracted corpuscle recedes; provided that the decrease is directly or inversely in some ratio of the distances.

...these forces [are represented] by the products **A** x **AZ** and **B** x **BZ**. Let **AB** be joined, and let it be cut at **G** so that **AG** is to **BG** as particle **B** is to particle **A**; and **G** will be the common <term>center of gravity</term><note>The point at which the entire weight of a body may be considered as concentrated.</note> of particles **A** and **B**. The force **A** x **AZ** (by Corollary 2 of the Laws <note>Referring to the introductory section of the Principia where Newton explains how to combine or resolve multiple forces into a single result.</note>) is resolved into forces **A** x **GZ** and **A** x **AG**, and the force **B** x **BZ** into forces **B** x **GZ** and **B** x **BG**. However, because the ratio of **A** to **B** is the same as the ratio of **BG** to **AG**, the forces **A** x **AG** and **B** x **BG** are equal; and therefore, since they are directed in opposite directions, they cancel each other out. The forces **A** x **GZ** and **B** x **GZ** remain. These tend from **Z** toward the center **G**, and together they compose the force (**A** + **B**) x **GZ**; that is, the same force as if the attractive particles **A** and **B** were located at their common center of gravity **G**, forming a sphere <note>original: "globum"; Newton often uses the term "globe" or "sphere" to represent a concentrated mass.</note> there.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a body bounded by points R, S, T, and V. A point Z is located outside the body to the left. Dotted lines extend from Z to points A and B inside the body. By the same argument, if a third particle **C** is added, and its force is combined with the force (**A** + **B**) x **GZ** tending toward center **G**; the resulting force will tend toward the common center of gravity of that sphere at **G** and particle **C**; that is, to the common center of gravity of the three particles **A, B, C**; and it will be the same as if the sphere and particle **C** were located at that common center, forming a larger sphere there. And so it proceeds to infinity. Therefore, the total force of all the particles of any body **RSTV** is the same as if that body, while maintaining its center of gravity, took on the shape of a sphere. *Which was to be demonstrated.* <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod erat demonstrandum).</note>

*Corollary.* From this, the motion of an attracted body **Z** will be the same as if the attracting body **RSTV** were spherical: and for that reason, if that attracting body either remains at rest or moves uniformly forward in a straight line; the attracted body will move in an ellipse having its center at the attractor’s center of gravity.

Therefore, the forces of the cone DPF and the conic segment EGCB are equal, and they cancel each other out due to their opposition. The same logic applies to all the matter located outside the innermost spheroid PCBM. Thus, the body P is attracted only by the innermost spheroid PCBM; and therefore (by Corollary 3, Proposition 72), its attraction is to the force with which body A is pulled by the entire spheroid AGOD, as the distance PS is to the distance AS. <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod Erat Demonstrandum - Which was to be demonstrated)</note>.

## PROPOSITION 93. THEOREM 47.

*If a solid is flat on one side and infinite in all other directions, and is composed of equal particles that attract equally, whose forces decrease as the distance from the solid increases according to any <term>power</term><note>Newton is referring to exponents, such as the square (power of 2) or cube (power of 3).</note> of the distances greater than the <term>quadratic</term><note>Meaning a power higher than 2, such as $1/r^3$ or $1/r^4$.</note>; and if a small body placed on either side of the plane is attracted by the force of the whole solid: I say that the attractive force of that solid, as the body moves away from its flat surface, will decrease in the ratio of a power whose <term>side</term><note>In this context, the "side" is the base value (the distance).</note> is the distance of the small body from the plane, and whose <term>index</term><note>An "index" is what we now call an exponent.</note> is three less than the index of the power of the distances.*

**Corollary 1.** From this, if the solid *LGIN* is bounded on both sides by two infinite parallel planes *LG* and *IN*; its attractive force becomes known by subtracting the attractive force of the further part *NIKO* (produced infinitely toward *KO*) from the attractive force of the whole infinite solid *LGKO*.

**Corollary 2.** If the further part of this infinite solid is discarded—when its attraction, compared with the attraction of the nearer part, is of almost no importance—the attraction of that nearer part will decrease, as the distance increases, as closely as possible in the ratio of the power $CG^{n-3}$.

**Corollary 3.** And hence, if any finite body that is flat on one side attracts a small body from the region of the middle of that plane, and the distance between the small body and the plane is very small compared to the dimensions of the attracting body; and if the attracting body consists of uniform particles whose attractive forces decrease in the ratio of any power of the distances greater than the <term>quadruplicate</term><note>The fourth power ($r^4$).</note>; then the attractive force of the whole body will decrease as closely as possible in the ratio of a power whose base is that very small distance, and whose exponent is three less than the exponent of the previous power. For a body consisting of particles whose attractive forces decrease in the ratio of the <term>triplicate</term><note>The third power ($r^3$).</note> power of the distances, the assertion does not hold; because, in this case, the attraction of that further part of the infinite body in the second corollary is always infinitely greater than the attraction of the nearer part.

<summary>Newton concludes the proof that the attraction of a semi-infinite solid follows a power law three degrees lower than the particle-to-particle force law. He also explains why this rule applies to finite bodies at very close range, provided the force law is sufficiently steep (greater than the inverse cube).</summary>

## Scholium.

If any body is drawn perpendicularly toward a given plane, and the motion of the body is sought from a given law of attraction: the problem is solved by seeking (through Prop. 39) the motion of a body descending in a straight line to this plane, and (through Corol. 2 of the Laws) by compounding <note>Combining two different motion vectors into one resultant path.</note> that motion with a uniform motion made along lines parallel to the same plane. And conversely, if the law of attraction toward a plane made along perpendicular lines is sought, under the condition that the attracted body moves in any given curved line, the problem is solved by working according to the example of the third problem.

However, the operations are usually shortened by resolving the <term>ordinates</term><note>In historical geometry, the "ordinate" (ordinatim applicata) refers to the vertical distance from a point on a curve to the base or x-axis.</note> into <term>converging series</term><note>What we now call a Taylor series or power series expansion; a method Newton pioneered to approximate complex functions.</note>. As if to the base *A* at any given angle an ordinate length *B* is applied, which is as any power of the base $A^{\frac{m}{n}}$ <note>original: "basis dignitas quælibet"</note>; and the force is sought by which a body, according to the position of the ordinate—either attracted toward the base or repelled from the base—can move in the curved line which the ordinate always touches at its upper limit: I suppose the base to be increased by the smallest possible part *O*, and I resolve the ordinate $\overline{A+O}|^{\frac{m}{n}}$ into an infinite series $A^{\frac{m}{n}} + \frac{m}{n} OA^{\frac{m-n}{n}} + \frac{mm-mn}{2nn} OOA^{\frac{m-2n}{n}}$ etc. and I suppose the force to be proportional to that term of this series in which *O* is of two dimensions <note>The term containing $O^2$. In Newton's fluxional calculus, the second-order term represents the acceleration or force.</note>, that is, the term $\frac{mm-mn}{2nn} OOA^{\frac{m-2n}{n}}$. Therefore, the sought force is as $\frac{mm-mn}{nn} A^{\frac{m-2n}{n}}$, or what is the same, as $\frac{mm-mn}{nn} B^{\frac{m-2n}{m}}$. For instance, if the ordinate touches a parabola, where $m = 2$ and $n = 1$: the force becomes as the given $2 B^0$, and therefore it will be given <note>Meaning the force is constant.</note>. With a given force, therefore, a body will move in a parabola, just as *Galileo* demonstrated. But if the ordinate touches a hyperbola, where $m = -1$ <note>original: "0 - 1"</note> and $n = 1$; the force becomes as $2 A^{-3}$ or $2 B^3$: and therefore by a force, which is as the cube of the ordinate, the body will move in a hyper-

<meta>The text cuts off mid-word "hyperbola" as indicated by the catchword "hyper-". This page introduces the application of Newton's "method of series" to celestial and terrestrial mechanics, specifically linking the geometric properties of curves to the physical forces that produce them.</meta>

<summary>Newton provides a general method for calculating the force required to make a body follow any specific curve by using binomial series expansions of the ordinates. He validates this by showing it results in a constant force for parabolas (Galileo's law) and a cubic force for hyperbolas.</summary>

<keywords>Scholium, law of attraction, converging series, binomial expansion, ordinates, Galileo, parabola, hyperbola, power of the base</keywords>

# SECTION 14.

## *Of the motion of very small bodies, which are driven by centripetal forces tending toward each of the parts of some large body.*

## PROPOSITION 94. THEOREM 48.

*If two similar media <note>Regions of different density or physical properties, such as air and water.</note>, separated from each other by a space bounded by parallel planes on both sides, and a body in its passage through this space is attracted or impelled perpendicularly toward either medium, and is not agitated or hindered by any other force; and if the attraction is everywhere the same at equal distances from either plane taken on the same side of it: I say that the sine of incidence <note>The ratio representing the angle at which the body enters the space.</note> onto either plane will be to the sine of emergence <note>The ratio representing the angle at which the body leaves the space.</note> from the other plane in a given <term>ratio</term><note>A fixed mathematical relationship or proportion.</note>.*

**Case 1.** Let *Aa* and *Bb* be two parallel planes. Let a body fall upon the first plane *Aa* along the line *GH*, and throughout its entire passage through the intermediate space let it be attracted or impelled toward the medium of incidence, and by that action let it describe the curved line *HI*, and emerge along the line *IK*. To the plane of emergence *Bb*, let the perpendicular *IM* be erected, meeting both the line of incidence *GH* produced <note>Extended in a straight line.</note> at *M*, and the plane of incidence *Aa* at *R*; and let the line of emergence *KI* produced meet *HM* at *L*. # PROPOSITION 95. THEOREM 49.

*The same conditions being assumed; I say that the velocity of the body before incidence is to its velocity after emergence, as the sine of emergence is to the sine of incidence.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing four parallel horizontal lines labeled Aa, Bb, Cc, and Dd from top to bottom. A diagonal line segment GH starts at a point G and ends at point H on line Aa. ### Scholium.

By the same method, one might proceed to three or more surfaces. However, for optical purposes, spherical figures are the most suitable. If the <term>objective glasses</term> <note>The main light-gathering lenses at the front of a telescope.</note> of telescopes were constructed from two spherical glasses shaped like shells and enclosing water between them, it might be possible for the errors of refraction—which occur at the outermost surfaces of the glass—to be corrected with sufficient accuracy by the refractions of the water. Such objective glasses are to be preferred to elliptical or hyperbolic glasses, not only because they can be formed more easily and accurately, but also because they refract <term>pencils of rays</term> <note>A 'pencil' is a technical term for a narrow beam of light rays coming from a single point.</note> located outside the axis of the glass more precisely.

Nevertheless, the different <term>refrangibility</term> <note>Newton's term for the discovery that different colors of light bend by different amounts, causing what we now call chromatic aberration (blurry color fringes).</note> of different rays is an obstacle that prevents optics from being perfected by spherical figures or any other figures whatsoever. Unless the errors arising from that source can be corrected, all the labor spent on correcting other errors will be unskillfully employed.

<summary>This page completes the proof for calculating the curvature of refracting surfaces and introduces Newton's observation that "different refrangibility" (color dispersion) is the primary obstacle to perfecting telescope lenses.</summary>

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY:
# ON THE MOTION OF BODIES
## BOOK TWO.

---

### S E C T I O N  I.

->*On the motion of bodies which are resisted in proportion to their velocity.*<-

### PROPOSITION I. THEOREM I.

->*For a body resisted in proportion to its velocity, the motion lost due to resistance is proportional to the distance traveled.*<-

For since the motion lost in each equal particle of time is as the velocity—that is, as the particle of the journey completed—it follows, <term>by addition</term> <note>original: *componendo*; a mathematical method of summing up the individual parts of a ratio to find the total.</note>, that the total motion lost over the entire time is as the total journey completed. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

*Corollary.* Therefore, if a body, stripped of all gravity, moves in free space by its <term>inherent force</term> <note>original: *vi insita*; this refers to the object's inertia, or its tendency to keep moving in a straight line.</note> alone; and if both the total motion at the start and the remaining motion after some distance has been traveled are known, then the total distance which the body can cover in an infinite time can be determined. For that total distance will be to the distance already traveled as the initial total motion is to the part of that motion which has been lost.

### L E M M A  I.

->*Quantities proportional to their own differences are continually proportional.*<-

Let A be to (A — B) as B is to (B — C) and C is to (C — D), and so on; then <term>by conversion</term> <note>original: *convertendo*; a geometric operation where if a:b = c:d, then a:(a-b) = c:(c-d).</note> it follows that A is to B as B is to C and C is to D, and so on. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

<meta>catchword: PROPOSITION</meta>

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Book Two of the Principia, shifting the focus from motion in a vacuum to motion through resisting mediums like air or water. Newton establishes the fundamental rule that when resistance is proportional to speed, the loss of momentum directly corresponds to the distance traveled.</summary>
<keywords>Book Two, fluid resistance, velocity, inertia, momentum, mathematical ratios, motion in mediums</keywords>

## PROPOSITION II. THEOREM II.

*If a body is resisted in proportion to its velocity, and the same moves by its inherent force alone through a uniform medium, and equal times are taken: the velocities at the beginnings of each time interval are in a geometric progression, and the distances described in each time interval are as the velocities.*

**Case 1.** Let time be divided into equal small parts; and if at the very beginnings of these parts a force of resistance acts with a single impulse, which is proportional to the velocity: the decrease in velocity in each small part of time will be as that same velocity. Therefore, the velocities are proportional to their differences, and for that reason (by Lemma 1, Book II) they are <term>continually proportional</term> <note>original: *continue proportionales*; this refers to a geometric progression where the ratio between successive terms remains constant (e.g., 8, 4, 2, 1).</note>. Consequently, if any equal time periods are composed of an equal number of these small parts, the velocities at the beginnings of those times will be as the terms in a continuous progression, which are taken <note>original: *per saltum*; by leaping or skipping.</note> by omitting an equal number of intermediate terms everywhere. However, the ratios of these terms are composed of the same ratios of the intermediate terms repeated equally, and therefore these composite ratios are also the same among themselves. Therefore, the velocities, which are proportional to these terms, are in a geometric progression. Now let those equal small parts of time be diminished and their number increased to infinity, so that the impulse of resistance is made continuous; the velocities at the beginnings of equal times, being always continually proportional, will in this case also be continually proportional. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

**Case 2.** And <term>by division</term> <note>original: *divisim*; a geometric method of comparing the differences of quantities to the quantities themselves.</note>, the differences of the velocities—that is, the parts of them lost in each time interval—are as the whole velocities: however, the distances traveled in each time interval are as the parts of velocity lost (by Proposition I, Book II) and therefore they are also as the whole velocities. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

**Corollary.** From this, if a hyperbola *BG* is described with <term>rectangular asymptotes</term> <note>original: *asymptotis rectangulis*; two lines at right angles that a curve approaches but never touches.</note> *AC* and *CH*, and *AB* and *DG* are perpendicular to the asymptote *AC*, and both the body's velocity and the resistance of the medium at the very start of motion are represented by any given line *AC*, but after some time has elapsed by the <term>indefinite line</term> <note>original: *lineam indefinitam*; a line segment whose length varies as the body moves.</note> *DC*: then the time can be represented by the area *ABGD*, and the distance...

## PROPOSITION III. PROBLEM I.

*To determine the motion of a body which, while it ascends or descends in a straight line in a uniform medium, is resisted in proportion to its velocity, and is acted upon by uniform gravity.*

When a body is ascending, let gravity be represented by any given rectangle $BACH$, and the resistance of the medium at the start of the ascent by the rectangle $BADE$, taken on the opposite side of the line $AB$. With the rectangular asymptotes <note>Rectangular asymptotes are fixed lines that a curve (like a hyperbola) approaches but never reaches, meeting at a 90-degree angle.</note> $AC, CH$, let a hyperbola be described passing through point $B$, cutting the perpendiculars $DE, de$ at $G, g$; then the body, in ascending for the time $DGgd$, will describe the space <note>In this context, "space" refers to the distance traveled.</note> $EGge$; in the time $DGBA$, it will describe the space of the entire ascent $EGB$; in the time $ABKI$, it will describe the space of descent $BFK$; and in the time $IKki$, the space of descent $KFfk$.

The velocities of the body (which are proportional to the resistance of the medium) in these periods of time will be $ABED, ABed$, zero, $ABFI, ABfi$ respectively; and the maximum velocity <term>terminal velocity</term> <note>original: *maxima velocitas*; the constant speed reached when the force of gravity is perfectly balanced by the resistance of the medium.</note> that the body can acquire by descending will be $BACH$.

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

<margin>BOOK TWO.</margin>

Let *AC* be to *AK*, or the rectangle *ABHC* to *ABkK*, as the force of gravity is to the resistance at the beginning of the second interval of time. If we then subtract the resistances from the force of gravity, the remaining areas *ABHC, KkHC, LlHC, MmHC*, etc., will represent the absolute forces <note>Newton uses "absolute forces" to describe the net force—the constant pull of gravity minus the opposing air resistance.</note> by which the body is urged at the beginning of each interval of time. Consequently, according to the second Law of Motion, these represent the increases in velocity—that is, the rectangles *Ak, Kl, Lm, Mn*, etc.—and are therefore (by Lemma 1, Book II) in a geometric progression <note>A geometric progression is a sequence of numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous one by a fixed, non-zero number.</note>. 

Therefore, if the straight lines *Kk, Ll, Mm, Nn*, etc., are extended until they meet the hyperbola at *q, r, s, t*, etc., the areas *ABqK, KqrL, LrsM, MstN*, etc., will be equal, and thus they are proportional to both the equal intervals of time and the constant forces of gravity. However, the area *ABqK* (by Corollary 3, Lemma VII, and Lemma VIII of Book I) is to the area *Bkq* as *Kq* is to half of *kq*, or *AC* to half of *AK*; that is, as the force of gravity is to the resistance in the middle of the first interval of time. By a similar argument, the areas *qKLr, rLMs, sMNt*, etc., are to the areas *qklr, rlms, smnt*, etc., as the forces of gravity are to the resistances in the middle of the second, third, and fourth intervals of time, and so on. 

Accordingly, since the equal areas *BAKq, qKLr, rLMs, sMNt*, etc., are proportional to the forces of gravity, the areas *Bkq, qklr, rlms, smnt*, etc., will be proportional to the resistances in the middle of each interval of time—which is to say (by our hypothesis) proportional to the velocities, and therefore to the spaces <note>In Newton's terminology, "space" (*spatium*) refers to the distance traveled.</note> described. If we take the sums of these proportional quantities, the areas *Bkq, Blr, Bms, Bnt*, etc., will be proportional to the total spaces described; and likewise, the areas *ABqK, ABrL, ABsM, ABtN*, etc., will be proportional to the times. Therefore, the body, while descending during any time *ABrL*, describes the space *Blr*; and in the time *LrtN*, it describes the space *rlnt*. **Which was to be demonstrated.** <note>original: "Q. E. D."</note> A similar demonstration applies to the motion described in the ascent. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

**Corollary 1.** Therefore, the maximum velocity that a body can acquire by falling is to the velocity acquired in any given time as the given force of gravity (which perpetually urges the body) is to the force of resistance which hinders it at the end of that time.

**Corollary 2.** If time increases in an arithmetic progression <note>An arithmetic progression is a sequence where the difference between consecutive terms is constant, like 1, 2, 3, 4.</note>, the sum of that maximum velocity and the velocity during ascent—as well as the difference between them during descent—decreases in a geometric progression.

**Corollary 3.** Furthermore, the differences between the spaces described in equal intervals of time decrease in that same geometric progression.

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK TWO.

### Scholium.

Furthermore, the hypothesis that the resistance of bodies is in the ratio of their velocity is more mathematical than natural. In mediums that lack all rigidity <note>original: "rigore omni vacant", referring to fluid mediums like air or water that offer no static resistance to being moved.</note>, the resistances of bodies are in a duplicate ratio <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>A historical mathematical term meaning the ratio of the squares ($v^2$).</note> of their velocities. Indeed, by the action of a faster body, a greater motion is communicated to the same quantity of the medium in less time, in proportion to the greater velocity; therefore, in an equal time, because of the greater quantity of the medium disturbed, the motion communicated is greater in a duplicate ratio; and resistance (by the second and third laws of motion) is as the motion communicated. Let us see, therefore, what kind of motions arise from this law of resistance.

---

## SECTION II.

->*On the motion of bodies that are resisted in a duplicate ratio of their velocities.*<-

### PROPOSITION 5. THEOREM 3.

> *If a body is resisted in the duplicate ratio of its velocity, and the same moves through a uniform <note>original: "similare", meaning a medium with consistent density throughout.</note> medium by its innate force <note>original: "sola vi insita", referring to its inertia or momentum without additional external propulsion.</note> alone; and if times are taken in a geometric progression proceeding from smaller terms to larger ones: I say that the velocities at the beginning of each of these times are in the same geometric progression inversely; and that the spaces described in each of those times are equal.*

### PROPOSITION VII. THEOREM V.

*Spherical bodies which are resisted in the <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>The ratio of the squares; for example, if velocity doubles, resistance quadruples.</note> of their velocities, will lose parts of their <term>motions</term> <note>In Newton’s physics, "motion" refers to momentum (mass multiplied by velocity).</note> proportional to the wholes in times which are as the initial motions directly and the initial resistances inversely; and they will describe spaces proportional to those times and initial velocities jointly.*

For the parts of the motions lost are as the resistances and the times jointly. Therefore, for those parts to be proportional to the wholes, the resistance and the time jointly must be proportional to the motion. Consequently, the time will be as the motion directly and the resistance inversely. Wherefore, if small intervals of time are taken in that ratio, the bodies will always lose parts of their motions proportional to the wholes, and therefore will retain velocities always proportional to their initial velocities. And because of the fixed ratio of the velocities, they will always describe spaces that are proportional to the initial velocities and the times jointly. <note>Which was to be demonstrated.</note>

*Corollary 1.* Therefore, if bodies of equal velocity are resisted in the duplicate ratio of their diameters: <term>homogeneous</term> <note>Bodies made of the same uniform material throughout.</note> spheres moved with any velocities whatever, by describing spaces proportional to their diameters, will lose parts of their motions proportional to the wholes. For the motion of any sphere will be as its velocity and its mass jointly—that is, as the velocity and the cube of the diameter; the resistance (by hypothesis) will be as the square of the diameter and the square of the velocity jointly; and the time (by this proposition) is in the former ratio directly and the latter ratio inversely—that is, as the diameter directly and the velocity inversely; and therefore the space, being proportional to the time and velocity, is as the diameter.

*Corollary 2.* If bodies of equal velocity are resisted in the <term>sesquiplicate ratio</term> <note>The ratio of the square root of the cubes, or the 3/2 power.</note> of their diameters: homogeneous spheres moved with any velocities whatever, by describing spaces in the sesquiplicate ratio of their diameters, will lose parts of their motions proportional to the wholes.

*Corollary 3.* And universally, if bodies of equal velocity are resisted in the ratio of any <term>power</term> <note>original: "dignitatis" — referring to a mathematical power or exponent.</note> of their diameters: the spaces in which homogeneous spheres, moved with any velocities whatever, will lose parts

# LEMMA II.

->*The <term>moment</term> <note>In this context, a "moment" is an infinitely small change in a variable—what we now call a differential ($dx$ or $dy$).</note> of any <term>generated quantity</term> <note>Original: "genitæ." Newton means any quantity produced by multiplication, division, or powers, such as $x \times y$ or $x^2$.</note> is equal to the moments of the individual generating sides multiplied by the indices of the powers of those same sides and their coefficients continually.*<-

I call a "generated quantity" any quantity which is produced from sides or terms in arithmetic by multiplication, division, and the extraction of roots; in geometry by the finding of either contents and sides, or extreme and mean proportionals, without addition and subtraction. Quantities of this kind are products, quotients, roots, rectangles, squares, cubes, square sides, cubic sides, and the like. These quantities—as being indeterminate and unstable, and as if increasing or decreasing by a perpetual motion or <term>flux</term> <note>Newton’s term for the rate of change; the root of his "calculus of fluxions."</note>—I consider here; and I understand their momentary increments or decrements under the name of **moments**: so that increments are held to be added or affirmative moments, and decrements to be subtracted or negative moments. Beware, however, of thinking of these as <term>finite particles</term> <note>Newton is emphasizing that these are "infinitesimals"—not small chunks of matter, but the very beginnings of a quantity as it starts to exist.</note>. Finite particles are not moments, but the quantities themselves generated from moments. They are to be understood as the just-now-nascent principles of finite—

...of magnitudes. For in this lemma, the magnitude of the moments is not considered, but rather the first proportion of them as they are born <note>original: *prima nascentium proportio*. This refers to the concept of limits—how variables behave as they just begin to change.</note>. It amounts to the same thing if, instead of moments, we use either the velocities of the increments and decrements (which may also be called the motions, changes, and <term>fluxions</term> <note>Newton's specific name for the rate of change or derivative.</note> of quantities) or any finite quantities proportional to these velocities. Moreover, the coefficient of each generating side is the quantity that arises by applying <note>In the mathematical language of the time, "applying" a product to a side meant dividing the product by that side.</note> the generated quantity to this side.

Therefore, the sense of the lemma is that if the moments, or the velocities of change proportional to them, of any quantities $A, B, C,$ etc., increasing or decreasing by a perpetual motion, are called $a, b, c,$ etc., then the moment or change of the generated rectangle $AB$ shall be $aB + bA$; and the moment of the generated solid $ABC$ shall be $aBC + bAC + cAB$; and the moments of the generated <term>powers</term> <note>original: *dignitatum*. Newton uses this to describe variables raised to an exponent.</note> $A^2, A^3, A^4, A^{1/2}, A^{3/2}, A^{1/3}, A^{2/3}, A^{-1}, A^{-2}, \text{ and } A^{-1/2}$ shall be $2aA, 3aA^2, 4aA^3, 1/2aA^{-1/2}, 3/2aA^{1/2}, 1/3aA^{-2/3}, 2/3aA^{-1/3}, -aA^{-2}, -2aA^{-3}, \text{ and } -1/2aA^{-3/2}$ respectively. And generally, that the moment of any power $A^{n/m}$ shall be $n/m \cdot aA^{\frac{n-m}{m}}$. Likewise, that the moment of the generated $A^2B$ shall be $2aAB + bA^2$; and the moment of the generated $A^3B^4C^2$ shall be $3aA^2B^4C^2 + 4bA^3B^3C^2 + 2cA^3B^4C$; and the moment of the generated $\frac{A^3}{B^2}$ or $A^3B^{-2}$ shall be $3aA^2B^{-2} - 2bA^3B^{-3}$: and so for the rest. The lemma is indeed demonstrated in this manner.

*Case 1.* Any rectangle $AB$ increased by a perpetual motion, when half of the moments $1/2a$ and $1/2b$ were lacking from the sides $A$ and $B$, was $A - 1/2a$ multiplied by $B - 1/2b$, or $AB - 1/2aB - 1/2bA + 1/4ab$; and as soon as the sides $A$ and $B$ are increased by the other halves of the moments, it becomes $A + 1/2a$ multiplied by $B + 1/2b$, or $AB + 1/2aB + 1/2bA + 1/4ab$. From this rectangle let the prior rectangle be subtracted, and the excess will remain $aB + bA$. Therefore, by the total increments of the sides $a$ and $b$, the increment of the rectangle $aB + bA$ is generated. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Case 2.* Let $AB$ be always equal to $G$, and the moment of the solid $ABC$ or $GC$ (by Case 1) will be $gC + cG$, that is (if $AB$ and $aB + bA$ are substituted for $G$ and $g$) $aBC + bAC + cAB$. And the reasoning is the same for a product composed of any number of sides. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

<summary>Newton defines the "Method of Fluxions" (calculus), specifically demonstrating the product rule and power rule for differentiation. He proves that the rate of change of a product of variables is found by summing the changes of each part multiplied by the other parts.</summary>

**Case 3.** Suppose the sides $A, B, C$ are always equal to one another; then for $A^2$, that is the <term>rectangle</term> <note>Newton uses "rectangle" to mean the product of two quantities.</note> $AB$, the moment $aB + bA$ will be $2aA$. For $A^3$, that is the solid $ABC$, the moment $aBC + bAC + cAB$ will be $3aA^2$. And by the same argument, the moment of any <term>power</term> <note>original: *dignitatis*. In early modern mathematics, this refers to a variable raised to an exponent.</note> $A^n$ is $naA^{n-1}$. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

**Case 4.** Since $1/A$ multiplied by $A$ is $1$, the moment of $1/A$ multiplied by $A$, together with $1/A$ multiplied by $a$, will be the moment of $1$, which is nothing <note>In calculus, the rate of change of a constant value is zero.</note>. Consequently, the moment of $1/A$ or $A^{-1}$ is $-a/A^2$. And generally, since $1/A^n$ multiplied by $A^n$ is $1$, the moment of $1/A^n$ multiplied by $A^n$ together with $1/A^n$ multiplied by $naA^{n-1}$ will be nothing. Therefore, the moment of $1/A^n$ or $A^{-n}$ will be $-na/A^{n+1}$. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

**Case 5.** And since $A^{1/2}$ multiplied by $A^{1/2}$ is $A$, the moment of $A^{1/2}$ multiplied by $2A^{1/2}$ will be $a$, by Case 3; therefore the moment of $A^{1/2}$ will be $a/(2A^{1/2})$ or $1/2 a A^{-1/2}$. **Case 6.** Therefore, the moment of any generated quantity $A^m B^n$ is the moment of $A^m$ multiplied by $B^n$, together with the moment of $B^n$ multiplied by $A^m$, which is $maA^{m-1} B^n + nbB^{n-1} A^m$; and this holds whether the <term>indices</term> <note>The exponents.</note> of the powers $m$ and $n$ are whole numbers or fractions, and whether they are positive or negative. The rule for a product of several powers is the same. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

### Scholium

In a certain letter to our countryman Mr. *J. Collins* <note>John Collins (1625–1683), a librarian and mathematician who acted as a hub for scientific correspondence in England.</note> dated December 10, 1672, when I had described the <term>method of tangents</term> <note>The method for finding the slope of a line touching a curve at a single point.</note> which I suspected was the same as the method of *Sluse* <note>René-François de Sluse (1622–1685), a mathematician whose work on tangents was published around the same time.</note> then not yet communicated; I added: *“This is one particular [case] or rather a corollary of a general method, which extends itself without any troublesome calculation, not only to drawing tangents to any curves, whether <term>geometric</term> or <term>mechanical</term> <note>"Geometric" curves were those defined by simple algebraic equations; "mechanical" (or transcendental) curves, like the cycloid, were considered more complex because they could not be expressed by standard algebra.</note>, whether respecting straight lines or other curves, but also to resolving other more abstruse types of problems concerning curvatures, areas, lengths, centers of gravity of curves, etc. nor (as is the method of *Hudde* <note>Johann Hudde (1628–1704), a Dutch mathematician who developed a rule for finding the maximum or minimum points of a polynomial.</note> concerning maxima and minima) is it restricted to those equations that are free from <term>surd</term> <note>An old term for irrational numbers or roots (like $\sqrt{x}$) that cannot be expressed as simple fractions.</note> quantities.”* I have interwoven this method with that other one by which I perform the explanation of equations by reducing them to infinite series. Thus far the letter. And these last words refer to a treatise which I had written on these matters in the year 1671. The foundation of this general method is contained in the preceding Lemma.

Since *AK* is as $AP^2$, the <term>moment</term> <note>An infinitely small change, similar to a differential in modern calculus.</note> of this, *KL*, will be as the moment of the other, $2 AP \times PQ$: that is, as *AP* multiplied by *KC*; for the increment of velocity *PQ* (by the Second Law of Motion) is proportional to the generating force *KC*.

But the ultimate ratio of the hyperbolic area *KNOL* to the rectangle $KL \times KN$, when the points *K* and *L* coincide, is one of equality. Therefore, that vanishing hyperbolic area is as *AP*. Thus, the whole hyperbolic area *ABOL* is composed of small parts *KNOL* always proportional to the velocity *AP*, and therefore it is proportional to the space described with that velocity. Now let that area be divided into equal parts *ABMI*, *IMNK*, *KNOL*, etc., and the absolute forces *AC*, *IC*, *KC*, *LC*, etc., will be in a geometric progression. <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod erat demonstrandum)</note> Which was to be demonstrated. And by a similar argument, in the ascent of the body, by taking equal areas *ABmi*, *imnk*, *knol*, etc., on the opposite side of point *A*, it will be established that the absolute forces *AC*, *iC*, *kC*, *lC*, etc., are continually proportional. And therefore if all the spaces in the ascent and descent are taken as equal, all the absolute forces *lC*, *kC*, *iC*, *AC*, *IC*, *KC*, *LC*, etc., will be continually proportional. Which was to be demonstrated.

*Corollary* 1. Hence, if the space described is represented by the hyperbolic area *ABNK*; the force of gravity, the velocity of the body, and the resistance can be represented [by the lines...].

## PROPOSITION 9. THEOREM 7. ##

*Based on what has already been demonstrated, I say that if the tangents of the angles of a circular sector and a hyperbolic sector are taken proportional to the velocities, with the radius being of the proper magnitude: then every time of ascending to the highest point will be as the sector of the circle, and every time of descending from the highest point will be as the sector of the hyperbola.*

Let the line $AD$ be drawn perpendicular and equal to the line $AC$, by which the force of gravity is represented. *Corollary 2.* The same follows also concerning the space described in an ascent. Namely, that the whole of that space is to the space described in the same time with a uniform velocity *AC*, as the area *ABnk* is to the sector *ADt*.

*Corollary 3.* The velocity of a body falling in time *ATD* is to the velocity which it would acquire in the same time in a non-resisting space <note>A vacuum or a theoretical space where no air resistance or friction exists.</note>, as the triangle *APD* is to the hyperbolic sector *ATD*. *Corollary 4.* By the same argument, the velocity in ascent is to the velocity by which a body in the same time in a non-resisting space could lose all its upward motion, as the triangle *ApD* is to the circular sector *AtD*; or as the straight line *Ap* is to the arc *At*.

*Corollary 5.* Therefore, the time in which a body acquires velocity *AP* by falling in a resisting medium is to the time in which it could acquire the maximum velocity *AC* <note>Terminal velocity; the constant speed reached when resistance equals the force of gravity.</note> by falling in a non-resisting space, as the sector *ADT* is to the triangle *ADC*: and the time in which it could lose velocity *Ap* by ascending in a resisting medium is to the time in which it could lose the same velocity by ascending in a non-resisting space, as the arc *At* is to its tangent *Ap*.

*Corollary 6.* Hence, from a given time, the space described in ascent or descent is given. For the maximum velocity of a body descending infinitely is given (by Corollaries 2 and 3 of Theorem 6, Book 2), and from that is given the time in which a body could acquire that velocity by falling in a non-resisting space. And by taking the sector *ADT* or *ADt* to the triangle *ADC* in the ratio of the given time to the time just found; there will be given both the velocity *AP* or *Ap*, and the area *ABNK* or *ABnk*, which is to the sector *ADT* or *ADt* as the space sought is to the space which can be uniformly described in the given time with that maximum velocity already found before.

*Corollary 7.* And by working backward <note>original: "regrediendo"</note>, from a given space of ascent or descent *ABnk* or *ABNK*, the time *ADt* or *ADT* will be given.

I distinguish series of this kind into successive terms in this manner. I call the first term that in which the <term>infinitely small quantity: a "fluxion" or "infinitesimal," a value so small it is almost zero, used to measure change at a specific point</term> $o$ does not appear; the second, in which that quantity is of one dimension <note>Meaning $o$ is raised to the first power ($o^1$).</note>; the third, in which it is of two dimensions; the fourth, in which it is of three; and so on to infinity. And the first term, which here is $e$, will always denote the length of the <term>ordinate: the vertical distance (y-coordinate) from the axis to a point on the curve</term> $CH$ standing at the beginning of the indefinite quantity $o$. The second term, which here is $\frac{ao}{e}$, will denote the difference between $CH$ and $DN$, that is, the small line $MN$, which is cut off by completing the parallelogram $HCDM$, and therefore always determines the position of the **tangent** $HN$; as in this case by taking $MN$ to $HM$ as $\frac{ao}{e}$ is to $o$, or $a$ to $e$. The third term, which here is $\frac{n^2 o^2}{2 e^3}$, will designate the small line $IN$, which lies between the tangent and the curve, and therefore determines the **angle of contact** $IHN$ or the **curvature** which the curved line has at $H$. If that small line $IN$ is of finite magnitude, it will be designated by the third term together with the following ones to infinity. But if that small line is diminished to infinity, the subsequent terms become infinitely smaller than the third, and therefore can be neglected. The fourth term determines the variation of curvature, the fifth the variation of the variation, and so on. From which, in passing, the not insignificant use of these series is evident in the solution of problems which depend on tangents and the curvature of curves.

But if the same body were to depart from location $P$, along a line perpendicular to $PQ$, and begin to move in the arc of the semicircle $PFQ$, the value $AC$ (or $a$) would have to be taken toward the opposite sides of the center $A$; and for that reason, its sign must be changed and written as $-a$ instead of $+a$. By this reasoning, the density of the medium would come out as $-\frac{a}{e}$. Nature, however, does not admit a **negative density**, that is, one which accelerates the motions of bodies; and therefore it cannot naturally happen that a body, by ascending from $P$, describes the quadrant of the circle $PF$. To achieve this effect, the body would have to be accelerated by an impelling medium, not hindered by a resisting one.

If the velocity is $V^n$ <note>Where $n$ represents the power or exponent of the velocity.</note>, the density of the medium will result as $\frac{S}{R^{\frac{4-n}{2}}} \times (\frac{AC}{HT})^{n-1}$. And therefore, if a curve can be found by that law, such that the ratio of $\frac{S}{R^{\frac{4-n}{2}}}$ to $(\frac{HT}{AC})^{n-1}$, or $\frac{S^2}{R^{4-n}}$ to $1+Q^2|^{n-1}$ is given: the body will move in this curve in a uniform medium with a resistance that is as the power of the velocity $V^n$. But let us return to simpler curves.

Since motion does not occur in a parabola except in a non-resisting medium <note>Newton refers to the idealized vacuum of Galilean physics, where only gravity acts on a body.</note>, whereas in the hyperbolas <note>A type of open curve formed by the intersection of a cone and a plane.</note> described here it occurs through perpetual resistance; it is clear that the line which a projectile describes in a uniformly resisting medium approaches these hyperbolas more closely than it does a parabola. That line is certainly of a hyperbolic kind, but one which, near the vertex <note>The highest or turning point of the curve.</note>, is further from the <term>asymptotes: lines that a curve approaches but never actually reaches</term>; in the parts further from the vertex, it approaches them more closely than the ratio of the hyperbolas I have described here requires. Yet the difference between these and that path is not so great that these cannot be used quite conveniently in practical matters in place of the more exact one. And these will perhaps be more useful than a more accurate and at the same time more complex hyperbola. Indeed, they shall be applied to use as follows.

*Rule 1.* If both the density of the medium at $A$ and the velocity with which the body is projected are kept the same, and the angle $NAH$ is changed; the lengths $AH, AI, HX$ will remain the same. *Rule 2.* If both the angle $NAH$ and the density of the medium at $A$ are kept the same, and the velocity with which the body is projected is changed; the length $AH$ will be preserved, and $AI$ will change in the reciprocal duplicate ratio <note>original: "duplicata ratione reciproce"; in modern terms, this means $AI$ is inversely proportional to the square of the velocity</note> of the velocity.

*Rule 4.* Since the density of the medium near the vertex of the hyperbola is greater than at position $A$; in order to obtain the average density, the ratio of the shortest of the tangents $GT$ to the tangent $AH$ must be found, and the density at $A$ should be increased in a ratio slightly greater than that of the half-sum of these tangents to the shortest tangent $GT$.

*Rule 5.* If the lengths $AH$ and $AI$ are given, and the figure $AGK$ is to be described: extend $HN$ to $X$, so that $HX$ is to $AI$ as $n + 1$ is to 1; and with center $X$ and <term>asymptotes</term> <note>The straight lines MX and NX that the curved hyperbola approaches but never touches.</note> $MX, NX$, let a hyperbola be described through point $A$, under the law that $AI$ is to any $VG$ as $XV^n$ is to $XI^n$.

Therefore, if the hyperbola is of this kind, and the point $K$—where the projected body falls upon any straight line $AN$ passing through point $A$—is sought: let the extended line $AN$ meet the asymptotes $MX$ and $NX$ at $M$ and $N$, and let $NK$ be taken equal to $AM$.

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES ###

<margin>BOOK TWO</margin>

...the hyperbola from observed phenomena. Let two similar and equal bodies be projected with the same velocity at different angles $HAK$ and $hAk$, and let them fall upon the horizontal plane at $K$ and $k$; then note the proportion of $AK$ to $Ak$. Let that ratio be $d$ to $e$. Then, having erected a perpendicular $AI$ of any length, assume a length for $AH$ or $Ah$ at will, and from there determine the lengths $AK$ and $Ak$ graphically using Rule 6. If the ratio of $AK$ to $Ak$ is the same as the ratio of $d$ to $e$, the length $AH$ was correctly assumed. If not, take a length $SM$ on an infinite line $SM$ <note>Newton is using a "graph within a graph" method. The line SM acts as a baseline to plot the errors of his guesses.</note> equal to the assumed $AH$, and erect a perpendicular $MN$ equal to the difference of the ratios $\frac{AK}{Ak} - \frac{d}{e}$ multiplied by any given line. By a similar method, from several assumed lengths of $AH$, multiple points $N$ are to be found, and a regular curved line $NNXN$ should be drawn through all of them, cutting the straight line $SMMM$ at $X$. Finally, let $AH$ be taken equal to the <term>abscissa</term> <note>The horizontal coordinate or distance along the baseline.</note> $SX$, and from this the length $AK$ is found once more; the lengths which are to the assumed length $AI$ and this final $AH$, as the length $AK$ known by experiment is to the last-found length $AK$, will be those true lengths $AI$ and $AH$ which were required to be found. With these values given, the resistance of the medium at position $A$ will also be given, since it is to the force of gravity as $AH$ is to $2AI$. However, the density of the medium must be increased by Rule 4, and the resistance just found, if increased in the same ratio, will become more accurate.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram used for a "method of false position." A horizontal baseline is labeled with points S, M, M, X, and M. Vertical lines (perpendiculars) rise from the M points to points labeled N. A smooth curve, labeled NNXN, connects these points and crosses the baseline at point X. This intersection point X represents the value where the error in the calculation becomes zero.</image-desc>

*Rule* 8. Having found the lengths $AH$ and $HX$; if the position of the line $AH$ is now required—according to which a projectile, launched with that given velocity, hits any point $K$: at points $A$ and $K$ let lines $AC$ and $KF$ be erected perpendicular to the horizon, of which $AC$ tends downward and is equal to $AI$ (or $\frac{1}{2}HX$). With $AK$ and $KF$ as <term>asymptotes</term> <note>The straight lines that a hyperbola approaches but never reaches.</note>, let a hyperbola be described whose <term>conjugate</term> <note>A secondary hyperbola that shares the same asymptotes and helps define the properties of the primary curve.</note> passes through point $C$; and with center $A$ and radius $AH$, let a circle be described cutting that hyperbola at point $H$; then the projectile launched along the line $AH$ will fall upon point $K$. <note>original: "Q. E. I." — Quod Erat Inveniendum; Which was to be found.</note> For point $H$, due to the given length $AH$, is located somewhere on the described circle. Let $CH$ be drawn meeting $AK$ and $KF$, the former at $E$ and the latter at $F$; and because $CH$ and $MX$ are parallel and $AC$ and $AI$ are equal, $AE$ will be equal to $AM$...

# SECTION III.

### *Of the motion of bodies that are resisted partly in the ratio of velocity, and partly in the square of the same.*

## PROPOSITION XI. THEOREM VIII.

*If a body is resisted partly in the ratio of the velocity, and partly in the square <note>original: "ratione duplicata," literally the duplicate ratio, meaning the square ($v^2$)</note> of the velocity, and the same moves by its inherent force alone in a uniform medium: and if times are taken in arithmetic progression; then quantities inversely proportional to the velocities, increased by a certain given quantity, will be in geometric progression.*

With center C and rectangular <term>asymptotes</term> <note>Lines that a curve approaches ever closer but never touches.</note> CADd and CH, let the hyperbola BEe be described, and let AB, DE, and de be parallel to the asymptote CH. On the asymptote CD, let points A and G be given. And if time is represented by the hyperbolic area ABED increasing uniformly; I say that the velocity can be represented by the length DF, whose reciprocal GD, together with the given length CG, composes the length CD, which increases in geometric progression.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a rectangular coordinate system with a vertical axis CH and a horizontal axis labeled with points C, G, A, D, and d. A hyperbolic curve BEe is drawn. Vertical lines AB, DE, and de connect the horizontal axis to the curve at points B, E, and e respectively. A vertical line segment DF extends downwards from point D on the horizontal axis. A horizontal line connects point H on the vertical axis to point E on the curve.</image-desc>

For let the small area DEed be a given very small increment of time, and Dd will be inversely as DE, and therefore directly as CD. Moreover, the decrease of 1/GD, which (by Lemma II of this book) is $Dd/GD^2$, will be as $CD/GD^2$ or $(CG + GD)/GD^2$, that is, as $1/GD + CG/GD^2$. Therefore, while the time ABED increases uniformly by the addition of the given particles <note>Small increments or differentials.</note> EDde, 1/GD decreases in the same ratio as the velocity. For the decrease in velocity is as the resistance, that is...

For, given the increment of space *EDde*, the small line *Dd*, which is the decrease of *GD* itself, will be reciprocally as *ED*, and therefore directly as *CD*, that is, as the sum of that same *GD* and the given length *CG*. But the decrease in velocity—in a time reciprocally proportional to the velocity, during which the given particle of space *DdeE* is described—is as the resistance and the time combined. *Corollary 3.* Hence, since (by Proposition 11) the velocity is determined from a given time, and by this proposition the space is determined from a given velocity, the space will be determined from a given time: and vice versa.

For since $AK$ is as the resistance, that is, as the square of $AP$ plus twice the rectangle $BAP$; let any given quantity $Z$ be assumed, and let $AK$ be set equal to $\frac{AP^2 + 2BAP}{Z}$; and (by Lemma II of this book) the momentum <note>In Newton’s calculus, a "momentum" is an infinitely small change in a quantity.</note> $KL$ of $AK$ itself will be equal to $\frac{2AP\dot{Q} + 2BA \times P\dot{Q}}{Z}$ or $\frac{2BP\dot{Q}}{Z}$ <note>The dot over the Q indicates a "fluxion," or the rate of change of the quantity Q.</note>, and the momentum $KLON$ of the area $AbNK$ will be equal to $\frac{2BP\dot{Q} \times LO}{Z}$ or $\frac{BP\dot{Q} \times BD^3}{2Z \times CK \times AB}$.

*Case 1.* Now if the body ascends, and gravity is as the sum of the squares $AB^2 + BD^2$, where $BET$ is a circle (in the first figure), the line $AC$, which is proportional to gravity, will be $\frac{AB^2 + BD^2}{Z}$, and $DP^2$ or $AP^2 + 2BAP + AB^2 + BD^2$ will be $AK \times Z + AC \times Z$ or $CK \times Z$; and therefore the area $DTV$ will be to the area $DP\dot{Q}$ as the square $DT^2$ or $DB^2$ is to $CK \times Z$.

*Case 2.* But if the body ascends, and gravity is as the difference of the squares $AB^2 - BD^2$, the line $AC$ (in the second figure) will be $\frac{AB^2 - BD^2}{Z}$, and $DT^2$ will be to the area $DP\dot{Q}$ as $DF^2$ or $DB^2$ is to $BP^2 - BD^2$ or $AP^2 + 2BAP + AB^2 - BD^2$, that is, to $AK \times Z + AC \times Z$ or $CK \times Z$. And therefore the area $DTV$ will be to the area $DP\dot{Q}$ as $DB^2$ is to $CK \times Z$.

*Case 3.* And by the same argument, if the body descends, and for that reason gravity is as the difference $BD^2 - AB^2$, and the line $AC$ (in the third figure) is equal to $\frac{BD^2 - AB^2}{Z}$, the area $DTV$ will be to the area $DP\dot{Q}$ as $DB^2$ is to $CK \times Z$: as above.

### Scholium.

The resistance of spherical bodies in fluids arises partly from tenacity, partly from friction, and partly from the density of the medium. And that part of the resistance which arises from the density of the fluid, we have said is in the duplicate ratio <note>original: "duplicata ratione"; this refers to the square of the velocity ($v^2$)</note> of the velocity; the other part, which arises from the tenacity <note>Tenacity refers to the viscosity or internal cohesiveness of the fluid</note> of the fluid, is uniform, or as the moment of time <term>moment of time: an infinitesimal increment of time, similar to $dt$ in modern calculus</term>: and therefore one might now proceed to the motion of bodies that are resisted partly by a uniform force (that is, in the ratio of the moments of time) and partly in the duplicate ratio of the velocity. 

But it is enough to have opened the way to this investigation in Propositions VIII and IX, which precede, and in their corollaries. In those instances, certainly, in place of the uniform resistance of an ascending body which arises from its gravity, one can substitute the uniform resistance which arises from the tenacity of the medium when the body is moved by its innate force <note>Newton uses "vis insita" to refer to inertia—the inherent power of a body to continue in its state of motion</note> alone; and when the body ascends in a straight line, one may add this uniform resistance to the force of gravity, and subtract the same when the body descends in a straight line. One might also proceed to the motion of bodies which are resisted partly uniformly, partly in the ratio of the velocity, and partly in the duplicate ratio of the velocity. And I have opened the way in the preceding Propositions XIII and XIV, in which also the uniform resistance arising from the tenacity of the medium can be substituted for the force of gravity, or combined with it, as before. But I hasten to other matters.

*Corollary 1.* The velocity at any location $P$ is always the same as that with which a body could revolve in a circle in a non-resisting medium, given the same centripetal force and the same distance $SP$ from the center.

*Corollary 2.* The density of the medium, if the distance $SP$ is known, is proportional to $\frac{OS}{OP}$; however, if that distance is not fixed, it is proportional to $\frac{OS}{OP \times SP}$. Consequently, a spiral path can be matched to any given density of a medium.

*Corollary 3.* The force of resistance at any location $P$ is to the centripetal force at that same location as $\frac{1}{2}OS$ is to $OP$. For those forces are to each other as $\frac{1}{2}Rr$ and $TQ$, or as $\frac{\frac{1}{4}VQ \times PQ^2}{SQ}$ and $\frac{\frac{1}{2}PQ^2}{SP}$; that is, as $\frac{1}{2}VQ$ and $PQ$, or $\frac{1}{2}OS$ and $OP$. Thus, if the spiral is given, the proportion of the resistance to the centripetal force is also given; and conversely, if that proportion is given, the spiral is determined.

*Corollary 4.* Therefore, a body cannot revolve in this spiral unless the force of resistance is less than half of the centripetal force. If the resistance were to become equal to half of the centripetal force, the spiral would coincide with the straight line $PS$, and the body would descend toward the center along this line. In this case, the velocity would be to the velocity of descent in a non-resisting medium (which we proved previously in the case of a parabola in Theorem 10, Book 1) in the square root ratio <term>subduplicata ratio: the square root of a ratio</term> of one to two. And the times of descent here will be inversely proportional to the velocities, and are therefore determined.

*Corollary 5.* And since at equal distances from the center the velocity is the same in the spiral $PQR$ as it is in the straight line $SP$, and the length of the spiral is in a given ratio to the length of the straight line $PS$ (namely, the ratio of $OP$ to $OS$);

truly the times will be directly as the perimeters of the orbits *AEB, BFC, CGD,* etc., and inversely as the velocities at the beginnings *A, B, C*; that is, as *AS*<sup>3/2</sup>, *BS*<sup>3/2</sup>, *CS*<sup>3/2</sup>. <note>Newton is applying Kepler’s Third Law logic here; since velocity in these orbits is inversely proportional to the square root of the distance, the time for a revolution relates to the distance raised to the power of 3/2.</note> And the total time, in which the body will reach the center, will be to the time of the first revolution, as the sum of all the <term>continued proportionals: a geometric progression where each term has a constant ratio to the one before it</term> *AS*<sup>3/2</sup>, *BS*<sup>3/2</sup>, *CS*<sup>3/2</sup>, proceeding to infinity, is to the first term *AS*<sup>3/2</sup>; that is, as that first term *AS*<sup>3/2</sup> is to the difference of the first two *AS*<sup>3/2</sup> — *BS*<sup>3/2</sup>, or as 2/3 *AS* to *AB* very nearly. <note>original: "quam proxime"</note> From which that total time is easily found.

*Corollary 8.* From these things one may also approximately gather the motions of bodies in mediums whose density is either uniform, or observes any other assigned law. With center *S*, and at continued proportional intervals *SA, SB, SC,* etc., describe any number of circles, and suppose the time of the revolutions between the perimeters of any two of these circles in the medium of which we have treated <note>This refers to the medium where density is inversely proportional to the distance from the center.</note>, to be to the time of the revolutions between the same in the proposed medium, as the mean density of the proposed medium between these circles is to the mean density of the medium of which we have treated between the same, very nearly: But also in that same ratio is the secant of the angle by which the predefined spiral, in the medium of which we have treated, cuts the radius *AS*, to the secant of the angle by which the new spiral cuts the same radius in the proposed medium: And also as the tangents of those same angles are, so are the numbers of all revolutions between those same two circles, very nearly. If these things are done everywhere between each pair of circles, the motion will be continued through all the circles. And in this way, we might without difficulty imagine in what manners and times bodies ought to revolve in any regular medium.

*Corollary 9.* And although eccentric motions are performed in spirals approaching the form of ovals; nevertheless, by conceiving that the individual revolutions of those spirals are separated from each other by the same intervals, and approach the center by the same degrees as the spiral described above, we shall also understand how the motions of bodies in such spirals are performed.

# PROPOSITION XVI. THEOREM XIII.

*If the density of a medium in individual places is inversely as the distance of those places from an immobile center, and if the centripetal force is inversely as any power of that same distance: I say that the body can revolve in a spiral which intersects all rays drawn from that center at a given angle.*

<margin>P</margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a spiral-like curve originating around a center point S. A radius SP connects the center to a point P on the curve. A tangent line PR is drawn at point P. A perpendicular line SO is dropped from the center S to the tangent. Another point Q on the curve is shown with a ray SQ. Various geometric construction lines (Rr, V, T, Q) define a small orbital sector used for mathematical derivation of force and resistance.</image-desc>

It is demonstrated by the same method as the preceding proposition. For if the centripetal force at *P* is inversely as any power <note>original: "dignitas." Newton uses this term for a mathematical power or exponent.</note> of the distance *SP*, specifically the power of *n+1* (where *n+1* is the index): it will be gathered, as above, that the time in which the body describes any arc *PQ* will be as the product of *PQ* and the square root of the *n*-th power of *SP* <note>original: "SP<sup>1/2n</sup>"</note>; and the resistance at *P* will be as $\frac{Rr}{PQ^2 \times SP^n}$, or as $\frac{1 - 1/2 n \times VQ}{PQ \times SP^n \times SQ}$, and therefore as $\frac{1 - 1/2 n \times OS}{OP \times SP^{n+1}}$. This is, because the term $\frac{1 - 1/2 n \times OS}{OP}$ is given <note>meaning it remains constant for a specific spiral path</note>, inversely as *SP*<sup>*n+1*</sup>. And therefore, since the velocity is inversely as the square root of the *n*-th power of *SP*, the density at *P* will be inversely as the distance *SP*.

*Corollary 1.* The resistance is to the centripetal force as $1 - 1/2 n \times OS$ is to *OP*.

*Corollary 2.* If the centripetal force is inversely as the <term>cube of the distance: a force proportional to 1 divided by the distance multiplied by itself three times (1/r³)</term> *SP*, then $1 - 1/2 n = 0$; and therefore the resistance and the density of the medium will be zero, as in the ninth proposition of the first book.

*Corollary 3.* If the centripetal force is inversely as any power of the radius *SP* whose index is greater than the number 3, the positive resistance will be changed into a negative one <note>A "negative resistance" would act as an accelerating force rather than a slowing one, pushing the body along its path.</note>.

## SECTION V.

->On the density and compression of fluids, and on hydrostatics.<- <note>Hydrostatics is the branch of physics that deals with fluids at rest and the pressure they exert.</note>

### Definition of a Fluid.

*A fluid is any body whose parts yield to any force applied to them, and by yielding are easily moved among themselves.* <note>Newton defines a fluid not by its chemical makeup, but by its mechanical behavior: its inability to resist "shearing" or being pushed aside.</note>

## PROPOSITION XIX. THEOREM XIV.

*If a homogeneous and motionless fluid is enclosed in any motionless vessel and compressed on all sides, all its parts (leaving aside the consideration of condensation, gravity, and all centripetal forces) are pressed equally on all sides, and remain in their places without any motion arising from that pressure.*

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram representing a spherical vessel. The circumference of the circle is marked with points A at the top, B at the middle-left, and C at the lower-right. Other points labeled G, H, and I are positioned within the lower half of the large circle. Dashed lines connect D to E, E to F, F to G, D to H, H to I, and I to C. A solid line extends from point D to the circumference at point A. This illustrates how pressure is transmitted through internal points of a fluid.</image-desc>

*Case 2.* I say now, that all the spherical parts of this fluid are pressed equally on all sides. For let *EF* be a spherical part of the fluid, and if this is not pressed equally on all sides, let the lesser pressure be increased until it is pressed equally on all sides; then its parts, according to the first case, will remain in their places. But they would also remain in their places before the pressure was increased, by that same first case, yet by the addition of new pressure they would be moved from their places by the very definition of a fluid. These two points are contradictory. Therefore, it was false to say that the sphere *EF* was not pressed equally on all sides. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Case 3.* I say further that the pressure of different spherical parts is equal. For contiguous spherical parts press each other equally at the point of contact, according to the <term>third law of motion</term> <note>Newton's Third Law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.</note>. But also, according to the second case, they are pressed on all sides by the same force. Therefore, any two spherical parts that are not touching—since an intermediate spherical part can touch both—will be pressed with the same force. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Case 4.* I say now that all parts of the fluid everywhere are pressed equally. For any two parts can be touched by spherical parts at any points whatever, and there they press those spherical parts equally, according to Case 3, and in turn are pressed equally by them, according to the third law of motion. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Case 5.* Since, therefore, any part **GHI** of the fluid is enclosed in the rest of the fluid as if in a vessel, and is pressed equally on all sides, and its own parts press each other equally and are at rest among themselves; it is manifest that all the parts of any fluid **GHI** which is pressed equally on all sides, press each other equally and are at rest among themselves. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Case 6.* Therefore, if that fluid is enclosed in a vessel that is not rigid, and is not pressed equally on all sides, the fluid will give way to the stronger pressure, by the definition of fluidity.

### PROPOSITION XX. THEOREM XV.

*If each of the parts of a spherical fluid, which is homogeneous at equal distances from the center, lying upon a concentric spherical bottom, gravitate toward the center of the whole; the bottom sustains the weight of a cylinder whose base is equal to the surface of the bottom, and whose height is the same as that of the incumbent fluid.* <note>Newton is describing a scenario like the Earth's atmosphere or a deep ocean. Therefore, the pressure by which each surface is pressed is not proportional to the solid quantity of the fluid resting upon it, but to the number of layers reaching to the top of the fluid; and it is equal to the gravity of the lowest layer multiplied by the number of layers. *Corollary 1.* Therefore, the bottom is not pressed by the total weight of the fluid resting upon it, but only supports that part of the weight described in the proposition; the remaining weight is supported by the arched shape of the fluid. <note>This explains why a small amount of water in a narrow tube can exert the same pressure as a vast ocean, provided they are the same height.</note>

*Corollary 2.* Moreover, at equal distances from the center, the quantity of pressure is always the same, whether the pressed surface is parallel to the horizon, or perpendicular, or oblique; whether the fluid, extending upward from the pressed surface, rises perpendicularly in a straight line, or creeps obliquely through twisted cavities and channels—whether those channels are regular or highly irregular, wide or very narrow. It is concluded that pressure is not changed by these circumstances, by applying the demonstration of this theorem to individual cases of fluids.

*Corollary 3.* By the same demonstration, it is also concluded (by Proposition 19) that the heavy parts of a fluid acquire no motion among themselves from the pressure of the resting weight, provided that motion arising from condensation is excluded.

*Corollary 4.* And therefore if another body of the same <term>specific gravity</term> <note>Specific gravity refers to the density of a substance compared to the density of the fluid.</note>, which is incapable of being condensed, is submerged in this fluid, it will acquire no motion from the pressure of the resting weight: it will not descend, it will not ascend, and it will not be forced to change its shape. If it is spherical, it will remain spherical, notwithstanding the pressure; if it is square, it will remain square; and this is true whether the body be soft or even highly fluid;

For every internal part of a fluid has the nature of a submerged body, and the same reasoning applies to all submerged bodies of the same size, shape, and <term>specific gravity</term> <note>Newton uses "specific gravity" to refer to what we now call density—the weight of a substance relative to the volume it occupies.</note>. *Corollary 5.* Consequently, a body that is specifically heavier than the fluid touching it will sink, and one that is specifically lighter will rise, and it will undergo motion and a change of shape as much as that excess or lack of gravity can cause. For that excess or lack acts as an impulse by which the body—which would otherwise be in equilibrium with the parts of the fluid—is urged; and it can be compared with the excess or lack of weight in either pan of a balance scale.

*Corollary 6.* There is, therefore, a twofold gravity for bodies placed in fluids: one true and absolute, the other apparent, common, and comparative. Absolute gravity is the total force by which a body tends downward; relative and common gravity is the excess of gravity by which a body tends downward more than the surrounding fluid. By gravity of the first kind, the parts of all fluids and bodies gravitate in their own places; and therefore, when their weights are joined, they compose the weight of the whole. For every "whole" is heavy, as can be experienced in vessels full of liquids; and the weight of the whole is equal to the weights of all its parts, and is therefore composed of them. By gravity of the other kind, bodies do not gravitate in their own places; that is, when compared among themselves, they do not outweigh one another, but by hindering each other’s attempts to descend, they remain in their places just as if they were not heavy. Things which are in the air and do not outweigh it are not judged "heavy" by the common people. Things which do outweigh it, the common people judge to be heavy, insofar as they are not supported by the weight of the air. The weights used by the common folk are nothing other than the excess of true weights over the weight of the air. Hence, those things are commonly called "light" which are less heavy, and which, by yielding to the weight of the air, seek higher places. They are comparatively light, but not truly so, because they descend in a vacuum <note>original: "in vacuo"</note>. So also in water, bodies which, due to a greater or lesser gravity, descend or ascend, are comparatively and

*Corollary 7.* Those things which are demonstrated concerning gravity hold true in any other <term>centripetal forces</term> <note>A force that pulls an object toward a center, such as gravity pulling toward the center of the Earth.</note> whatever.

*Corollary 8.* Accordingly, if a medium in which some body moves is urged either by its own gravity or by any other centripetal force whatever, and the body is urged more strongly by that same force, the difference of the forces is that moving force which we considered in the preceding propositions as centripetal force. But if the body is urged more lightly by that force, the difference of the forces ought to be regarded as <term>centrifugal force</term> <note>While we now often think of centrifugal force as an "apparent" force in a rotating frame, Newton here uses it to describe the relative outward tendency when the surrounding medium is pulled more strongly toward the center than the object itself is.</note>.

*Corollary 9.* Furthermore, since fluids by pressing upon enclosed bodies do not change their external shapes, it is also evident (by the corollary to Proposition 19) that they will not change the arrangement of the internal parts among themselves. Therefore, if animals are submerged, and all sensation arises from the motion of parts, the fluids will neither injure the submerged bodies nor excite any sensation, except insofar as these bodies can be condensed by compression <note>Newton is explaining why deep-sea creatures or divers are not "crushed" by the immense pressure of the water; because the pressure is equalized on all sides, the internal structure remains undisturbed unless the material itself is compressible.</note>. And the reasoning is equal for any system of bodies surrounded by a compressing fluid. All parts of the system will be agitated by the same motions as if they were placed in a <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "vacuo"; a space entirely devoid of matter.</note>, and would retain only their comparative gravity, except insofar as the fluid either resists their motions somewhat or is required to bind them together by compression.

## PROPOSITION XXII. THEOREM XVII.

> *Let the density of a certain fluid be proportional to the compression, and let its parts be drawn downward by a gravity inversely proportional to the squares of their distances from the center: I say that, if the distances are taken in musical progression, the densities of the fluid at these distances will be in geometric progression.* <note>Newton uses the term "musical progression" to refer to what we now call a harmonic progression, where the reciprocals of the numbers are in arithmetic progression.</note>

Let S designate the center, and SA, SB, SC, SD, SE the distances in a <term>geometric progression</term> <note>A sequence of numbers where each term after the first is found by multiplying the previous one by a fixed, non-zero number.</note>. Let the perpendiculars AH, BI, CK, etc., be erected, which are as the densities of the fluid in locations A, B, C, D, E, etc., and the <term>specific gravities</term> <note>original: "gravitates specificæ" — the weight per unit volume of the fluid at a specific point.</note> in those same locations will be AH/SA², BI/SB², CK/SC², etc. Imagine these gravities to be uniformly continued, the first from A to B, the second from B to C, the third from C to D, etc. And these [gravities] multiplied by the altitudes AB, BC, CD, DE, etc., or, what is the same thing, by the distances SA, SB, SC, etc., which are proportional to those altitudes, will produce the exponents of the pressures.
