### *Scholium.*

By a similar argument, it can be proved that if the gravity of the particles of a fluid decreases in the triplicate ratio <note>The cube of the distance.</note> of the distances from the center, and the reciprocals of the squares of the distances *SA, SB, SC*, etc. (namely, $\frac{SA^3}{SA^2}, \frac{SA^3}{SB^2}, \frac{SA^3}{SC^2}$) are taken in arithmetic progression; the densities *AH, BI, CK*, etc., will be in geometric progression. And if gravity decreases in the quadruplicate ratio <note>The fourth power.</note> of the distances, and the reciprocals of the cubes of the distances (say $\frac{SA^4}{SA^3}, \frac{SA^4}{SB^3}, \frac{SA^4}{SC^3}$, etc.) are taken in arithmetic progression; the densities *AH, BI, CK*, etc., will be in geometric progression. And so on to infinity. Again, if the gravity of the particles of the fluid is the same at all distances, and the distances are in arithmetic progression, the densities will be in geometric progression, as the famous <term>Edmund Halley</term> <note>A contemporary of Newton and the astronomer who calculated the orbit of the comet that now bears his name.</note> discovered. If gravity is as the distance, and the squares of the distances are in arithmetic progression, the densities will be in geometric progression. And so on to infinity. These things hold true when the density of a fluid condensed by compression is as the force of compression, or, what is the same thing, the space occupied by the fluid is inversely as this force <note>This describes what we now call Boyle’s Law.</note>. Other laws of condensation can be imagined, such as that the cube of the compressing force is as the biquadrate <note>The fourth power.</note> of the density, or the triplicate ratio of the force is the same as the quadruplicate ratio of the density. In which case, if gravity is inversely as the square of the distance from the center, the density will be inversely as the cube of the distance. ## PROPOSITION XXIII. THEOREMA XVIII.

*If the density of a fluid composed of particles which flee one another <note>Newton is describing what we now call repulsive forces.</note> is as the compression, the centrifugal forces of the particles are inversely proportional to the distances of their centers. And vice versa, particles fleeing one another with forces that are inversely proportional to the distances of their centers compose an elastic fluid, whose density is proportional to the compression.*

<image-desc>Two line-drawn diagrams of cubes side-by-side, used for geometric proof. The larger cube on the right has vertices labeled A, B, C, D on the front face, with E, F, G, H on the back. In the plane side $ABCD$ of the larger cube, let a square $DP$ be taken equal to the plane side $db$ of the smaller cube; and by the hypothesis, the pressure, by which the square $DP$ urges the enclosed fluid, will be to the pressure, by which that square $db$ urges the enclosed fluid, as the densities of the medium to each other, that is, as $ab$ cubed to $AB$ cubed.

...equally, the pressure with which the square *DB* urges the fluid is to the pressure with which the square *db* urges the fluid, as *ab* is to *AB*. With the planes *FGH* and *fgh* drawn through the middles of the cubes, the fluid is divided into two parts, and these parts will press each other with the same forces with which they are pressed by the planes *AC* and *ac*; that is, in the proportion of *ab* to *AB*. Therefore, the centrifugal forces <note>Newton uses "centrifugal force" here to mean the repulsive force that causes particles to flee from one another.</note> by which these pressures are sustained are in the same ratio. Because of the same number of particles and their similar positions in both cubes, the forces which all the particles exert on all the others along the planes *FGH* and *fgh* are as the forces which individuals exert on individuals. Therefore, the forces which individuals exert on individuals along the plane *FGH* in the larger cube are to the forces which individuals exert on individuals along the plane *fgh* in the smaller cube as *ab* is to *AB*; that is, inversely as the distances of the particles from each other. **Which was to be demonstrated.** <note>original: "Q. E. D."</note>

And vice versa, if the forces of individual particles are inversely as the distances—that is, inversely as the sides of the cubes *AB* and *ab*—the sums of the forces will be in the same ratio; and the pressures of the sides *DB* and *db* will be as the sums of the forces; and the pressure of the square *DP* <note>The OCR likely refers to a surface area related to the pressure calculation.</note> will be to the pressure of the side *DB* as the square of *ab* is to the square of *AB*. ## Scholium.

By a similar argument, if the centrifugal forces of the particles are inversely in the duplicate ratio <note>The square of the distance ($1/r^2$).</note> of the distances between their centers, the cubes of the compressing forces will be as the fourth powers <note>original: "quadrato-quadrata"; literally the "square-square."</note> of the densities. If the centrifugal forces are inversely in the triplicate or quadruplicate ratio <note>The third power ($1/r^3$) or fourth power ($1/r^4$).</note> of the distances, the cubes of the compressing forces will be as the fifth powers <note>original: "quadrato-cubi."</note> or sixth powers <note>original: "cubo-cubi."</note> of the densities. And universally, if *D* is put for the distance and *E* for the density of the compressed fluid, and the centrifugal forces are inversely as any power of the distance $D^n$ whose index is the number *n*, the compressing forces will be as the cubic roots of the power $E^{n+2}$ whose index is $n+2$; and vice-versa. <note>Newton is providing a general formula: if the repulsive force $F \propto 1/D^n$, then the Pressure $P \propto E^{(n+2)/3}$. We have an example in magnetic bodies. The attractive power of these is terminated almost within bodies of their own kind that are nearest to them. The power of a magnet [is exerted] through an interposed plate <note>The Latin text ends abruptly here: "Magnetis virtus per interpositam laminam."</note>.

## On the motion and resistance of pendulums. <note>original: "funependulorum," literally "bodies hanging from a rope."</note>

### PROPOSITION XXIV. THEOREMA XIX.

*The quantities of matter in pendulous bodies, whose centers of oscillation are at an equal distance from the center of suspension, are in a ratio compounded of the ratio of the weights and the squared ratio <note>original: "ratione duplicata," a mathematical term meaning the ratio of the squares.</note> of the times of the oscillations in a vacuum.*

For the velocity, which a given force can generate in a given quantity of matter <note>Newton’s term for "mass."</note> in a given time, is as the force and the time directly, and the matter inversely. The greater the force or the longer the time, or the smaller the matter, the greater will be the velocity generated. This is manifest from the second law of motion. Now, if pendulums are of the same length, the motive forces in places equally distant from the perpendicular are as the weights; and therefore, if two bodies in oscillating describe equal arcs, and those arcs are divided into equal parts; since the times in which the bodies describe the individual corresponding parts of the arcs are as the times of the total oscillations, the velocities will be to each other in corresponding parts of the oscillations as the motive forces and the total times of oscillation directly, and the quantities of matter inversely: and therefore the quantities of matter are as the forces and the times of oscillation directly, and the velocities inversely. ...therefore the times directly and the velocities inversely are as the squares of the times, and for that reason the **quantities of matter** <note>Newton uses "quantitas materiæ" to define what we now call "mass"—the amount of "stuff" in an object regardless of its volume.</note> are as the **motive forces** and the squares of the times, that is, as the weights and the squares of the times. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Corollary 1.* And therefore if the times are equal, the quantities of matter in individual bodies will be as their weights.

*Corollary 2.* If the weights are equal, the quantities of matter will be as the squares of the times.

*Corollary 3.* If the quantities of matter are equal, the weights will be inversely as the squares of the times.

*Corollary 4.* Whence, since the squares of the times, other things being equal, are as the lengths of the pendulums; if both the times and the quantities of matter are equal, the weights will be as the lengths of the pendulums.

*Corollary 5.* And universally, the quantity of matter in a swinging body is as the weight and the square of the time directly, and the length of the pendulum inversely.

*Corollary 6.* But even in a non-resisting medium <note>A "non-resisting medium" refers to a vacuum or an idealized space where air resistance does not slow the object down.</note>, the quantity of matter in a swinging body is as the **comparative weight** and the square of the time directly and the length of the pendulum inversely. For the comparative weight is the motive force of a body in any heavy medium, as I have explained above; and therefore it performs the same function in such a non-resisting medium as absolute weight does in a vacuum.

*Corollary 7.* And from this, the method is clear both for comparing bodies with one another regarding the quantity of matter in each, and for comparing the weights of the same body in different locations to understand the variation of gravity. Moreover, by performing the most accurate experiments, I have always found the quantity of matter in individual bodies to be proportional to their weight. <note>This is a landmark statement in physics; Newton's experiments with pendulums of different materials (gold, silver, wood, etc.) proved that mass and weight are proportional, a concept central to the "Equivalence Principle."</note>

## PROPOSITION XXVI. THEOREMA XXI. ##

*The oscillations of **pendulous bodies** <note>original: "funependulorum"; literally "rope-hanging," referring to a pendulum bob on a string.</note> in a **cycloid** <note>A specific mathematical curve that allows a pendulum to be "isochronous," meaning its period is independent of its amplitude.</note>, where the resistance is in the ratio of the velocities, are isochronous.*

For if two bodies, at an equal distance from their centers of suspension, describe unequal arcs while oscillating, and the velocities in the corresponding parts of the arcs are to each other as the total arcs; the resistances, being proportional to the velocities, will also be to each other as those same arcs. Consequently, if these resistances are subtracted from or added to the **motive forces** <note>original: "viribus motricibus". Newton uses this to describe the total force acting to move a body.</note> arising from gravity (which are as those same arcs), the differences or sums will be to each other in that same ratio of the arcs. And since the increases or decreases in velocity are as these differences or sums, the velocities will always be as the total arcs. Therefore, if the velocities are in any case as the total arcs, they will always remain in that same ratio. But at the beginning of the motion, where the bodies begin to descend and describe those arcs, the forces (since they are proportional to the arcs) will generate velocities proportional to the arcs. Therefore, the velocities will always be as the total arcs to be described, and for that reason, those arcs will be described simultaneously.

# PROPOSITION XXVII. THEOREM XXII.

*If **pendulous bodies** <note>original: "funependulis"; literally "roped-pendulums." Newton is referring to a weight suspended by a string.</note> are resisted in the **duplicate ratio** <note>original: "duplicata ratione"; this means the resistance is proportional to the square of the velocity ($v^2$).</note> of their velocities, the differences between the times of oscillations in a resisting medium and the times of oscillations in a medium of the same specific gravity that does not resist, will be proportional to the arcs described in the oscillation, or very nearly so.*

For let unequal arcs $A$ and $B$ be described by equal pendulums in a resisting medium; and the resistance of the body in arc $A$ will be to the resistance in the corresponding part of arc $B$ in the duplicate ratio of the velocities, that is, as $AA$ to $BB$, or very nearly so. If the resistance in arc $B$ were to the resistance in arc $A$ as $AB$ to $AA$, the times in arcs $A$ and $B$ would be equal, by the preceding proposition. Therefore, the resistance $AA$ in arc $A$, or $AB$ in arc $B$, causes the excess of time in arc $A$ over the time in a non-resisting medium; and the resistance $BB$ causes the excess of time in arc $B$ over the time in a non-resisting medium. Moreover, those excesses are as the efficient forces $AB$ and $BB$ very nearly, that is, as the arcs $A$ and $B$. **Which was to be demonstrated.** <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod Erat Demonstrandum)</note>

**Corollary 1.** Hence, from the times of oscillations performed in unequal arcs in a resisting medium, the times of oscillations in a medium of the same specific gravity that does not resist can be determined. For the difference of the times will be to the excess of the time in the smaller arc over the time in the non-resisting medium, as the difference of the arcs is to the smaller arc.

**Corollary 2.** Shorter oscillations are more **isochronous** <note>original: "isochronæ"; from the Greek for "equal time." This refers to a pendulum taking the same amount of time to complete a swing regardless of its width.</note>, and the shortest ones are completed in nearly the same times as in a non-resisting medium. However, for those oscillations occurring in larger arcs, the times are slightly longer, because the resistance during the body's descent (by which the time is lengthened) becomes greater in proportion to the length described in the descent than the resistance in the subsequent ascent (by which the time is shortened). But even so, the time of both short and long oscillations seems to be somewhat lengthened by the motion of the medium. For bodies that are slowing down are resisted slightly less, in proportion to their velocity, and accelerated bodies slightly more than those which move uniformly: and this is because the medium, by that [motion] which it has received from the bodies...

<summary>Newton demonstrates that when air or fluid resistance is proportional to the square of a pendulum's speed, the delay caused by that resistance is directly proportional to the width of the swing's arc. He notes that while all resisted swings are slowed down, shorter swings remain more consistent in their timing (isochronous) than wider ones.</summary>

Therefore, if the area $(\frac{OR}{OQ}) \times IEF - IGH$ is called $Y$, and the decrement of the area $PIGR$ is given, the increment of the area $Y$ will be as $PIGR - Y$.

But if $V$ designates the force arising from gravity, proportional to the arc $CD$ to be described, by which the body is urged at $D$, and $R$ is put for the resistance; then $V - R$ will be the total force by which the body is urged at $D$. The increment of velocity is, therefore, as the total force $V - R$ and the small particle of time in which it is made, combined. But the velocity itself is as the contemporaneous increment of the space described directly, and that same particle of time inversely. Whence, since the resistance is by hypothesis as the square of the velocity, the increment of the resistance (by Lemma II) <note>Newton refers back to his "Lemma II" in Book II, which provides the rules for the "moments" (derivatives) of squares and other products.</note> will be as the velocity and the increment of velocity combined; that is, as the momentum <note>In Newton's work, a "momentum" refers to an infinitely small change or increment in a quantity—the precursor to the modern differential.</note> of space and $V - R$ combined; and therefore, if the momentum of space is given, it is as $V - R$. That is, if for the force $V$ its exponent $PIGR$ is written, and the resistance $R$ is represented by some other area $Z$, then the increment of $Z$ is as $PIGR - Z$.

Therefore, while the area $PIGR$ decreases uniformly through the subtraction of given moments, the area $Y$ increases in the ratio $PIGR - Y$, and the area $Z$ in the ratio $PIGR - Z$. And on that account, if the areas $Y$ and $Z$ begin together and are equal at the start, they will continue to be equal through the addition of equal moments, and likewise by equal moments

**Corollary.** From this, based on the law of resistance and the difference *Aa* <note>The difference between the arc of descent and the arc of ascent.</note> between the arcs *Ca* and *CB*, the ratio of the resistance to gravity can be determined very nearly.

For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle formed by *Ba* and *DK*; and therefore the rectangle formed by $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle formed by *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to $\frac{1}{2} Aa$. Therefore, since *DK* represents <term>the resistance|Newton uses the word 'exponent' here to mean a geometric line that represents a physical quantity</term>, and the length of the pendulum represents gravity, the resistance will be to gravity as $\frac{1}{2} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum; exactly as was demonstrated in Proposition 28.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be an ellipse, or nearly so. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, described the length *BA* in one complete oscillation, the velocity at any point *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* <note>The vertical line reaching from the horizontal axis to the curve of the circle.</note> of the circle described with diameter *AB*. Accordingly, since the arc *Ba* in a resisting medium and the arc *BA* in a non-resisting medium are described in approximately equal times, and therefore the velocities at individual points of *Ba* are very nearly in the same ratio to the velocities at corresponding points of the length *BA* as *Ba* is to *BA*, the velocity at point *D* in the resisting medium will be as the ordinate of a circle or ellipse described on the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be very nearly an ellipse. Since the resistance is assumed proportional to the velocity, let *OV* represent the resistance at the midpoint *O*; and the ellipse *BRVSa*, described with center *O* and semi-axes *OB* and *OV*, will be nearly equal to the figure *BKVT a* and to its equivalent rectangle *Aa* x *BO*. Therefore, *Aa* x *BO* is to *OV* x *BO* as the area of this ellipse is to *OV* x *BO*: that is, *Aa* is to *OV* as the area of a semicircle is to the square of its radius, or roughly as 11 to 7 <note>Newton is using the approximation of $\pi$ as 22/7; the area of a semicircle is $\frac{1}{2}\pi r^2$, so the ratio to $r^2$ is roughly 11/7.</note>. And consequently, $\frac{7}{11} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the duplicate ratio <note>Proportional to the square of the velocity.</note> of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be almost a parabola having its vertex at *V* and axis *OV*, and therefore will be nearly equal to two-thirds of the rectangle formed by *Ba* and *OV*. Thus, the rectangle formed by $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle formed by $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ and *OV*, and so *OV* is equal to $\frac{3}{4} Aa$. Therefore, the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as $\frac{3}{4} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum.

### PROPOSITION XXXI. THEOREMA XXV.

*If the resistance of an oscillating body in each of the proportional parts of the arcs described is increased or diminished in a given ratio; the difference between the arc described during the descent and the arc described in the subsequent ascent will be increased or diminished in the same ratio.*

For that difference arises from the retardation of the pendulum caused by the resistance of the medium, and is therefore proportional to the total retardation and the retarding resistance that causes it. In the preceding proposition, the rectangle formed by the line 1/2 *aB* and the difference *Aa* between those arcs *CB* and *Ca* was equal to the area

**Corollary 3.** And universally, if the resistance is in the triple <note>original: "triplicata," meaning proportional to the cube</note> or any other ratio of the velocity, the difference <note>the difference between the arc of descent and the arc of the subsequent ascent</note> will be in the same ratio as the whole arc: and vice versa.

**Corollary 4.** And if the resistance is partly in the simple ratio <note>proportional to velocity</note> and partly in the double ratio <note>proportional to the square of velocity</note> of the same, the difference will be partly in the ratio of the whole arc and partly in the double ratio of it: and vice versa. The law and ratio of resistance for velocity will be the same as the law and ratio of that difference for the length of the arc.

**Corollary 5.** Therefore, if a pendulum describes unequal arcs successively, and the ratio of the increase and decrease of this difference can be found relative to the length of the arc described, we will also have the ratio of the increase and decrease of the resistance for a greater or lesser velocity.

From these propositions, one may find the resistance of <term>mediums</term> <note>A "medium" is the substance through which an object moves, such as air, water, or oil.</note> by the oscillations of pendulums in any such medium. I investigated the resistance of air by the following experiments. I fashioned a wooden globe weighing $57 \frac{7}{22}$ Roman ounces <note>The Roman ounce was slightly lighter than the modern ounce, used here as a standard of measurement common in scientific circles of the time</note>, with a diameter of $6 \frac{7}{8}$ London inches, and suspended it by a thin thread from a sufficiently firm hook, so that the distance between the hook and the center of oscillation of the globe was $10 \frac{1}{2}$ feet. I marked a point on the thread ten feet and one inch distant from the center of suspension; and opposite that point I placed a ruler divided into inches, by which I might mark the lengths of the arcs described by the pendulum. 

Then I counted the oscillations by which the globe would lose an eighth part of its motion. If the pendulum was drawn back from the perpendicular to a distance of two inches and then released, so that in its entire descent it described an arc of two inches, and in the whole first oscillation—composed of the descent and the subsequent ascent—it described an arc of nearly four inches: that same pendulum lost an eighth part of its motion in 164 oscillations, so that in its last ascent it described an arc of one inch and three-fourths of an inch. 

If in the first descent it described an arc of four inches, it lost an eighth part of its motion in 121 oscillations, so that in its last ascent it described an arc of $3 \frac{1}{2}$ inches. If in the first descent it described an arc of eight, sixteen, thirty-two, or sixty-four inches, it lost an eighth part of its motion in 69, $35 \frac{1}{2}$, $18 \frac{1}{2}$, and $9 \frac{2}{3}$ oscillations, respectively. For those differences in a cycloid ought to be increased, along with the resistance, in approximately the duplicate ratio of the arc to the chord, because the velocity is increased in that simple ratio; and they ought to be decreased, along with the square of the time, in that same duplicate ratio. Thus, to make a reduction to the cycloid, the same differences of arcs are to be taken as were observed in the circle, but the maximum velocities are to be set as proportional to the arcs, either halved or whole—that is, to the numbers 1/2, 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16. Moreover, the diameters of the globes are 18 3/4 and 6 7/8; and their squares, 351 9/16 and 47 17/64, are as 7.438 to 1, that is, as the resistances of the globes, 7 to 1, very nearly. The difference of the ratios is hardly greater than what could have arisen from the resistance of the string. Therefore, those parts of the resistances which, for equal globes, are as the squares of the velocities, are also, for equal velocities, as the squares of the diameters of the globes.

Now, let $AV + CV^2$ represent the difference of the arcs described in the descent and the subsequent ascent by a globe moving in air with a maximum velocity $V$. Since the maximum velocity in the case of the fourth column is to the maximum velocity in the case of the first column as 1 to 8; and the difference of those arcs in the fourth column is to the difference in the first column as $2/535$ to $16/85 \frac{1}{2}$, or as $85 \frac{1}{2}$ to 4280: let us write 1 and 8 for the velocities in these cases, and $85 \frac{1}{2}$ and 4280 for the differences of the arcs. It then follows that $A + C = 85 \frac{1}{2}$ and $8A + 64C = 4280$ (or $A + 8C = 535$). Through the reduction of these equations, it results that $7C = 449 \frac{1}{2}$, so $C = 64 \frac{3}{14}$ and $A = 21 \frac{1}{7}$. Therefore, the resistance—being expressed as $\frac{1}{11} AV + \frac{3}{4} CV^2$ <note>Newton uses these coefficients to balance the linear resistance (proportional to velocity, $V$) and quadratic resistance (proportional to velocity squared, $V^2$).</note>—will be as $13 \frac{1}{11} V + 48 \frac{3}{28} V^2$. Consequently, in the case of the fourth column where the velocity was 1, the total resistance is to its part proportional to the square of the velocity as $13 \frac{1}{11} + 48 \frac{3}{28}$ (which is $61 \frac{1}{7}$) is to $48 \frac{3}{28}$. 

Therefore, the resistance of the pendulum in water is to that part of the resistance in air which is proportional to the square of the velocity (which is the only part that needs to be considered in faster motions) as $61 \frac{1}{7}$ to $48 \frac{3}{28}$ and 535 to $1 \frac{1}{5}$ combined—that is, as 571 to 1. If the entire string of the pendulum oscillating in the water had been submerged, the resistance would have been even greater; so much so that the resistance of a pendulum oscillating in water (that part proportional to the square of the velocity, which is the only part considered for faster bodies) is to the resistance of the same whole pendulum oscillating with the same velocity in air as roughly 850 to 1. This is very nearly the same as the ratio of the <term>density</term> <note>The mass per unit volume; Newton is showing that fluid resistance is directly related to how "heavy" or thick the medium is.</note> of water to the density of air.

In this calculation, one ought to have also taken that part of the pendulum's resistance in water which was proportional to the square of the velocity, but (what may perhaps seem strange) the resistance in water increased in a ratio greater than the square of the velocity. Investigating the cause of this, I hit upon the fact that the chest was too narrow for the size of the pendulum globe, and by its narrowness, it hindered the motion of the water as it gave way <note>This is a classic observation of "wall effects" in fluid dynamics, where the boundaries of a container change the flow patterns around an object.</note>. For if a pendulum globe with a diameter of only one <term>digit</term> <note>About 0.75 inches.</note> were submerged, the resistance increased almost exactly in the squared ratio of the velocity. I tested this by constructing a pendulum from two globes, where the lower and smaller one oscillated in water, while the upper and larger one was fixed to the string just above the water; by oscillating in the air, this larger globe helped sustain the motion of the pendulum.

When I used a slightly larger pendulum globe—say, one whose diameter was about 1/3 or 2/3 parts of an inch—the resistance of the quicksilver came out in a ratio to the resistance of water of about 12 or 10 to 1. But more trust should be placed in the first experiment, because in these latter cases the vessel was too narrow for the size of the submerged globe. If the globe were enlarged, the vessel ought to be enlarged as well.

I had indeed intended to repeat experiments of this kind in larger vessels and with other liquids, such as molten metals and others, both hot and cold; but I do not have the leisure to try everything. From what has already been described, it is sufficiently clear that the resistance of rapidly moving bodies is, as nearly as possible, proportional to the density of the fluids in which they move. I do not say this is perfectly accurate. Finally, since it is the opinion of some that a certain <term>ethereal medium<note>A hypothetical "invisible fluid" that 17th-century scientists believed filled all space and the gaps between atoms.</note></term> exists, which is far more subtle than air and permeates all the pores and passages of all bodies most freely; and since resistance ought to arise from such a medium flowing through the pores of bodies: I devised an experiment to test this. I wanted to see if the resistance we experience in moving bodies occurs entirely on their external surface, or whether the internal parts also feel a notable resistance on their own surfaces. 

From a sufficiently firm steel hook, by means of a steel ring, I suspended a round <term>fir-wood box<note>original: "pyxidem abiegnam"; a light container made of deal or fir timber.</note></term> with a thread eleven feet in length, to form a pendulum of that length. The hook was sharpened at the top with a concave edge, so that the ring, resting with its upper arc upon the edge, might move most freely. To the lower arc, however, the thread was attached. The pendulum thus constructed I moved away from the <term>perpendicular<note>The "plumb line" or the resting vertical position of the pendulum.</note></term> to a distance of about six feet. I did this in a plane perpendicular to the edge of the hook, so that the ring would not slide back and forth over the hook's edge while the pendulum oscillated. For the point of suspension, where the ring touches the hook, must remain unmoved. 

I therefore accurately noted the place to which I had drawn the pendulum; then, letting the pendulum go, I noted three other places to which it returned at the end of the first, second, and third oscillation. I repeated this several times, so that I might find those locations as accurately as I could. 

Then I filled the box with lead and other heavier metals that were at hand. But first I weighed the empty box, together with the part of the thread that was wound around the box and half of the remaining part of the thread stretched between the hook and the box. (For a stretched thread, by half of its weight, always urges the pendulum once it has moved from the perpendicular). To this weight I added the weight of the air which the box contained. The total weight of the empty box [plus air and string] was about one seventy-eighth part of the box when it was full of metals. 

Then, because the box full of metals increased the length of the pendulum by stretching the thread with its weight, I shortened the thread so that the length of the pendulum while oscillating would be exactly the same as before. Then, having pulled the pendulum back to the first noted spot and let it go, I counted about seventy-seven oscillations until the box returned to the second noted spot, and just as many thereafter until the box returned to the...

From this I conclude that the total resistance of the full box had no greater proportion to the resistance of the empty box than 78 to 77. For if the resistances of both were equal, the full box—owing to its <term>inherent force<note>original: "vim suam insitam"; Newton's term for what we now call inertia, the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion.</note></term> being seventy-eight times greater than the inherent force of the empty box—ought to have preserved its oscillatory motion that much longer, and therefore, with 78 oscillations completed, always return to those marked places. However, it returned to them after 77 completed oscillations.

Therefore, let *A* designate the resistance of the box on its external surface, and *B* the resistance of the empty box in its internal parts; and if the resistances of bodies moving at equal speeds in their internal parts are as the matter, or the number of particles which are resisted: then 78 *B* will be the resistance of the full box in its internal parts. Therefore, the total resistance of the empty box (*A* + *B*) will be to the total resistance of the full box (*A* + 78 *B*) as 77 is to 78; and <term>by division<note>A classical mathematical technique (proportional division) used to simplify ratios.</note></term>, *A* + *B* is to 77 *B* as 77 is to 1, and hence *A* + *B* is to *B* as 77 $\times$ 77 is to 1, and by division *A* is to *B* as 5928 is to 1. Therefore, the resistance of the empty box in its internal parts is more than five thousand times smaller than its resistance on the external surface. Thus we argue from the hypothesis that the greater resistance of the full box does not arise from some other hidden cause, but solely from the action of some <term>subtle fluid<note>original: "fluidi subtilis"; a reference to the hypothetical aether, which many scientists of the time believed filled the universe and permeated solid matter.</note></term> upon the metal enclosed within.

I have recounted this experiment from memory. For the paper on which I had once described it has been lost. Consequently, I have been forced to omit certain fractional parts of the numbers which have escaped my memory.

For I do not have the leisure to try everything again. The first time, when I used a weak hook, the full box was slowed down more quickly. Seeking the cause, I found that the weak hook yielded to the weight of the box, and by yielding to its oscillations, it bent in all directions. I therefore prepared a firm hook, so that the point of suspension might remain unmoved, and then everything turned out just as we have described above.

# SECTION VII. #

### *On the motion of fluids and the resistance of projectiles.* ###

## PROPOSITION XXXII. THEOREM XXVI. ##

*If two similar systems of bodies consist of an equal number of particles, and the corresponding particles are similar and proportional—each in one system to each in the other—and are similarly situated among themselves, and have a given ratio of density to one another; and if they begin to move among themselves in similar ways during proportional times (those in one system among themselves, and those in the other among themselves); and if the particles within the same system do not touch each other except at the moments of reflection, nor attract or repel each other except by <term>accelerative forces<note>original: "viribus acceleratricibus"; forces that cause a change in velocity regardless of the mass of the particle, similar to how gravity acts on all objects equally.</note></term> which are as the diameters of the corresponding particles inversely and the squares of the velocities directly: then I say that those particles of the systems will continue to move among themselves in a similar manner during proportional times.*

I say that similar and similarly situated bodies move similarly among themselves in proportional times when their positions relative to each other at the end of those times are always similar: for instance, if the particles of one system are compared with the corresponding particles of the other. From this, the times will be proportional in which similar and proportional parts of similar figures are described by the corresponding particles. Therefore, if there are two systems of this kind, the corresponding particles, because of the similarity of their initial motions, will continue to move similarly until they encounter one another. For if they are driven by no forces, they will proceed uniformly in straight lines by the <term>first law of motion<note>original: "motus leg. 1"; Newton’s Law of Inertia, stating that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a force.</note></term>. If they drive each other by any forces, and those forces are as the diameters of the corresponding particles inversely and the squares of the velocities directly; since the positions of the particles are similar and the forces are proportional, the total forces by which the corresponding particles are driven, consisting of the individual forces driv—

[forces] composed of these (by the second corollary to the laws) will have similar directions, just as if they were directed toward centers situated similarly among the particles; and those total forces will be to one another as the individual component forces—that is, inversely as the diameters of the corresponding particles and directly as the squares of the velocities—and therefore they will cause the corresponding particles to continue describing similar figures. This will be the case (by Corol. 1 and 8 of Prop. IV, Book 1) provided that those centers are at rest. But if they move, since their positions among the particles of the systems remain similar due to the similarity of their translations, similar changes will be induced in the figures that the particles describe. Therefore, the motions of corresponding and similar particles will be similar until their first encounters, and hence there will be similar encounters and similar reflections, and thereafter (by what has already been shown) similar motions among themselves until they collide with each other again, and so on to infinity. **Which was to be demonstrated.**

*Corol.* 1. Hence, if any two bodies, which are similar and situated similarly relative to the corresponding particles of the systems, begin to move similarly among them in proportional times, and if their sizes and densities are to each other as the sizes and densities of the corresponding particles, these will continue to move similarly in proportional times. For the ratio of the larger parts of each system is the same as that of the particles.

*Corol.* 2. And if all similar and similarly positioned parts of the systems are at rest among themselves, and two of them, which are larger than the others and correspond to each other in both systems, begin to move in any way with a similar motion along similarly situated lines, these will excite similar motions in the remaining parts of the systems, and will continue to move similarly among them in proportional times; and therefore they will describe spaces proportional to their diameters.

partly from the forces by which the particles of the systems agitate each other, and partly from the collisions and reflections of the particles and larger parts. Resistances of the first kind are to each other as the total <term>motive forces</term><note>Motive force refers to the total force acting to change the motion of a body, equivalent to mass times acceleration.</note> from which they arise—that is, as the total <term>accelerating forces</term> and the quantities of matter in the corresponding parts. This is (by hypothesis) as the squares of the velocities directly, and the distances of the corresponding particles inversely, and the quantities of matter in the corresponding parts directly. Therefore, since the distances of the particles of one system are to the corresponding distances of the particles of another as the diameter of a particle or part in the first system is to the diameter of the corresponding particle or part in the other; and the quantities of matter are as the densities of the parts and the cubes of the diameters; the resistances are to each other as the squares of the velocities and the squares of the diameters and the densities of the parts of the systems. *Which was to be demonstrated.* Resistances of the second kind are as the numbers of corresponding reflections and the forces combined. Now, the numbers of reflections are to each other as the velocities of the corresponding parts directly, and the spaces between their reflections inversely. And the forces of the reflections are as the velocities, magnitudes, and densities of the corresponding parts combined; that is, as the velocities, the cubes of the diameters, and the densities of the parts. And by combining all these ratios, the resistances of the corresponding parts are to each other as the squares of the velocities, the squares of the diameters, and the densities of the parts combined. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Corollary 1.* Therefore, if those systems are two elastic fluids in the manner of air, and their parts are at rest among themselves; and two similar bodies—proportional in size and density to the parts of the fluids and situated similarly among those parts—are projected in any way along similarly positioned lines; and if the accelerating forces, by which the particles of the fluids agitate each other, are inversely as the diameters of the projected bodies and directly as the squares of the velocities: those bodies will excite similar motions in the fluids in proportional times, and will describe similar spaces proportional to their diameters.

*Corollary 2.* Accordingly, in the same fluid, a swift projectile encounters a resistance that is in the <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>In modern terms, the "duplicate ratio" of the velocity means the square of the velocity ($v^2$).</note> of the velocity very nearly. For if the forces by which the distant particles agitate each other were increased in the duplicate ratio of the velocity, the resistance would be accurately in that same duplicate ratio; and therefore in a medium whose parts are distant from each other

<margin>SECOND BOOK.</margin>
...particles agitate each other with no forces, the resistance is exactly in the <term>duplicate ratio</term><note>That is, proportional to the square of the velocity.</note> of the velocity. Let there be, therefore, three media, *A, B, C*, consisting of similar and equal parts regularly arranged at equal distances. Let the parts of media *A* and *B* flee <note>original: "fugiant"; Newton uses this to describe particles repelling each other.</note> one another with forces which are to each other as *T* and *V*, while those of medium *C* are entirely destitute of such forces. And if four equal bodies *D, E, F, G* move in these media—the first two, *D* and *E*, in the first two media, *A* and *B*, and the other two, *F* and *G*, in the third medium, *C*; and let the velocity of body *D* be to the velocity of body *E*, and the velocity of body *F* to the velocity of body *G*, in the <term>subduplicate ratio</term><note>The square root of the ratio.</note> of the forces *T* to the forces *V*: the resistance of body *D* will be to the resistance of body *E*, and the resistance of body *F* to the resistance of body *G*, in the duplicate ratio of the velocities; and therefore the resistance of body *D* will be to the resistance of body *F* as the resistance of body *E* is to the resistance of body *G*. Let bodies *D* and *F* be of equal velocity, as also bodies *E* and *G*; and by increasing the velocities of bodies *D* and *F* in any ratio, and diminishing the forces of the particles of medium *B* in the same duplicate ratio, the medium *B* will approach the form and condition of medium *C* at will; and therefore the resistances of the equal and equally swift bodies *E* and *G* in these media will perpetually approach equality, so that their difference finally becomes less than any given value. Consequently, since the resistances of bodies *D* and *F* are to each other as the resistances of bodies *E* and *G*, these will also similarly approach a ratio of equality. Therefore, of the bodies *D* and *F*, when they move very swiftly, the resistances are as near as possible to equal: and therefore, since the resistance of body *F* is in the duplicate ratio of the velocity, the resistance of body *D* will be in the same ratio as near as possible.

*Corol.* 3. The resistance of a body moving very swiftly in any <term>elastic fluid</term><note>A fluid that can be compressed or expanded, like air.</note> is almost the same as if the parts of the fluid were destitute of their <term>centrifugal forces</term><note>In this context, Newton means the repulsive forces between particles that cause the fluid to expand.</note> and did not flee one another: provided that the elastic force of the fluid arises from the centrifugal forces of the particles, and the velocity is so great that the forces do not have enough time to act.

*Corol.* 4. Therefore, since the resistances of similar and equally swift bodies, in a medium whose distant parts do not flee one another, are as the squares of the diameters; the resistances of equally swift and very rapidly moving bodies in an elastic fluid are also as the squares of the diameters, as near as possible.

<summary>Newton concludes that at high velocities, the resistance of a body in an elastic fluid (like air) is proportional to the square of its velocity and the square of its diameter, because the repulsive forces between fluid particles do not have time to interact.</summary>

*Corollary 5.* And since similar, equal, and equally fast bodies—moving in media of the same density where the particles do not repel one another—strike against an equal quantity of matter in equal times and impart an equal quantity of motion to it (regardless of whether those particles are many and smaller, or fewer and larger), and in turn (by the <term>third law of motion</term><note>Newton’s law that every action has an equal and opposite reaction.</note>) suffer an equal reaction from that matter—that is, they are resisted equally: it is also manifest that in elastic fluids of the same density, where bodies move very swiftly, their resistances are nearly equal, whether those fluids consist of coarser particles or are composed of the most subtle particles of all. The resistance of projectiles moving very rapidly is not much diminished by the <term>subtlety</term><note>The "fineness" or smallness of the individual particles making up the fluid.</note> of the medium.

*Corollary 6.* All these things hold true in fluids whose <term>elastic force</term><note>original: "vis elastica"</note> arises from the <term>centrifugal forces</term><note>original: "viribus centrifugis"; here Newton refers to particles that push away from one another to create pressure.</note> of the particles. But if that force should arise from another source, such as from the expansion of particles in the manner of wool or the branches of trees, or from any other cause by which the motions of the particles among themselves are rendered less free: the resistance, because of the lesser fluidity of the medium, will be greater than in the preceding corollaries.

## PROPOSITION XXXIV. THEOREM XXVIII.

*If a globe and a cylinder described with equal diameters move with equal velocity in a rare medium consisting of equal particles freely disposed at equal distances from one another, along the direction of the cylinder’s axis: the resistance of the globe will be half as great as the resistance of the cylinder.*

For since the action of the medium upon a body is the same (by Corollary 5 of the Laws) whether the body moves through a resting medium, or the particles of the medium strike against a resting body with the same velocity: let us consider the body as resting, and see with what force it will be urged by the moving medium. ...particle of the medium, striking the sphere obliquely at point *B* along the straight line *FB*, hits the sphere with a force that is to the force with which the same particle would perpendicularly hit the cylinder *ONGQ* (described around the sphere with axis *ACI*) at point *b*, as *LD* is to *LB* or *BE* to *BC*. It is a known fact of geometry that a paraboloid is exactly half the volume of its circumscribing cylinder. Therefore, the total force of the medium on the sphere is twice as small as the total force on the cylinder. And thus, if the particles of the medium were at rest, and the cylinder and sphere moved with equal velocity, the resistance of the sphere would be half the resistance of the cylinder. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

## PROPOSITION 35. PROBLEM 7.

*If a <term>rare medium</term><note>Newton uses the concept of a "rare medium"—a vacuum filled with widely spaced, non-interacting particles—to simplify the complex physics of fluid resistance into basic collisions.</note> consists of very small, equal, and freely arranged particles at equal distances from one another: find the resistance of a globe moving uniformly in this medium.*

*Case 1.* Suppose a cylinder described with the same diameter and height is understood to move at the same velocity along the length of its axis in the same medium. And let us assume that the particles of the medium, which the globe or cylinder strikes, bounce back with the greatest possible force of reflection <note>This refers to perfectly elastic collisions where kinetic energy is conserved.</note>. And since the resistance of the globe (by the most recent proposition) is twice as small as the resistance of the cylinder, and the globe's volume is to the cylinder's as two to three, and the cylinder, by striking the particles perpendicularly and reflecting them as much as possible, communicates twice its own velocity to them: the cylinder, in the time it describes half the length of its axis by moving uniformly, will communicate motion to the particles which is to the total motion of the cylinder as the density of the medium is to the density of the cylinder; and the globe, in the time it describes the whole length of its diameter by moving uniformly, will communicate that same motion to the particles; and in the time it describes two-thirds of its diameter, it will communicate motion to the particles which is to the total motion of the globe as the density of the medium to the density of the globe. And therefore the globe suffers a resistance, which is to the force by which its total motion could be either taken away or generated in the time it describes two-thirds of its diameter by moving uniformly, as the density of the medium is to the density of the globe.

*Case 2.* Let us assume that the particles of the medium striking the globe or cylinder are not reflected; then the cylinder, by striking the particles perpendicularly, will communicate its own simple velocity to them, and therefore suffers a resistance twice as small as in the first case, and the resistance of the globe will also be twice as small as before.

All these things are evident through Corollary 1 and 3 of Proposition 5, Book II.

## Scholium.

In this proposition I have explained the resistance and the slowing down of spherical projectiles in non-continuous media <note>By "non-continuous," Newton refers to a medium made of individual, scattered particles rather than a solid fluid like water.</note>, and I have shown that this resistance is to the force by which the entire motion of the globe could either be taken away or generated—in the time the globe describes two-thirds of its own diameter with its velocity uniformly continued—as the density of the medium is to the density of the globe; provided that the globe and the particles of the medium are <term>perfectly elastic</term><note>Meaning they bounce back with no loss of kinetic energy.</note> and possess the greatest power of reflecting. I have also shown that this force is twice as small where the globe and the particles of the medium are infinitely hard and entirely devoid of any power of reflection.

In continuous media, however, such as water, hot oil, and quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, in which the globe does not strike immediately against all the particles of the fluid that generate resistance, but presses only the nearest particles, and these press others, and those others in turn, the resistance is yet twice as small. Indeed, a globe in such highly fluid media suffers a resistance which is to the force by which its entire motion could be taken away or generated—in the time that it describes eight-thirds of its diameter with its motion uniformly continued—as the density of the medium is to the density of the globe. This is what we shall attempt to show in the following pages.

We do assume that the parts of the water cohere slightly, and through this <term>cohesion</term> during the fall, they move toward each other in paths parallel to the horizon so that they form only a single cataract rather than dividing into several; but we do not consider the horizontal motion itself that arises from that cohesion.

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK TWO.

...[it must be] generated as before, and the bottom of the vessel will support the weight of the ice surrounding the column.

Now let the ice in the vessel melt; and the outflow of water, as far as velocity is concerned, will remain the same as before. It will not be less, because the ice resolved into water will still strive to descend; nor will it be greater, because the ice resolved into water cannot descend without hindering the descent of other water by an amount equal to its own descent. The same force must generate the same velocity in the flowing water.

But the opening in the bottom of the vessel, on account of the oblique <note>Meaning the water particles do not move in straight lines but curve toward the hole from the sides.</note> motions of the particles of water flowing out, must be a little larger than before. For the particles of water no longer all pass through the opening perpendicularly; but flowing together from all sides of the vessel and converging into the opening, they pass through with oblique motions; and bending their course downward, they combine into a <term>stream of water</term> <note>Latin: *vena aquae*. In fluid mechanics, this is called the "vena contracta." Because the water converges from the sides, the stream continues to narrow even after it has left the physical opening.</note> springing out, which is a little narrower just below the opening than in the opening itself. Its diameter is to the diameter of the opening as 5 to 6, or 5 ½ to 6 ½ approximately, if I have measured the diameters correctly.

I prepared a very thin flat plate, perforated in the middle, the diameter of the circular hole being five-eighths of an inch. And so that the stream of springing water would not be accelerated by falling (and thus rendered narrower by that acceleration), I fixed this plate not to the bottom but to the side of the vessel so that the stream would exit along a line parallel to the horizon. Then, when the vessel was full of water, I opened the hole so that the water would flow out; and the diameter of the stream, at a distance of about half an inch from the hole, measured as accurately as possible, came out to be twenty-one fortieths of an inch. Therefore, the diameter of this circular hole was to the diameter of the stream as 25 to 21 approximately. 

The water, therefore, in passing through the opening, converges from all sides, and after it has flowed out of the vessel, it is made narrower by this convergence; by this narrowing, it is accelerated until it reaches a distance of half an inch from the opening. At that distance, it becomes narrower and faster than in the opening itself in the ratio of 25 × 25 to 21 × 21, or nearly 17 to 12. This is approximately in the <term>subduplicate ratio</term> <note>This is the ratio of the square roots. Newton is noting that the increase in velocity is roughly equal to the square root of 2 (about 1.414 to 1).</note> of two to one. Through experiments, it is established that the quantity of water which flows out in a given time through a circular hole made in the bottom of a vessel is that which, with the predicted velocity, ought to flow in the same time—not through that hole—but through a circular hole whose diameter is to the diameter of the first hole as 21 to 25. Therefore—

### L E M M A IV.

*The resistance of a cylinder, which moves forward uniformly along its length, is not changed by the increase or decrease of its length; and therefore it is the same as the resistance of a circle described with the same diameter and moving with the same velocity along a straight line perpendicular to its own plane.*

For the sides of the cylinder do not oppose its motion in the least; and a cylinder, once its length is infinitely diminished, is turned into a circle.

## PROPOSITION XXXVII. THEOREM XXIX.

*The resistance of a cylinder, which moves uniformly along its length in an infinite, compressed, and non-elastic <note>In modern terms, "non-elastic" here refers to an incompressible fluid, like water, which does not change volume under pressure.</note> fluid, which arises from the size of its cross-section, is to the force by which its total motion—during the time it travels four times its own length—could be either destroyed or generated, as the density of the medium is to the density of the cylinder, approximately.*

For if the vessel *ABDC* touches the surface of stagnant water with its bottom *CD*, and water flows out of this vessel through a cylindrical channel *EFTS* perpendicular to the horizon into the stagnant water, and a little circle *PQ* is placed parallel to the horizon anywhere in the middle of the channel, and *CA* is extended to *K*, so that *AK* is to *CK* in the duplicate ratio <note>original: *duplicata ratione*; this means the square of the ratio.</note> of the excess of the channel's opening *EF* over the little circle *PQ* to the circle *AB*: it is manifest (by cases 5 and 6 and corollary 1 of Proposition 36) that the velocity of the water passing through the annular space <note>The "annular space" is the ring-shaped gap between the small disk and the walls of the tube.</note> between the little circle and the sides of the vessel will be that which the water can acquire by falling and, in its fall, describing the height *KC* or *IG*.

But the velocity of the little circle will be to the velocity which water acquires by falling and in its fall describing height $IG$, as $EF^2 - PQ^2$ to $EF^2$.

Let the width of the channel be increased to infinity: and those ratios between $EF^2 - PQ^2$ and $EF^2$, and between $EF^2$ and $EF^2 - 1/2 PQ^2$ will ultimately approach ratios of equality. And therefore the velocity of the little circle will now be that which water can acquire by falling and in its fall describing height $IG$, its resistance indeed will become equal to the weight of a cylinder whose base is that little circle and whose height is half the height $IG$, from which the cylinder must fall in order to acquire the velocity of the ascending little circle; and with this velocity, in the time of its falling, the cylinder will travel four times its own length. <note>In Newtonian physics, a body falling from a certain height reaches a speed that, if maintained, would carry it twice that height in the same time it took to fall. Here, he extends this logic to the displacement of fluid.</note> But the resistance of a cylinder, moving at this velocity along its length, is the same as the resistance of the little circle (by Lemma 4) and is therefore equal to the force by which its motion—during the time it travels four times its length—can be generated, very nearly.

If the length of the cylinder is increased or decreased: its motion as well as the time in which it travels four times its length will increase or decrease in the same ratio; and therefore that force, by which the increased or decreased motion can be generated or removed in a similarly increased or decreased time, will not change; and consequently it is still equal to the resistance of the cylinder, for this also remains unchanged by Lemma 4.

If the density of the cylinder is increased or decreased: its motion as well as the force by which the motion can be generated or removed in the same time will increase or decrease in the same ratio. Therefore the resistance of any cylinder will be to the force by which its total motion—during the time it [travels] four times...

<margin>ON THE MOTION OF BODIES</margin>of its own length, can either be generated or taken away, as the density of the medium is to the density of the cylinder, very nearly. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

Moreover, a fluid must be compressed so as to be a continuum, and it must be a continuum and non-elastic so that all pressure arising from its compression may be transmitted instantaneously, and by acting equally on all parts of the moved body, may not change the resistance. Certainly, the pressure which arises from the motion of the body is spent in generating the motion of the parts of the fluid and thus creates resistance. However, the pressure which arises from the compression of the fluid, however strong it may be, if it is transmitted instantaneously, generates no motion in the parts of a continuous fluid and induces no change of motion at all; therefore, it neither increases nor diminishes the resistance. Surely the action of the fluid arising from its compression cannot be stronger on the rear parts of the moved body than on its front parts, and therefore cannot diminish the resistance described in this proposition; and it will not be stronger on the front parts than on the rear parts, provided its transmission is infinitely swifter than the motion of the pressed body. But it will be infinitely swifter and will be transmitted instantaneously, provided the fluid is a continuum and non-elastic <note>Newton assumes an idealized "perfect" fluid that does not compress or expand (incompressible) to simplify the calculation of drag.</note>.

*Corollary 1.* For cylinders that move uniformly according to their lengths in infinite continuous media, the resistances are in a ratio compounded of the squared ratio of the velocities, the squared ratio of the diameters, and the ratio of the density of the media <note>In modern terms: Resistance $\propto v^2 \cdot d^2 \cdot \rho$.</note>.

# LEMMA V.

*If a cylinder, a sphere, and a spheroid, whose widths are equal, are placed successively in the middle of a cylindrical canal in such a way that their axes coincide with the axis of the canal: these bodies will equally impede the flow of water through the canal.*

For the spaces between the canal and the cylinder, the sphere, and the spheroid, through which the water passes, are equal; and water passes through equal spaces equally.

These things hold true based on the hypothesis that all the water above the cylinder, sphere, or spheroid is frozen <note>original: "congeletur" — Newton uses the idea of "frozen" fluid to describe a stagnant region of water that stays with the object, effectively changing its shape to be more streamlined.</note>, since its fluidity is not required for the fastest passage of water, as I explained in Corollary 7, Proposition 36.

## LEMMA VI.

*Under the same conditions, the aforementioned bodies are equally urged by water flowing through a channel.*

This is evident by Lemma 5 and the third law of motion <note>Newton's Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.</note>. For the water and the bodies certainly act upon each other with equal force.

## LEMMA VII.

*If the water remains at rest in the channel, and these bodies are moved through the channel in opposite directions with equal velocity: their resistances among themselves will be equal.*

This is established from the previous lemma, for the relative motions <note>Newton is applying the principle of relativity: it does not matter if the water moves past the object or the object moves through the water; the physical resistance remains the same.</note> remain the same among themselves.

->Scholium<-

The same reasoning applies to all convex and round bodies whose axes coincide with the axis of the channel. Some difference may arise from greater or lesser friction; but in these lemmas, we suppose the bodies to be perfectly polished, and the <term>tenacity</term> <note>original: "tenacitatem" — Newton uses this term to describe what we now call viscosity, or the "stickiness" of a fluid.</note> and friction of the medium to be zero. We also suppose that the parts of the fluid—which, by their oblique and superfluous motions, could disturb, impede, and retard the flow of water through the channel—rest among themselves as if constrained by frost <note>original: "gelu constrictæ" — a famous Newtonian metaphor where he imagines the turbulent parts of water as being "frozen" or solid to simplify his mathematical model of fluid flow.</note>, and adhere to the bodies at their front and back parts, just as I explained in the scholium of the preceding proposition. For in the following sections, we are dealing with the minimum possible resistance that round bodies, defined by their largest cross-sections, can have.

Bodies floating in fluids, when they move in a straight line, cause the fluid to rise at the front part and sink at the back part, especially if their shapes are blunt; and because of this, they feel a resistance slightly greater than if their "head" and "tail" <note>original: "capite & cauda"</note> were sharp. Furthermore, bodies moving in <term>elastic fluids</term> <note>original: "fluidis elasticis" — Newton is referring to gases, such as air, which can be compressed and expanded.</note>, if they are blunt in front and back, compress the fluid a bit more at the front and allow it to relax or expand a bit more at the back; and thus they feel a resistance slightly greater than if their head and tail were sharp. ## PROPOSITION XXXVIII. THEOREM XXX.

*The resistance of a sphere, moving uniformly through an infinite, compressed, and non-elastic fluid, is to the force by which its entire motion could be either destroyed or generated—in the time it takes to describe eight-thirds of its diameter—as the density of the fluid is to the density of the sphere, very nearly.*

For a sphere is to its circumscribed cylinder <note>The cylinder that perfectly fits the sphere inside it.</note> as two is to three; and therefore that force which could destroy all the motion of the cylinder while the cylinder describes a length of four diameters, will destroy all the motion of the sphere while the sphere describes two-thirds of this length—that is, eight-thirds of its own diameter. <note>original: "octo tertias partes diametri suæ" — Newton uses these specific ratios because the volume of a sphere is 2/3 that of a cylinder with the same height and diameter.</note> Now, the resistance of the cylinder is to this force very nearly as the density of the fluid is to the density of the cylinder or sphere (by Proposition 37); and the resistance of the sphere is equal to the resistance of the cylinder (by Lemmas 5, 6, and 7). Which was to be demonstrated.

*Corollary* 1. For spheres in infinite compressed media, the resistances are in a ratio composed of the square of the velocity, the square of the diameter, and the density of the media. <note>This is a foundational statement of the modern drag equation, where resistance increases with the area (diameter squared) and the square of the speed.</note>

*Corollary* 2. The maximum velocity <note>This is what we now call "terminal velocity."</note> with which a sphere, by the force of its comparative weight <note>original: "vi ponderis sui comparativi" — this refers to the weight of the object minus the buoyancy of the fluid.</note>, can descend in a resisting fluid, is that which the same sphere could acquire by falling with that same weight without resistance and, in its fall, describing a space that is to four-thirds of its diameter as the density of the sphere is to the density of the fluid. For a sphere in the time of its fall, with the velocity acquired by falling, will describe a space which will be to eight-thirds of its diameter as the density of the sphere is to the density of the fluid; and the force of the weight generating this motion will be to the force that could generate the same motion in the time the sphere describes eight-thirds of its diameter with the same velocity, as the density of the fluid...

# PROPOSITION XXXIX. THEOREM XXXI.

*The resistance of a sphere, advancing uniformly through a fluid enclosed and compressed within a cylindrical channel, is to the force by which its entire motion could be either generated or destroyed—in the time it takes to describe eight-thirds of its diameter—in a ratio compounded of the ratio of the opening of the channel to the excess of this opening over half of the sphere's greatest circle, and the squared ratio <note>original: "ratione duplicata" — in geometry, this refers to the ratio of the squares of the terms.</note> of the opening of the channel to the excess of this opening over the sphere's greatest circle, and the ratio of the density of the fluid to the density of the sphere, very nearly.*

This is clear through Corollary 2 of Proposition <term>XXXVII</term>; indeed, the proof proceeds in the same manner as in the preceding proposition.

->*Scholium*<-
<note>A "scholium" is an explanatory note or commentary added to a mathematical proof to provide context or address practical considerations.</note>

In the two most recent propositions (just as in Lemma <term>V</term>), I assume that all the water preceding the sphere is frozen, as its fluidity increases the sphere's resistance. If all that water were to liquefy, the resistance would be increased slightly. But that increase in these propositions will be small and can be disregarded, because the convex surface of the sphere performs almost the same function as the ice. <note>Newton uses the "frozen water" metaphor to simplify the fluid dynamics, treating the water immediately in front of the object as a solid cap to calculate the pressure and resistance more easily.</note>

### PROPOSITION XL. PROBLEM IX.

*To find the resistance of a sphere, advancing in a highly fluid compressed medium, by means of observable phenomena.* <note>original: "per phænomena" — Newton uses this to mean empirical evidence or experimental data.</note>

Let **A** be the weight of the sphere in a vacuum, **B** its weight in the resistant medium, and **D** the diameter of the sphere. Let **F** be a distance that stands to 4/3 of the diameter **D** as the density of the sphere stands to the density of the medium (that is, as **A** stands to **A – B**). Let **G** be the time in which the sphere, with weight **B** and without resistance, falling from rest, describes the distance **F**; and let **H** be the velocity which the sphere acquires by this fall. Then **H** will be the maximum velocity <note>This is what we now call terminal velocity—the point where the force of gravity is balanced by the force of resistance.</note> with which the sphere can descend by its own weight **B** in the resistant medium, according to Corollary 2 of Proposition XXXVIII; and the resistance which the sphere experiences when descending with that velocity will be equal to its weight **B**. Furthermore, the resistance it experiences at any other velocity will be to the weight **B** in the squared ratio <note>original: "duplicata ratione" — in the ratio of the squares of the values.</note> of this velocity to that maximum velocity **H**, according to Corollary 1 of Proposition XXXVIII.

This is the resistance that arises from the <term>inertia of matter</term> <note>the resistance of the fluid's mass to being moved out of the way</note> in the fluid. However, the resistance that arises from its elasticity, tenacity <note>original: "tenacitate" — what we now refer to as viscosity or the internal "stickiness" of the fluid.</note>, and the friction of its parts, shall be investigated as follows.

Let the sphere be dropped so that it descends in the fluid by its own weight **B**; and let **P** be the time of falling, expressed in seconds if the time **G** is also given in seconds. Find the absolute number **N** which corresponds to the logarithm 0.4342944819 $\frac{2P}{G}$, and let **L** be the logarithm of the number $\frac{N+1}{N}$. Then the velocity acquired by falling will be $\frac{N-1}{N+1}$ **H**, and the height described will be $\frac{2PF}{G}$ — 1.3862943611 **F** + 4.605170186 **LF**. If the fluid is deep enough, the term 4.605170186 **LF** can be neglected; and the height described will be approximately $\frac{2PF}{G}$ — 1.3862943611 **F**. These things are evident through the ninth proposition of the second book and its corollaries, based on the hypothesis that the sphere experiences no resistance other than that arising from the <term>inertia of matter</term>. If, however, it experiences an additional resistance, the descent will be slower, and the amount of this resistance will become known from that retardation.

To investigate the resistances of fluids through experiments, I prepared a square wooden vessel, nine inches in internal length and width <note>The "London foot" used here was the standard unit of measurement in England at the time, approximately 30.48 centimeters.</note>, and nine and a half feet in depth, and filled it with rainwater. A solid cubic London foot contains 76 <term>Roman pounds</term> <note>A Roman pound (libra) was a historical unit of weight, lighter than the modern pound, roughly equal to 327 grams.</note> of rainwater, and a solid inch of this foot contains 19/36 ounces of this pound, or 253 1/3 grains; and a globe of water described by a diameter of one inch contains 132.645 grains in the midst of air, or 132.8 grains in a vacuum; and any other globe is as the excess of its weight in a vacuum above its weight in water.

*Exper. 1.* A globe, whose weight was 156 1/3 grains in air and 77 grains in water, described the total height of 112 inches in a time of four seconds. And with the experiment repeated, the globe fell again in the same time of four seconds.

From this, the diameter of the globe is produced as 0.84224 parts of an inch. Moreover, as that excess is to the weight of the globe in a vacuum, so is the density of water to the density of the globe, and so are eight-third parts of the diameter of the globe (*viz.* 2.24597 inches) to the space 2 F, which accordingly will be 4.4256 inches. The globe in the time of one second, falling in a vacuum with its total weight of 156 13/30 grains, will describe 193 1/3 inches; and with a weight of 77 grains, in the same time, falling without resistance in water, it will describe 95.219 inches; and in time G, which is to one second in the <term>subduplicate ratio</term> <note>The "subduplicate ratio" refers to the square root of the ratio, a common phrasing in 17th-century mathematics.</note> of the space F or 2.2128 inches to 95.219 inches, it will describe 2.2128 inches, and will acquire the maximum velocity H <note>terminal velocity</note> with which it can descend in water. Therefore, time G is 0.15244 seconds. And in this time G, with that maximum velocity H, the globe will describe the space 2 F of 4.4256 inches; and therefore in the time of four seconds, it will describe a space of 116.1245 inches. In the experiment, it traveled 112 inches. The difference is imperceptible.

*Exper. 4.* I began the experiments described thus far in order to investigate the resistances of fluids before the theory explained in the immediately preceding propositions became known to me. ***Exper. 12.*** Three equal globes, with a weight of 141 grains in air and 4 1/8 in water, having been dropped several times, fell in times of 61, 62, 63, 64, and 65 oscillations, describing a height of 182 inches <note>original: "digitorum" — Newton uses "digits" to refer to inches.</note>.

And according to the theory, they ought to have fallen in a time of 64 8/10 oscillations, as nearly as possible.

Through these experiments, it is clear that where the globes fell slowly, as in the second, fourth, fifth, eighth, eleventh, and twelfth experiments, the times of falling are correctly shown by the theory; but where the globes fell more quickly, as in the sixth, ninth, and tenth experiments, the resistance stood a little higher than in the squared ratio <note>original: "duplicata ratione" — the square of the velocity ($v^2$)</note> of the velocity. For the globes oscillate a little while falling; and this oscillation in lighter and slower-falling globes quickly ceases due to the weakness of the motion; but in heavier and larger ones, it lasts longer due to the strength of the motion, and cannot be restrained by the surrounding water except after many oscillations. Furthermore, the faster the globes are, the less they are pressed by the fluid at their rear parts; and if the velocity were perpetually increased, they would eventually leave a vacuum behind them, unless the compression of the fluid were increased at the same time. However, the compression of the fluid (by Propositions 32 and 33) ought to be increased in the squared ratio of the velocity, so that the resistance might be in that same squared ratio. Since this does not happen, the faster globes are pressed a little less from behind, and by the lack of this pressure, their resistance becomes a little greater than in the squared ratio of the velocity.

The theory, therefore, agrees with the phenomena of bodies falling in water; it remains for us to examine the phenomena of those falling in air.

***Exper. 13.*** From the top of St. Paul’s Cathedral in the city of *London*, in the month of June 1710, two glass globes were dropped at the same time, one full of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi" — mercury</note>, the other of air; and in falling they described a height of 220 *London* feet. A wooden board was suspended by iron poles at one end and rested on a wooden bolt at the other; and the two globes, placed upon this board, were dropped together by pulling away the bolt with the help of an iron wire let down all the way to the ground, so that the board, leaning only on the iron poles, would swing down around them; and at the same moment of time, a pendulum oscillating to seconds [of time], by a wire...

The second and fourth bladders fell more straightly in the first trial, and the first and third in the second trial. The fifth bladder was wrinkled and was somewhat slowed down by its wrinkles. I derived the diameters of the bladders from their circumferences, measured with a very thin thread wound around twice. And I compared the theory with the experiments in the following table, assuming the density of the air to be to the density of rainwater as 1 to 860, and calculating the spaces which the globes ought to have described by falling according to the theory.
