<margin>BOOK TWO.</margin>
In the Scholium <note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary added to a mathematical proof.</note> that followed the sixth section, we showed through experiments with pendulums that the resistances of equal globes moving at the same speed in air, water, and quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; this is the historical term for mercury.</note> are proportional to the densities of those fluids. We are now demonstrating this more accurately through experiments with bodies falling in air and water. Indeed, with every swing, pendulums stir up a motion in the fluid that is always contrary to the motion of the pendulum as it returns. This resistance arising from that counter-motion, as well as the resistance of the wire by which the pendulum was suspended, made the total resistance of the pendulum greater than the resistance found through the experiments with falling bodies. 

For according to the pendulum experiments described in that Scholium, a globe of the same density as water, in traveling a distance equal to its own semi-diameter <note>The radius of the sphere.</note> in the air, ought to lose <margin>1/3342.</margin> part of its motion. But according to the theory explained in this seventh section and confirmed by the experiments with falling bodies, that same globe, in traveling the same distance, ought to lose only 1/4586 part of its motion—assuming the density of water is to the density of air as 860 to 1. Therefore, the resistances found through the pendulum experiments were larger (for the reasons already described) than those found by the experiments with falling globes, and this by a ratio of approximately 4 to 3. Nevertheless, since the resistances of pendulums oscillating in air, water, and quicksilver are increased in a similar way by similar causes, the proportion of the resistances in these mediums will be quite correctly shown both by pendulum experiments and by experiments with falling bodies. From this, it can be concluded that the resistances of bodies moving in any highly fluid mediums are, other things being equal, proportional to the densities of the fluids.

With these points established, we may now state approximately what portion of its motion any globe, thrown into any fluid, will lose in a given time. Let **D** be the diameter of the globe, **V** its velocity at the beginning of the motion, and **T** the time in which the globe, moving with velocity **V** in a vacuum, would describe a space that is to the space 8/3 **D** as the density of the globe is to the density of the fluid. If the globe is thrown into that fluid, in any other time **t**, it will lose a portion of its velocity equal to $\frac{t V}{T+t}$, while the portion $\frac{TV}{T+t}$ remains; and it will describe a space which is to the space described in a vacuum in the same time with uniform velocity **V**, as the logarithm of the number $\frac{T+t}{T}$ multiplied by...

the number 2.302585093 <note>This number is the natural logarithm of 10, used here for logarithmic calculations of resistance.</note> is to the number <gloss>t</gloss>/T, by Corollary 7, Proposition 35. In slow motions, the resistance can be a little less, because the shape of a globe is a little better suited for motion than the shape of a cylinder described with the same diameter. In swift motions, the resistance can be a little greater, because the elasticity and compression of the fluid do not increase in the squared ratio <note>original: "duplicata ratione"; in Newtonian physics, this refers to a relationship where one value increases as the square of another (v²).</note> of the velocity. And although air, water, quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; the historical term for mercury.</note>, and similar fluids might be refined by the division of their parts into infinity and become infinitely fluid mediums; nevertheless, they would resist projected globes no less. For the resistance discussed in the preceding propositions arises from the inertia of matter; and the inertia of matter is essential to bodies and always proportional to the quantity of matter. By the division of the parts of a fluid, the resistance which arises from the tenacity <note>Newton uses "tenacity" to describe what we now call viscosity—the "stickiness" or internal friction of a fluid.</note> and friction of the parts can indeed be diminished: but the quantity of matter is not diminished by the division of its parts; and while the quantity of matter remains, its force of inertia remains, to which the resistance discussed here is always proportional. For this resistance to be diminished, the quantity of matter in the spaces through which bodies move must be diminished. And for that reason, the celestial spaces—through which the globes of the planets and comets move perpetually in all directions most freely and without any sensible diminution of motion—are devoid of all bodily fluid, if perhaps you except the most thin vapors and the rays of light passing through.

Projectiles certainly stir up motion in fluids as they move forward, and this motion arises from the excess of the fluid's pressure on the front parts of the projectile over the pressure on its back parts; it can be no less in infinitely fluid mediums than in air, water, and quicksilver, in proportion to the density of the matter in each. Moreover, this excess of pressure, according to its magnitude, not only stirs up motion in the fluid but also acts upon the projectile to retard its motion: and therefore, resistance in every fluid is as the motion excited in the fluid by the projectile, nor can it be less in the most subtle ether <note>Many scientists in Newton's time believed space was filled with "ether," an invisible, weightless fluid. Newton argues here that if ether had any mass at all, it would eventually stop the planets.</note> according to the density of that ether, than in air, water, and quicksilver according to the densities of those fluids.

# SECTION VIII.
## *On motion propagated through fluids.*
### PROPOSITION 41. THEOREM 32.

*Pressure is not propagated through a fluid along straight lines, except where the particles of the fluid lie in a direct line.*

<image-desc>A diagram illustrating particle interaction. A horizontal line of circles is labeled a, b, c, d, and e. From circle e, the arrangement branches out to the right in a staggered, hexagonal-like packing. The first branching layer contains circles f (top) and g (bottom). The second layer contains h (top), i (middle), and k (bottom). The third layer contains l (top) and m (bottom).</image-desc>

If the particles *a, b, c, d, e* lie in a straight line, pressure can indeed be propagated directly from *a* to *e*; but the particle *e* will urge the obliquely <note>at an angle; not in a straight line</note> positioned particles *f* and *g* obliquely, and those particles *f* and *g* will not sustain the pressure applied to them unless they are supported by the further particles *h* and *k*; and insofar as they are supported, they press upon the supporting particles; and these will not sustain the pressure unless they are supported by the further particles *l* and *m* and press upon them, and so on indefinitely. Therefore, as soon as the pressure is propagated to particles that do not lie in a direct line, it will begin to divaricate <note>to branch off or spread out</note> and will be propagated obliquely indefinitely; and after it begins to be propagated obliquely, if it falls upon further particles which do not lie in a direct line, it will divaricate again; and this will happen as often as it falls upon particles not lying accurately in a direct line. Which was to be demonstrated. <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod erat demonstrandum)</note>

*Corollary.* If some part of the pressure propagated from a given point through a fluid is intercepted by an obstacle, the remaining part, which is not intercepted, will divaricate into the spaces behind the obstacle. This can also be demonstrated as follows. Let pressure be propagated in all directions from point *A*, and if possible, let this happen along straight lines; and let all of it be intercepted by an obstacle *NBCK* perforated at *BC*, except for the cone-shaped part *APQ* which passes through the circular hole *BC*. Let the cone *APQ* be divided into frustums <note>a section of a cone with the top cut off, like a stack of tapering disks</note> by the transverse planes *de, fg, hi*; and while the cone *ABC*, by propagating the pressure, urges the further conical frustum *degf* at the surface *de*, and this frustum urges the next frustum *fgih* at the surface *fg*, and that frustum urges the third frustum, and so on indefinitely; it is manifest (by the third law of motion) <note>Newton’s law stating that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.</note> that the frustum

## PROPOSITION 42. THEOREM 33.

*All motion propagated through a fluid diverges from a straight path into the motionless spaces.* <note>original: "Motus omnis per fluidum propagatus divergit a recto tramite in spatia immota." This is Newton's fundamental statement on the diffraction of waves.</note>

**Case 1.** Let motion be propagated from point *A* through an opening *BC*, and let it proceed, if possible, in the conical space *BCQP*, along straight lines diverging from point *A*. And let us first suppose that this motion is that of waves on the surface of stagnant water. Let *de, fg, hi, kl,* etc., be the highest parts <note>the crests</note> of the individual waves, separated from each other by as many intervening valleys <note>troughs</note>.

Therefore, since the water at the ridges of the waves is higher than in the motionless parts of the fluid *LK, NO*, it will flow down from the ends of the ridges *e, g, i, l,* etc., and *d, f, h, k,* etc., on either side toward *KL* and *NO*. And since the water in the valleys of the waves is lower than in the motionless parts of the fluid *KL, NO*, the water will flow from those motionless parts into the valleys of the waves. By the former outflow, the wave ridges are widened, and by the latter, the valleys are widened on both sides and propagated toward *KL* and *NO*. 

<note>Newton is explaining that because a wave consists of high points (crests) and low points (troughs), the laws of gravity and pressure force the water at the crest to spill sideways into the still water, while the still water spills into the troughs. This dual action causes the wave front to expand laterally, rather than traveling in a perfectly straight line like a solid projectile might.</note>

<summary>Newton demonstrates that waves traveling through an opening do not stay within a straight "beam" but spread sideways into quiet areas. He uses the physical behavior of water wave crests and troughs to explain why motion in a fluid inevitably diverges from a linear path.</summary>

<keywords>diffraction, wave propagation, fluid dynamics, Newton's laws of motion, wave crests, troughs, lateral expansion</keywords>

## PROPOSITION XLIII. THEOREM XXXIV.

> *Every vibrating body in an elastic medium will propagate the motion of pulses everywhere in a straight line; but in a non-elastic medium it will excite a circular motion.*

*Case 1.* For the parts of a vibrating body, by going and returning in alternating turns, will in this way urge and propel the parts of the medium closest to themselves, and by urging, will compress and condense them; then by their return, they will allow the compressed parts to recede and expand themselves. Therefore the parts of the medium closest to the vibrating body will go and return by turns, in the manner of the parts of that vibrating body: and by the same reasoning as the parts of this body agitated these parts of the medium, these [parts], agitated by similar vibrations, will agitate the parts closest to them, and those similarly agitated will agitate the ones further away, and so on infinitely. We have an example of this in water waves, which if excited by a vibrating finger, will not only proceed here and there according to the direction of the finger’s motion, but, in the manner of concentric circles, will immediately surround the finger and be propagated everywhere. *Case 2.* But if the medium is not elastic: since its parts, being pressed by the vibrating parts of the body, cannot be compressed, the motion will be propagated in an instant to the parts where the medium yields most easily, that is, to the parts which the vibrating body would otherwise leave empty behind it. The case is the same as that of a body projected in any medium. A medium, in yielding to projectiles, does not recede to infinity; but by moving in a circle, it proceeds to the spaces which the body leaves behind. Therefore, as often as the vibrating body moves in any direction, the medium by yielding will move in a circle to the parts which the body is leaving; and as often as the body returns to its former place, the medium will be repelled from there and return to its former place. And although the vibrating body might not be rigid, but flexible in every way, if it remains of a given size, since by its vibrations it cannot press the medium in one place without the medium simultaneously yielding to it elsewhere; it will cause the medium,

## PROPOSITION XLIV. THEOREM XXXV.

The force also, by which a weight *P* in any place *Q* is accelerated and retarded in a cycloid <note>A cycloid is the curve traced by a point on the rim of a circular wheel as it rolls along a straight line; Newton uses it here because a pendulum swinging in a cycloid is perfectly isochronous, meaning every swing takes the same time regardless of its width.</note> (by the corollary to proposition 51), is to its whole weight as its distance *PQ* from the lowest place *P* is to the length of the cycloid *PR*. Wherefore the motive forces of the water and of the pendulum, as they describe equal spaces *AE* and *PQ*, are as the weights to be moved; and therefore, if the water and the pendulum are at rest in the beginning, those forces will move them equally in equal times, and will cause them to go and return together in a reciprocal motion. Which was to be demonstrated. <note>original: "Q. E. D."</note>

**Corollary 1.** Therefore, whether the motion of the ascending and descending water be more intense or more sluggish, all its cycles are isochronous <note>original: "isochronæ"; meaning they take exactly the same amount of time.</note>.

**Corollary 2.** If the total length of the water in the channel is $6 \frac{1}{9}$ Parisian feet <note>The "Paris foot" was a common unit of measurement in 17th-century science, slightly longer than the English foot (about 32.5 cm).</note>: the water will descend in the time of one second, and ascend in the time of another second; and so on by turns forever. For a pendulum $3 \frac{1}{18}$ feet in length oscillates in the time of one second.

**Corollary 3.** Moreover, if the length of the water is increased or diminished, the time of the reciprocation is increased or diminished in the subduplicate ratio <note>This is a classical mathematical term meaning the "square root" of the ratio.</note> of the length.

# PROPOSITION XLV. THEOREM XXXVI.

*The velocity of waves is in the square root ratio <note>original: "subduplicata ratione"; Newton is stating that if you quadruple the wavelength, the speed only doubles.</note> of their breadths.*

This follows from the construction of the following proposition.

# PROPOSITION XLVI. PROBLEM X.

->*To find the velocity of waves.*<-

Let a pendulum be established whose length, between the point of suspension and the center of oscillation <note>The point in a swinging object where all its mass could be concentrated without changing its period.</note>, is equal to the breadth <note>What we now call wavelength.</note> of the waves: and in the time that this pendulum performs its individual oscillations, the waves will, in moving forward, nearly complete their own breadth.

I call the "breadth" of the waves the transverse measure that lies either between the lowest valleys or the highest peaks. Let $ABCDEF$ represent the surface of stagnant water, rising and falling in successive waves; and let $A, C, E,$ etc., be the peaks of the waves, and $B, D, F,$ etc., be the intermediate valleys. And since the motion of waves occurs through the successive rise and fall of the water, so that those parts $A, C, E,$ etc.,

<image-desc>A line drawing of a regular transverse wave oscillating around a central horizontal dotted line. Peaks are labeled A, C, and E. Troughs are labeled B, D, and F. The wave moves from left to right through these points.</image-desc>

which are now the highest, will soon become the lowest; and the motive force by which the highest parts descend and the lowest rise is the weight of the elevated water; that alternating rise and fall will be analogous to the reciprocal motion of water in a channel <note>Referring back to the U-shaped tube experiment in Proposition 44.</note>, and will observe the same laws of time: and therefore (by Proposition 44) if the distances between the highest points of the waves $A, C, E$ and the lowest points $B, D, F$ are equal to double the length of the pendulum, the highest parts $A, C, E$ will become the lowest in the time of one oscillation, and in the time of another oscillation they will rise again. Therefore, the time between the passage of individual waves will be the duration of two oscillations; that is, the wave will cover its breadth in the time that the pendulum oscillates twice. But in that same time, a pendulum whose length is four times greater, and which therefore equals the breadth of the waves, will oscillate exactly once. 
*Which was to be found.* <note>original: "Q. E. I." (*Quod Erat Inveniendum*)</note>

## PROPOSITION XLVII. THEOREM XXXVII.

*When pulses are propagated through a fluid, the individual particles of the fluid, moving back and forth in a very short <term>reciprocal motion<note>original: "motu reciproco"; a repetitive back-and-forth movement, similar to a pendulum or a piston.</note></term>, are always accelerated and retarded according to the law of an oscillating pendulum.*

<image-desc>A vertical linear diagram on the right margin consisting of a vertical axis with horizontal segments of varying lengths extending from points labeled from top to bottom: A, B, E, F, G, Ω, τ, G, F, E, B, A. This illustrates the varying displacement of particles in a wave pulse.</image-desc>

Let *AB*, *BC*, *CD*, etc., designate the equal distances of successive pulses; *ABC* the direction of the motion of the pulses propagated from *A* toward *B*; *E*, *F*, *G* three physical points of the medium at rest, situated at equal distances from one another along the straight line *AC*; *Ee*, *Ff*, *Gg* equal, very short spaces through which those points, in their reciprocal motion, go and return during each individual vibration; $\epsilon$, $\phi$, $\gamma$ any intermediate locations of those same points; and *EF*, *FG* the physical lines—or the linear parts of the medium—lying between those points, and successively transferred into the locations $\epsilon\phi$, $\phi\gamma$ and *ef*, *fg*. Let a straight line *PS* be drawn equal to the straight line *Ee*. Let the same be bisected at *O*, and with center *O* and radius *OP*, let the circle *SIPi* be described. Let the entire time of one vibration, along with its parts, be represented by this whole circumference and its parts.

For the physical lineola $\epsilon \gamma$, as soon as it has returned to its first location, will rest; nor will it be moved thereafter unless it is stirred by a new motion, either from the impulse of the tremulous body or from the impulse of the pulses propagated from the tremulous body. It will therefore rest as soon as the pulses cease to be propagated from the tremulous body.

Nevertheless, unless the contractions and expansions are very intense, it will not stray noticeably, and therefore can be considered physically accurate. The elastic moving forces are as the contractions and expansions; and the velocities of equal parts generated at the same time are as the forces. Therefore, equal and corresponding parts of corresponding <term>pulses<note>In this context, Newton uses "pulses" to describe what we now call sound waves or longitudinal waves.</note></term> will complete their forward and backward movements through spaces proportional to the contractions and expansions, with velocities that are as those spaces, at the same time: and for that reason the pulses, which in the time of one forward and backward movement complete their own breadth by moving forward, and always succeed into the locations of the pulses immediately preceding them, will, due to the equality of distances, proceed with equal velocity in both media.

*Case 2.* But if the distances or lengths of the pulses are greater in one medium than in another; let us suppose that the corresponding parts describe spaces proportional to the breadths of the pulses in each forward and backward motion: and their contractions and expansions will be equal. Therefore, if the media are <term>homogeneous<note>Uniform in structure or composition throughout.</note></term>, those elastic moving forces by which they are agitated in reciprocal motion will also be equal. However, the matter to be moved by these forces is as the breadth of the pulses; and in the same ratio is the space through which they must be moved in each forward and backward motion. And the time of one forward and backward motion is in a ratio compounded of the <term>square root ratio<note>original: *ratione subduplicata*. Newton uses this classical terminology to describe what we mathematically express as the square root ($\sqrt{x}$).</note></term> of the matter and the square root ratio of the space, and is therefore as the space. But pulses, in the times of one forward and backward movement, complete their own breadths by moving forward—that is, they traverse spaces proportional to the times; and therefore they are equally swift.

*Case 3.* Therefore, in media with equal density and elastic force, all pulses are equally swift. But if either the density or the elastic force of the medium is increased, since the moving force increases in the ratio of the elastic force, and the matter to be moved increases in the ratio of the density; the time in which the same motions may be completed as before will increase in the square root ratio of the density, and decrease in the square root ratio of the elastic force. And therefore the velocity of the pulses will be in a ratio compounded of the inverse square root ratio of the density of the medium and the direct square root ratio of the elastic force.
*Which was to be demonstrated.*

**Corollary 1.** The velocity of the pulses is that which heavy bodies acquire by falling with an equally accelerated motion and describing half of the height *A* in their fall. For in the time of this fall, with the velocity acquired by falling, the pulse would traverse a space that will be equal to the entire height *A*; and therefore, in the time of one oscillation composed of an outward and return motion, it will traverse a space equal to the circumference of a circle described with radius *A*: for the time of the fall is to the time of oscillation as the radius of a circle is to its circumference.

**Corollary 2.** Hence, since that height *A* is as the <term>elastic force<note>What we now call the bulk modulus or pressure of the fluid.</note></term> of the fluid directly and its density inversely; the velocity of the pulses will be in a ratio compounded of the subduplicate ratio of the density inversely and the subduplicate ratio of the elastic force directly. <note>In modern terms: $v = \sqrt{P/\rho}$.</note>

## PROPOSITION 50. PROBLEM 12.

### *To find the distances between pulses.*

Find the number of vibrations of a body—whose trembling excites the pulses—within a given time. Divide the space that a pulse can travel in that same time by that number, and the part found will be the width of a single pulse. <note>Which was to be found.</note>

### *Scholium.*

The most recent propositions relate to the motion of light and sounds. For since light is propagated along straight lines, it cannot consist in action alone (by Propositions 41 and 42) <note>Newton is arguing that if light were merely a wave like sound, it would "bend" into shadows more readily; he uses this to support his corpuscular (particle) theory of light.</note>. Sounds, however, because they arise from trembling bodies, are nothing other than propagated pulses of air, as shown by Proposition 43. This is confirmed by the tremors they excite in surrounding bodies, provided they are forceful and deep, such as the sounds of drums. For faster and shorter tremors are excited with greater difficulty. Moreover, it is very well known that any sounds, when they strike strings that are <term>unison<note>In harmony or at the same pitch.</note></term> with the sounding bodies, excite tremors. 

It is also confirmed by the velocity of sounds. For since the specific weights of rain water and quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi" (mercury)</note> are to each other as about 1 to 13 2/3, and where the mercury in the *Barometer* reaches a height of 30 *English* inches, the specific weights of air and rain water are to each other as about 1 to 870: the specific weights of air and quicksilver will be as 1 to 11890. Accordingly, since the height of the quicksilver is 30 inches, the height of a uniform atmosphere <note>original: "aëris uniformis". This refers to an idealized atmosphere of constant density that would exert the same pressure as our actual atmosphere.</note>, the weight of which could compress our underlying air, would be 356,700 inches, or 29,725 *English* feet. And this height is that very same one which we named *A* in the construction of the preceding problem. 

The circumference of a circle described with a radius of 29,725 feet is 186,768 feet. And since a pendulum 39 1/5 inches long completes an oscillation composed of an outward and return motion in the time of two seconds, as is well known; a pendulum 29,725 feet (or 356,700 inches) long must complete a similar oscillation in the time of 190 3/4 seconds. Therefore, in that time, sound by moving forward will cover 186,768 feet, and therefore in the time of one second, it covers 979 feet.

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

Furthermore, in this calculation, no account is taken of the thickness of the solid particles of air, through which sound is certainly propagated in an <margin>BOOK TWO.</margin> instant. Since the weight of air is to the weight of water as 1 to 870, and salts are nearly twice as dense as water; if the particles of air are assumed to be of approximately the same density as the particles of either water or salts, and the rarity of air arises from the intervals between the particles: the diameter of a particle of air will be to the interval between the centers of the particles as about 1 to 9 or 10, and to the interval between the particles as 1 to 8 or 9. Accordingly, to the 979 feet which sound travels in the time of one second according to the calculation above, we may add about 979/9 feet, or roughly 109 feet, due to the thickness of the air particles; and thus, in the time of one second, sound will cover about 1088 feet.

Add to this that the vapors lurking in the air, since they are of a different <term>elasticity<note>original: "elateris"</note></term> and a different tone, hardly—if at all—participate in the motion of the true air by which sounds are propagated. While these vapors remain at rest, that motion will be propagated more quickly through the true air alone, and that in the <term>subduplicate ratio<note>This refers to the square root of the ratio. Newton is applying his discovery that the speed of a wave is proportional to the square root of the medium's elasticity divided by its density.</note></term> of the lesser matter. For instance, if the atmosphere consists of ten parts true air and one part vapors, the motion of sounds will be faster in the subduplicate ratio of 11 to 10, or in approximately the whole ratio of 21 to 20, than if it were propagated through eleven parts of true air; and therefore the motion of sounds found above must be increased in this ratio. In this way, sound will travel 1142 feet in the time of one second.

These things ought to be so in the Spring and Autumn, when the air is thinned by temperate heat and its elastic force is somewhat intensified. But in the Winter, when the air is condensed by cold and its elastic force is weakened, the motion of sounds ought to be slower in the subduplicate ratio of the density; and conversely, in the Summer, it ought to be faster.

Moreover, it is established by experiments that sounds, in the time of one second, travel more or less 1142 *London* feet, or 1070 *Paris* feet. <note>Before the Metric System, "feet" varied by region; a Paris foot was slightly longer than a London foot.</note>

Once the velocity of sounds is known, the intervals between pulses also become known. For <term>Mr. Sauveur<note>Joseph Sauveur (1653–1716), a French mathematician and physicist known as the founder of acoustics.</note></term> found, through experiments he conducted, that an open pipe, the length of which is approximately five *Paris* feet, emits a sound of the same tone as a string which returns one hundred times in the space of one second. There are, therefore, about one hundred pulses in the space of 1070 *Paris* feet, which sound [travels] in the time of...

## SECTION IX.
### On the circular motion of fluids.

## HYPOTHESIS.

*The resistance which arises from a lack of <term>slipperiness<note>original: "lubricitatis"—Newton is here defining what we now call "viscosity," the internal friction or "thickness" of a fluid that resists flow.</note></term> in the parts of a fluid, other things being equal, is proportional to the velocity by which the parts of the fluid are separated from one another.*

## PROPOSITION LI. THEOREM XXXIX.

*If a solid cylinder of infinite length revolves with a uniform motion in a uniform and infinite fluid around an axis given in position, and the fluid is driven into a swirl by this impulse alone, and every part of the fluid continues uniformly in its motion; I say that the <term>periodic times<note>The time required for a particle to complete one full revolution around the axis.</note></term> of the parts of the fluid are as their distances from the axis of the cylinder.*

Let AFL be a cylinder driven uniformly in a circle around the axis *S*, and let the fluid be distinguished by the concentric circles *BGM, CHN, DIO, EKP*, and so forth.

...the fluid into countless concentric solid cylindrical <term>shells<note>Newton uses "orbes," which in this context refers to thin, nested cylindrical layers similar to the layers of an onion.</note></term> of the same thickness. And since the fluid is <term>homogeneous<note>Uniform in composition throughout.</note></term>, the <term>forces<note>original: "impressiones"—referring to the internal friction or viscosity between the layers of the fluid.</note></term> exerted by neighboring shells upon each other will be (by hypothesis) proportional to their <term>relative motions<note>original: "translationes"—the sliding motion of one layer against another.</note></term> from each other and the shared surface areas where these forces occur. If the force acting on any shell is greater or lesser on the concave (inner) side than on the convex (outer) side, the stronger force will prevail, and will either accelerate or retard the motion of the shell, depending on whether it is directed in the same direction as the motion or the opposite. Therefore, for each shell to continue uniformly in its motion, the forces on both sides must be equal to each other and act in opposite directions. Since the forces are proportional to the contact surfaces and their relative motions, the relative motions will be inversely as the surfaces—that is, inversely as the distances of the surfaces from the axis. However, the differences in the angular motions around the axis are proportional to these relative motions applied to the distances, or as the relative motions directly and the distances inversely; that is,

**Corollary 1.** From this, the angular motions of the fluid particles are inversely as their distances from the axis of the cylinder, and the absolute velocities are equal.

*Corollary* 2. If a fluid is contained in a cylindrical vessel of infinite length and contains another interior cylinder, and both cylinders revolve around a common axis, and the <term>periodic times<note>The time it takes to complete one full revolution.</note></term> of their revolutions are proportional to their <term>radii<note>original: "semidiametri"</note></term>, and every part of the fluid persists in its motion: then the periodic times of the individual parts will be proportional to their distances from the axis of the cylinders.

*Corollary* 3. If any common <term>angular motion<note>Rotational or spinning motion.</note></term> is added to or subtracted from the system of cylinders and fluid moving in this manner; since this new motion does not change the mutual <term>friction<note>original: "attritus"—Newton's term for the internal resistance or viscosity of the fluid.</note></term> of the parts of the fluid, the motions of the parts relative to each other will not be changed. For the relative shifting of the parts from one another depends upon friction. Any part will persist in that motion which, with friction acting on both sides in opposite directions, is accelerated no more than it is retarded.

*Corollary* 4. Hence, if all angular motion of the exterior cylinder is removed from the whole system of cylinders and fluid, one will have the motion of the fluid in a resting cylinder.

*Corollary* 5. Therefore, if the fluid and the exterior cylinder are at rest, and the interior cylinder is rotated uniformly; circular motion will be communicated to the fluid and will be propagated gradually through the whole fluid; nor will it cease to increase until the individual parts of the fluid acquire the motion defined in the fourth corollary.

*Corollary* 6. And because the fluid endeavors to propagate its motion even further, the exterior cylinder will also be rotated by its <term>impetus<note>The force or energy of the moving fluid.</note></term> unless it is forcibly held back; and its motion will be accelerated until the periodic times of both cylinders are equal to each other. But if the exterior cylinder is forcibly held back, it will endeavor to retard the motion of the fluid; and unless the interior cylinder, by some force applied from without, maintains that motion, it will cause the same to gradually cease.

## PROPOSITION 52. THEOREM 40.

> *If a solid sphere, in a uniform and infinite fluid, revolves with a uniform motion about an axis given in position, and the fluid is driven into a whirlpool by the impulse of this alone; and every part of the fluid persists uniformly in its motion: I say that the <term>periodic times<note>The time required for a single complete revolution.</note></term> of the parts of the fluid will be as the squares of the distances from the center of the sphere.*

**Case 1.** Let AFL be a sphere driven uniformly around axis S, and let the fluid be divided into innumerable concentric <term>orbs<note>Spherical shells or layers, like the layers of an onion.</note></term> of the same thickness by the concentric circles BGM, CHN, DIO, EKP, and so on. Imagine, moreover, that those orbs are solid; and since the fluid is <term>homogeneous<note>Of a uniform consistency throughout.</note></term>, the <term>impressions<note>original: "impressiones"—Newton uses this to mean the force of friction or viscous resistance between the layers.</note></term> of contiguous orbs made upon each other will be (by hypothesis) as their <term>translations<note>original: "translationes"—the relative sliding or shifting speed of one layer against the next.</note></term> from each other and the contiguous surfaces in which the impressions are made. If the impression on any orb is greater or less on the concave side than on the convex side, the stronger impression will prevail, and will either accelerate or retard the velocity of the orb, according to whether it is directed in the same direction as its motion or in the opposite direction. Therefore, in order for each orb to persist uniformly in its motion, the impressions on both sides must be equal to each other, and occur in opposite directions.

Hence, since the impressions are as the contiguous surfaces and their translations from each other; the translations will be inversely as the surfaces—that is, inversely as the squares of the distances of the surfaces from the center. If $Dd, Ee,$ etc., are <term>reciprocally proportional<note>This means that as one value increases, the other decreases at a specific rate. Here, the force or motion decreases as the cube of the distance ($1/r^3$) from the center.</note></term> to the cubes of the distances $SA, SB, SC, SD, SE,$ etc., then the sums of the differences—that is, the total **angular motions**—will be as the corresponding sums of the lines $Aa, Bb, Cc, Dd, Ee$. This means (if we imagine the number of layers increasing and their thickness decreasing to infinity, in order to create a <term>uniformly fluid medium<note>A liquid or gas that has the same consistency everywhere.</note></term>) that these motions are as the <term>hyperbolic areas<note>Newton uses the geometry of a hyperbola to calculate the total effect of friction throughout the fluid; in modern terms, this is similar to integration in calculus.</note></term> $AaQ, BbQ, CcQ, DdQ, EeQ,$ etc., which are analogous to those sums. Consequently, the **periodic times** (being reciprocally proportional to the angular motions) will also be reciprocally proportional to these areas. Therefore, the periodic time of any orbit $DIO$ is reciprocally as the area $DdQ$; that is, by the known <term>quadratures<note>The historical term for calculating the area under a curve.</note></term> of curves, it is directly as the **square of the distance** $SD$. This is what I first intended to demonstrate.

**Case 2.** From the center of the sphere, let an infinite number of straight lines be drawn, separated by equal angles from a given axis. Imagine the fluid orbits to be sliced into innumerable **rings** (annuli) by revolving these lines around that axis. Each ring will have four other rings touching it: one on the inside, one on the outside, and two on its sides. Because of the <term>friction<note>original: "attritu"—the resistance caused by fluid layers sliding against one another.</note></term> of the inner and outer rings, any single ring can only be urged equally and in opposite directions if the motion follows the law established in Case 1. This is clear from the proof of Case 1. Furthermore, any series of rings extending in a straight line from the globe to infinity will move according to the law of Case 1, unless hindered by the friction of the rings at their sides. But in a motion governed by this law, there is no friction between the rings at their sides; therefore, it will not hinder the motion from occurring this way. If the rings at an equal distance from the center revolved either faster or slower near the poles than near the <term>ecliptic<note>The "equator" or midline of the rotating sphere.</note></term>, the slower ones would be accelerated and the faster ones retarded by their mutual friction. Thus, the periodic times would always tend toward equality, according to the law of Case 1. Therefore, this friction does not prevent the motion from happening according to the law of Case 1, and consequently, that law will hold: that is, the **periodic times** of the individual rings will be as the **squares of their distances** from the center of the sphere. This is what I intended to demonstrate in the second place.

**Case 3.** Now let each ring be divided by transverse sections into countless particles constituting an absolutely and uniformly fluid substance; and since these sections do not pertain to the law of circular motion, but only contribute to the makeup of the fluid, the circular motion will continue as before. By these sections, all the smallest rings will either not change their <term>roughness<note>Newton uses "asperitas" (roughness) to describe the physical quality of the fluid particles that causes friction (attritus) between the layers.</note></term> and the force of mutual friction, or they will change them equally. And as the proportion of causes remains the same, the proportion of effects will also remain—that is, the proportion of motions and **periodic times**. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

Furthermore, since the circular motion, and the **centrifugal force** arising from it, is greater at the <term>ecliptic<note>original: "eclipticam"; here Newton refers to the equator of the rotating sphere, the "great circle" furthest from the poles.</note></term> than at the poles, some cause must be present by which individual particles are kept in their circles; otherwise, the matter at the ecliptic would always move away from the center and migrate through the outer parts of the **vortex** toward the poles, and from there return via the axis to the ecliptic in a perpetual circulation.

**Corollary 1.** Hence, the **angular motions** of the parts of the fluid around the axis of the globe are <term>reciprocally<note>Inversely proportional: as the distance from the center increases, the angular motion decreases by the square of that distance.</note></term> as the squares of the distances from the center of the globe, and the absolute velocities are reciprocally as the same squares applied to the distances from the axis.

**Corollary 2.** If a globe revolves with a uniform motion around an axis in a given position within a resting, similar, and infinite fluid, the motion will be communicated to the fluid in the manner of a **vortex**, and this motion will gradually propagate out to infinity; nor will it cease to accelerate in the individual parts of the fluid until the **periodic times** of those individual parts are as the squares of the distances from the center of the globe.

**Corollary 3.** Since the inner parts of the vortex, on account of their greater velocity, rub against and press upon the outer parts, and by that action perpetually communicate motion to them, and those outer parts simultaneously transfer the same quantity of motion to others even further out, and by that action keep their own quantity of motion entirely unchanged; it is clear that motion is perpetually transferred from the center to the circumference of the vortex, and is absorbed by the infinity of the circumference. The matter between any two spherical surfaces concentric to the vortex will never be accelerated, because it always transfers all the motion received from the inner matter to the outer matter.

**Corollary 4.** Therefore, for the conservation of a vortex constantly in the same state of motion, some <term>active principle<note>Newton suggests that because friction constantly "absorbs" motion, a mechanical system like a vortex cannot run forever on its own; it requires an external source or "active principle" to keep the central globe spinning.</note></term> is required, from which the globe may always receive the same quantity of motion that it impresses upon the matter

</margin>the material of the vortex. Without such a principle, it is inevitable that the globe and the inner parts of the vortex—which are constantly passing their motion to the outer parts and receiving no new motion in return—would gradually slow down and eventually cease to spin in a circle.

**Corollary 5.** If a second globe were to float in this **vortex** <note>Newton is critiquing René Descartes' theory that planets are carried by "vortices" of celestial fluid. Here, he shows that multiple rotating bodies would create conflicting currents.</note> at a fixed distance from its center, and were kept constantly revolving around its own axis by some force at a given inclination; the fluid would be drawn into a vortex by its motion. Initially, this new and small vortex would revolve along with its globe around the center of the first vortex; meanwhile, its motion would creep further outward and be gradually propagated to infinity, in the same manner as the first vortex. And by the same reasoning that this second globe would be carried by the motion of the first vortex, the first globe would also be carried by the motion of the second, such that the two globes would revolve around some intermediate point. Because of that circular motion, they would flee from one another <note>This "fleeing" refers to centrifugal force pushing the bodies apart.</note> unless held back by some force. Afterward, if the constantly impressed forces by which the globes persist in their motions were to cease, and everything were left to the **laws of mechanics**, the motion of the globes would gradually fade away (for the reason assigned in **Corollaries 3 and 4**) and the vortices would finally come to rest.

**Corollary 6.** If many globes in fixed locations were constantly rotated at specific velocities around axes in set positions, just as many vortices would be created, extending out infinitely. For each individual globe, by the same reasoning that any single one propagates its motion to infinity, will also propagate its own motions to infinity, so much so that every part of the infinite fluid would be agitated by the motion resulting from the actions of all the globes. Therefore, the vortices would not be confined by fixed limits, but would gradually run into one another; and the globes, through the actions of the vortices upon each other, would be perpetually moved from their positions, as was explained in the previous corollary; nor would they maintain any fixed position relative to each other unless held back by some force. However, if those forces which are constantly impressed upon the globes to preserve these motions were to cease, the matter—for the reason assigned in the third and fourth corollaries—would gradually come to rest and cease to be driven into vortices.

**Corollary 7.** If a uniform fluid is enclosed in a spherical vessel, and is driven into a vortex by the uniform rotation of a globe located at the center, and both the globe and the vessel are rotated in the same direction around the same axis, and their **periodic times** <note>The time taken to complete one full revolution.</note> are as the squares of the <term>semidiameters<note>The radius of the sphere.</note></term>: the parts of the fluid will not continue in their motions without acceleration

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "tione," which completes the word "acceleratione" (acceleration) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Newton argues that vortices require a continuous source of energy to persist, otherwise friction causes them to slow and stop. ### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

<margin>BOOK TWO.</margin>
...acceleration and retardation, so that their periodic times <note>The time taken to complete one full revolution.</note> are as the squares of the distances from the center of the vortex. No other constitution of a vortex can be permanent.

*Corollary 8.* If a vessel, the fluid contained within it, and the globe maintain this motion, and furthermore revolve with a common angular motion around any given axis; because this new motion does not change the friction <note>original: "attritus"</note> of the parts of the fluid against one another, the motions of the parts relative to each other will not be changed. For the relative movements of the parts depend on friction. Any part will persevere in that motion by which it happens that it is slowed down by friction on one side no more than it is accelerated by friction on the other.

*Corollary 9.* Hence, if the vessel is at rest and the motion of the globe is given, the motion of the fluid will be determined. For conceive of a plane passing through the axis of the globe and revolving with a contrary motion; and let the sum of the time of this revolution and the revolution of the globe be to the time of the revolution of the globe, as the square of the semi-diameter <note>The radius of the vessel.</note> of the vessel is to the square of the semi-diameter of the globe: then the periodic times of the parts of the fluid with respect to this plane will be as the squares of their distances from the center of the globe.

*Corollary 10.* Therefore, if the vessel moves either around the same axis as the globe, or around some different axis with any given velocity, the motion of the fluid will be determined. For if the angular motion of the vessel is subtracted from the whole system, all the motions relative to each other will remain the same as before, by Corollary 8. And those motions will be determined by Corollary 9.

*Corollary 11.* If the vessel and the fluid are at rest and the globe revolves with a uniform motion, the motion will be propagated gradually through the whole fluid to the vessel, and the vessel will be turned around unless forcibly held back; nor will the fluid and the vessel stop being accelerated until their periodic times are equal to the periodic times of the globe. But if the vessel is held back by some force or revolves with any constant and uniform motion, the medium will gradually reach the state of motion defined in Corollaries 8, 9, and 10, and will never persist in any other state. Then, if those forces by which the vessel and globe were revolving with certain motions cease, and the whole system is left to the **laws of mechanics**; the vessel and the globe will act upon each other through the medium of the fluid, and they will not stop propagating their motions to each other through the fluid until their periodic times are equal to one another, and the whole system revolves together like a single solid body.

<summary>Newton describes how friction within a fluid eventually forces a vessel, its contained fluid, and a rotating inner globe to synchronize their motions. He argues that without external force, any system of fluid and solids will eventually rotate as a single, solid mass, further debunking the idea of independent, self-sustaining celestial vortices.</summary>

**On the Motion of Bodies**

### Scholium. <note>An explanatory note or commentary following a mathematical proof.</note>

In all of these investigations, I suppose the fluid to consist of matter that is uniform in both density and fluidity. It is a fluid in which the same globe, moving with the same motion in the same interval of time, is able to propagate similar and equal motions at always equal distances from itself, wherever it is placed in the fluid. To be sure, matter attempts by its circular motion to recede from the axis of the vortex, and therefore presses upon all the matter further out. From this pressure, the friction <note>original: "attritus"</note> of the parts becomes stronger and their separation from one another more difficult; and consequently, the fluidity of the matter is diminished. Again, if the parts of the fluid are anywhere thicker or larger, the fluidity there will be less, due to having fewer surfaces where the parts may separate from one another. In cases of this kind, I suppose the deficient fluidity to be restored either by the slipperiness of the parts or by their suppleness <note>original: "lentore" – Newton is suggesting that if friction or particle size reduces fluidity, some other physical property must compensate to keep his mathematical model consistent.</note> or some other condition. Unless this happens, the matter where it is less fluid will cohere more and be more sluggish, and therefore will receive motion more slowly and propagate it further than according to the ratio assigned above. 

If the shape of the vessel is not spherical, the particles will move in lines that are not circular but conform to the shape of that same vessel, and the periodic times will be as the squares of the average distances from the center, very nearly. In the parts between the center and the circumference, where the spaces are wider, the motions will be slower; where they are narrower, they will be faster; yet the faster particles will not seek the circumference. For they will describe arcs that are less curved, and the endeavor to recede from the center will be diminished by the decrease of this curvature no less than it will be increased by the increase of velocity. Moving from narrower spaces into wider ones, they will recede a little further from the center, but by that recession they will slow down; and approaching afterwards from wider to narrower spaces, they will be accelerated, and thus by turns each individual particle will slow down and accelerate forever. These things will be so in a rigid vessel. For in an infinite fluid, the constitution of vortices is known through the sixth corollary of this proposition.

Now, I have attempted to investigate the properties of vortices in this proposition so that I might test whether by any means celestial phenomena <note>The observable movements of the stars and planets.</note> can be explained by vortices. For it is an observed phenomenon that the periodic times of the planets revolving around Jupiter are in the sesquialteral <note>original: "sesquiplicata" – The "three-halves" power ratio (x^1.5), now known as Kepler's Third Law. Newton is testing if a vortex of fluid can produce this specific mathematical result.</note> ratio of their distances from the center of Jupiter; and the same rule holds for the planets that revolve around the sun. These rules hold, moreover, in the planets

If this is granted, the periodic times of the parts of the vortex will be in a ratio greater than the duplicate ratio <note>greater than r²</note> of the distances from its center. But if the vortices (as is the opinion of some) move faster near the center, then slower up to a certain limit, then again faster near the circumference; certainly neither the sesquiplicate ratio nor any other certain and determined ratio can be maintained. Let philosophers <note>Here Newton refers to "Natural Philosophers," the 17th-century term for scientists, particularly the Cartesians who defended the vortex theory.</note> therefore consider how that phenomenon of the sesquiplicate ratio can be explained by vortices.

## PROPOSITION LIII. THEOREM XLI.

*Bodies that are carried in a vortex and return in an orbit are of the same density as the vortex, and move by the same law as the parts of the vortex in terms of velocity and the determination of their course.*

*Corol. 2.* And if the vortex is of uniform density, the same body can be revolved at any distance from the center of the vortex.

These two things contradict each other. 

Thus, at the beginning of the sign of Virgo, where the aphelion of Mars is now located, the distance between the orbits of Mars and Venus is to the distance of those same orbits at the beginning of the sign of Pisces as approximately three to two; and therefore, the matter of the vortex between those orbits at the beginning of Pisces must be faster than at the beginning of Virgo in a ratio of three to two. For the narrower the space through which the same quantity of matter passes in the same time of one revolution, the greater the velocity with which it must pass. 

Therefore, if the Earth, being relatively at rest in this celestial matter, were carried by it and revolved together around the Sun, its velocity at the beginning of Pisces would be to its velocity at the beginning of Virgo in a sesquialterate <note>A ratio of 3:2, or 1.5 times.</note> ratio. From this, the Sun’s apparent daily motion <note>Newton is using the apparent motion of the Sun as seen from Earth to describe the Earth's actual orbital speed.</note> at the beginning of Virgo would be greater than seventy minutes of a degree, and at the beginning of Pisces less than forty-eight minutes; yet (as experience proves), that apparent motion of the Sun is greater at the beginning of Pisces than at the beginning of Virgo, and therefore the Earth is faster at the beginning of Virgo than at the beginning of Pisces. 

Therefore, the hypothesis of vortices is utterly at odds with astronomical phenomena, and serves not so much to explain as to disturb the celestial motions. How these motions are actually performed in free spaces without vortices can be understood from Book I, and will now be taught more fully in *The System of the World*.

## BOOK THREE.

In the preceding books, I have presented the principles of philosophy <note>In Newton’s time, "Natural Philosophy" was the term for what we now call "Physics."</note>, yet these were not so much philosophical as they were strictly mathematical—the foundations, as it were, from which one may argue in philosophical matters. These consist of the laws and conditions of motions and forces, which relate most closely to philosophy. Nevertheless, so that these principles might not appear sterile, I have illustrated them with certain philosophical scholia <note>original: "scholiis," meaning explanatory notes or commentaries</note>, treating topics that are general and upon which philosophy seems to be most firmly based, such as the density and resistance of bodies, spaces empty of matter, and the motion of light and sound. It remains for us now to demonstrate, from these same principles, the constitution of the System of the World.

Regarding this subject, I had originally composed this third book in a popular method <note>Newton initially wrote a more prose-heavy version of this book, now known as "The System of the World," before deciding it was too risky to publish in a non-mathematical format.</note>, so that it might be read by a wider audience. But for those who have not sufficiently understood the principles I have laid down, they will hardly perceive the force of the conclusions, nor will they set aside the prejudices to which they have been accustomed for many years. Therefore, to prevent the subject from being dragged into endless disputes, I have reduced the essence of that book into the form of propositions, in the mathematical manner, so that they may be read only by those who have first mastered the principles. 

However, since a great many propositions occur there which might cause even mathematically learned readers to pause too long, I do not wish to suggest that anyone should study them all. It will suffice if someone reads the definitions, the laws of motion, and the first three sections of Book I with diligence; then, let them pass to this book on the System of the World, and consult the remaining propositions of the previous books cited here at their own discretion.

# RULES

# OF REASONING IN PHILOSOPHY. <note>original: "Philosophandi." In Newton's era, "Natural Philosophy" was the term for what we now call science, specifically physics.</note>

---

### RULE I.

*No more causes of natural things should be admitted than those which are both true and sufficient to explain their phenomena.*

As philosophers <note>By "philosophers," Newton refers to the natural philosophers or scientists who preceded him, such as Aristotle or those following the principle known as Ockham’s Razor.</note> say: Nature does nothing in vain, and it is in vain to do with more what can be done with fewer. For Nature is simple and does not indulge in superfluous <note>original: "luxuriat," meaning to run riot or be excessive</note> causes of things.

### RULE II.

*Therefore, to natural effects of the same kind, the same causes must be assigned, as far as possible.*

Such as respiration in humans and in animals; the falling of stones in Europe and in America; the light in a kitchen fire and in the sun; the reflection of light on the Earth and on the planets.

### RULE III.

*Those qualities of bodies that cannot be increased or diminished, and which belong to all bodies on which experiments can be performed, are to be considered qualities of all bodies universally.*

And this is the foundation of all philosophy. <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers to Natural Philosophy, or science.</note> Furthermore, we know from phenomena that the divided parts of bodies, which are mutually touching, can be separated from one another; and it is certain from mathematics that undivided parts can be distinguished by reason into smaller parts. Whether those distinct but as-yet undivided parts can be divided and separated from each other by the forces of nature is uncertain. But if it were established by even a single experiment that any undivided particle suffered division by the breaking of a hard and solid body, we would conclude by the power of this rule that not only were divided parts separable, but even that undivided parts could be divided to infinity.

Finally, if it is universally established through experiments and astronomical observations that all bodies on the circuit of the earth are heavy toward the earth—and this in proportion to the quantity of matter in each—and that the moon is heavy toward the earth in proportion to the quantity of its matter, and in turn our sea is heavy toward the moon, and all the planets are heavy toward each other, and the gravity of comets toward the sun is similar, it must be said by this rule that all bodies gravitate toward each other. ## RULE IV.

*In <term>experimental philosophy</term> <note>The 17th-century term for science based on observation and experiment rather than pure logic.</note>, propositions collected from phenomena by <term>induction</term> <note>The logical process of reaching a general conclusion by looking at specific instances.</note>, despite any contrary <term>hypotheses</term> <note>In Newton's usage, "hypotheses" are speculative explanations that lack experimental evidence. ### *Distances of the satellites from the center of Saturn in semidiameters of the ring.*

The maximum <term>elongation</term> <note>The greatest angular distance between a moon and its planet as seen from Earth.</note> of the fourth satellite from the center of Saturn is usually gathered from observations to be approximately eight semidiameters. However, the maximum elongation of this same satellite from the center of Saturn, taken with an excellent <term>micrometer</term> <note>An instrument used with a telescope to measure very small distances between celestial objects.</note> in a <term>Huygenian telescope</term> <note>A type of refracting telescope designed by Christiaan Huygens; this one was notably long at 123 feet to reduce optical distortions.</note> 123 feet long, was found to be eight semidiameters and seven-tenths. And from this observation and the periodic times, the distances of the satellites from the center of Saturn in semidiameters of the ring are 2.1, 2.69, 3.75, 8.7, and 25.35. In the same telescope, the diameter of Saturn was to the diameter of the ring as 3 is to 7; and on the days of May 28 and 29 in the year 1719, the diameter of the ring was found to be 43''. From this, the diameter of the ring at Saturn's average distance from the Earth is 42'', and the diameter of Saturn is 18''. These measurements are found in the longest and best telescopes because the apparent sizes of celestial bodies in longer telescopes have a greater proportion to the <term>dilation of light</term> <note>Newton is referring to "irradiation" or optical blurring that makes bright objects look larger than they are; larger telescopes minimize this effect relative to the object's size.</note> at the edges of those bodies than in shorter telescopes. If all stray light is excluded, the diameter of Saturn will remain no greater than 16''.

## PHENOMENON III.

### *That the five primary planets—Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn—encircle the Sun in their orbits.*

That Mercury and Venus revolve around the Sun is demonstrated by their lunar-like phases. When they shine with a full face, they are situated beyond the Sun; when they appear halved, they are in a region level with the Sun; and when <term>falcate</term> <note>Crescent-shaped, like a sickle.</note>, they are on this side of the Sun, sometimes passing across its disk in the manner of spots. From the full face of Mars near its <term>conjunction</term> <note>When a planet is on the opposite side of the Sun from the Earth.</note> with the Sun, and its <term>gibbous</term> <note>Appearing more than half-illuminated but less than full.</note> appearance in <term>quadratures</term> <note>When a planet is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun as seen from Earth.</note>, it is certain that it orbits the Sun. Regarding Jupiter and Saturn, the same is demonstrated from their phases, which are always full: for it is manifest that these shine with light borrowed from the Sun by the shadows of their satellites cast upon them.

## PHENOMENON 4.

*The periodic times of the five primary planets—and either of the sun around the earth or the earth around the sun—(the fixed stars being at rest), are in the <term>sesquialteral ratio</term> <note>original: "ratione sesquiplicata"; this refers to a 3/2 power ratio, where the square of the time is proportional to the cube of the distance. This is now known as Kepler's Third Law.</note> of their average distances from the sun.*

This ratio, discovered by <term>Kepler</term> <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), the German astronomer who first formulated the laws of planetary motion.</note>, is acknowledged by all. Indeed, the periodic times are the same, and the dimensions of the orbits are the same, whether the sun revolves around the earth or the earth around the sun. Concerning the measurement of the periodic times, all astronomers are in agreement. However, Kepler and <term>Bullialdus</term> <note>Ismaël Boulliau (1605–1694), a French astronomer. Although he rejected Kepler's physical theories, his precise astronomical tables were highly regarded.</note> have determined the magnitudes of the orbits most diligently from observations; and the average distances that correspond to the periodic times do not differ perceptibly from the distances which they found, and for the most part, they fall between them, as can be seen in the following table.

->*The periodic times of the planets and of the earth around the sun with respect to the fixed stars, in days and decimal parts of a day.*<-

| Saturn (♄) | Jupiter (♃) | Mars (♂) | Earth (♁) | Venus (♀) | Mercury (☿) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 10,759.275 | 4,332.514 | 686.9785 | 365.2565 | 224.6176 | 87.9692 |

->*The average distances of the planets and of the earth from the sun.*<-

| | Saturn (♄) | Jupiter (♃) | Mars (♂) | Earth (♁) | Venus (♀) | Mercury (☿) |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| According to *Kepler* | 951,000 | 519,650 | 152,350 | 100,000 | 72,400 | 38,806 |
| According to *Bullialdus* | 954,198 | 522,520 | 152,350 | 100,000 | 72,398 | 38,585 |
| According to periodic times | 954,006 | 520,096 | 152,369 | 100,000 | 72,333 | 38,710 |

There is no room for dispute regarding the distances of Mercury and Venus from the sun, since these are determined by their <term>elongations</term> <note>The angular distance between the planet and the sun as seen from Earth.</note> from the sun. Also, all dispute regarding the distances of the superior planets <note>The "superior" planets are those with orbits further from the sun than Earth's (Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn).</note> from the sun is removed by the eclipses of the satellites of Jupiter. For through those eclipses, the position of the shadow which Jupiter casts is determined, and by that means the <term>heliocentric longitude</term> <note>The position of the planet as viewed from the center of the sun.</note> of Jupiter is obtained. Moreover, from the heliocentric and <term>geocentric</term> <note>The position as viewed from the center of the earth.</note> longitudes compared with one another, the distance of Jupiter is determined.

## PHENOMENON 5.

*That the primary planets, by <term>radii</term> <note>Imaginary lines (now called position vectors) connecting the center of a planet to the center of its orbital focus.</note> drawn to the earth, describe areas not at all proportional to the times; but by radii drawn to the sun, they traverse areas proportional to the times.*

For with respect to the earth, they sometimes move forward, sometimes are stationary, and sometimes even move backward <note>Newton is describing "retrograde motion," an optical illusion where planets appear to move backward in the sky because the Earth is overtaking them in its own orbit.</note>. But with respect to the sun, they always move forward, and do so with a nearly uniform motion, yet a little faster in <term>perihelion</term> <note>original: "periheliis"; the point in an orbit closest to the sun.</note> and slower in <term>aphelion</term> <note>original: "apheliis"; the point in an orbit furthest from the sun.</note>, so that the description of the areas is uniform. This proposition is very well known to astronomers, and is especially demonstrated in Jupiter by the eclipses of its satellites; by which eclipses, as we have said, the <term>heliocentric</term> <note>Sun-centered; measuring the positions as they would appear from the center of the sun.</note> longitudes and distances of this planet from the sun are determined.

## PHENOMENON 6.

*That the moon, by a radius drawn to the center of the earth, describes an area proportional to the time.*

This is evident from the apparent motion of the moon compared with its apparent diameter. However, the lunar motion is disturbed slightly by the force of the sun, but I ignore the imperceptible details of these errors in these phenomena.

# PROPOSITIONS.

## PROPOSITION I. THEOREM I.

*The forces by which the <term>circumjovial</term> <note>original: "circumjoviales"; planets or moons orbiting Jupiter.</note> planets are continually drawn away from <term>rectilinear motions</term> <note>Straight-line motion; according to Newton's First Law, an object will move in a straight line unless acted upon by a force.</note> and are retained in their orbits, look toward the center of Jupiter, and are inversely as the squares of the distances of their places from that same center.*

The first part of this proposition is evident from the first phenomenon and the second or third proposition of the first book; and the latter part from the first phenomenon and the sixth corollary of the fourth proposition of the same book.

Understand the same regarding the planets that accompany <term>Saturn</term>, based on the second phenomenon.

## PROPOSITION II. THEOREM II.

*The forces by which the <term>primary planets</term> <note>The major planets orbiting the sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn).</note> are continually drawn away from rectilinear motions and are retained in their orbits, look toward the sun, and are inversely as the squares of the distances from its center.*

The first part of the proposition is evident from the fifth phenomenon and the second proposition of the first book; and the latter part from the fourth phenomenon and the fourth proposition of the same book. This part of the proposition is demonstrated most accurately, however, by the <term>stillness of the aphelia</term> <note>original: "quietem apheliorum"; the observation that the long axis of a planet's elliptical orbit remains fixed in space rather than rotating.</note>. For even the smallest deviation from the <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>The "inverse square" law; if the force was not exactly the square of the distance, the orbits would noticeably shift.</note> (by the 1st corollary of proposition 45, book 1) would necessarily produce a noticeable motion of the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center (perihelion and aphelion).</note> in single revolutions, and an enormous motion in many.

### PROPOSITION III. THEOREM III.

->*The force by which the moon is retained in its orbit looks toward the earth, and is inversely as the square of the distance of its places from the center of the same.*<-

The first part of the assertion is evident through the sixth phenomenon <note>Phenomenon 6 describes the moon's motion relative to the Earth's center.</note>, and the second or third proposition of the first book: and the latter part through the very slow motion of the lunar <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the moon's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth.</note>. For that motion, which in individual revolutions is only three degrees and three minutes <term>in consequence</term> <note>original: "in consequentia"; moving in the order of the signs of the zodiac, or prograde motion.</note>, can be neglected. For it is evident (through corollary 1, proposition 45, book 1) that if the distance of the moon from the center of the earth be to the semi-diameter of the earth as D to 1; the force from which such a motion arises would be inversely as D<sup>2 <sup>4</sup>/<sub>243</sub></sup>, that is, inversely as that power of D itself whose index is 2 <sup>4</sup>/<sub>243</sub>, that is, in a ratio of the distance a little greater than the <term>inverse square</term> <note>original: "duplicata inverse"; the mathematical relationship where force decreases by the square of the distance.</note>, but which comes 59 ¾ parts closer to the square than to the triplicate ratio. But it arises from the action of the sun (as will be said hereafter) and therefore is to be neglected here. The action of the sun, insofar as it draws the moon away from the earth, is very nearly as the distance of the moon from the earth; and therefore (through those things said in corollary 2, proposition 45, book 1) it is to the moon’s centripetal force as about 2 to 357.45, or 1 to 178 <sup>29</sup>/<sub>40</sub>. And neglecting so small a force of the sun, the remaining force by which the moon is retained in its orbit will be inversely as D². This will also be established more fully by comparing this force with the force of gravity, as is done in the following proposition.

*Corollary.* If the mean centripetal force by which the moon is retained in its orbit be increased first in the ratio of 177 <sup>29</sup>/<sub>40</sub> to 178 <sup>29</sup>/<sub>40</sub>, then also in the duplicate ratio of the semi-diameter of the earth to the mean distance of the center of the moon from the center of the earth: the lunar centripetal force at the surface of the earth will be obtained, provided that this force, in descending to the surface of the earth, increases perpetually in the inverse duplicate ratio of the height.

And by this same force, heavy bodies do in fact descend to the earth. For the length of a pendulum, oscillating to individual seconds in the latitude of Paris, is three Paris feet and 8 1/2 lines, as *Huygens* observed. and 1/12) is that very force which we are accustomed to call <term>gravity</term> <note>The Latin word "gravitas" literally means "heaviness." Newton is famously unifying the force that makes an apple fall with the force that keeps the moon in its orbit.</note>. For if gravity were different from this force, bodies seeking the earth by both forces joined together would descend twice as fast, and in the space of one second of time would describe 30 1/6 Paris feet in falling: entirely contrary to experience.

This calculation is based on the hypothesis that the earth is at rest. For if the earth and moon are moved around the sun, and meanwhile also revolve around the common center of gravity: while the law of gravity remains, the distance of the centers of the moon and earth from each other will be about 60 1/2 terrestrial radii; as will be evident to someone entering into the computation. However, the computation can be entered through Proposition 60, Book I.

### *Scholium.*

The demonstration of the proposition can be explained more fully in this way. If several moons were revolving around the earth, just as happens in the system of Saturn or Jupiter: their <term>periodic times</term> <note>The time taken to complete one full orbit.</note> (by the argument of induction) would observe the law of the planets discovered by <term>Kepler</term> <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), who discovered that the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its distance from the sun.</note>, and therefore their <term>centripetal forces</term> <note>original: "vires centripetæ"; the "center-seeking" force directed toward the Earth.</note> would be inversely as the squares of the distances from the center of the earth, by Proposition 1 of this book. And if the lowest of them were small, and nearly touched the tops of the highest mountains: its centripetal force by which it was retained in its orbit would very nearly equal the gravities of bodies on the peaks of those mountains (by the preceding calculation), and would cause that same little moon, if it were deprived of all the motion with which it proceeds in its orbit, due to the lack of <term>centrifugal force</term> <note>The "center-fleeing" force that arises from the moon's velocity, which balances the pull of gravity to keep it in orbit.</note> by which it had remained in orbit, to descend to the earth, and that with the same velocity with which heavy things fall on the peaks of those mountains, because of the equality of the forces by which they descend. And if that force by which that lowest little moon descends were different from gravity, and that little moon were also heavy toward the earth in the manner of bodies on the peaks of mountains: the same little moon would descend twice as fast by the two forces joined together. Therefore, since both forces—both those of heavy bodies and those of the moons—look toward the center of the earth and are similar and equal to each other, they (by <term>Rules 1 and 2</term> <note>Referring to Newton's "Rules of Reasoning in Philosophy" at the beginning of Book III, which state that we should assign the same causes to the same natural effects.</note>) will have the same cause. And therefore that force, by which the moon is retained in its orbit, will be that very one which we are accustomed to call gravity: and this is especially so lest the little moon on the mountain peak either lack gravity or fall twice as fast as heavy bodies are accustomed to fall.

<summary>Newton concludes his proof that the force keeping the moon in orbit is identical to terrestrial gravity by showing that their mathematical values match perfectly. He uses a thought experiment involving a hypothetical "little moon" orbiting at mountain-top height to illustrate that orbital force and gravity must be the same single cause.</summary>
