## PROPOSITION 5. THEOREM 5.

*The moons revolving around Jupiter gravitate toward Jupiter, those around Saturn toward Saturn, and the planets around the sun gravitate toward the sun; and by the force of their gravity they are always drawn back from straight-line motions and kept in curved orbits.*

For the revolutions of the <term>circumjovial planets</term> <note>The "Moons of Jupiter," discovered by Galileo in 1610.</note> about Jupiter, of the <term>circumsaturnian</term> <note>The moons of Saturn.</note> about Saturn, and of Mercury, Venus, and the other <term>circumsolar</term> <note>Planets orbiting the sun.</note> planets about the sun, are phenomena of the same kind as the revolution of the Moon about the Earth; and therefore (by <term>Rule 2</term> <note>One of Newton's "Rules of Reasoning" stated at the beginning of Book 3, which says that the same natural effects must be assigned the same causes.</note>) they depend on causes of the same kind; especially since it has been demonstrated that the forces on which those revolutions depend look toward the centers of Jupiter, Saturn, and the Sun, and decrease as they recede from Jupiter, Saturn, and the Sun in the same ratio and by the same law as the force of gravity decreases as it recedes from the Earth.

**Corollary 1.** Gravity, therefore, is found in all planets. For no one doubts that Venus, Mercury, and the others are bodies of the same kind as Jupiter and Saturn. And since every attraction is mutual by the <term>third law of motion</term> <note>"To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction."</note>, Jupiter will gravitate toward all its satellites, Saturn toward its own, the Earth toward the Moon, and the Sun toward all the primary planets.

**Corollary 2.** The gravity that relates to each individual planet is <term>inversely as the square</term> <note>The "Inverse Square Law": if you double the distance, the force becomes four times weaker.</note> of the distance of places from its center.

**Corollary 3.** All planets are heavy toward one another by Corollaries 1 and 2. And hence Jupiter and Saturn, by attracting each other when they are near <term>conjunction</term> <note>When two planets appear closest to each other in the sky.</note>, noticeably disturb each other's motions; the sun disturbs the lunar motions; and the sun and moon disturb our sea, as will be explained in what follows.

->Scholium.<-

Hitherto we have called that force by which the celestial bodies are kept in their orbits <term>centripetal</term> <note>From the Latin "centrum" (center) and "petere" (to seek).</note>. It is now established that this same force is <term>gravity</term>, and therefore we shall call it gravity from now on. For the cause of that centripetal force by which the moon is kept in its orbit ought to be extended to all the planets by Rules 1, 2, and 4.

<meta>catchword: PROPO.</meta>

<summary>Newton generalizes his theory of gravity, arguing that the same force that pulls an apple to Earth also keeps the moons of Jupiter and Saturn in their orbits and governs the entire solar system. He officially identifies "centripetal force" as "gravity."</summary>

## PROPOSITION 6. THEOREM 6.

*That all bodies gravitate toward each of the planets, and at any given equal distance from the center of a planet, their weight toward that planet is proportional to the quantity of matter <note>original: "quantitati materiæ"; Newton is defining what we now call "mass."</note> they contain.*

Others have long observed that the descent of all heavy bodies toward the earth (setting aside the slight delay caused by the very small resistance of the air) occurs in equal times; and one may observe this equality of times most accurately in <term>pendulums</term> <note>Newton used pendulums because they allowed him to observe the effects of gravity over a long period, making small differences in speed easier to detect than in a simple free-fall.</note>. I tested this with gold, silver, lead, glass, sand, common salt, wood, water, and wheat. I compared two round, equal wooden boxes. I filled one with wood and suspended an equal weight of gold (as exactly as I could) at the <term>center of oscillation</term> <note>The specific point in a pendulum where all its mass can be considered concentrated for the purpose of its swinging time.</note> of the other. These boxes, hanging from equal eleven-foot threads, formed pendulums entirely equal in terms of weight, shape, and air resistance: and when placed side by side, they swung back and forth together with equal oscillations for a very long time.

Accordingly, the amount of matter in the gold (according to <term>corollaries 1 and 6, proposition 24, book 2</term> <note>Earlier sections of the *Principia* where Newton established the mathematical rules for pendulum motion.</note>) was to the amount of matter in the wood as the action of the <term>motive force</term> <note>The total force of gravity acting on the object.</note> upon all the gold is to the action of the same force upon all the wood; that is, as weight is to weight. And so it was for the rest of the materials. In bodies of the same weight, a difference in matter even smaller than a thousandth part of the whole could have been clearly detected by these experiments.

Now, there is no doubt that the nature of gravity toward the planets is the same as it is toward the Earth. For let us imagine these terrestrial bodies to be raised all the way to the orbit of the Moon, and, being deprived of all motion along with the Moon, let them be dropped so that they fall to the Earth together. It is certain, from what has been shown before, that in equal times they would describe the same distances as the Moon; and therefore, they are to the quantity of matter in the Moon as their weights are to its weight.

Furthermore, since the <term>satellites of Jupiter</term> <note>The four moons discovered by Galileo.</note> revolve in times that are in the <term>sesquialterate ratio</term> <note>original: "ratione sesquiplicata"; this refers to Kepler's Third Law, where the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the distance (3/2 power).</note> of their distances from the center of Jupiter, their <term>accelerative gravities</term> <note>original: "gravitates acceleratrices"; what we now call gravitational acceleration or *g*.</note> toward Jupiter will be inversely as the squares of their distances from the center of Jupiter; and therefore, at equal distances from Jupiter, their accelerative gravities would turn out to be equal. Thus, falling from equal heights in equal times, they would describe equal spaces; just as...

And by the same argument, the planets circling the sun, if let fall from equal distances from the sun, would describe equal spaces in equal times during their descent toward the sun. Moreover, the forces by which unequal bodies are equally accelerated are as the bodies themselves; that is, weights are as the quantities of matter in the planets. Furthermore, it is clear from the highly regular motion of the satellites that the weights of Jupiter and its satellites toward the sun are proportional to their quantities of matter; this is per <term>corollary 3, proposition 65, book 1</term> <note>In the first book of the Principia, Newton established the mathematical laws for how multiple bodies attract each other. Therefore, if at equal distances from the sun, the accelerative gravity of any satellite toward the sun were greater or less than the accelerative gravity of Jupiter toward the sun by even a thousandth part of the total gravity, the distance of the center of the satellite’s orbit from the sun would be greater or less than Jupiter's distance from the sun by a 1/2000 part of the total distance—that is, a fifth part of the distance of the outermost satellite from the center of Jupiter. Such an <term>eccentricity</term> <note>A measurement of how much an orbit deviates from being a perfect circle.</note> of the orbit would be very noticeable. But the orbits of the satellites are concentric to Jupiter, and therefore the accelerative gravities of Jupiter and its satellites toward the sun are equal to one another. And by the same argument, the weights of Saturn and its companions <note>Newton refers to the moons of Saturn as its "companions" (comites).</note> toward the sun, at equal distances from the sun, are as the quantities of matter in them; and the weights of the moon and the earth toward the sun are either zero, or accurately proportional to their masses. That there are indeed such weights is clear from <term>corollaries 1 and 3, proposition 5</term>.

Furthermore, the weights of the individual parts of any planet toward any other are toward each other as the matter in the individual parts. For if some parts weighed more and others less than their quantity of matter would warrant, the whole planet—depending on the kind of parts it most abounded in—would weigh more or less than its total quantity of matter would warrant.

Nor does it matter whether those external parts are on the outside or the inside. For if, for example, terrestrial bodies that are here with us were imagined to be raised to the orbit of the moon and compared with the body of the moon: if the weights of these were to the weights of the external parts of the moon as the quantities of matter in them, but to the weights of the internal parts in a greater or lesser ratio, they would be to the weight of the whole moon in a greater or lesser ratio: contrary to what was shown above <note>Newton is referring to the previous proof that the moon and terrestrial objects at the same distance would be accelerated equally by gravity.</note>.

*Corollary 1.* Hence the weights of bodies do not depend on their forms and textures. For if they could vary with forms, they would be greater or lesser, according to the variety of forms, in equal matter: entirely contrary to experience.

*Corollary 2.* All bodies which are around the earth are heavy toward the earth; and the weights of all, which are equally distant from the center of the earth, are as the quantities of matter <note>Newton's term for "mass."</note> in them. This is the quality of all things in which it is possible to perform experiments, and therefore by <term>Rule 3 of Reasoning</term> <note>A principle Newton established earlier in Book III stating that properties we find in all bodies we can test should be assumed to apply to all bodies in the universe.</note> it is to be affirmed of all things universally. If the <term>ether</term> <note>A hypothetical weightless fluid that many 17th-century scientists believed filled all space.</note> or any other body whatsoever were either entirely devoid of gravity, or gravitated less in proportion to its quantity of matter: since it (according to the mind of <term>Aristotle</term>, <term>Descartes</term>, and others) does not differ from other bodies except in the form of its matter, the same could be gradually transformed through a change of form into a body of the same condition as those which gravitate most for their quantity of matter; and conversely, the heaviest bodies, by gradually taking on its form, could gradually lose their gravity. And therefore weights would depend on the forms of bodies, and could vary with the forms, contrary to what was proven in the previous corollary.

*Corollary 3.* All spaces are not equally full. For if all spaces were equally full, the <term>specific gravity</term> <note>The density of a substance compared to another; here, Newton argues that if space were a "plenum" (totally full), everything would be as dense as the densest materials.</note> of the fluid with which the region of the air is filled, on account of the extreme density of the matter, would not yield at all to the specific gravity of quicksilver <note>Mercury.</note>, or gold, or any other most dense body; and therefore neither gold nor any other body could descend in the air. For bodies in fluids, unless they are specifically heavier, do not descend at all. But if the quantity of matter in a given space can be diminished through any rarefaction whatsoever, why can it not be diminished to infinity?

*Corollary 4.* If all the solid particles of all bodies are of the same density, and cannot be rarefied without pores <note>Small gaps or spaces within a material.</note>, a <term>vacuum</term> exists.

*Corollary 5.* The force of gravity is of a different kind from magnetic force. For magnetic attraction is not proportional to the matter attracted. ## PROPOSITION VII. THEOREM VII.

***That gravity occurs in all bodies universal, and that it is proportional to the quantity of matter in each.***

We have already proved before that all planets are heavy toward one another, and that gravity toward each one viewed separately is inversely as the square of the distance of positions from the center of the planet. And from this it follows (by Proposition 69, Book 1, and its corollaries) that gravity toward all planets is proportional to the matter in them.

Furthermore, since all parts of any planet *A* are heavy toward any planet *B*, and the gravity of each part is to the gravity of the whole as the matter of the part is to the matter of the whole, and to every action there is an equal reaction (by the <term>third law of motion</term> <note>Newton's law stating that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.</note>); the planet *B* will in turn gravitate toward all parts of planet *A*, and its gravity toward each part will be to its gravity toward the whole as the matter of the part is to the matter of the whole. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

*Corollary 1.* Gravity toward a whole planet, therefore, arises and is composed of the gravity toward the individual parts. We have examples of this in magnetic and electric attractions. For every attraction toward a whole arises from the attractions toward the individual parts. The matter will be understood in gravity by conceiving of many smaller planets coming together into one globe and composing a larger planet. For the force of the whole must arise from the forces of the component parts. If anyone should object that all bodies which are around us ought to gravitate toward each other by this law, whereas gravity of this kind is in no way felt, I reply that...

### PROPOSITION VIII. THEOREM VIII.

*If the matter of two globes gravitating toward each other is homogeneous in all regions that are equally distant from the centers: then the weight of either globe toward the other will be inversely as the square of the distance between the centers.*

After I had discovered that gravity toward a whole planet arises from and is composed of the gravities toward its parts, and that for each individual part it is inversely proportional to the squares of the distances from those parts: I was in doubt whether that same inverse duplicate proportion <note>original: *proportio illa duplicata* — another term for the inverse square law.</note> would hold accurately for a total force composed of many individual forces, or whether it would only be approximate. For it might be possible that a proportion which holds accurately enough at greater distances might deviate noticeably near the surface of a planet, due to the unequal distances of the particles and their differing positions. At last, however, through Propositions 75 and 76 of Book 1 and their corollaries, I understood the truth of the proposition treated here.

### PROPOSITION X. THEOREM X.

->*That the motions of the planets in the heavens can be preserved for a very long time.*<-

In the <term>scholium</term> <note>A scholium is an explanatory note or remark added to a mathematical proof.</note> of Proposition 40, Book 2, it was shown that a globe of frozen water <note>original: *aquæ congelatæ* — referring to ice.</note>, moving freely in our air and traveling a distance equal to its own <term>semi-diameter</term> <note>The radius of the sphere.</note>, would lose $\frac{1}{4586}$ part of its motion due to the resistance of the air. If this globe were entirely <term>aqueous</term> <note>Made of water.</note>, anything less dense than water would, on account of its lesser <term>specific gravity</term> <note>The ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a standard, usually water.</note>, emerge and float on the surface. For that reason, a terrestrial globe covered on all sides by waters, if it were less dense than water, would emerge somewhere, and all the water flowing away from there would gather in the opposite region. This same logic applies to our Earth, which is largely surrounded by seas. If the Earth were not denser than water, it would emerge from the seas, and a part of it—according to its degree of lightness—would stand out from the water, while all the seas flowed together to the opposite side of the world. By the same argument, <term>sunspots</term> <note>original: *maculæ solares* — dark spots on the Sun's surface. Newton correctly deduces they must be less dense than the surrounding solar material because they "float" on the surface.</note> are lighter than the bright solar matter upon which they float. Hence, since the common soil on the Earth’s surface is about twice as heavy as water, and a bit deeper in mines is found to be three, four, or even five times heavier, it is probable that the total quantity of matter in the Earth is about five or six times greater than if it were made entirely of water. But because the resistance of mediums decreases in proportion to their weight and density—just as water, being $13\frac{3}{4}$ times lighter than <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum* — mercury.</note>, offers less resistance in that same proportion; and air, being 860 times lighter than water, resists less in the same way—if we were to ascend into the heavens where the weight of the medium in which the planets move is immensely reduced, resistance will almost completely vanish. We have already demonstrated in the <term>scholium</term> <note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary following a proof.</note> to Proposition 22, Book 2, that at a height of two hundred miles above the Earth, the air is thinner than at the surface in a ratio of about 7,500,000,000,000 to 1. Consequently, the planet Jupiter <note>original: *stella jovis* — literally "the star of Jove."</note>, moving through such a thin medium, would not lose even a one-millionth <note>original: *decimam centesimam millesimam* — a ten-hundred-thousandth.</note> part of its motion due to the resistance of the medium over a period of 1,000,000 years. In the regions closest to Earth, certainly nothing is found that creates resistance except air, exhalations, and vapors. When these are very carefully exhausted from a hollow glass cylinder, heavy objects fall within the glass quite freely and without any noticeable resistance; gold itself and the thinnest feather, let down at the same time, fall with equal velocity, and in their fall, covering a height of four, six, or eight feet, they strike the bottom at the same time, as has been found by experience.

And for that reason, if one ascends into the heavens, which are void of air and exhalations, planets and comets will move through those spaces for a very long time without any noticeable resistance.

<summary>Newton argues that the vacuum of space offers almost no resistance to planetary motion, calculating that Jupiter could orbit for millions of years without slowing down. He supports this using the "coin and feather" vacuum experiment to show that resistance is a property of the medium (air) rather than the objects themselves.</summary>

## HYPOTHESIS I.

->*The center of the system of the world is at rest.*<-

This is acknowledged by everyone, although some contend that the Earth, and others that the Sun, stays at rest in the center of the system. Let us see what follows from this.

### PROPOSITION XI. THEOREM XI.

->*The common center of gravity of the Earth, the Sun, and all the planets is at rest.*<-

For that center (by Corollary 4 of the Laws <note>Referring to the foundational laws of motion established at the beginning of the *Principia*.</note>) will either be at rest or move forward uniformly in a straight line. But if that center were always moving forward, the center of the world would also move, which contradicts the hypothesis.

### PROPOSITION XII. THEOREMA XII.

->*The Sun is moved by a perpetual motion, but never recedes far from the common center of gravity of all the planets.*<-

For since (by Corollary 2, Proposition 8) the quantity of matter in the Sun is to the matter in Jupiter as 1067 to 1, and the distance of Jupiter from the Sun is in a ratio slightly greater than the <term>semi-diameter</term> <note>The radius of the Sun.</note> of the Sun; the <term>common center of gravity</term> <note>The "balance point" between two or more objects where their masses effectively cancel each other out.</note> of Jupiter and the Sun will fall at a point just above the Sun's surface. By the same argument, since the matter in the Sun is to the matter in Saturn as 3021 to 1, and the distance of Saturn from the Sun is in a ratio slightly less than the semi-diameter of the Sun, the common center of gravity of Saturn and the Sun will fall at a point just below the Sun's surface. And following the tracks of the same calculation, if the Earth and all the planets were to stand on one side of the Sun, the common center of gravity of them all would scarcely be distant from the center of the Sun by a full solar diameter. In other cases, the distance between the centers is always less. And therefore, since that center of gravity is perpetually at rest, the Sun—depending on the varying positions of the planets—will move in all directions, but will never recede far from that center.

*Corollary.* Hence the common center of gravity of the Earth, the Sun, and all the planets is to be regarded as the center of the world. For since the Earth,

the sun and all the planets gravitate toward one another, and therefore, according to the laws of motion, are in perpetual agitation in proportion to the force of their gravity: it is evident that their moving centers cannot be considered as the resting center of the world. If that body in which all bodies gravitate most (as is the common opinion) were to be placed in the center, that privilege should be granted to the sun. However, since the sun moves, a stationary point must be chosen from which the center of the sun departs as little as possible, and from which it would depart even less if the sun were denser and larger, so that it moved less.

### PROPOSITION XIII. THEOREM XIII.

*The planets move in ellipses having a focus in the center of the sun, and by radii drawn to that center they describe areas proportional to the times.*

We discussed these motions above based on phenomena <note>Referring to the observed data provided by astronomers like Kepler.</note>. Now that the principles of motion are known, we infer the celestial motions *a priori* <note>original: "a priori"; meaning: through theoretical deduction from established laws rather than through observation alone.</note>. Since the weights of the planets toward the sun are inversely as the squares of their distances from the sun's center; if the sun were at rest and the remaining planets did not act upon one another, their orbits would be elliptical, having the sun in a common focus, and areas would be described proportional to the times (by Proposition 1 and 11, and Corollary 1 of Proposition 13, Book 1). However, the actions of the planets upon one another are very small (so much so that they can be ignored), and they disturb the motions of the planets in ellipses around the moving sun less (by Proposition 66, Book 1) than if those motions were carried out around a stationary sun.

Indeed, the action of Jupiter upon Saturn is not entirely to be ignored. For the gravity toward Jupiter is to the gravity toward the sun (at equal distances) as 1 to 1067; and therefore in the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The point in time when two planets are closest to each other in their orbits as seen from the sun.</note> of Jupiter and Saturn, since the distance of Saturn from Jupiter is to the distance of Saturn from the sun as nearly 4 to 9, the gravity of Saturn toward Jupiter will be to the gravity of Saturn toward the sun as 81 to 16 x 1067, or about 1 to 211. And from this arises a perturbation of the orbit of Saturn in each of this planet's conjunctions with Jupiter, so noticeable that astronomers are troubled by it. According to the varying positions of the planet in these conjunctions, its <term>eccentricity</term> <note>A measure of how much an orbit deviates from being a perfect circle.</note> is now increased and now diminished, its <term>aphelion</term> <note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is furthest from the sun.</note> is now advanced and now perhaps retracted, and its mean

## PROPOSITION XIV. THEOREMA XIV.

->*The aphelia and nodes of the orbits are at rest.*<-

The <term>aphelia</term> <note>The points in a planet's orbit furthest from the sun.</note> are at rest, according to Proposition 11, Book 1, as are the planes of the orbits, according to Proposition 1 of the same book; and while the planes remain at rest, the <term>nodes</term> <note>The points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note> are at rest. Nevertheless, from the actions of the revolving planets and comets upon one another, some inequalities will arise, but these are so small they can be ignored here.

*Corollary 1.* The fixed stars also remain at rest, because they maintain their given positions relative to the aphelia and nodes.

*Corollary 2.* And therefore, since there is no sensible <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent change in position of a star when viewed from different sides of the Earth's orbit.</note> of them arising from the Earth’s annual motion, their forces, due to the immense distance of the bodies, will produce no sensible effects in the region of our system. Indeed, the fixed stars, being equally dispersed in all parts of the heavens, destroy their mutual forces through contrary attractions, according to Proposition 70, Book 1.

## Scholium.

Since the planets closer to the sun (namely Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars) act very little on one another due to the smallness of their bodies, their aphelia <note>The points in an orbit farthest from the sun.</note> and nodes <note>The points where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note> will remain stationary, except insofar as they are disturbed by the gravitational forces of Jupiter, Saturn, and the higher bodies. From this it can be gathered through the theory of gravity that their aphelia move slightly forward <note>original: "in consequentia" — meaning in the same direction as the planet's travel</note> relative to the fixed stars, and this happens in the sesquiplicate proportion <note>A ratio where one value is proportional to the 3/2 power of another; specifically, the square root of the cube.</note> of the distances of these planets from the sun. For example, if the aphelium of Mars in a hundred years completes 33' 20'' <note>33 minutes and 20 seconds of arc.</note> forward relative to the fixed stars, then the aphelia of the Earth, Venus, and Mercury in a hundred years will complete 17' 40'', 10' 53'', and 4' 16'' respectively. These motions, because they are so small, are neglected in this proposition.

## PROPOSITION XV. PROBLEM I.

->*To find the principal diameters of the orbits.*<-

These are to be taken in the subsesquiplicate ratio <note>The ratio of the 2/3 power; this relates the size of an orbit to the time it takes to complete a revolution.</note> of the periodic times, according to Proposition 15, Book 1; then they must be increased individually in the ratio of the sum of the masses of the sun and each revolving planet to the first of two mean proportionals <note>A geometric method for finding values between two given numbers to account for the shared center of gravity.</note> between that sum and the sun, according to Proposition 60, Book 1.

## PROPOSITION XVI. PROBLEM II.

->*To find the eccentricities and aphelia of the orbits.*<-

The problem is solved by Proposition 18, Book 1.

## PROPOSITION XVIII. THEOREM XVI.

->*The axes of the planets are smaller than the diameters drawn perpendicularly to those same axes.*<-

If all daily circular motion were removed, the planets ought to take on a spherical shape because of the equal gravity of their parts on every side. By that circular motion, it happens that the parts receding from the axis endeavor to rise near the equator. And therefore, if the material is fluid, it will increase the diameters by its ascent at the equator, but diminish the axis by its descent at the poles. Thus the diameter of Jupiter (by the agreeing observations of astronomers) is found to be shorter between the poles than from east to west. By the same argument, unless our Earth were a little higher under the equator than at the poles, the seas would sink at the poles, and by rising near the equator, they would flood everything there.

Now let these three ratios be combined—126 to 125, 126 to 125½, and 100 to 101—and the gravity at place $Q$ toward the earth will be to the gravity at place $A$ toward the earth as $126 \times 126 \times 100$ to $125 \times 125 \frac{1}{2} \times 101$, or as 501 to 500.

Now, since (according to Corollary 3 of Proposition 91, Book 1) the gravity in either leg of the canal, *ACca* or *QCcq*, is proportional to the distance of those places from the center of the earth; if those legs are divided by transverse and equidistant surfaces into parts proportional to the whole, the weights of the individual parts in leg *ACca* will be to the weights of the corresponding parts in the other leg as their sizes and <term>accelerative gravities</term> <note>The measure of the force of gravity at a specific point, independent of the mass of the object being weighed.</note> combined; that is, as 101 to 100 and 500 to 501, which results in a ratio of 505 to 501. And therefore I say, according to the <term>Golden Rule</term> <note>A historical term for the "Rule of Three" or simple proportion.</note>, that if a centrifugal force of 4/505 causes the height of the water in leg *ACca* to exceed the height of the water in leg *QCcq* by one-hundredth part of the total height: then a centrifugal force of 1/289 will cause the excess height in leg *ACca* to be only 1/229 of the height in the other leg *QCcq*. And so, since the average semi-diameter of the earth, according to *Picard’s* measurement <note>Jean-Félix Picard (1620–1682) was a French astronomer whose precise measurement of the Earth's size was used by Newton.</note>, is 19,615,800 Parisian feet, or 3,923.16 miles (assuming a mile is a measure of 5,000 feet), the earth will be higher at the equator than at the poles by an excess of 85,472 feet, or 17 1/15 miles. And its height at the equator will be approximately 19,658,600 feet, and at the poles 19,573,000 feet.

If a planet were larger or smaller than the earth while its density and the periodic time of its daily revolution remained the same, the proportion of centrifugal force to gravity would remain the same, and therefore the proportion of the diameter between the poles to the diameter at the equator would also remain the same. But if the daily motion were accelerated or retarded in any ratio, the centrifugal force would increase or decrease in the <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>The ratio of the squares; for example, if the speed doubles, the force quadruples.</note>, and therefore the difference of the diameters would increase or decrease in that same duplicate ratio very nearly. Concerning the System of the World

...of diminished gravity. Since the Earth rotates relative to the fixed stars in 23 hours and 56 minutes, but Jupiter in 9 hours and 56 minutes, the squares of these times are as 29 to 5. Furthermore, the <term>densities</term><note>The amount of matter packed into a given space.</note> of the two planets are as 400 to 94 1/2. By calculation, the difference in Jupiter's diameters will be to its lesser diameter as 29/5 times 400/94 1/2 times 1/229 to 1, or approximately 1 to 9 1/3. Therefore, the diameter of Jupiter measured from east to west is to its diameter between the poles as 10 1/3 to 9 1/3, approximately. Given that its major diameter is 37 seconds of a degree, its minor diameter (lying between the poles) would be 33 seconds and 25 thirds <note>In historical measurement, a "third" is 1/60th of a second.</note>. If we add about 3 seconds to account for <term>erratic light</term><note>Newton refers to "optical glare" or "irradiation," an effect where bright objects appear slightly larger to the eye than they actually are.</note>, the apparent diameters of this planet become 40 seconds and 36 seconds, 25 thirds. These are to each other as 11 1/12 to 10 1/12, approximately.

This holds true under the hypothesis that Jupiter’s body is of uniform density. However, if its body is denser toward the plane of the equator than toward the poles, its diameters might be in a ratio of 12 to 11, or 13 to 12, or perhaps 14 to 13. Indeed, **Cassini** <note>Giovanni Domenico Cassini (1625–1712), a renowned Italian-French astronomer.</note> observed in the year 1691 that Jupiter’s diameter stretched from east to west exceeded the other diameter by about one-fifteenth part. Our own **Pound** <note>James Pound (1669–1724), an English astronomer and mentor to James Bradley.</note>, using a telescope 123 feet in length and an excellent <term>micrometer</term><note>An instrument used with a telescope to measure very small distances between celestial objects.</note>, measured the diameters of Jupiter in the year 1719 as follows:

The theory, therefore, agrees with the observed phenomena. For planets are heated more by the light of the sun toward their equators, and for that reason are "cooked" <note>original: "decoquuntur"—Newton suggests the sun's heat slightly alters the material density or consistency of the planet's equatorial regions.</note> a little more there than toward the poles.

Furthermore, that gravity is diminished at the equator by the daily rotation of our Earth, and therefore the Earth rises higher there than at the poles (provided its matter is of uniform density), will be made clear by the experiments with <term>pendulums</term> which are reviewed in the following proposition.

MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK THREE.

# PROPOSITION XX. PROBLEM IV.

->*To find and compare the weights of bodies in different regions of this earth.*<-

Since the weights of the unequal branches of the water-filled channel $ACQqca$ <note>Newton uses a thought experiment involving a channel of water running from the pole to the Earth's center and then out to the equator to model equilibrium.</note> are equal; and the weights of the parts, which are proportional to the whole branches and similarly situated within them, are to each other as the weights of the wholes, and are therefore also equal to each other; it follows that the weights of equal parts similarly situated in the branches will be inversely as the branches themselves—that is, inversely as 230 to 229. The same reasoning applies to any homogeneous and equal bodies similarly situated in the branches of the channel. Their weights are inversely as the branches, which is to say, inversely as the distances of the bodies from the center of the earth. Therefore, if bodies are placed on the highest parts of the channels, or on the surface of the earth, their weights will be to each other inversely as their distances from the center. By the same argument, the weights in any other regions across the entire surface of the earth are inversely as the distances of those places from the center; and therefore, under the hypothesis that the earth is a <term>spheroid</term><note>An ellipsoid that is nearly, but not quite, a perfect sphere; in this case, flattened at the poles.</note>, these weights are given by that proportion.

From this arises the following theorem: that the increase in weight in traveling from the equator to the poles is very nearly as the <term>versed sine</term><note>The "versed sine" (1 minus the cosine) was a common trigonometric function in Newton's time, used here to map the curve of the Earth.</note> of double the latitude, or, what amounts to the same thing, as the square of the sine of the latitude. The arcs of the degrees of latitude on the <term>meridian</term><note>The imaginary line running North-South through the poles.</note> increase in roughly the same proportion. Therefore, since the latitude of **Paris** <note>original: "Lutetiæ Parisiorum"</note> is 48° 50', that of places under the equator is 00° 00', and that of places at the poles is 90°; and the double versed sines are 11334, 00000, and 20000 (where the radius is 10000); and since the gravity at the pole is to the gravity at the equator as 230 to 229, and the excess of gravity at the pole over the gravity at the equator is as 1 to 229: the excess of gravity at the latitude of **Paris** compared to the gravity at the equator will be as $1 \times \frac{11334}{20000}$ to 229, or 5667 to 2290000. Consequently, the total gravities in these places will be to each other as 2295667 to 2290000. Because the lengths of <term>pendulums</term><note>Newton uses the swing of a pendulum as a precise way to measure the strength of gravity; a stronger gravitational pull makes a pendulum swing faster, requiring a longer rod to maintain the same time interval.</note> vibrating in equal times are proportional to the gravities, and in the latitude of **Paris** the length of a pendulum vibrating every second is three **Paris feet** and 8 1/2 **lines** <note>A "line" is a historical unit equal to 1/12th of an inch.</note>, or rather 8 5/9 lines to account for the weight of the air: the length of a pendulum at the equator will be exceeded by the length of a synchronous Paris pendulum by the difference of one line and 87 thousandths of a line. A similar calculation produces the following table.

In the month of *August* <note>original: "mense Augusto." This refers to Jean Richer's expedition to Cayenne in 1672.</note>, he found his clock to move more slowly than the <term>mean motion of the sun</term><note>the average rate at which the sun appears to move, used to keep consistent time</note>, with a difference of 2 minutes and 28 seconds every day. Then, by making a <term>simple pendulum</term><note>a weight suspended from a pivot so that it can swing freely</note> oscillate to individual seconds as measured by an excellent clock, he noted the length of the simple pendulum; and he did this frequently every week for ten months. Then, having returned to *France*, he compared the length of this pendulum with the length of the Parisian pendulum (which was three Parisian feet and eight lines with three-fifths of a line) and found it to be shorter, with a difference of one line and a quarter <note>a "line" is 1/12th of an inch</note>.

Afterward, our friend *Halley* <note>Edmond Halley, the astronomer famous for the comet that bears his name</note>, sailing to the island of *Saint Helena* around the year 1677, found that his pendulum clock moved more slowly there than in *London*, but he did not note the difference. However, he made the pendulum shorter by more than an eighth part of an inch, or one and a half lines. And to accomplish this, since the length of the screw at the bottom of the pendulum was not sufficient, he placed a wooden ring between the housing of the screw and the pendulum weight.

Then, in the year 1682, Mr. *Varin* and Mr. *Des Hayes* found the length of a pendulum oscillating to individual seconds in the Royal Observatory at Paris to be 3 feet, 8 5/9 lines. And on the island of *Goree* <note>off the coast of Senegal</note>, by the same method, they found the length of a synchronous pendulum to be 3 feet, 6 5/9 lines, there being a difference in lengths of 2 lines. And in the same year, sailing to the islands of *Guadeloupe* and *Martinique*, they found the length of a synchronous pendulum in these islands to be 3 feet, 6 1/2 lines.

After this, Mr. *Couplet* the younger, in the month of *July* 1697, adjusted his pendulum clock to the mean motion of the sun at the Royal Observatory in Paris, so that for a sufficiently long time the clock agreed with the motion of the sun. Then, sailing to *Lisbon* <note>original: "Ulyssipponem"</note>, he found that in the following month of *November* the clock went more slowly than before, there being a difference of 2 minutes and 13 seconds in 24 hours. And in the following month of *March*, sailing to *Paraiba* <note>in Brazil</note>, he found his clock went more slowly there than in *Paris*, with a difference of 4 minutes and 12 seconds in 24 hours. And he asserts that the pendulum oscillating to seconds was shorter at *Lisbon* by 2 1/2 lines and at *Paraiba* by 3 2/3 lines than at *Paris*. He would have more correctly stated the differences to be 1 1/3 and 2 5/9. For these differences correspond to the time differences of 2 minutes 13 seconds, and 4 minutes 12 seconds. These cruder observations of his are less to be trusted.

In the following years (1699 and 1700), *Mr. Des Hayes*, sailing again to *America*, determined that in the islands of *Cayenne* and *Grenada*, the length of a pendulum oscillating to <term>seconds</term><note>one "swing" per second</note> was slightly less than 3 feet and 6 1/2 lines. He also found that on the island of *Saint Christopher*, that length was 3 feet and 6 3/4 lines, and on the island of *Saint Domingo*, the same was 3 feet and 7 lines <note>A "line" is a historical unit of length equal to 1/12th of an inch</note>.

And in the year 1704, *Father Feuillée* found in *Portobelo* in *America* that the length of the pendulum oscillating to seconds was only three *Parisian* feet and 5 7/12 lines—that is, almost three lines shorter than in *Paris* <note>original: "Lutetiæ Parisiorum"</note>—but this observation was in error. For afterward, sailing to the island of *Martinique*, he found the length of an <term>isochronous pendulum</term><note>a pendulum that keeps the same time</note> to be only three *Parisian* feet and 5 10/12 lines.

Now, the latitude of *Paraiba* is 6 degrees and 38 minutes to the south <note>original: "ad austrum"</note>, and that of *Portobelo* is 9 degrees and 33 minutes to the north <note>original: "ad boream"</note>. The latitudes of the islands of *Cayenne*, *Goree*, *Guadeloupe*, *Martinique*, *Grenada*, *Saint Christopher*, and *Saint Domingo* are respectively 4° 55', 14° 40', 14° 00', 14° 44', 12° 6', 17° 19', and 19° 48' to the north. The amounts by which the length of the Parisian pendulum exceeds the lengths of the isochronous pendulums observed in these latitudes are slightly greater than those calculated in the table of pendulum lengths above. Therefore, the Earth is somewhat higher <note>meaning further from the center, or "bulging"</note> at the equator than the previous calculation suggested, and denser at the center than in mines near the surface—unless, perhaps, the heat in the <term>torrid zone</term><note>the region of the Earth between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn</note> has slightly increased the length of the pendulums.

Certainly, *Mr. Picard* observed that an iron rod which, in winter time when the cold was freezing, was one foot in length, became one foot and a quarter-part of a line when heated by fire. Then *Mr. de la Hire* observed that an iron rod which in similar winter time was six feet in length, became six feet and two-thirds of a line when exposed to the summer sun. In the first case, the heat was greater than in the second; but in the latter, the heat was greater than that of the external parts of the human body. For metals grow very hot in the summer sun. But the rod of a pendulum in a <term>pendulum clock</term><note>original: "horologio oscillatorio"</note> is never usually exposed to the heat of the summer sun, nor does it ever absorb a heat equal to the heat of the external surface of the human body. Therefore, a pendulum rod in a clock three feet long will indeed be slightly longer in the summer than in the winter, but only by an excess of a fourth <meta>catchword: fourth.</meta>

...scarcely exceeding a fourth part of a single line <note>A "line" is a historical unit of length, equal to 1/12th of an inch</note>. Therefore, the total difference in the length of pendulums which are <term>isochronous</term><note>pendulums that swing with the exact same time period</note> in different regions cannot be attributed to differing levels of heat. But nor should this difference be attributed to the errors of the astronomers sent from *France* <note>original: "Gallia"</note>. For although their observations do not perfectly agree with each other, nevertheless the errors are so small that they can be disregarded. And in this they all agree: that isochronous pendulums are shorter under the equator than in the Royal Observatory in *Paris*, the difference being no less than one line and a quarter, and no more than 2 1/3 lines. By the observations of *Mr. Richer* made in *Cayenne*, the difference was one line and a quarter. By those of *Mr. Des Hayes*, that corrected difference turned out to be one line and a half, or one and three-quarter lines. By those of others, which were less accurate, it came out as nearly two lines. And this discrepancy could arise partly from errors in observation, partly from the dissimilarity of the Earth’s internal parts and the height of mountains, and partly from the various temperatures of the air.

An iron rod three feet long is shorter in the winter time in *England* than in the summer time by a sixth part of a line, as far as I can tell. On account of the heat under the equator, let this quantity be subtracted from the difference of one line and a quarter observed by *Richer*, and there will remain 1 1/12 lines; which matches well with the 1 87/1000 lines already gathered before by theory. Moreover, *Richer* repeated his observations made in *Cayenne* every week for ten months, and compared the lengths of the pendulum on the iron rod noted there with its lengths similarly noted in *France*. Such diligence and caution seem to have been lacking in other observers. If his observations are to be trusted, the Earth will be higher at the equator than at the poles by an excess of about seventeen miles, as was shown above through theory.

### PROPOSITION 21. THEOREM 17.

*That the equinoctial points recede, and that the Earth's axis, by nodding, inclines toward the ecliptic twice in each annual revolution and returns twice to its former position.*

This is clear by Corollary 20 of Proposition <term>66, Book 1</term> <note>Newton refers to his earlier mathematical proofs regarding the gravitational pull of a third body on an orbiting system</note>. However, this motion of nodding must be very small, and hardly, if at all, perceptible.

### PROPOSITION 22. THEOREM 18.

*That all lunar motions and all the irregularities of those motions follow from the principles established.*

It is clear from Proposition <term>65, Book 1</term> that major planets, while they are carried around the sun, can carry other smaller planets revolving around them, and that those smaller ones must revolve in ellipses having their foci <note>the two central points of an ellipse</note> in the centers of the larger ones. However, by the action of the sun, their motions will be disturbed in many ways, and they will be affected by those irregularities which are observed in our moon. This moon indeed (per Corollaries 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Proposition <term>66</term>) moves faster and, with a radius drawn to the Earth, describes a larger area for the time, and has an orbit less curved—and therefore approaches closer to the Earth—in <term>syzygies</term> <note>the points where the Moon, Earth, and Sun are aligned, such as a New or Full Moon</note> than in <term>quadratures</term> <note>the points where the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun as seen from Earth</note>, except insofar as the motion of eccentricity prevents it. For the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>the measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note> is greatest (per Corollary 9 of Proposition <term>66</term>) when the moon's <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth</note> is in syzygies, and smallest when the same remains in quadratures; and thus the moon in its <term>perigee</term> <note>the point in the orbit closest to the Earth</note> is faster and closer to us, and in its apogee slower and further away, in syzygies than in quadratures. Furthermore, the apogee moves forward, and the <term>nodes</term> <note>the two points where the Moon's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit around the Sun</note> move backward, but with an uneven motion. And the apogee indeed (per Corollaries 7 and 8 of Proposition <term>66</term>) advances faster in its syzygies, retreats more slowly in its quadratures, and by the excess of the progress over the retreat is carried annually forward <note>original: "in consequentia," referring to the direction of the zodiac signs</note>. The nodes, however (per Corollary 2 of Proposition <term>66</term>), remain still in their syzygies and retreat most rapidly in their quadratures. But also, the moon's maximum latitude is greater in its quadratures (per Corollary 10 of Proposition <term>66</term>) than in syzygies; and the mean motion is slower in the Earth's <term>perihelion</term> <note>the point where the Earth is closest to the Sun</note> (per Corollary 6 of Proposition <term>66</term>) than in its <term>aphelion</term> <note>the point where the Earth is furthest from the Sun</note>. And these are the more notable irregularities observed by astronomers.

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

<margin>BOOK THREE.</margin>

There are also certain other inequalities not observed by previous astronomers, by which the lunar motions are so disturbed that, until now, they could not be reduced to any certain rule by any law. For the velocities or hourly motions of the moon's <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in the orbit farthest from Earth</note> and <term>nodes</term> <note>the points where the Moon's orbit intersects the Earth's orbital plane</note>, and their equations, as well as the difference between the maximum eccentricity in <term>syzygies</term> <note>alignment of Sun, Earth, and Moon, i.e., new or full moon</note> and the minimum in <term>quadratures</term> <note>when the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun</note>, and the inequality called the <term>variation</term> <note>a specific periodic fluctuation in the Moon's speed</note>, increase and decrease annually (by Corollary 14, Proposition 66) in the <term>triplicate ratio</term> <note>the cube</note> of the sun's apparent diameter. Furthermore, the variation increases or decreases in approximately the <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>the square</note> of the time between quadratures (by Corollaries 1 and 2, Lemma 10, and Corollary 16, Proposition 66, Book 1). But in astronomical calculations, this inequality is usually referred to the moon's <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>the difference between the true position of a planet and its mean position</note> and is confused with it.

## PROPOSITION XXIII. PROBLEM V.

->*To derive the unequal motions of the satellites of Jupiter and Saturn from the lunar motions.*<-

From the motions of our moon, the analogous motions of the moons or satellites of Jupiter are derived in this way. The mean motion of the nodes of the outermost Jovian satellite is to the mean motion of our moon's nodes in a ratio compounded of the square of the periodic time of the Earth around the sun to the periodic time of Jupiter around the sun, and the simple ratio of the periodic time of the satellite around Jupiter to the periodic time of the moon around the Earth (by Corollary 16, Proposition 66, Book 1); and therefore, in a hundred years, that node completes 8 degrees 24 minutes <term>in precedence</term> <note>original: "in antecedentia"; this refers to retrograde motion, or moving backward through the zodiac</note>. The mean motions of the nodes of the interior satellites are to the motion of this [outermost] one as their periodic times are to its periodic time (by the same corollary) and are determined from that. Moreover, the motion of the <term>apsis</term> <note>original: "augis"; the point of an orbit closest or farthest from the center</note> of each satellite <term>in consequence</term> <note>original: "in consequentia"; this refers to prograde motion, or moving forward through the zodiac</note> is to its motion of nodes in precedence as the motion of our moon's apogee is to its motion of nodes (by the same corollary), and is determined from that. However, the motion of the apsis así found must be diminished in a ratio of about 5 to 9 or 1 to 2, for a reason I do not have time to explain here. The maximum equations of the nodes and the apsis of each satellite are nearly to the maximum equations of the nodes and apogee of the moon respectively, as the motions of the nodes and apsides of the satellites during the time of one revolution of the former equations are to the motions of the nodes and apogee of the moon during the time of one revolution of the [equa-]

The variation of a satellite as seen from Jupiter is to the variation of the moon as the respective total motions of the nodes are to each other during the times in which the satellite and moon revolve toward the sun, by the same corollary; and therefore in the outermost satellite it does not exceed 5'' 12''' <note>5 seconds and 12 thirds of a degree—a measurement of extremely small arc</note>.

## PROPOSITION XXIV. THEOREM XIX.

->*The flow and ebb of the sea arise from the actions of the sun and the moon.*<-

That the sea ought to swell and flow back twice during each day, both lunar and solar <note>original: "tam lunaribus quam solaribus"</note>, is clear from Corollaries 19 and 20 of Proposition 66, Book 1. It is also clear that the maximum height of the water in deep and open seas follows the <term>appulse</term> <note>the arrival or crossing</note> of the celestial bodies to the <term>meridian</term> <note>the imaginary line in the sky directly above the observer</note> of that place by a space of less than six hours; as happens in the whole eastern tract of the *Atlantic* and *Ethiopian* <note>The "Ethiopian Sea" was a historical name for the South Atlantic Ocean</note> oceans between *France* and the *Cape of Good Hope*, as well as on the *Chilean* and *Peruvian* shores of the *Pacific* ocean. In all these coastal areas, the tide falls at approximately the second, third, or fourth hour, unless where the motion, propagated from the deep ocean through shallow places, is delayed until the fifth, sixth, or seventh hour or even further. I number the hours from the appulse of each celestial body to the local meridian, both below the horizon and above; and by the hours of a lunar day, I mean the twenty-fourth parts of the time in which the moon, by its apparent daily motion, returns to the local meridian. The force of the sun or moon to raise the sea is greatest at the very arrival of the celestial body at the local meridian. But the force impressed upon the sea at that time remains for a while, and is increased by the new force subsequently impressed upon it, until the sea has reached its maximum height, which will happen in the space of one or two hours, but more often at the shores in the space of about three hours, or even more if the sea is shallow.

Furthermore, the two motions which the two celestial bodies excite will not be perceived distinctly, but will produce a certain mixed motion. In the <term>conjunction</term> or <term>opposition</term> <note>when the Sun and Moon are aligned, either together or on opposite sides of Earth</note> of the celestial bodies, their effects will be combined, and the greatest flow and ebb will be composed <note>these are known today as "spring tides"</note>. In the <term>quadratures</term> <note>when the Sun and Moon are at a 90-degree angle to each other from Earth's perspective</note>, the sun will raise the water where the moon depresses it, and depress it where the moon raises it; and from the difference of the effects, the smallest tide of all will arise <note>known today as "neap tides"</note>. And since, as experience witnesses, the effect of the moon is greater than that of the sun, the maximum height of the water will fall at approximately the third lunar hour. Outside of the <term>syzygies</term> <note>the points of alignment, i.e., new and full moon</note> and quadratures, the maximum tide—which by the lunar force alone ought always to fall at the third lunar hour, and by the solar force alone at the third solar hour—

<summary>Newton explains that the Earth's tides are caused by the combined gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon, noting that high tides lag behind the celestial bodies' crossing of the meridian due to the momentum of the water.</summary>

These things are so in the open sea. For in the mouths of rivers, the greater flows (other things being equal) will come to their peak <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\kappa\mu\grave{\eta}\nu$" (akmēn)</note> more slowly.

The effects of the luminaries <note>the sun and moon</note> also depend upon their distances from the earth. For at smaller distances their effects are greater, and at greater distances smaller, and that in the <term>triplicate ratio</term> <note>an inverse-cube relationship; as the distance increases, the tidal force decreases by the cube of that change</note> of their apparent diameters. Therefore the sun in the winter time, being in <term>perigee</term> <note>its closest point to Earth</note>, produces greater effects, and causes the tides in the syzygies to be a little greater, and in the quadratures a little smaller (other things being equal) than in the summer time; and the moon in perigee each month stirs up greater tides than fifteen days before or after, when it is situated in <term>apogee</term> <note>its furthest point from Earth</note>. From this it happens that two absolutely maximum tides in consecutive syzygies do not follow one another.

The effect of each luminary also depends on its own <term>declination</term> <note>the angle or distance of a celestial body from the celestial equator</note> or distance from the equator. For if the luminary were placed at the pole, it would draw the individual parts of the water constantly, without the intensification and remission of action, and therefore would stir up no reciprocation of motion. Therefore, as the luminaries recede from the equator toward the pole, they will gradually lose their effects, and for that reason will stir up smaller tides in the <term>solstitial</term> syzygies <note>at the summer and winter solstices</note> than in the <term>equinoctial</term> ones. In the solstitial quadratures, however, they will stir up greater tides than in the equinoctial quadratures; because the effect of the moon, now situated on the equator, most greatly exceeds the effect of the sun. Therefore, the maximum tides fall at the syzygies and the minimum at the quadratures of the luminaries, around the times of each equinox. And the maximum tide at the syzygies is always accompanied by the minimum at the quadratures, as has been found by experience. Moreover, because of the smaller distance of the sun from the earth in the winter time than in the summer time, it happens that the maximum and minimum tides more often precede the vernal equinox than follow it, and more often follow the autumnal than precede it.

The effects of the luminaries also depend upon the latitude of places. Hence, in the daily revolution of any place *F*, the <term>afflux</term> <note>the incoming flow or high tide</note> will be greatest at *F* at the third hour after the moon’s arrival at the <term>meridian</term> <note>the imaginary line running through the sky from north to south, passing directly overhead</note> above the horizon; afterward the greatest <term>deflux</term> <note>the outgoing flow or low tide</note> will be at *Q* at the third hour after the setting of the moon; then the greatest afflux at *f* at the third hour after the arrival of the moon at the meridian below the horizon <note>meaning when the moon is on the opposite side of the Earth</note>; finally, the greatest deflux at *Q* at the third hour after the rising of the moon. And the second afflux at *f* will be smaller than the first afflux at *F*. For the entire sea is divided into exactly two hemispherical waves: one in the hemisphere *KHk* tending toward the north, and the other in the opposite hemisphere *Khk*; these we may therefore call the northern wave and the southern wave. These waves, always directly opposite to one another, arrive in turn at the meridians of individual locations with an interval of twelve lunar hours between them. And since northern regions participate more in the northern wave, and southern regions more in the southern, it follows that tides arise which are alternately greater and smaller in every place outside the equator where the <term>luminaries</term> <note>the sun and moon</note> rise and set. Specifically, the greater tide—with the moon declining toward the <term>vertex</term> <note>the zenith, or the point directly overhead</note> of the place—will occur at approximately the third hour after the moon’s arrival at the meridian above the horizon; and as the moon changes its declination <note>its angular distance north or south of the celestial equator</note>, this will turn into the smaller tide. The maximum difference between these flows will occur at the times of the solstices; especially if the moon’s <term>ascending node</term> <note>the point where the moon's orbit crosses the Earth's orbital plane moving northward</note> is located at the start of Aries <note>the point of the vernal equinox</note>.

Thus experience has found that the morning tides in the winter time exceed the evening ones, and the evening ones in the summer time exceed the morning ones; at Plymouth indeed by a height of about one foot, but at Bristol by a height of fifteen inches: according to the observations of <note>original: "Colepressio & Sturmio"</note> Colepress and Sturm.

However, the motions described so far are changed somewhat by that force of reciprocation of the waters, by which the tide of the sea could persevere for some time even if the actions of the <term>luminaries</term> <note>the sun and the moon</note> ceased. This conservation of impressed motion diminishes the difference of the alternating tides; and it makes the tides nearest after the <term>syzygies</term> <note>the points when the sun, moon, and earth are in a direct line, such as at a new or full moon</note> greater, and diminishes those nearest after the <term>quadratures</term> <note>the points when the sun and moon are at right angles to each other relative to the earth, such as at the first and last quarter moon</note>. From this it happens that the alternating tides at Plymouth and Bristol do not differ much more from one another than by a height of one foot or fifteen inches; and that the greatest tides of all in those same ports are not the first from the syzygies, but the third. All motions are also retarded in transit through shallows, so much so that the greatest tides of all, in certain straits and the mouths of rivers, are the fourth or even the fifth from the syzygies.

Furthermore, it can happen that a tide is propagated from the ocean through different straits to the same port, and passes more quickly through some straits than through others: in which case the same tide, divided into two or more arriving successively, can compose new motions of various kinds. Let us imagine two equal tides coming from different places into the same port, the first of which precedes the other by a space of six hours, and falls upon the third hour from the moon’s approach to the <term>meridian</term> <note>the imaginary longitudinal line through the sky directly above the port</note> of the port. If the moon in this approach of hers to the meridian was positioned on the equator, equal <term>affluxes</term> <note>incoming flows or high tides</note> will come every six hours, which, by falling upon the mutual <term>refluxes</term> <note>ebb tides or outgoing flows</note>, will equal them, and thus in the space of that day will cause the water to stand still. If the moon then <term>declined</term> <note>moved north or south</note> from the equator, the tides in the ocean will become larger and smaller by alternating turns, as has been said; and from there two larger and two smaller affluxes will be propagated into this port by alternating turns. Moreover, two larger affluxes will compose the highest water in the middle between both; a larger and a smaller afflux will cause the water to rise to a medium height in their middle; and between two smaller affluxes the water will rise to the minimum height. Thus in the space of twenty-four hours, the water will reach the maximum height not twice as is usually the case, but only once, and the minimum height once; and the maximum height, if the moon declines toward the

An example of all these things was revealed by <note>original: "Halleius"</note> Edmond Halley, based on the observations of sailors, in the port of the kingdom of *Tonkin* at *Batsham* <note>modern-day Vietnam; Batsham likely refers to Bát Tràng or a similar coastal station</note> at a northern latitude of 20° 50'. There, on the day following the Moon's passage through the equator, the water is stagnant; then, as the Moon moves toward the north, the water begins to flow and ebb, not twice, as in other ports, but only once each day; and high tide happens at moonset, while the maximum ebb occurs at moonrise. This tide increases with the Moon's declination until the seventh or eighth day; then, through the next seven days, it decreases by the same degrees as it had previously increased; and when the Moon changes its declination <note>crosses the equator again</note>, the tide ceases and soon changes into an ebb. For thereafter, the ebb occurs at moonset and the flow at moonrise, until the Moon again changes its declination. The approach to this port and the neighboring straits is two-fold: one from the *Chinese* Ocean between the continent and the island of *Luzon*, the other from the *Indian* Sea between the continent and the island of *Borneo*. Whether the tides—coming through those straits from the *Indian* Sea in the space of twelve hours and from the *Chinese* sea in the space of six hours, and thus falling upon the third and ninth lunar hours—compose motions of this kind, or whether there is some other condition of those seas, I leave to be determined by observations of the neighboring shores.

Thus far I have rendered the causes of the motions of the Moon and the seas. It is now appropriate to subjoin something regarding the quantity of these motions.

Let $LM$ be drawn parallel to $PT$ such that $SK$ is to $SP$ as the square of $SP$ is to the square of $SK$; and if the <term>accelerating gravity</term> <note>The acceleration caused by gravity, independent of the mass being moved</note> of the earth toward the sun is represented by the distance $ST$ or $SK$, then $SL$ will be the accelerating gravity of the moon toward the sun. This force is composed of the parts $SM$ and $LM$, of which $LM$ and the part $TM$ of $SM$ disturb the moon's motion, as has been explained in Book I, Proposition 66 and its corollaries. Insofar as the earth and moon revolve around their common <term>center of gravity</term> <note>The point around which two or more bodies orbit each other</note>, the motion of the earth around that center will also be disturbed by similar forces; but we may refer the sums of both the forces and the motions to the moon, and designate the sums of the forces by the lines $TM$ and $ML$ which are analogous to them. 

The force $ML$, in its mean quantity, is to the <term>centripetal force</term> <note>The inward-pulling force that keeps a body in its orbit</note> by which the moon could revolve in its orbit around a stationary earth at the distance $PT$, in the <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>The ratio of the squares; a common way of expressing geometric proportions in 17th-century mathematics</note> of the periodic times of the moon around the earth and the earth around the sun (by Corollary 17, Proposition 66, Book I); that is, in the duplicate ratio of 27 days, 7 hours, 43 minutes to 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes; which is as 1,000 to 178,725, or 1 to $178\frac{29}{40}$. 

We found, however, in Proposition 4, that if the earth and moon revolve around their common center of gravity, their mean distance from each other will be approximately $60\frac{1}{2}$ mean <term>semidiameters</term> <note>The radius of the earth</note> of the earth. And the force by which the moon could revolve in an orbit around a stationary earth at the distance $PT$ of $60\frac{1}{2}$ terrestrial semidiameters, is to the force by which it could revolve in the same time at a distance of 60 semidiameters, as $60\frac{1}{2}$ to 60; and this force is to the force of gravity among us as 1 to 60 x 60 approximately. Therefore, the mean force $ML$ is to the force of gravity at the surface of the earth as $1 \times 60\frac{1}{2}$ to $60 \times 60 \times 60 \times 178\frac{29}{40}$, or 1 to 638,092.6. From this, and from the proportion of the lines $TM$ and $ML$, the force $TM$ is also given: and these are the forces of the sun by which the moon's motions are disturbed. <note>original: "Q. E. I." And the velocity which the maximum force could generate in any time *CP* will be to the velocity which any lesser force *EL* generates in the same time, as the rectangle $\frac{1}{2} TP \times CP$ to the area *KCGF*; but in the whole time *CPA*, the generated velocities will be to each other as the rectangle $\frac{1}{2} TP \times CA$ and the triangle *TCG*, or as the quadrantal arc *CA* and the radius *TP*. And therefore (by Proposition 9, Book 5 of the <term>Elements</term> <note>Referring to Euclid's *Elements*, the standard geometry textbook of Newton's time.</note>), the latter velocity, generated in the whole time, will be the $\frac{100}{11,915}$ part of the velocity of the moon. To this velocity of the moon, which is analogous to the mean moment of the area, let half of the other velocity be added and subtracted; and if the mean moment is represented by the number 11,915, the sum 11,915 + 50 or 11,965 will show the maximum moment of the area in the <term>syzygy</term> <note>The points where the Moon, Earth, and Sun are in a straight line; the New and Full Moon.</note> *A*, and the difference 11,915 - 50 or 11,865 will show the minimum moment of the same in the <term>quadratures</term> <note>The points where the Moon is at a right angle to the Sun as seen from Earth; the First and Third Quarter Moon.</note>. Therefore, the areas described in equal times in the syzygies and quadratures are to each other as 11,965 to 11,865. To the minimum moment 11,865, add the moment which is to the difference of the moments (100) as the trapezoid *FKCG* is to the triangle *TCG* (or what is the same thing, as the square of the sine *PK* to the square of the radius *TP*, that is, as *Pd* to *TP*), and the sum will show the moment of the area when the moon is in any intermediate position *P*.

<summary>Newton calculates the specific mathematical ratios for the variation in the Moon's orbital speed (the rate of area description) caused by solar gravity, finding that the Moon sweeps out area faster at syzygy than at quadrature.</summary>

All these things hold true on the hypothesis that the sun and earth are at rest, and the moon revolves in a <term>sidereal period</term> <note>Newton uses the term "synodic" here in the original Latin, but the value of 27 days, 7 hours, 43 minutes actually refers to the sidereal month. He corrects this for the true synodic month in the next sentence.</note> of 27 days, 7 hours, 43 minutes. However, since the lunar <term>synodic period</term> <note>The time from one New Moon to the next.</note> is truly 29 days, 12 hours, and 44 minutes, the increments of the <term>moments</term> <note>The instantaneous rates at which the area is swept out.</note> must be increased in the ratio of the time, that is, in the ratio of 1,080,853 to 1,000,000. In this way, the total increment, which was a 1/11023 part of the average moment, now becomes a 1/10973 part of the same. Therefore, the moment of the area in the moon’s <term>quadrature</term> <note>The points where the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun; the first and third quarters.</note> will be to its moment in <term>syzygy</term> <note>The points where the Moon is in line with the Sun; New Moon and Full Moon.</note> as 11,023—50 to 11,023+50, or 10,973 to 11,073; and to its moment when the moon is in any other intermediate place *P*, as 10,973 to 10,973+*Pd*, with *TP* <note>The radius from the Earth to the Moon.</note> being equal to 100.

Therefore, the area which the moon describes with a radius drawn to the earth in equal particles of time is very nearly as the sum of the number 219.46 and the <term>versed sine</term> <note>An old trigonometric function: $versin(\theta) = 1 - \cos(\theta)$.</note> of the doubled distance of the moon from the nearest quadrature, in a circle whose radius is unity. These things hold true where the <term>variation</term> <note>A specific inequality or "wobble" in the Moon’s motion caused by the Sun’s gravity.</note> in the octants is of average magnitude. But if the variation there is greater or less, that versed sine ought to be increased or decreased in the same ratio.

## PROPOSITION XXVII. PROBLEM VIII.
### *To find the moon’s distance from the earth from its hourly motion.*

The area which the moon describes with a radius drawn to the earth in individual moments of time is as the hourly motion of the moon and the square of the distance of the moon from the earth jointly; and therefore the distance of the moon from the earth is in a ratio compounded of the <term>subduplicate ratio</term> <note>In modern terms, the square root.</note> of the area directly and the subduplicate ratio of the hourly motion inversely. <note>original: "Q. E. I." — *Quod erat inveniendum*, meaning "Which was to be found."</note>

*Corollary* 1. From this, the moon’s apparent diameter is given: since it is reciprocally as its distance from the earth. Let astronomers test how well this rule agrees with the phenomena.

*Corollary* 2. From this also, the lunar orbit can be defined from the phenomena more accurately than before.

<summary>Newton adjusts his calculations of the Moon's motion to account for the Earth's orbit around the Sun, resulting in a formula to determine the Moon's distance based on its observed speed.</summary>

## PROPOSITION 28. PROBLEM 9.

<margin>BOOK THREE.</margin>

->*To find the diameters of the orbit in which the moon, without eccentricity, ought to move.*<-

The curvature of a trajectory described by a moving body—if it is drawn by a force perpendicular to that trajectory—is directly proportional to the attraction and inversely proportional to the square of the velocity. I assume the curvatures of lines to be to one another in the ultimate ratio of the sines or tangents of the angles of contact belonging to equal radii, where those radii are diminished to infinity. <note>Newton is using "angles of contact" to describe how sharply the path curves at any given point.</note> Now, the attraction of the moon toward the earth in the **syzygies** <note>The points of New and Full Moon, where Earth, Moon, and Sun are aligned.</note> is the excess of its gravity toward the earth over the solar force 2 PK (see the *figure on page* 428) by which the accelerating gravity of the moon toward the sun exceeds the accelerating gravity of the earth toward the sun, or is exceeded by it. In the **quadratures** <note>The first and third quarters of the lunar cycle, when the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun relative to Earth.</note>, however, that attraction is the sum of the moon’s gravity toward the earth and the solar force KT, by which the moon is drawn toward the earth. And these attractions, if $\frac{AT+CT}{2}$ is called N, are as $\frac{178725}{AT^2} - \frac{2000}{CT \times N}$ and $\frac{178725}{CT^2} + \frac{1000}{AT \times N}$ approximately; or as 178725 N $\times$ CT$^2$ — 2000 AT$^2$ $\times$ CT and 178725 N $\times$ AT$^2$ + 1000 CT$^2$ $\times$ AT. 

For if the accelerating gravity of the moon toward the earth is represented by the number 178725, the average force ML, which in the quadratures is PT or TK and draws the moon toward the earth, will be 1000; and the average force TM in the syzygies will be 3000. If the average force ML is subtracted from this, there will remain the force 2000 by which the moon in the syzygies is pulled away from the earth, which I have already called 2 PK. The velocity of the moon in the syzygies A and B is to its velocity in the quadratures C and D as CT is to AT and the **moment** <note>The rate at which the area is swept out by the Moon’s radius.</note> of the area which the moon describes with a radius drawn to the earth in the syzygies to the moment of the same area in the quadratures combined; i.e., as 11073 CT to 10973 AT. Let this ratio be taken twice inversely and the prior ratio once directly, and the curvature of the lunar orbit in the syzygies to its curvature in the quadratures will become as 120406729 $\times$ 178725 AT$^2$ $\times$ CT$^2$ $\times$ N — 120406729 $\times$ 2000 AT$^4$ $\times$ CT to 122611329 $\times$ 178725 AT$^2$ $\times$ CT$^2$ $\times$ N + 122611329 $\times$ 1000 CT$^4$ $\times$ AT; i.e., as 2151969 AT $\times$ CT $\times$ N — 24081 AT$^3$ to 2191371 AT $\times$ CT $\times$ N + 12261 CT$^3$.

Therefore the velocity of the nodes is as *IT* × *PH* × *AZ*, or as the product of the sines of the three angles *TPI*, *PTN*, and *STN*.
