**Corollary 2.** In any given position of the nodes, the average hourly motion is half of the hourly motion in the syzygies <note>original: "syzygiis lunæ" — the points where the Moon, Earth, and Sun are in a straight line, i.e., New and Full Moon.</note> of the moon, and therefore it is to 16'' 35''' 16<sup>iv</sup> 36<sup>v</sup> <note>Newton is using sexagesimal fractions of a degree: seconds (''), thirds ('''), fourths (iv), and fifths (v).</note> as the square of the sine of the distance of the nodes from the syzygies is to the square of the radius, or as the *square of AZ* is to the *square of AT*. For if the moon moves with a uniform motion through the semicircle *QAq*, the sum of all the areas *PDdM*, during the time the moon travels from *Q* to *M*, will be the area *QMdE* which is terminated at the tangent of the circle *QE*; and during the time the moon reaches point *n*, that sum will be the entire area *EQAn* which the line *PD* describes; then, as the moon proceeds from *n* to *q*, the line *PD* will fall outside the circle, and will describe the area *nqe* terminated at the tangent of the circle *qe*; which, since the nodes were previously regressing but are now progressing <note>Regression is backward movement; progression is forward movement. Newton is describing the shifting "wobble" of the orbit.</note>, must be subtracted from the former area, and since it is equal to the area *QEN*, it leaves the semicircle *NQAn*. Therefore, the sum of all the areas *PDdM*, during the time the moon describes a semicircle, is the area of the semicircle; and the sum of all of them during the time the moon describes a full circle is the area of the entire circle. But the area *PDdM*, when the moon is positioned in the syzygies, is the rectangle formed by the arc *PM* and the radius *PT*; and the sum of all such equal areas during the time the moon describes a circle is the rectangle formed by the entire circumference and the radius of the circle; and this rectangle, since it is equal to two circles, is twice as large as the former area. Accordingly, the nodes, if they continued uniformly with that velocity which they have in the lunar syzygies, would describe a space twice as large as they truly describe; and for that reason, the average motion—by which, if continued uniformly, they could describe the space actually completed by their unequal motion—is half of the motion they have in the syzygies of the moon. Hence, since the maximum hourly motion, if the nodes are positioned in the quadratures <note>Quadratures are the points in the orbit 90 degrees away from the Sun.</note>, is 33'' 10''' 33<sup>iv</sup> 12<sup>v</sup>, the average hourly motion in this case will be 16'' 35''' 16<sup>iv</sup> 36<sup>v</sup>. And since the hourly motion of the nodes is always as the *square of AZ* and the area *PDdM* combined, and therefore the hourly motion of the nodes in the syzygies of the moon is as the *square of AZ* and the area *PDdM* combined, that is (because of the given area *PDdM* described in the syzygies) as the *square of AZ*, the average motion will also be as the *square of AZ*; and therefore this motion, where the nodes are positioned outside of the quadratures, will be to 16'' 35''' 16<sup>iv</sup> 36<sup>v</sup> as the *square of AZ* is to the *square of AT*. *Which was to be demonstrated.*

For if $PF$ is a tangent to the circle at point $P$, and when extended meets the line $TN$ at $F$, and $pf$ is a tangent to the ellipse at point $p$ and when extended meets the same line $TN$ at $f$, let these tangents meet on the axis $TQ$ at the point $\Upsilon$ <note>The Greek letter Upsilon.</note>; and if $ML$ designates the space which the moon revolving in a circle, in the time it describes the arc $PM$, could describe by the urging and impelling force mentioned before, $3IT$ or $3PK$, <note>original: "urgente & impellente vi prædicta 3IT, seu 3PK." This refers to the solar perturbing force calculated in Proposition 25.</note> by a transverse motion, and $ml$ designates the space which the moon revolving in an ellipse in the same time, also by the force $3IT$ or $3PK$, could describe; and let $LP$ and $lp$ be extended until they meet the plane of the ecliptic <note>The plane of the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note> at $G$ and $g$; and let $FG$ and $fg$ be joined, of which $FG$ extended cuts $pf, pg$ and $TQ$ at $c, e$ and $R$ respectively, and $fg$ extended cuts $TQ$ at $r$. 

Since the force $3IT$ or $3PK$ in a circle is to the force $3IT$ or $3PK$ in an ellipse as $PK$ is to $pK$, or $AT$ to $aT$; the space $ML$ produced by the first force will be to the space $ml$ produced by the second force as $PK$ is to $pK$, that is, because of the similar figures $P\Upsilon Kp$ and $F\Upsilon Rc$, as $FR$ to $cR$. However, $ML$ is to $FG$ (because of the similar triangles $PLM, PGF$) as $PL$ to $PG$, which is (because of the parallel lines $Lk, PK, GR$) as $pl$ to $pe$, that is (because of the similar triangles $plm, cpe$) as $lm$ to $ce$; and inversely as $LM$ is to $lm$, or $FR$ to $cR$, so is $FG$ to $ce$. 

And therefore if $fg$ were to $ce$ as $f\Upsilon$ to $c\Upsilon$, that is, as $fr$ to $cR$ (that is, as $fr$ to $FR$ and $FR$ to $cR$ combined, that is, as $f\Upsilon$ to $F\Upsilon$ and $FG$ to $ce$ combined) since the ratio of $FG$ to $ce$ taken away from both sides leaves the ratios $fg$ to $FG$ and $f\Upsilon$ to $F\Upsilon$, $fg$ would be to $FG$ as $f\Upsilon$ to $F\Upsilon$; and thus the angles, which $FG$ and $fg$ would subtend <note>To subtend an angle means to form the base of an angle at a specific point, in this case, the Earth at point T.</note> at the earth $T$, would be equal to each other. 

But those angles (by what we explained in the preceding proposition) are the motions of the nodes, during the time the moon traverses the arc $PM$ in a circle, and the arc $pm$ in an ellipse: and therefore the motion of the nodes in the circle and the ellipse would be equal to each other. This would be so, if only $fg$ were to $ce$ as $f\Upsilon$ to $c\Upsilon$, that is, if $fg$ were equal to $\frac{ce \times f\Upsilon}{c\Upsilon}$. 

But because of the similar triangles $fgp, cep$, $fg$ is to $ce$ as $fp$ to $cp$; and therefore $fg$ is equal to $\frac{ce \times fp}{cp}$; and therefore the angle, which $fg$ actually subtends, is to the previous angle, which $FG$ subtends—that is, the motion of the nodes in an ellipse to the motion of the nodes in a circle—as this $fg$ or $\frac{ce \times fp}{cp}$ is to the previous $fg$ or $\frac{ce \times f\Upsilon}{c\Upsilon}$, that is, as $fp \times c\Upsilon$ to $f\Upsilon \times cp$, or $fp$ to $f\Upsilon$ and $c\Upsilon$ to $cp$.

Therefore, the corrected mean hourly motion, in any given position of the nodes, is to 16'' 16''' 37<sup>iv</sup> 42<sup>v</sup> as the square of *AZ* is to the square of *AT*; that is, as the square of the sine of the distance of the nodes from the <term>syzygies</term> <note>New or Full Moon positions.</note> is to the square of the radius.

# PROPOSITION 32. PROBLEM 13.

->*To find the mean motion of the moon's nodes.*<-

The <term>mean annual motion<gloss>the average movement calculated over a full year</gloss></term> is the sum of all the mean hourly motions in a year. Imagine the node <note>the point where the Moon's orbit intersects the plane of the Earth's orbit</note> to be located at *N*, and at the completion of each hour it is drawn back into its previous position so that, notwithstanding its own proper motion, it always maintains a given position relative to the fixed stars. Meanwhile, let the Sun *S*, through the motion of the earth, move away from the node and uniformly complete its apparent annual circuit. Let *Aa* be a given very small arc which the straight line *TS* (always drawn to the sun) describes by its intersection with the circle *NAn* in a very small given time: and the mean hourly motion (as already shown) will be as the square of *AZ*, that is (because *AZ* and *ZY* are proportional) as the rectangle contained by *AZ* and *ZY*, which is to say, as the area *AZYa*.

...of such a length that the rectangle formed by *dZ* and *Z$\Upsilon$* is to the small part of the <term>sector<gloss>a portion of a circle bounded by two radii and an arc</gloss></term> *ATa* as the <note>original: "AZq" (AZ quadratum)</note> square of *AZ* is to 9.0827646 times the square of *AT* + the square of *AZ*; that is, so that *dZ* is to 1/2 *AZ* as the square of *AT* is to 9.0827646 times the square of *AT* + the square of *AZ*. This rectangle of *dZ* and *Z$\Upsilon$* will represent the reduction in time arising from the motion of the node during the entire time that the arc *Aa* is traversed. 

And if the point *d* touches the curve *NdGn*, the curvilinear area *NdZ* will be the total reduction in time during which the entire arc *NA* is traversed; and therefore the excess of the sector *NAT* over the area *NdZ* will be that total time. And since the motion of the node is smaller in a shorter time in proportion to that time, the area *Aa$\Upsilon$Z* must also be diminished in the same proportion. This will be achieved if a length *eZ* is taken on *AZ* which is to the length *AZ* as the square of *AZ* is to 9.0827646 times the square of *AT* + the square of *AZ*. 

For in this way, the rectangle of *eZ* and *Z$\Upsilon$* will be to the area *AZ$\Upsilon$a* as the reduction in time during which arc *Aa* is traversed is to the total time in which it would be traversed if the node were stationary; and therefore that rectangle will correspond to the reduction in the node's motion. And if the point *e* touches the curve *NeFn*, the whole area *NeZ*, which is the sum of all these reductions, will correspond to the total reduction during the time the arc *AN* is traversed; and the remaining area *NAe* will correspond to the remaining motion, which is the true motion of the node during the time the entire arc *NA* is traversed by the combined motions of the Sun and the node. 

Now, the area of the semicircle is to the area of the figure *NeFn* (sought through the <term>method of infinite series<gloss>Newton's early version of calculus used to solve complex areas and curves</gloss></term>) as approximately 793 to 60. Moreover, the motion that corresponds to the whole circle was 19 degrees, 49 minutes, 3 seconds, and 55 thirds. Therefore, the motion that corresponds to the doubled figure *NeFn* is 1 degree, 29 minutes, 58 seconds, and 2 thirds. 

When this is subtracted from the prior motion, it leaves 18 degrees, 19 minutes, 5 seconds, and 53 thirds as the total motion of the node relative to the fixed stars between its own conjunctions with the Sun. And this motion, when subtracted from the Sun’s annual motion of 360 degrees, leaves 341 degrees, 40 minutes, 54 seconds, and 7 thirds as the Sun’s motion between those same conjunctions. 

This motion is to the annual motion of 360 degrees as the node’s motion just found (18 degrees, 19 minutes, 5 seconds, and 53 thirds) is to its own annual motion, which will therefore be 19 degrees, 18 minutes, 1 second, and 23 thirds. This is the <term>mean motion<gloss>the average speed of a celestial body, ignoring small periodic fluctuations</gloss></term> of the nodes in a <term>sidereal year<gloss>the time it takes for the Sun to return to the same position relative to the stars</gloss></term>. 

According to astronomical tables, this same value is 19 degrees, 21 minutes, 21 seconds, and 50 thirds. The difference is less than a three-hundredth part of the total motion, and it appears to arise from the <term>eccentricity<gloss>the degree to which the Moon's orbit deviates from a perfect circle</gloss></term> of the lunar orbit and its <term>inclination<gloss>the tilt of the Moon's orbit</gloss></term> to the plane of the <term>ecliptic<gloss>the Earth's orbital path around the Sun</gloss></term>. By the eccentricity of the orbit, the motion of the nodes is accelerated too much, and by its inclination, it is in turn retarded slightly and reduced to the correct velocity.

### Scholium.

By another method, *John Machin, Professor of Astronomy at Gresham College*, and *Henry Pemberton, M.D.*, independently discovered the motion of the nodes. Some mention of this method has been made elsewhere. Both of their papers, which I have seen, contained two propositions and were consistent with each other. However, since the paper by *Mr. Machin* was the first to come into my hands, I shall include it here.

> “ 386° 50' 15'', as is deduced from observations used in the theory of the moon:
> “ then the mean motion of the nodes in a sidereal year will be 19°
> “ 20' 31'' 58'''. And *TH* will be to *HK* as 360 degrees is to 19° 20' 31'' 58''',

> “ in the quadratures becomes 16'' 18''' 48<sup>iv</sup>. And the maximum

### OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>BOOK THREE.</margin>...of the <term>mean motion<gloss>The average speed of a celestial body, assuming it moves in a perfect circle at a constant speed</gloss></term> of the moon arises from the varying dilation of the moon’s orbit by the force of the sun, according to Corollary 6, Proposition 66, Book 1. This force is greater at the <term>perigee<gloss>The point in an orbit closest to the center of attraction; here, when the Earth is closest to the sun</gloss></term> of the sun and dilates the moon’s orbit; at its <term>apogee<gloss>The point in an orbit furthest from the center of attraction</gloss></term> it is smaller and allows that orbit to contract. In a dilated orbit, the moon revolves more slowly; in a contracted one, it revolves more quickly. The <term>annual equation<gloss>A periodic correction applied to the moon's position to account for the Earth's elliptical orbit around the sun</gloss></term>, through which this inequality is compensated, is zero at the apogee and perigee of the sun; at a mean distance of the sun from the earth, it rises to about 11 minutes and 50 seconds; in other places, it is proportional to the equation of the sun’s center. It is added to the mean motion of the moon when the earth proceeds from its <term>aphelion<gloss>The point in Earth's orbit furthest from the sun</gloss></term> to its <term>perihelion<gloss>The point in Earth's orbit closest to the sun</gloss></term>, and in the opposite part of the orbit, it is subtracted. Assuming the radius of the great orbit <note>Newton refers to the Earth's orbit around the sun as the "great orbit" (orbis magnus)</note> is 1000 and the eccentricity of the earth is 16 7/8, this equation, where it is at its maximum, resulted in 11' 49'' through the theory of gravity. But the eccentricity of the earth seems to be a little larger, and with an increased eccentricity, this equation must be increased in the same ratio. Let the eccentricity be 16 11/12, and the maximum equation will be 11' 51''.

I also found that at the earth's perihelion, because of the greater force of the sun, the moon's apogee and <term>nodes<gloss>The two points where the moon's path crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit</gloss></term> move faster than at its aphelion, and this occurs in the <term>inverse triplicate ratio<gloss>A mathematical relationship where a value changes according to the inverse of the cube (1/x³)</gloss></term> of the distance of the earth from the sun. From this arise annual equations for these motions that are proportional to the equation of the sun’s center. However, the motion of the sun is in the <term>inverse duplicate ratio<gloss>The inverse square (1/x²), which is the fundamental law of gravity</gloss></term> of the distance of the earth from the sun, and the maximum equation of the center, which this inequality generates, is 1 degree, 56 minutes, and 20 seconds, corresponding to the aforementioned solar eccentricity of 16 11/12. But if the motion of the sun were in the inverse triplicate ratio, this inequality would generate a maximum equation of 2 degrees, 54 minutes, and 30 seconds. Therefore, the maximum equations that the inequalities of the motions of the moon's apogee and nodes generate are to 2° 54' 30'' as the mean daily motion of the apogee and the mean daily motion of the moon's nodes are to the mean daily motion of the sun. From this, the maximum equation of the mean motion of the apogee emerges as 19' 43'', and the maximum equation of the mean motion of the nodes as 9' 24''. The former equation is added and the latter is subtracted when the earth proceeds from its perihelion to its aphelion; and the contrary occurs in the opposite part of the orbit.

Through the theory of gravity, it was also established that the sun’s action on the moon is a little greater when the transverse diameter of the lunar orbit passes through the sun than when the same is at right angles with the line joining the earth and the sun; and therefore the lunar orbit is a little larger in the former case than in the latter. ### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES.

I

<margin>ON THE SYSTEM OF THE WORLD</margin>
...of the moon, depending on the position of the moon’s <term>apogee<gloss>The point in the moon's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth</gloss></term> relative to the sun; this is indeed greatest when the moon’s apogee is located in an <term>octant<gloss>An orbital position at a 45-degree angle from the sun</gloss></term> with the sun, and is zero when it reaches the <term>quadratures<gloss>The points where the moon and sun are 90 degrees apart (half moon)</gloss></term> or <term>syzygies<gloss>The points where the moon, Earth, and sun are in a straight line (new moon or full moon)</gloss></term>. This is added to the <term>mean motion<gloss>The theoretical average speed of the moon</gloss></term> during the passage of the moon’s apogee from the sun’s quadrature to the syzygy, and is subtracted during the passage of the apogee from the syzygy to the quadrature. This correction, which I shall call the <term>semestral equation<gloss>A "six-monthly" correction; "semestrem" in the original Latin</gloss></term>, rises to about 3 minutes and 45 seconds at the octants of the apogee when it is at its maximum, as far as I have been able to gather from the phenomena. This is its quantity at the average distance of the sun from the earth. However, it increases and decreases in the <term>inverse triplicate ratio<gloss>The inverse cube (1/d³); as distance increases, the effect drops off very sharply</gloss></term> of the sun's distance, and therefore at the sun’s greatest distance it is 3' 34'', and at its minimum distance about 3' 56''; but where the moon’s apogee is located outside the octants, it becomes smaller; and it is to the maximum equation as the sine of double the distance of the moon’s apogee from the nearest syzygy or quadrature is to the radius.

By the same theory of gravity, the action of the sun upon the moon is slightly greater when the straight line drawn through the moon’s <term>nodes<gloss>The two points where the moon's path crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit</gloss></term> passes through the sun, than when that line is at right angles to the line joining the sun and the earth. And from this arises another equation of the lunar mean motion, which I shall call the **second semestral equation**, and which is greatest when the nodes are located in the sun’s octants, and vanishes when they are in the syzygies or quadratures; and in other positions of the nodes, it is proportional to the sine of double the distance of either node from the nearest syzygy or quadrature. It is added to the moon’s mean motion if the sun is at a distance from the node nearest to it in <term>precedence<gloss>Moving westward or contrary to the order of the zodiac signs</gloss></term>, and subtracted if in <term>consequence<gloss>Moving eastward or following the order of the zodiac signs</gloss></term>; and in the octants, where it is greatest, it rises to 47'' at the average distance of the sun from the earth, as I calculate from the theory of gravity. At other distances of the sun, this maximum equation in the octants of the nodes is inversely as the cube of the sun’s distance from the earth, and therefore at the sun's <term>perigee<gloss>The point where the sun is closest to the Earth</gloss></term> it rises to about 49'' and at its apogee to about 45''.

By the same theory of gravity, the moon’s apogee moves forward most when it is either joined with the sun <note>in conjunction/new moon</note> or opposed to it <note>in opposition/full moon</note>, and moves backward when it is at a quadrature with the sun. And the <term>eccentricity<gloss>The degree to which the moon's elliptical orbit is "stretched" or flattened</gloss></term> becomes greatest in the former case and smallest in the latter, according to Corollaries 7, 8 and 9 of Proposition 66, Book 1. And these inequalities, according to the same Corollaries, are very large and produce the principal equation of the apogee, which I shall call **semestral**. And the maximum semestral equation is about 12 degrees and 18 minutes, as far as I could gather from observations. Our *Horrocks* <note>Jeremiah Horrocks (1618–1641), a brilliant English astronomer whose work on lunar theory Newton greatly admired</note> was the first to describe the moon moving in an ellipse...

He also introduces the variation in the moon's orbital eccentricity and apogee movement, citing the observations of Jeremiah Horrocks.</summary>

...was the first to establish that the moon revolves in an ellipse around the Earth, which is positioned at its lower <term>focus<gloss>The original Latin uses "umbilico," or navel; in geometry, this refers to the focal point of an ellipse</gloss></term>. *Halley* <note>original: "Halleius"</note> placed the center of the ellipse on an <term>epicycle<gloss>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle</gloss></term>, the center of which revolves uniformly around the Earth. And from the motion in this epicycle arise the already mentioned inequalities in the advancement and retreat of the <term>apogee<gloss>The point where the moon is furthest from Earth</gloss></term> and the degree of <term>eccentricity<gloss>The amount by which the orbit deviates from a perfect circle</gloss></term>. Let it be understood that the average distance of the moon from the earth is divided into 100,000 parts, and let *T* represent the Earth and *TC* the average eccentricity of the moon of 5,505 parts. Let *TC* be extended to *B*, so that *CB* is the <term>sine<gloss>A trigonometric ratio</gloss></term> of the maximum <term>semestral equation<gloss>A correction occurring twice a year</gloss></term> of 12 degrees 18 minutes to the radius *TC*; and the circle *BDA*, described with center *C* and the interval *CB*, will be that epicycle in which the center of the lunar orbit is located and revolves according to the order of the letters *BDA*. Let the angle *BCD* be taken equal to twice the <term>annual argument<gloss>The angular measurement used to track the sun's position relative to the moon's orbit over a year</gloss></term>, or twice the distance of the sun's true place from the moon's apogee (once corrected), and *CTD* will be the semestral equation of the moon's apogee, and *TD* will be the eccentricity of its orbit tending toward the apogee after it has been corrected a second time. Having obtained the moon's <term>mean motion<gloss>The average speed/position</gloss></term>, its apogee, and its eccentricity, as well as the orbit's <term>major axis<gloss>The longest diameter of the elliptical orbit</gloss></term> of 200,000 parts; from these, the true position of the moon in its orbit and its distance from the earth will be drawn out, and that by the most well-known methods.

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES

<margin>BOOK THREE</margin>

...the angle *CDF* is equal to the complement of the sun's <term>true anomaly<gloss>The actual angular distance of the sun from its closest point to Earth (perigee) at a given time</gloss></term> to 360 degrees. And let *DF* be to *DC* as the double <term>eccentricity<gloss>The measurement of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</gloss></term> of the great orbit <note>the Earth's orbit around the sun</note> is to the mean distance of the sun from the earth, and the mean daily motion of the sun from the moon’s <term>apogee<gloss>The point where the moon is furthest from Earth</gloss></term> to the mean daily motion of the sun from its own apogee taken together; that is, as 33 7/8 to 1000 and 52' 27'' 16''' to 59' 8'' 10''' combined, or as 3 to 100. And imagine the center of the moon's orbit to be located at point *F*, and to revolve in an <term>epicycle<gloss>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle</gloss></term>, whose center is *D* and radius is *DF*, while the point *D* moves forward on the circumference of the circle *DABD*. For by this reasoning, the velocity with which the center of the moon’s orbit will move in a certain curved line described around center *C* will be inversely as the cube of the sun’s distance from the earth, or very nearly so, as it ought to be.

The calculation of this motion is difficult, but it will be made easier by the following approximation. If the mean distance of the moon from the earth is 100,000 parts, and the eccentricity *TC* is 5,505 parts as stated above: the straight line *CB* or *CD* will be found to be 1,172 3/4 parts, and the line *DF* to be 35 1/12 parts. And this line subtends an angle at the earth relative to the distance *TC* which the shifting of the orbit’s center from place *D* to place *F* generates in the motion of this center: and the same line doubled, in a position parallel to the distance of the upper <term>focus<gloss>The original Latin "umbilici" literally means navel, used here to describe the focal point of the elliptical orbit</gloss></term> of the moon’s orbit from the earth, subtends the same angle, which indeed that shifting generates in the motion of the focus, and at the distance of the moon from the earth it subtends the angle which the same shifting generates in the motion of the moon, and which for that reason can be called the **second equation of the center**. And this equation, at the mean distance of the moon from the earth, is very nearly as the <term>sine<gloss>A trigonometric ratio</gloss></term> of the angle which that line *DF* makes with the line drawn from point *F* to the moon; and where it is at its maximum, it becomes 2' 25''. Moreover, the angle which the line *DF* and the line drawn from point *F* to the moon encompass is found either by subtracting the angle *EDF* from the moon's <term>mean anomaly<gloss>The angular distance from the apogee the moon would have if it moved at a constant speed</gloss></term>, or by adding the moon's distance from the sun to the distance of the moon's apogee from the sun's apogee. And as the radius is to the sine of the angle thus found, so 2' 25'' are to the second equation of the center—to be added if that sum is less than a semicircle, and subtracted if it is greater. Thus its longitude will be obtained in the <term>syzygies<gloss>The points where the sun, earth, and moon are in a straight line, specifically at new and full moons</gloss></term> themselves.

Since the earth's atmosphere refracts sunlight up to an altitude of 35 or 40 miles, and by refracting scatters the same into the earth's <term>shadow<gloss>Latin: "umbram"</gloss></term>, and by scattering the light at the edge of the shadow expands the shadow: I add one minute to the diameter of the shadow produced by <term>parallax<gloss>The apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different points</gloss></term> during lunar eclipses, or one minute and twenty seconds.

The theory of the moon should be examined and established by observations, first at the <term>syzygies<gloss>The times of the new and full moon, when the Earth, Moon, and Sun are aligned</gloss></term>, then at the <term>quadratures<gloss>The first and third quarters of the moon, when it is at a right angle to the sun from Earth's perspective</gloss></term>, and finally at the <term>octants<gloss>The points halfway between the syzygies and quadratures (the 45-degree points of the orbit)</gloss></term>. However, the mean motions of the moon and its apogee are not yet known with sufficient accuracy.

## PROPOSITION 36. PROBLEM 17.

->*To find the force of the sun to move the sea.*<-

The sun’s force *ML* or *PT*, at the lunar quadratures, to disturb the lunar motions was (by Proposition 25 of this book) to the force of gravity among us as 1 to 638,092.6. And the force *TM - LM* or *2 PK* at the lunar syzygies is twice as great. These forces, however, if one descends to the surface of the earth, are diminished in the ratio of the distances from the center of the earth—that is, in the ratio of 60 2/5 to 1 <note>This ratio represents the distance of the moon in Earth radii</note>. Therefore, the first force at the surface of the earth is to the force of gravity as 1 to 38,604,600. By this force, the sea is depressed in places that are 90 degrees away from the sun. By the other force, which is twice as great, the sea is raised both under the sun and in the region opposite to the sun. The sum

This will have the same effect as if the entire force raised the sea in the regions under and opposite the sun, while doing nothing in the regions that are 90 degrees distant from the sun.

This is the force of the sun for moving the sea at any given location, when the sun is both at the <term>zenith<gloss>The point directly overhead</gloss></term> of that place and at its mean distance from the earth. In other positions of the sun, the force for raising the sea is directly proportional to the <term>versed sine<gloss>A trigonometric value calculated as 1 minus the cosine of an angle</gloss></term> of twice the sun's altitude above the local horizon, and inversely proportional to the cube of the sun's distance from the earth.

*Corollary.* Since the <term>centrifugal force<gloss>The outward force acting on an object moving in a circular path</gloss></term> of the parts of the earth arising from the earth's daily rotation—which is to the force of gravity as 1 to 289—causes the height of the water at the equator to exceed its height at the poles by a measure of 85,472 <term>Parisian feet<gloss>A unit of length used in 17th-century French science, approximately 32.5 centimeters or 1.066 English feet</gloss></term> (as shown above in Proposition 19); the solar force of which we have treated—since it is to the force of gravity as 1 to 12,868,200, and therefore to that centrifugal force as 289 to 12,868,200 or 1 to 44,527—will cause the height of the water in the regions under and opposite the sun to exceed its height in places 90 degrees distant from the sun by a measure of only one Parisian foot and eleven inches, plus a thirtieth part of an inch <note>Original: "pedis unius Parisiensis & digitorum undecim cum tricesima parte digiti"</note>. For this measure is to the measure of 85,472 feet as 1 is to 44,527.

## PROPOSITION 37. PROBLEM 18.

->*To find the force of the moon to move the sea.*<-

The force of the moon to move the sea is to be gathered from its proportion to the force of the sun, and this proportion is to be gathered from the proportion of the movements of the sea that arise from these forces. Before the mouth of the **River Avon**, at the third milestone below **Bristol**, during the spring and autumn, the total rise of the water at the <term>syzygies<gloss>The times of the new or full moon when the Earth, Moon, and Sun are aligned</gloss></term> is, according to the observations of **Samuel Sturmy**, approximately 45 feet; however, at the <term>quadratures<gloss>The quarter-moons, when the moon is at a right angle to the sun</gloss></term> it is only 25 feet. The first height arises from the sum of the forces, the latter from their difference. Therefore, let the forces of the sun and moon (when they are in the equator and at their mean distance from the earth) be represented by *S* and *L*. Thus, *L+S* will be to *L-S* as 45 is to 25, or 9 to 5.

# THE PRINCIPLES OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>
ON THE SYSTEM OF THE WORLD
</margin>

In the harbor of Plymouth, according to the observations of Samuel Colepress <note>Colepress was a 17th-century researcher who contributed tidal data to the Royal Society</note>, the sea tide rises to an average height of about sixteen feet; and in the spring and autumn seasons, the height of the tide at the <term>syzygies<gloss>The points in an orbit when the Earth, Sun, and Moon are in a straight line, such as a new or full moon</gloss></term> can exceed its height at the <term>quadratures<gloss>The points when the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun as seen from Earth, such as a half-moon</gloss></term> by more than seven or eight feet. If the greatest difference between these heights is nine feet, then the sum of the Lunar and Solar forces ($L+S$) will be to their difference ($L-S$) as $20 \frac{1}{2}$ to $11 \frac{1}{2}$, or 41 to 23. This proportion agrees closely enough with the previous calculation. However, because of the great magnitude of the tides in the port of Bristol, it seems that more trust should be placed in the observations of <term>Sturm<gloss>Johann Christoph Sturm (1635–1703), a German mathematician and philosopher</gloss></term>; therefore, until something more certain is established, we shall use the proportion of 9 to 5.

Furthermore, due to the reciprocal motions of the waters, the highest tides do not fall exactly upon the syzygies of the <term>luminaries<gloss>A traditional term for the Sun and the Moon</term></term> themselves, but are the third tides from the syzygies, as has been said, or follow most closely after the third arrival of the moon at the local <term>meridian<gloss>The imaginary line in the sky passing directly overhead from north to south; the "noon" line</gloss></term> after the syzygy. Or rather (as noted by Sturm), they are the third tides after the day of the new or full moon—that is, about twelve hours after the third day from the new or full moon—and thus they fall approximately forty-three hours after the new or full moon. Indeed, in this port, they fall about the seventh hour after the moon's transit across the local meridian; therefore, they closely follow the moon's arrival at the meridian when the moon is distant from the sun (or from opposition to the sun) by about eighteen or nineteen degrees <term>in consequence<gloss>An astronomical term meaning moving in the same direction as the signs of the Zodiac (west to east)</gloss></term>. Summer and winter reach their greatest intensity not at the <term>solstices<gloss>The longest and shortest days of the year</gloss></term> themselves, but where the sun is distant from the solstices by about a tenth part of the entire circuit, or roughly 36 to 37 degrees. In a similar way, the greatest tide of the sea arises from the arrival of the moon at the local meridian when the moon is distant from the sun by about a tenth part of the total motion from one tide to the next. Let that distance be approximately $18 \frac{1}{2}$ degrees. The force of the sun at this distance of the moon from the syzygies and quadratures will be less effective at increasing or decreasing the movement of the sea arising from the moon’s force than it is at the syzygies and quadratures themselves, in the ratio of the radius to the sine of the complement of this distance doubled (that is, an angle of 37 degrees), which is in the ratio of 10,000,000 to 7,986,355. Therefore, in the above analogy, $0.7986355 S$ should be written instead of $S$.

But the force of the moon at the quadratures must also be diminished because of the moon's <term>declination<gloss>The angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator</gloss></term> from the equator. For the moon in the quadratures, or rather at $18 \frac{1}{2}$ degrees after the quadratures, is positioned at a declination of approximately $22^\circ 13'$. And the force of a luminary declining from the equator to move the sea...

Furthermore, the diameters of the orbit in which the moon would move without eccentricity are to each other as 69 to 70; therefore, the distance of the moon from the earth at the <term>syzygies<gloss>The points in an orbit when the Earth, Sun, and Moon are in a straight line, such as a new or full moon</gloss></term> is to its distance at the quadratures as 69 to 70, all else being equal. From which it follows that $1.017522 L + 0.7986355 S$ to $0.9830427 \times 0.8570327 L - 0.7986355 S$ is as 9 to 5. And $S$ to $L$ <note>The ratio of the Sun's force to the Moon's force</note> is as 1 to 4.4815. Thus, since the force of the sun is to the force of gravity as 1 is to 12,868,200, the force of the moon will be to the force of gravity as 1 is to 2,871,400.

**Corollary** 1. Since water agitated by the force of the sun rises to a height of one foot and eleven <term>inches<gloss>Newton uses the Latin 'digiti,' which typically refers to a digit (about 0.75 inches), but in his English translations, it is usually rendered as inches</gloss></term> with a thirtieth part of an inch, by the same force of the moon it will rise to a height of eight feet and $7 \frac{4}{25}$ inches, and by both forces together to a height of ten and a half feet; and when the moon is at <term>perigee<gloss>The point in the orbit where the moon is closest to the Earth</gloss></term> it rises to a height of twelve and a half feet and more, especially when the tide is aided by blowing winds. Such a great force is abundantly sufficient to excite all the motions of the sea, and it corresponds well to the magnitude of those motions. For in the seas which lie open widely from east to west, as in the *Pacific* Ocean, and the parts of the *Atlantic* and *Ethiopic* <note>The "Ethiopic Ocean" was a common 17th-century name for the South Atlantic Ocean</note> oceans outside the tropics, the water is accustomed to be raised to a height of six, nine, twelve, or fifteen feet. In the *Pacific* Ocean, however, which is deeper and wider, the tides are said to be greater than in the *Atlantic* and *Ethiopic*. For in order for the tide to be full, the width of the sea from east to west ought not to be less than ninety degrees. In the *Ethiopic* sea, the rise of water within the tropics is less than in the temperate zones, because of the narrowness of the sea between *Africa* and the southern part of *America*. In the middle of the sea, the water cannot rise unless it descends simultaneously at both the eastern and western shores:

# ON NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>
ON THE SYSTEM OF THE WORLD
</margin>

...since however it must descend to those shores in our narrow seas in alternate turns. For that reason, the ebb and flow <note>original: "fluxus & refluxus"</note> in islands that are furthest from the shores is usually very small. In certain ports where the water is forced to flow in and out with great impetus through shallow places to fill and empty the bays in alternate turns, the ebb and flow must be larger than usual, as at *Plymouth* and the *Chepstow* bridge in *England*; at the <term>Mounts of St. Michael<gloss>Mont Saint-Michel, famous for its dramatic tidal range</gloss></term> and the city of the *Abrincatui* (commonly called *Avranches*) in *Normandy*; and at *Cambay* and *Pegu* in the *East Indies*. In these places the sea, by approaching and receding with great velocity, now floods the shores and now leaves them dry for many miles. Nor can the <term>impetus<gloss>The kinetic energy or momentum of the moving water</gloss></term> of the inflow and return be broken before the water is raised or depressed to 30, 40, or 50 feet and more. And the reasoning is the same for long and shallow straits, such as the *Magellanic* <note>The Strait of Magellan at the southern tip of South America</note> and that by which *England* is surrounded. The tide <note>original: "æstus"</note> in such ports and straits is increased beyond measure by the force of the flow and return. But at shores that face the deep and open sea with a steep descent, where the water can rise and subside without the force of flowing and returning, the magnitude of the tide corresponds to the forces of the sun and moon.

*Corollary* 2. Since the force of the moon for moving the sea is to the force of gravity as 1 to 2,871,400, it is clear that this force is far less than what can be felt either in pendulum experiments or in any static or hydrostatic experiments. It is only in the tides of the sea that this force produces a sensible effect.

*Corollary* 3. Since the force of the moon for moving the sea is to the similar force of the sun as 4.4815 to 1, and those forces (by corollary 14, proposition 66, book 1) are as the densities of the bodies of the moon and sun and the cubes of their <term>apparent diameters<gloss>How large the objects look from Earth, rather than their actual physical size</gloss></term> combined; the density of the moon will be to the density of the sun as 4.4815 to 1 directly, and the cube of the moon’s diameter to the cube of the sun’s diameter inversely: that is (since the average apparent diameters of the moon and sun are 31 minutes, 16 1/2 seconds and 32 minutes, 12 seconds) as 4891 to 1000. But the density of the sun was to the density of the earth as 1000 to 4000; and therefore the density of the moon is to the density of the earth as 4891 to 4000, or roughly 11 to 9. Therefore, the body of the moon is denser and more terrestrial <note>Newton is arguing the Moon is made of "heavier" or more compact earth-like material than the Earth itself</note> than our earth.

<summary>Newton explains how geography—specifically narrow channels and shallow bays—amplifies tidal heights far beyond the open ocean's levels. He also calculates that the Moon is approximately 22% denser than the Earth based on their respective gravitational effects on the tides.</summary>

## LEMMA III.

> *With the same conditions established: I say thirdly that the motion of the whole Earth around the axis already described—being composed of the motions of all its particles—will be to the motion of the aforementioned ring around the same axis in a ratio compounded of the ratio of the matter in the Earth to the matter in the ring, and the ratio of three squares of the quadrantal arc of any circle to two squares of the diameter; that is, in the ratio of the matter to the matter and of the number 925,275 to the number 1,000,000.*

For the motion of a cylinder revolving around its own fixed axis is to the motion of an inscribed and simultaneously revolving sphere, as any four equal squares are to three of the circles inscribed within them. And the motion of the cylinder is to the motion of an extremely thin ring (which surrounds the sphere and cylinder at their common contact point) as twice the matter in the cylinder is to three times the matter in the ring. Furthermore, that motion of the ring, if continued uniformly around the axis of the cylinder, is to its own uniform motion around its own diameter (made in the same periodic time) as the circumference of a circle is to twice its diameter.

## HYPOTHESIS II.

*If the aforementioned ring, with all the rest of the Earth removed, were carried alone in the Earth's orbit by an annual motion around the sun, and meanwhile rotated with a daily motion around its own axis, inclined to the plane of the ecliptic at an angle of 23 1/2 degrees: the motion of the equinoctial points would be the same, whether that ring were fluid or consisted of rigid and solid matter.*

### PROPOSITION XXXIX. PROBLEM XX.

The mean hourly motion of the nodes of the moon in a circular orbit, when the nodes are in quadratures, was 16'' 35''' 16iv 36v <note>Newton uses these symbols for sexagesimal divisions: seconds (''), thirds ('''), fourths (iv), and fifths (v) of a degree.</note>, and half of this, 8'' 17''' 38iv 18v (for reasons explained above), is the mean hourly motion of the nodes in such an orbit; and in a whole sidereal year it becomes 20° 11' 46''. Since, therefore, the nodes of the moon in such an orbit would complete 20° 11' 46'' annually in a retrograde direction <note>original: "in antecedentia," meaning moving westward against the stars</note>; and if there were several moons, the motions of the nodes of each (by corollary 16, proposition LXVI, book I) would be as their periodic times; if a moon revolved in the space of a sidereal day near the surface of the earth, the annual motion of the nodes would be to 20° 11' 46'' as the sidereal day <term>sidereal day: the time Earth takes to rotate once relative to the distant stars (approx. 23 hours, 56 minutes), rather than relative to the Sun</term> of 23 hours 56' is to the periodic time of the moon of 27 days 7 hours 43'; that is, as 1436 to 39343. And the ratio is the same for the nodes of a ring of moons surrounding the earth; whether those moons do not touch each other, or are melted and formed into a continuous ring, or finally, whether that ring becomes rigid and is made inflexible.

Therefore, the annual motion of the equinoctial points of a body composed of the ring and the globe will be to the motion of 20° 11' 46" as 1436 to 39343 and 4590 to 489813 combined; that is, as 100 to 292369. Furthermore, the forces by which the nodes of the moons (as I explained above) and thus by which the equinoctial points of the ring retreat (that is, the forces 3 *IT* in the figure on pages 437 & 438) are, in individual particles, as the distances of those particles from the plane *QR*, and by these forces those particles flee the plane; and therefore (<italic>by Lemma II</italic>) if the matter of the ring were spread over the entire surface of the globe in the manner of the figure *Pa p A P e p E* to constitute that upper part of the earth, the total force and efficacy of all the particles to rotate the earth about any diameter of the equator, and thus to move the equinoctial points, would become less than before in the ratio of 2 to 5. Moreover, this motion must be diminished because of the inclination of the plane of the equator to the plane of the ecliptic <note>The ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note>, and that in the ratio of the sine 91706 (which is the sine of the complement of 23 ½ degrees) to the radius 100000. By this ratio, that motion will now become 9'' 7''' 20<sup>iv</sup>. This is the annual precession of the equinoxes arising from the force of the sun.

But the force of the moon to move the sea was to the force of the sun as about 4.4815 to 1. And the force of the moon to move the equinoxes is to the force of the sun in the same proportion. From this, there results an annual precession of the equinoxes arising from the lunar force of 40'' 52''' 52<sup>iv</sup>, and a total annual precession arising from both forces of 50'' 00''' 12<sup>iv</sup>. And this motion agrees with the phenomena. For the precession of the equinoxes, according to astronomical observations, is approximately fifty seconds annually.

If the altitude of the earth at the equator exceeds its altitude at the poles by more than 17 ⅙ miles, its matter will be rarer <note>Less dense.</note> at the circumference than at the center: and the precession of the equinoxes ought to be increased because of that altitude, and decreased because of the rarity.

We have now described the system of the sun, earth, moon, and planets: it remains for something to be added concerning comets.

->*That Comets are higher than the moon and move in the region of the planets.*<-

Just as the lack of daily parallax <note>Daily or "diurnal" parallax is the change in the apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from different points on Earth's surface. If a body is far away, this shift is too small to measure.</note> lifted comets above the sublunary <note>Historically, "sublunary" referred to the region between the Earth and the Moon, which Aristotle believed was the only place where change and decay occurred.</note> regions, so by the annual parallax their descent into the regions of the planets is proven. For comets, which move forward according to the order of the [Zodiacal] signs, are all at the end of their appearance either slower than usual or retrograde <note>Appearing to move backward across the sky.</note>, if the Earth is between them and the sun; but faster than usual if the Earth moves toward opposition. And conversely, those which proceed against the order of the signs <note>Retrograde or "contrary" motion in their orbits.</note> are faster than usual at the end of their appearance, if the Earth is situated between them and the sun; and slower than usual or retrograde, if the Earth is situated on the opposite side. This happens mostly because of the motion of the Earth in its various positions, just as occurs with the planets, which—depending on whether the Earth's motion is in the same or opposite direction—now appear retrograde, now appear to move forward more slowly, and now more quickly. 

If the Earth moves in the same direction as the comet, and is carried with an angular motion around the sun so much faster that a straight line drawn through the Earth and the comet perpetually converges toward parts beyond the comet, the comet viewed from Earth appears to be retrograde because of its slower motion; but if the Earth is carried more slowly,

The proximity of comets is also confirmed by the light of their heads. For when a celestial body is illuminated by the sun and departs into distant regions, its splendor decreases in the quadruplicated ratio <note>The fourth power ($1/d^4$). Newton reasons that as distance increases, the intensity of light hitting the object decreases by the square, and its apparent size also decreases by the square, making the total perceived light drop off much faster than distance alone.</note> of its distance: namely, in a duplicate ratio because of the increased distance of the body from the sun, and in another duplicate ratio because of its diminished apparent diameter. Let us suppose that Saturn with its ring was about four times brighter: and since the light of the ring nearly equaled the light of the intermediate globe, and the apparent diameter of the globe was about 21'', and thus the light of the globe and ring together would equal the light of a globe whose diameter was 30''; the distance of the comet will be to the distance of Saturn as 1 to $\sqrt{4}$ inversely, and 12'' to 30'' directly; that is, as 24 to 30, or 4 to 5. # NATURAL PHILOSOPHY #

It is clear that all comets at their perihelia <note>original: *periheliis* — the point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note> are to be placed either below Saturn, or not far above it. Those who banish comets to the region of the fixed stars err by the whole width of heaven <note>original: *errant toto cœlo* — a Latin idiom meaning to be completely or fundamentally mistaken.</note>; for if that were the case, comets would no more be illuminated by our sun than the planets here are illuminated by the fixed stars.

We have discussed these things without even considering the obscuration of comets by that very abundant and thick smoke <note>Newton uses the word "smoke" (*fumus*) to describe what modern astronomers call the coma—the envelope of gas and dust surrounding the nucleus.</note> with which the head is surrounded, which always shines with a dull light, as if through a cloud. For the more the body is darkened by this smoke, the closer it must approach the Sun so that the abundance of light reflected from it might rival the planets. From this it becomes likely that comets descend far below the sphere of Saturn, as we have proved from their parallax. The same is confirmed most strongly by their tails. These arise either from the reflection of smoke scattered through the heavens, or from the light of the head itself. In the first case, the distance of the comets must be reduced, lest the smoke always arising from the head be spread through too vast a space with incredible velocity and expansion. In the latter case, all the light of both the tail and the hair <gloss>original: *capillitii* — the "hair" or coma of the comet</gloss> must be referred back to the nucleus of the head. Therefore, if we imagine all this light being gathered together and compressed within the disk of the nucleus, that nucleus—whenever it emits a very large and shining tail—would certainly far surpass Jupiter itself in its splendor. Thus, since it emits more light with a smaller apparent diameter, it must be much more intensely illuminated by the sun, and therefore must be much closer to the sun. Furthermore, those heads which hide beneath the sun’s glare and sometimes emit tails that are both very large and very brilliant, like fiery beams, must by the same argument be placed below the orbit of Venus. For if all that light were supposed to be gathered into a single star, it would sometimes surpass Venus itself, not to say several Venuses joined together.

Finally, the same conclusion is gathered from the light of the heads, which increases as comets move away from the Earth toward the Sun, and decreases as they move away from the Sun toward the Earth. Thus, the later comet of the year 1665 (observed by *Hevelius* <note>Johannes Hevelius (1611–1687), a leading Polish astronomer known for his detailed lunar maps and observations of comets.</note>), from the time it began to be seen, was always losing its apparent motion, and therefore had passed its perigee <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Earth.</note>; nevertheless, the splendor of its head increased daily until the comet, covered by the solar rays, ceased to be visible. The comet of the year 1683 (observed by the same *Hevelius*) at the end of the month of July, when it was first seen, was moving very slowly, about 40 or 45 minutes of a degree each day in its orbit...

This is also gathered from the diameter of the head as measured with a micrometer: for <term>Hevelius</term><note>Johannes Hevelius (1611–1687) was a prominent Polish astronomer known as the "father of lunar topography."</note> found on August 6 that it was only 6' 5'' including the hair <note>original: *coma* — the envelope of gas and dust around the comet's nucleus.</note>, but on September 2 it was 9' 7''. The comet of the year 1618 around the middle of the month of December, and that of the year 1680 around the end of the same month, moved most rapidly, and therefore were then in their <term>perigees</term><note>The perigee is the point in an orbit where a body is closest to the Earth.</note>. The head of the former comet, according to the observations of <term>Cysatus</term><note>Johann Baptist Cysat (1587–1657), a Swiss Jesuit mathematician and astronomer.</note>, on December 1 appeared larger than stars of the first magnitude <note>In the magnitude scale, "first magnitude" refers to the brightest stars visible to the naked eye.</note>, and on December 16 (being now at its perigee) it had faded little in size, but had diminished greatly in brilliance or clarity of light. On January 7, <term>Kepler</term>, uncertain about the head, ceased his observations. 

On the 12th day of the month of December, the head of the latter comet was sighted and observed by <term>Flamsteed</term><note>John Flamsteed (1646–1719), the first Astronomer Royal of England.</note> at a distance of nine degrees from the Sun; a visibility that would hardly have been granted to a star of the third magnitude. On December 15 and 17, the same appeared as a star of the third magnitude, its brightness certainly diminished by the clouds near the setting sun. On December 26, moving most swiftly and being almost at its perigee, it gave way to <note>original: *cedebat* — was surpassed by or appeared fainter than.</note> the "mouth of Pegasus," a star of the third magnitude. On January 3, it appeared as a star of the fourth magnitude; on January 9, as a star of the fifth; on January 13, it disappeared due to the brightness of the waxing moon. On January 25, it barely equaled stars of the seventh magnitude. 

If equal times from the perigee are taken on either side, the heads—which at those times were placed in distant regions and ought to have shone equally because of their equal distances from the Earth—shone most brightly when in the region of the Sun and vanished on the other side of the perigee. Therefore, from the great difference in light in both positions, it is concluded that there was a great proximity between the Sun and the comet in the first position. For the light of comets is usually regular, and appears greatest where the heads move most swiftly and are thus at their perigees—except insofar as that light is greater in the vicinity of the Sun.

<meta>This page continues Newton’s discussion of comets in Book III of his Principia. Having previously established their distance and brightness, he now moves into three significant corollaries regarding their physical nature—specifically that they reflect sunlight, why they are mostly seen near the Sun, and why their orbits prove that outer space is a vacuum without resistance.</meta>

## NATURAL PHILOSOPHY ##

<margin>
ON THE SYSTEM OF THE WORLD
</margin>

*Corollary 1.* Comets, therefore, shine by the light of the sun reflected from them.

*Corollary 2.* From what has been said, it is also understood why comets so frequently visit the region of the sun. If they were seen in regions far beyond <term>Saturn</term><note>At the time of writing, Saturn was the most distant known planet.</note>, they ought to appear more often in those parts of the sky opposite to the sun. For those situated in these parts would be nearer to the Earth, and the sun, placed between them, would obscure the others. But by searching through the histories of comets, I have found that four or five times more have been detected in the hemisphere toward the sun than in the opposite hemisphere—besides, no doubt, many others which the sun’s brilliance has hidden. Surely, in their descent to our regions, they neither emit tails nor are they so illuminated by the sun as to show themselves to the naked eye before they are closer than <term>Jupiter</term> itself. Moreover, of the space traced around the sun in such a small interval, by far the greater part is situated on the side of the Earth that faces the sun; and in that larger part, comets, being for the most part nearer to the sun, are usually more brightly illuminated.

*Corollary 3.* From this it is also evident that the heavens lack resistance. For comets, following oblique paths and sometimes ones contrary to the course of the planets, move in every direction with the utmost freedom, and preserve their motions for a very long time, even against the course of the planets. <note>Newton uses this observation to argue against the "Vortex Theory" of René Descartes, which suggested the planets were carried by a fluid medium. If such a fluid existed, comets moving "against the grain" would be slowed down or blocked.</note> I am mistaken if they are not a kind of planet, returning in a perpetual circuit by their motion. For as to what some writers wish—that they are <term>meteors</term><note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred broadly to any atmospheric phenomenon (like clouds or lightning), not just space rocks. Newton is refuting the idea that comets are just temporary weather-like events in Earth's atmosphere.</note>, drawing an argument from the perpetual changes of their heads—that seems to lack foundation. The heads of comets are surrounded by huge atmospheres, and these atmospheres ought to be denser at the bottom. Hence, it is the clouds, not the bodies of the comets themselves, in which those changes are seen. Thus, if the Earth were viewed from the planets, it would no doubt shine by the light of its clouds, and the solid body would lie hidden beneath those clouds. So too the <term>belts of Jupiter</term> are formed in the clouds of that planet, which change their positions relative to each other, and the solid body of Jupiter is seen with more difficulty through those clouds. And much more so must the bodies of comets be hidden under atmospheres that are both deeper and thicker.

<summary>Newton concludes that comets are solid, planet-like bodies that shine by reflected sunlight and move through a vacuum (void of resistance). He explains that their changing appearance is due to their thick atmospheres rather than changes to the comet's actual body.</summary>

<keywords>comets, reflection of light, celestial mechanics, vacuum, planetary motion, Jupiter's belts, atmospheric density, Saturn, orbital frequency</keywords>

-> MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK THREE. <-

## PROPOSITION 40. THEOREM 20. ##

*That comets move in conic sections having their foci in the center of the sun, and by radii drawn to the sun describe areas proportional to the times.*

This is evident from corollary 1 of proposition 13 of the first book, combined with propositions 8, 12, and 13 of the third book. <note>Newton is cross-referencing his earlier mathematical proofs that a body moving under an inverse-square law of gravity must follow a conic section (an ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola).</note>

*Corollary 1.* Hence, if comets return in an orbit, those orbits will be ellipses, and their <term>periodic times</term><note>The time taken to complete one full orbit.</note> will be to the periodic times of the planets in the <term>sesquiplicate ratio</term><note>The 3/2 power ratio; for example, if the distance is 4 times greater, the time is 8 times longer (the square root of 4 cubed).</note> of their principal axes. And therefore, comets, which for the most part wander above the planets and on that account describe orbits with larger axes, will revolve more slowly. For instance, if the axis of a comet’s orbit is four times larger than the axis of Saturn’s orbit, the time of the comet’s revolution will be to the time of Saturn’s revolution (which is 30 years) as 8 is to 1 (that is, $4 \sqrt{4}$ to 1); and therefore, it will be 240 years.

*Corollary 2.* Moreover, their orbits will be so close to parabolas that parabolas may be used in their place without sensible <note>meaning "noticeable" or "measurable"</note> errors.

*Corollary 3.* And for that reason (by corollary 7 of proposition 16, book 1), the velocity of every comet will always be to the velocity of any planet revolving around the sun in a circle, in the <term>subduplicate ratio</term><note>The ratio of the square roots.</note> of the double distance of the planet from the center of the sun, to the distance of the comet from the center of the sun, very nearly. Let us suppose the radius of the <term>great orbit</term><note>The mean radius of the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note>, or the maximum semi-diameter of the ellipse in which the Earth revolves, to be 100,000,000 parts: then the Earth, by its mean daily motion, will describe 1,720,212 parts, and by its hourly motion 71,675 1/2 parts. Therefore, a comet at the same mean distance from the sun as the Earth, with a velocity which is to the velocity of the Earth as $\sqrt{2}$ to 1, will describe in its daily motion 2,432,747 parts, and in its hourly motion 101,364 1/2 parts. At greater or lesser distances, however, both the daily and hourly motion will be to this daily and hourly motion in the inverse subduplicate ratio of the distances, and is therefore given.

*Corollary 4.* From which, if the <term>latus rectum</term><note>The chord passing through the focus of a conic section, perpendicular to its major axis; it defines the "width" of the curve.</note> of the parabola is four times larger than the radius of the great orbit, and the square of that radius is set at 100,000,000 parts: the area which the comet describes each day by a radius drawn to the sun...

<summary>In this proposition, Newton applies Kepler's Laws to comets, proving they move in elliptical or nearly parabolic orbits with the Sun at one focus. He provides the mathematical ratios to calculate a comet's orbital period and velocity relative to the Earth and other planets.</summary>

*Corollary.* From this, the areas of all curves can be found very nearly. For if some points are found for any curve that needs to be <term>squared</term><note>original: "quadrandæ"; quadrature or "squaring" a curve is the historical term for calculating the area underneath it.</note>, and a parabola is understood to be drawn through those same points, the area of this parabola will be very nearly the same as the area of the curve to be squared. Moreover, a parabola can always be squared geometrically by well-known methods.

## LEMMA VI.

### *From several observed places of a comet, to find its place at any given intermediate time.*

Let *HI, IK, KL, LM* designate the times between observations (as in the preceding figure); let *HA, IB, KC, LD, ME* be the five observed <term>longitudes</term><note>In astronomy, longitude measures the position of a celestial body along the ecliptic, the sun's apparent path.</note> of the comet, and *HS* the given time between the first observation and the longitude being sought. And if a regular curve *A B C D E* is understood to be drawn through the points *A, B, C, D, E*; and through the lemma above its ordinate *RS* is found, *RS* will be the sought longitude.

By the same method, from five observed latitudes, the latitude at a given time is found.

*...I $\mu$ and vertex $\mu$. On $I \mu$ produced <note>In geometry, "produced" means extending a line segment further in the same direction.</note>, let $\mu O$ be taken equal to half of $I \mu$. Let $OS$ be joined, and let it be produced to $\xi$, so that $S\xi$ is equal to twice $SO$. And if a comet $B$ moves in the arc $CBA$, and $\xi B$ is drawn cutting the chord $AC$ at $E$: I say that the point $E$ will cut off from the chord $AC$ a segment $AE$ proportional to the time, very nearly.*

For let $EO$ be joined, cutting the parabolic arc $ABC$ at $\Upsilon$ <note>The Greek letter Upsilon, used here to mark a specific point on the curve.</note>, and let $\mu X$ be drawn, which touches the same arc at the vertex $\mu$, and meets the drawn line $EO$ at $X$; and the curvilinear area <note>The area bounded by the curve and the straight lines.</note> $AEX\mu A$ will be to the curvilinear area $ACY\mu A$ as $AE$ is to $AC$. And therefore, since the triangle $ASE$ is to the triangle $ASC$ in the same ratio, the whole area $ASEX\mu A$ will be to the whole area $ASC\Upsilon\mu A$ as $AE$ is to $AC$. Moreover, since $\xi O$ is to $SO$ as 3 to 1, and $EO$ to $XO$ is in the same ratio, $SX$ will be parallel to $EB$: and therefore if $BX$ is joined, the triangle $SEB$ will be equal to the triangle $XEB$. Hence if the triangle $EXB$ is added to the area $ASEX\mu A$, and the triangle $SEB$ is subtracted from the sum, the area $ASBX\mu A$ will remain equal to the area $ASEX\mu A$, and thus it is to the area $ASC\Upsilon\mu A$ as $AE$ is to $AC$. But the area $ASBX\mu A$ is very nearly equal to the area $ASB\Upsilon\mu A$, and this area $ASB\Upsilon\mu A$ is to the area $ASC\Upsilon\mu A$ as the time of the described arc $AB$ is to the time of the entire described arc $AC$ <note>Newton relies on Kepler's Second Law here: that a line connecting a celestial body to its focus sweeps out equal areas in equal times.</note>. Therefore $AE$ is to $AC$ in the ratio of the times, very nearly. <note>original: "Q. E. D." (Quod erat demonstrandum); "Which was to be demonstrated."</note>

*Corollary.* When the point $B$ falls on the vertex $\mu$ of the parabola, $AE$ is to $AC$ in the ratio of the times exactly.

### Scholium.

If $\mu\xi$ is joined cutting $AC$ at $\delta$, and on it a point $\eta$ is taken so that $\xi\eta$ is to $\mu B$ as $27 MI$ is to $16 M\mu$: the line $B\eta$ drawn will cut the chord $AC$ in the ratio of the times more accurately than before. However, the point $\eta$ should lie beyond the point $\xi$ if the point $B$ is further from the principal vertex of the parabola than point $\mu$; and on this side <note>meaning closer to point μ</note> if it is less distant from the same vertex.

# LEMMA XI.

*If a comet, deprived of all motion, were dropped from the height SN or S $\mu$ +* $\frac{2}{3}$ *I $\mu$ so that it fell into the sun, and were urged toward the sun by that same force uniformly continued with which it is urged at the beginning; the same comet, in half the time in which it describes the arc AC in its orbit, would by its descent describe a space equal to the length I $\mu$.*

For a comet, in the time it describes the parabolic arc $AC$, would describe the chord $AC$ with the velocity it has at height $SP$ (by the last lemma); and therefore (by corollary 7, proposition 16, book 1) in the same time, revolving in a circle whose radius is $SP$ by the force of its own gravity, it would describe an arc whose length would be to the chord $AC$ of the parabolic arc in the <term>subduplicate ratio<gloss>A historical mathematical term for the ratio of the square roots—in this case, $1 : \sqrt{2}$.</gloss></term> of one to two. And for that reason, with the weight <note>Newton uses "weight" (pondus) to mean the gravitational force acting on the comet at a specific distance from the Sun.</note> it has toward the sun at height $SP$, falling from that height toward the sun, it would in half that time (by corollary 9, proposition 4, book 1) describe a space equal to the square of half that chord <note>original: "quadrato semissis chordæ"</note> divided by <note>original: "applicato ad" — literally "applied to," a geometric way of expressing division.</note> four times the height $SP$, that is, the space $\frac{AI^2}{4 SP}$. Hence, since the weight of the comet toward the sun at height $SN$ is to its weight toward the sun at height $SP$ as $SP$ is to $S \mu$: the comet, with the weight it has at height $SN$, falling toward the sun in the same time, will describe the space $\frac{AI^2}{4 S \mu}$, which is to say, a space equal to the length $I \mu$ or $M \mu$. Which was to be demonstrated.

# PROPOSITION 41. PROBLEM 21.

## To determine the trajectory <note>The path or orbit an object follows through space.</note> of a comet moving in a parabola from three given observations.

Having attacked this most difficult problem in many ways, I composed certain problems in the first book which relate to its solution. Afterwards, I thought of the following, slightly simpler solution.

Let three observations be selected, spaced at nearly equal intervals of time from each other. However, let that interval of time in which the comet moves more slowly be slightly larger than the other, specifically so that the difference in times is to the sum of the times as the sum of the times is to approximately six hundred days; or so that point *E* (in the figure for Lemma 8) falls as close as possible to point *M*, and deviates from there toward *I* rather than toward *A*. If such observations are not available, a new position for the comet must be found using Lemma 6.

->MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK THREE.<-

[the comet] <note>Newton is completing a sentence from the previous page regarding the distance a comet travels.</note> must describe in its own orbit between the first and third observation, and therefore it would be equal to $MN$ itself, provided that $B$ is the true position of the comet in the plane of the ecliptic <term>ecliptic</term><note>The plane of Earth's orbit around the Sun; the "path" the Sun appears to follow through the stars.</note>.

Moreover, it is fitting to choose the points $B, b, \beta$ not at random, but as close to the true position as possible. If the angle $A\curlyvee t$, in which the trace of the orbit described in the plane of the ecliptic cuts the straight line $tB$, is known approximately; in that angle, a hidden straight line $AC$ must be drawn, which is to $\frac{4}{3} T\tau$ in the subduplicate ratio <term>subduplicate ratio</term><note>original: "subduplicata ratione"; in modern terms, this means the ratio of the square roots.</note> of $S\Omega$ to $St$. And by drawing the straight line $SEB$, whose part $EB$ is equal to the length $V\tau$, the point $B$ will be determined, which may be used for the first time. Then, after the straight line $AC$ is deleted and redrawn according to the preceding construction, and the length $MP$ is also found; a point $b$ should be taken on $tB$ by this rule: if $TA$ and $\tau C$ intersect each other at $\curlyvee$ <note>The symbol $\curlyvee$ represents a specific point of intersection in the diagram, often associated with the Greek letter Upsilon.</note>, the distance $\curlyvee b$ should be to the distance $\curlyvee B$ in a ratio compounded <note>A "compounded ratio" involves multiplying two ratios together.</note> of the ratio of $MP$ to $MN$ and the subduplicate ratio of $SB$ to $Sb$. And by the same method, a third point $\beta$ is to be found, if one wishes to repeat the operation a third time. But by this method, two operations will generally suffice. For if the distance $Bb$ comes out very small; after the points $F, f$ and $G, g$ are found, the drawn straight lines $Ff$ and $Gg$ will intersect $TA$ and $\tau C$ at the sought points $X$ and $Z$.

From observations of this kind, through the construction of figures and calculations, I derived the longitudes and latitudes of the comet; and our friend <term>Pound<note>James Pound (1669–1724), an English astronomer and clergyman who provided Newton and Halley with highly accurate astronomical data.</note></term> corrected the comet's locations based on corrected positions of the fixed stars; these corrected locations are recorded above. I used a <term>micrometer<note>An instrument used with a telescope to measure very small angular distances between celestial objects.</note></term> that was somewhat crudely constructed, yet the errors in longitude and latitude (insofar as they arise from our observations) hardly exceed one <term>arcminute<note>A unit of angular measurement equal to 1/60th of a degree.</note></term>. Toward the end of its movement, the comet (according to our observations) began to deflect notably toward the north, away from the <term>parallel<note>A line of constant latitude on the celestial sphere, parallel to the celestial equator.</note></term> it had held at the end of the month of February.

Now, to determine the comet's orbit, I selected three from the observations described so far, which <term>Flamsteed<note>John Flamsteed (1646–1719), the first Astronomer Royal, whose meticulous observations of the 1680 comet were vital to Newton's work.</note></term> made on December 21, January 5, and January 25. From these, I found $S t$ to be 9842.1 parts and $V t$ to be 455 parts, where 10,000 parts represent the <term>semi-diameter of the great orbit<note>The average distance from the Earth to the Sun, known today as an Astronomical Unit (AU).</note></term>. Then, for the first operation, assuming $t B$ to be 5657 parts, I found $S B$ to be 9747, $BE$ (in the first instance) 412, $S \mu$ 9503, $i \lambda$ 413; $BE$ (in the second instance) 421, $OD$ 10186, $X$ 8528.4, $MP$ 8450, $MN$ 8475, and $NP$ 25. From this, for the second operation, I gathered the distance $t b$ to be 5640. And through this operation, I finally found the distances $T X$ to be 4775 and $\tau Z$ to be 11322. 

Defining the orbit from these values, I found its <term>nodes<note>The two points where the comet's path intersects the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic).</note></term>—the descending node in Cancer [♋] and the ascending node in Capricorn [♑] at 1 degree 53 minutes; the <term>inclination<note>The tilt of the comet's orbital plane relative to the Earth's orbital plane.</note></term> of its plane to the plane of the ecliptic to be 61 degrees 20½ minutes; its vertex (or the comet's <term>perihelion<note>The point in the comet's orbit where it is closest to the Sun.</note></term>) to be 8 degrees 38 minutes from the node, located in Sagittarius [♐] at 27 degrees 43 minutes with a southern latitude of 7 degrees 34 minutes. Its <term>latus rectum<note>A geometric parameter that defines the width of the orbital curve (a parabola or ellipse) at the focus (the Sun).</note></term> was 236.8, and the area described each day by a radius drawn to the Sun was 93,585 (where the square of the semi-diameter of the great orbit is set at 100,000,000). The comet indeed proceeded in this orbit according to the <term>order of the signs<note>Prograde or "direct" motion, moving through the zodiac in the standard sequence (Aries, Taurus, etc.).</note></term>, and reached the vertex of its orbit (the perihelion) on December 8th at 4 minutes past noon. I determined all these things graphically using a scale of equal parts and <term>chords<note>Straight lines connecting two points on a curve, used to measure angles in geometric constructions.</note></term> of angles collected from a table of natural sines; I constructed a sufficiently large diagram in which the semi-diameter of the great orbit (10,000 parts) was equal to 16⅓ English <term>inches<note>Original: "digitis... pedis Anglicani". Newton is describing a large physical drawing with a radius of about 1.36 feet.</note></term>.

Finally, to confirm whether the comet truly moved in the orbit thus found, I gathered the comet's locations in this orbit at the times of certain observations through operations that were partly arithmetic and partly graphic, as may be seen in the following table.
