### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES

<margin>BOOK THREE</margin>

...its position relative to the nearest fixed stars having been observed with sufficient accuracy by means of a telescope, sometimes two feet and sometimes ten feet in length, and with the difference in longitude between **Coburg** <note>A city in Bavaria, Germany; the observations there were made by Gottfried Kirch.</note> and **London** being eleven degrees, and the locations of the fixed stars having been observed by our friend **Pound** <note>James Pound (1669–1724), a clergyman and skilled astronomer who provided Newton and Halley with precise stellar data.</note>, our friend **Halley** determined the locations of the comet as follows:

**Nov.** 3, at 17 hours 2 minutes, apparent time in **London**, the comet was in Leo (♌) at 29° 51' with a northern latitude of 1° 17' 45".
**Nov.** 5, at 15 hours 58 minutes, the comet was in Virgo (♍) at 3° 23' with a northern latitude of 1° 6'.
**Nov.** 10, at 16 hours 31 minutes, the comet was equally distant from the stars Sigma ($\sigma$) and Tau ($\tau$) of Leo according to **Bayer** <note>Johann Bayer, whose 1603 star atlas *Uranometria* assigned Greek letters to stars.</note>; it had not yet reached the straight line joining them, but was a short distance from it. In **Flamsteed’s** catalog of stars, Sigma then held 14° 15' of Virgo (♍) with a northern latitude of nearly 1° 41', while Tau held 17° 3 1/2' of Virgo (♍) with a southern latitude of 0° 34'. And the midpoint between these stars was 15° 39 1/4' of Virgo (♍) with a northern latitude of 0° 33 1/2'. Let the distance of the comet from that straight line be about 10' or 12', and the difference in longitude of the comet and that midpoint will be 7', and the difference in latitude about 7 1/2'. And from this, the comet was in 15° 32' of Virgo (♍) with a northern latitude of about 26'.

The first observation, based on the position of the comet relative to certain small fixed stars, was abundantly accurate. The second was also sufficiently accurate. In the third, which was less accurate, an error of six or seven minutes might have occurred, but hardly more. The longitude of the comet in the first observation, which was more accurate than the others, was calculated in the aforesaid parabolic orbit as 29° 30' 22" of Leo (♌); the northern latitude was 1° 25' 7"; and its distance from the sun was 115,546.

Furthermore, **Halley**, observing that a remarkable comet had appeared four times at intervals of 575 years—specifically in the month of **September** after the murder of **Julius Caesar** <note>The "Sidus Iulium" or Caesar's Comet of 44 BC.</note>; in the year of Christ 531 during the consulship of **Lampadius** and **Orestes**; in the year of Christ 1106 in the month of **February**; and toward the end of the year 1680—and this with a long and remarkable tail (except that after the death of **Caesar**, the tail appeared less visible due to the unfavorable position of the earth): he sought an elliptical orbit whose major axis would be 1,382,957 parts (where the average distance of the earth from the sun is 10,000 parts), in which orbit the comet could indeed revolve in 575 years. And by placing the ascending <term>node<note>The point where the comet crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic) moving northward.</note></term> in 2° 2' of Cancer (♋); the inclination of the plane of the orbit to the plane of the ecliptic at 61° 6' 48"; the <term>perihelion<note>The point in the orbit closest to the Sun.</note></term> of the comet in this plane at 22° 44' 25" of Sagittarius (♐); the equalized time of perihelion on **Dec.** 7, at 23 hours 9 minutes; the distance of the perihelion from the node...

The observations of this comet from the beginning to the end match the motion of the comet in the orbit already described no less closely than the motions of the planets are accustomed to match their theories; and by this agreement, they prove that it was one and the same comet that appeared during all this time, and that its orbit has been correctly defined here.

...**Ponthæus** <note>Jean-Dominique Ponthée, a French Jesuit and astronomer.</note> published his findings concerning this comet. **Cellius**, who was present and sent his observations in a letter to **Mr. Cassini**, saw the comet at the same hour at 8 degrees 30' of **Libra** <note>original: "♎"</note> with a southern latitude of 0 degrees 30'. At the same hour **Galletius** at **Avignon** (that is, 5:42 a.m. in **London**) saw the comet at 8 degrees of Libra without any latitude. According to the theory, however, the comet was then at 8 degrees 16' 45'' of Libra with a southern latitude of 0 degrees 53' 7''.

**November 18**, at 6:30 a.m. in **Rome** (that is, 5:40 a.m. in London), **Ponthæus** saw the comet at 13 degrees 30' of Libra with a southern latitude of 1 degree 20'. **Cellius** saw it at 13 degrees 30' of Libra with a southern latitude of 1 degree 00'. **Galletius**, however, at 5:30 a.m. in Avignon, saw the comet at 13 degrees 00' of Libra with a southern latitude of 1 degree 00'. On the same day at **Boston** in **New England**, at a latitude of 42½ degrees, at 5:00 a.m. (that is, 9:44 a.m. in London), the comet was seen near 14 degrees of Libra with a southern latitude of 1 degree 30', as I received from the famous **Mr. Halley**.

**November 19**, at 4:30 a.m. at **Cambridge**, the comet (as observed by a certain young man) was about 2 degrees distant from **Spica Virginis** <note>The brightest star in the constellation Virgo.</note> toward the **north-west** <term>boreazephyrum: a classical term for the wind or direction between north (Boreas) and west (Zephyrus).</term>. **Spica** was then at 19 degrees 23' 47'' of Libra with a southern latitude of 2 degrees 1' 59''. On the same day on the island of **Jamaica**, the comet was at a distance of about one degree from Spica. On the same day, **Mr. Arthur Storer** at the **Patuxent River**, near **Hunting Creek** in **Maryland**, on the border of **Virginia** at a latitude of 38½ degrees, at 5:00 a.m. (that is, 10:00 a.m. London time), saw the comet above Spica, and almost joined with Spica, the distance between them being about ¾ of a degree. From these observations compared with one another, I conclude that at 9:44 a.m. in London, the comet was at 18 degrees 50' of Libra with a southern latitude of approximately 1 degree 25'. However, by the theory, the comet was then at 18 degrees 52' 15'' of Libra with a southern latitude of 1 degree 26' 54''.

At **Boston** in **New England**, however, it appeared at approximately 3 degrees of Scorpio, with nearly the same latitude as before, that is, 1 degree 30'. On the same day at five o'clock in the morning at Balasore, the comet was observed at 1 degree 50' of Scorpio; and therefore at five o'clock in the morning in London, the comet was at approximately 3 degrees 5' of Scorpio. On the same day in London at 6:30 a.m., our own **Hooke** <note>Robert Hooke, the English polymath</note> saw the comet at approximately 3 degrees 30' of Scorpio, and this was in a straight line that passes through Spica in Virgo and **the Heart of the Lion** <note>original: "cor leonis," the star Regulus</note>, not exactly indeed, but deviating a very little from that line toward the north. **Montanari** likewise noted that the line drawn from the comet through Spica, on this day and the following ones, passed through the southern side of the Heart of the Lion, with a very small interval interposed between the Heart of the Lion and this line. A straight line passing through the Heart of the Lion and Spica in Virgo intersected the **ecliptic** <note>the apparent path of the sun through the stars</note> at 3 degrees 46' of Virgo at an angle of 2 degrees 51'. And if the comet had been placed on this line at 3 degrees of Scorpio, its latitude would have been 2 degrees 26'. But since the comet, by the agreement of **Hooke** and **Montanari**, was somewhat distant from this line toward the north, its latitude was a little less. On the 20th, from the observation of **Montanari**, its latitude almost equaled the latitude of Spica, and was approximately 1 degree 30', and according to the agreement of **Hooke**, **Montanari**, and **Ango**, it was continuously increasing, and therefore it was now sensibly greater than 1 degree 30'. Between the limits now established of 2 degrees 26' and 1 degree 30', at a medium magnitude, the latitude will be approximately 1 degree 58'. The observations of **Ponthaeus** and **Cellius** are less precise <note>original: "craſſiores", literally 'thicker' or 'coarser'</note>, especially those taken by <term>azimuths</term> <note>the horizontal angle of a celestial object from the North or South</note> and altitudes, as are those of **Gallet**: better are those made by the positions of the comet relative to the fixed stars by **Montanari**, **Hooke**, **Ango**, and the observer in **New England**, and occasionally by **Ponthaeus** and **Cellius**. According to the theory, however, the comet was now at approximately 18 1/2 degrees of Scorpio.

These observations, therefore, agree with the theory as much as they agree with one another, and by agreeing they prove that it was one and the same comet which appeared throughout the entire time from the fourth day of **November** until the ninth of **March**. The <term>trajectory</term> <note>the path of the comet through space</note> of this comet crossed the plane of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>the apparent path of the Sun through the sky</note> twice, and therefore it was not a straight line. It crossed the ecliptic not in opposite parts of the heavens, but at the end of Virgo and the beginning of Capricorn, at an interval of approximately 98 degrees; and therefore the course of the comet turned <note>original: "deflecte-", catchword for 'deflectebatur' on the following page</note>...

...was deflected from the great circle <note>A great circle is the largest possible circle that can be drawn on a sphere; in astronomy, it refers to the path across the celestial sphere</note>. For even in the month of November, its course declined by at least three degrees from the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky</note> toward the south, and afterward in the month of December it leaned 29 degrees from the ecliptic toward the north in those parts of the orbit where the comet tended toward the sun and returned from the sun, with the apparent angle of more than thirty degrees declining from each other, as **Montanari** <note>original: "Montenarus"; Geminiano Montanari, an Italian astronomer and contemporary of Newton</note> observed. This comet passed through nine signs <note>the divisions of the Zodiac</note>, namely from the last degree of Leo to the beginning of Gemini, besides the sign of Leo through which it passed before it began to be seen; and no other theory exists by which a comet might traverse such a large part of the heavens with a regular motion. Its motion was extremely uneven. For around the twentieth day of **November**, it described about five degrees each day; then with its motion slowed down between **Nov. 26** and **Dec. 12**, in a space of fifteen and a half days, it described only 40 degrees; but afterward, with its motion accelerated again, it described nearly five degrees each day before its motion began to slow down once more. And a theory which corresponds so well to such an uneven motion through the greatest part of the heavens, and which observes the same laws as the theory of the planets, and accurately agrees with precise astronomical observations, cannot but be true.

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK THREE.

*G H* represents the intersection of the sphere of the great orbit <note>The "great orbit" refers to the Earth's annual path around the Sun</note> with the plane of the comet's trajectory; *I* is the location of the comet on *Nov. 4, 1680*; *K* its location on *Nov. 11*; *L* its location on *Nov. 19*; *M* on *Dec. 12*; *N* on *Dec. 21*; *O* on *Dec. 29*; *P* on the following *Jan. 5*; *Q* on *Jan. 25*; *R* on *Feb. 5*; *S* on *Feb. 25*; *T* on *Mar. 5*; and *V* its location on *Mar. 9*. I have employed the following observations in defining the tail.

*Nov. 4 & 6.* The tail had not yet appeared. *Nov. 11.* The tail had now begun to show, but was seen to be only half a degree long through a ten-foot telescope.

*Nov. 17.* The tail appeared more than fifteen degrees long to **Ponthaeus** <note>Matteo Ponatoni, an Italian Jesuit mathematician and astronomer</note>.

*Nov. 18.* The tail was 30 degrees long, directly opposite the sun, and was observed in **New England** <note>This likely refers to observations by Thomas Brattle or Arthur Storer; Newton was keen to use data from the American colonies to provide a wider baseline for his calculations</note>; it reached as far as the star Mars, which was then in 9 degrees 54 minutes of Virgo. *Nov. 19.* In **Maryland**, the tail was seen to be 15 or 20 degrees long. *Dec. 10.* The tail (according to the observations of **Flamsteed** <note>John Flamsteed, the first Astronomer Royal of England</note>) passed through the middle of the distance between the tail of the serpent in the constellation *Ophiuchus* and the star delta in the southern wing of the *Eagle* <note>the constellation Aquila</note>, and ended near the stars *A*, omega, and *b* in **Bayer’s** charts <note>Johann Bayer’s "Uranometria," the standard star atlas of the 17th century</note>. Its end was therefore in 19 1/2 degrees of Capricorn, with a northern latitude of about 34 1/4 degrees. *Dec. 11.* The tail rose as far as the head of the *Arrow* <note>the constellation Sagitta</note> (labeled alpha and beta by Bayer), ending in 26 degrees 43 minutes of Capricorn, with a northern latitude of 38 degrees 34 minutes. *Dec. 12.* The tail passed through the middle of the *Arrow*, and did not extend much further beyond it, ending in 4 degrees of Aquarius, with a northern latitude of about 42 1/2 degrees. These measurements refer to the length of the brighter part of the tail. For in a fainter light, perhaps in a clearer sky, on *Dec. 12* at 5:40 PM at **Rome** (as observed by **Ponthaeus**), the tail extended 10 degrees above the rump of the *Swan* <note>the constellation Cygnus</note>; and from this star, its side toward the west and north stood off by 45 minutes. Moreover, the tail on these days was 3 degrees wide near its upper end; therefore, its middle was 2 degrees 15 minutes away from that star toward the south, and the upper end was in 22 degrees of Pisces, with a northern latitude of 61 degrees. From this, the tail was approximately 70 degrees long. *Dec. 21.* It rose almost to the chair of *Cassiopeia*, being equally distant from beta and *Schedir* <note>the brightest star in Cassiopeia</note>, and having a distance from each equal to the distance between the two stars themselves; it ended, therefore, in 24 degrees of Aries, with a latitude of 47 1/2 degrees. *Dec. 29.* The tail touched *Scheat* <note>a star in the constellation Pegasus</note> located on the left, and accurately filled the interval between the two stars in the northern foot of *Andromeda*, and was 54 degrees long; it therefore ended in 19 degrees of Taurus, with a latitude of 35 degrees. *Jan. 5.* The tail touched the star pi in the breast of *Andromeda* on its right side, and the star mu in her belt on the left side; and (according to our observations

For if they were nothing other than vapors or exhalations of the earth, the sun, and the planets, this comet ought to have been immediately dissipated during its passage through the vicinity of the sun. For the heat of the sun is as the density of its rays, that is, inversely as the square of the distance of the places from the sun. <note>Newton is applying the inverse-square law to thermal radiation: if you are 10 times closer to the sun, the heat is 100 times greater</note>. But the heat of boiling water is about three times greater than the heat which dry earth receives from the summer sun, as I have experienced; and the heat of red-hot iron (if I conjecture correctly) is about three or four times greater than the heat of boiling water; therefore, the heat which dry earth at the comet could have received from the solar rays while at perihelion was about 2000 times greater than the heat of red-hot iron. A comet, therefore, at its <term>perihelion</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the sun.</note> conceived an immense heat from the sun, and it is able to preserve that heat for a very long time. For a globe of red-hot iron one inch wide, if left standing in the air, would scarcely lose all its heat in the space of one hour. However, a larger globe would preserve its heat longer in proportion to its diameter, because the surface (by the measure of which it is cooled through contact with the surrounding air) is smaller in that proportion relative to the quantity of its included hot matter. And therefore, a globe of red-hot iron equal to this Earth—that is, roughly 40,000,000 feet wide—would scarcely cool in as many days, and therefore in 50,000 years. I suspect, however, that the duration of heat, due to hidden causes, increases in a smaller ratio than that of the diameter; and I would wish that the true ratio be investigated through experiments.

Furthermore, it should be noted that in the month of *December*, when the comet had just been heated near the sun, it emitted a tail far larger and more splendid than before in the month of *November*, when it had not yet reached perihelion. And universally, all the largest and most shining tails arise from comets immediately after their passage through the region of the sun. Therefore, the heating of the comet contributes to the magnitude of the tail. And from this I seem to conclude that the tail is nothing other than a very thin vapor, which the head or nucleus of the comet emits by its heat.

Regarding the tails of comets, however, there is a triple opinion: that they are either a sunbeam <note>original: "jubar," a radiant beam of light</note> propagated through the translucent heads of the comets; or that they arise from the refraction of light in its progress from the comet’s head to the earth; or, finally, that they are a cloud or vapor continually rising from the head of the comet and moving away into the regions facing away from the sun. The first opinion belongs to those who are not yet imbued with the science of **optics**. For a sunbeam is not perceived in a dark room except insofar as the light is reflected from particles of dust and smoke always flying through the air; therefore, in air infected with thicker smoke, it is more splendid and strikes the sense more strongly; in clearer air, it is thinner and more difficult to perceive; but in the heavens, without reflecting matter, there can be none. Light is not perceived insofar as it is in the beam, but insofar as it is reflected from there to our eyes. For vision does not occur except through rays that strike the eyes. The second opinion <note>The theory that comet tails are an optical illusion caused by the refraction (bending) of light as it passes through celestial matter.</note> is burdened with many difficulties. Tails are never variegated with colors, which are nevertheless the inseparable companions of refractions. The light of the fixed stars <note>Stars that appear to maintain a permanent position relative to each other, unlike the "wandering" planets.</note> and planets, transmitted distinctly to us, demonstrates that the celestial medium possesses no refractive power. For as to the claim that fixed stars were sometimes seen as comets by the *Egyptians*, this, because it happens so rarely, must be ascribed to the accidental refraction of clouds. The radiation and twinkling <note>original: *scintillatio*</note> of the fixed stars are also to be attributed to the refractions of both the eyes and the shimmering air, since these disappear when telescopes are applied to the eye. It is the trembling of the air and ascending vapors that causes rays to be easily diverted by turns from the narrow space of the pupil, but not at all from the wider aperture of the objective glass <note>The large primary lens of a telescope.</note>. This is why twinkling is generated in the first case, but ceases in the second; and the cessation in the latter case demonstrates a regular transmission of light through the heavens without any sensible refraction.

Lest anyone should contend that tails are not usually seen around comets <note>Referring here to stars appearing as comets.</note> because their light is not strong enough—claiming that the secondary rays <note>Fainter, scattered rays of light.</note> lack the strength to move the eyes, and therefore the tails of fixed stars are not perceived—it should be known that the light of fixed stars can be increased more than a hundredfold by means of telescopes, yet no tails are seen. The light of planets is also more abundant, yet they have no tails; but comets are often extremely long-tailed even when the light of their heads is thin and very dull. For so it was that the comet of the year 1680, in the month of December, at which time its head scarcely equaled the stars of the second magnitude in its light, emitted a tail of notable splendor reaching 40, 50, 60 or 70 degrees in length and beyond. on December 29, 1577, the comet <note>Newton is referencing the Great Comet of 1577, a famous celestial event observed by astronomers across Europe.</note> was located at 8 degrees 41 minutes of Sagittarius with a northern latitude of 28 degrees 40 minutes, while the sun was also positioned at approximately 18 degrees 26 minutes of Capricorn. In both cases, the Earth was located in the same spot, and the comet appeared in the same part of the sky; however, in the first case, the comet's tail (based on my observations and those of others) deviated at an angle of 4 ½ degrees from the direction opposite the sun toward the north; whereas in the latter case (from the observations of *Tycho Brahe* <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was a Danish nobleman and astronomer whose accurate planetary observations provided the data for Kepler’s laws and Newton’s physics.</note>), the deviation was 21 degrees toward the south. Therefore, having rejected the idea of celestial refraction, it remains that the phenomena of tails must be derived from some matter that reflects light.

Moreover, that tails arise from the heads and ascend into the regions facing away from the sun is confirmed by the laws they observe. For instance, lying in the planes of the comets' orbits passing through the sun, they deviate from the direction opposite the sun toward those parts which the heads leave behind as they progress in those orbits. To a spectator positioned in these planes, the tails appear in parts directly opposite the sun; but as the spectator moves away from these planes, the deviation is gradually perceived and appears greater day by day. This deviation, all else being equal, is smaller where the tail is more oblique to the comet's orbit, and also where the comet’s head approaches closer to the sun—especially if the angle of deviation is viewed near the comet's head. Furthermore, tails that do not deviate appear straight, while those that do deviate are curved. This curvature is greater where the deviation is greater, and more noticeable where the tail, all else being equal, is longer; for in shorter tails, the curvature is hardly noticed. The angle of deviation is smaller near the comet’s head and larger toward the other extremity of the tail; and therefore, the tail, with its convex side, faces the parts from which the deviation occurs—parts which are in a straight line drawn from the sun through the comet's head to infinity. Finally, those tails which are longer and wider, and shine with a more vigorous light, are a little more splendid on their convex sides and are terminated by a less indistinct boundary than on their concave sides. The phenomena of the tail, therefore, depend on the motion of the head, and not on the region of the heaven in which the head is seen; and for that reason, they are not caused by the refraction of the heavens, but arise from the head supplying the matter. For just as in our air the smoke of any ignited body seeks the upper regions—and does so either perpendicularly if the body is at rest, or obliquely if the body moves sideways—so in the heavens, where bodies gravitate toward the sun, smoke and vapors ought to ascend away from the sun (as has already been said)

Regarding the sudden and erratic flickering of the tails, and their irregular shapes which some observers occasionally describe, I add nothing here; this is because they may arise either from changes in our own atmosphere and the movements of clouds partially obscuring the tails, or perhaps from parts of the Milky Way, which might be confused with the passing tails and seen as if they were parts of them.

Moreover, that vapors sufficient for filling such immense spaces can arise from the atmospheres of comets can be understood from the thinness <term>rarity: the quality of being low in density; Newton is explaining how matter expands in a vacuum</term> of our own air. For air near the surface of the earth occupies a space nearly 850 times greater than water of the same weight, and therefore a cylindrical column of air 850 feet high is of the same weight as a column of water one foot high of the same width. A column of air rising to the very top of the atmosphere equals in its weight a column of water about 33 feet high; and therefore, if the lower part of the entire air column (the 850 feet of height) is removed, the remaining upper part will equal in weight a column of water 32 feet high. From this basis (following the rule confirmed by many experiments, that the compression of air is proportional to the weight of the incumbent atmosphere, and that gravity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the center of the earth), and by performing a calculation using the corollary to Proposition 22, Book 2, I have found that if air is ascended from the surface of the earth to the height of one terrestrial semi-diameter <note>The "semi-diameter" is the radius of the Earth, roughly 4,000 miles.</note>, it becomes thinner than it is here by a ratio far greater than that of the entire space below the orbit of Saturn compared to a globe only one digit <note>A "digit" was a standard measurement of approximately 0.75 inches.</note> wide. Therefore, a globe of our air only one digit wide, if it had the thinness it would possess at the height of one Earth radius, would fill all the regions of the planets all the way to the sphere of Saturn and far beyond. Accordingly, since air even higher up thins out immensely, and since the coma or atmosphere of a comet, in ascending from its center, becomes nearly ten times higher...

And although—on account of the far thicker atmosphere of comets, the great gravitation of bodies toward the sun, and the gravitation of particles of air and vapors toward each other—it is possible that air in the celestial spaces and in the tails of comets does not become so thinned out; nevertheless, it is clear from this calculation that a very small quantity of air and vapor is abundantly sufficient for all those phenomena of tails. For the remarkable rarity of the tails is also inferred from the stars shining through them. The terrestrial atmosphere, glowing with the light of the sun, in its thickness of only a few miles, obscures and entirely extinguishes both all the stars and the moon itself; yet through the immense thickness of the tails, which are likewise illuminated by solar light, the smallest stars are known to shine through without any loss of brightness. Nor is the splendor of most tails usually greater than the light of our own air in a darkened room when it reflects a beam of sunlight the width of only one or two fingers.

In what space of time the vapor ascends from the head to the end of the tail can be known approximately by drawing a straight line from the end of the tail to the sun, and noting the place where that line cuts the trajectory <note>The "trajectory" refers to the path or orbit of the comet.</note>. For the vapor at the end of the tail—if it were to ascend in a straight line from the sun—began to ascend from the head at the time when the head was at that point of intersection. But the vapor does not ascend in a perfectly straight line from the sun; instead, by retaining the motion which the comet had before the vapor's ascent, and by combining that with the motion of its ascent, it rises obliquely <note>Newton is describing the effect of inertia; the vapor keeps moving forward with the comet even as it is pushed away from the sun.</note>. Hence, a more accurate solution to the problem will be that the straight line which cuts the orbit should be parallel to the length of the tail, or rather (on account of the curved motion of the comet) that it should diverge slightly from the line of the tail. By this method I found that the vapor which was at the end of the tail on *January* 25 had begun to ascend from the head before *December* 11, and therefore had spent more than 45 days in its entire ascent. But all that tail which appeared on *December* 10 had ascended in the space of those two days which had elapsed from the time of the comet’s perihelion <term>perihelion: the point in an orbit where a celestial body is closest to the sun</term>. Therefore, the vapor at the beginning, in the vicinity of the sun, was ascending very quickly, and afterward continued to ascend with a motion always slowed down by its own gravity; and by ascending, it increased the length of the tail. The tail, however, as long as it appeared, consisted of almost all the vapor that had ascended from the time of perihelion; and the vapor that first ascended and formed the tip of the tail did not vanish until it ceased <note>original: "desiit"</note> to be seen because of its excessive distance both from the illuminating sun and from our eyes.

From this it also follows that the tails of other comets, which are short, do not ascend with a swift and perpetual motion from the heads and then quickly vanish, but are permanent columns of vapors and exhalations, propagated from the heads by a very slow motion of many days; these, by participating in that motion of the heads which they had at the beginning, continue to move through the heavens together with the heads. And from this it is again inferred that celestial spaces are devoid of the power of resistance; since in them not only the solid bodies of planets and comets, but also the extremely thin <term>rarissimi: the least dense or most "spread out" state of matter</term> vapors of the tails, perform their very swift motions most freely and preserve them for a very long time.

*Kepler* ascribes the ascent of the tails from the atmospheres of the heads, and their progress into the regions away from the sun, to the action of rays of light carrying the matter of the tail along with them <note>Johannes Kepler proposed that the "pressure" of sunlight physically pushed comet material away, a remarkably prophetic idea now known as radiation pressure.</note>. And that a far thinner aura <note>original: "aura" — a term for a gentle breeze or thin vaporous atmosphere</note> in the most free spaces should yield to the action of rays is not at all contrary to reason, notwithstanding that thick substances in our highly obstructed regions <note>meaning on Earth, where air resistance is high</note> cannot be sensibly propelled by the sun’s rays. Another thinks that there can be particles as light as they are heavy, and that the matter of tails is light, and by its own lightness <note>original: "levitare" — Newton is referring to the concept of "levity," a historical idea that some objects have an inherent quality to rise, just as gravity makes them fall.</note> rises from the sun. But since the gravity of terrestrial bodies is proportional to the matter in the bodies, and therefore cannot be increased or diminished while the quantity of matter remains the same, I suspect that this ascent arises rather from the **rarefaction** of the matter of the tails. Smoke ascends in a chimney by the impulse of the air in which it floats. That air, thinned by heat <note>original: "per calorem rarefactus"</note>, rises because of its diminished specific gravity, and carries the entangled smoke along with it. Why should a comet’s tail not ascend from the sun in the same way? For solar rays do not agitate the media they pass through, except in reflection and refraction. The reflecting particles, heated by that action, will heat the ethereal aura in which they are entangled. That aura, by the heat communicated to it, will be rarefied, and because of the diminished specific gravity resulting from that rarity—by which it previously tended toward the sun—it will ascend and carry with it the reflecting particles from which the tail is composed. To the ascent of the vapors it also contributes that these revolve around the sun and by that action attempt to recede from the sun, while the sun's atmosphere and the matter of the heavens either rest entirely or, by only the motion which they received from the sun's rotation, revolve more slowly. These are the causes of the ascent of tails in the vicinity of the sun, where the orbits are more curved, and the comets exist within the denser and for that reason heavier atmosphere of the sun, and soon emit the longest tails. For the tails that are then born, by preserving their motion and meanwhile gravitating toward the sun, will be

For the gravity of the vapors toward the sun will no more cause the tails to fall away from the heads toward the sun than the gravity of the heads could cause them to fall away from the tails. By their common gravity, they will either fall together toward the sun or be retarded together in their ascent; and therefore, that gravity does not prevent the tails and heads from most easily assuming any position relative to each other from the causes already described, or any others whatsoever, and afterward most freely preserving it.

Therefore, the tails which are produced at the perihelia <note>the points in an orbit closest to the sun</note> of comets will depart with their heads into distant regions, and either return to us with them from there after a long series of years, or rather, having been rarefied there, they will gradually vanish. For afterward, in the descent of the heads toward the sun, new, somewhat short tails must be propagated from the heads with a slow motion, and thereafter, at the perihelia of those comets which descend even to the sun’s atmosphere, they will increase immensely. For the vapor in those most free spaces perpetually rarefies and expands. By which reasoning it happens that every tail is broader at its upper extremity than near the head of the comet.

Moreover, it seems consistent with reason that by that rarefaction, the perpetually expanding vapor is finally diffused and scattered through the entire heavens, and then gradually attracted into the planets by its own gravity and mixed with their atmospheres. For just as the seas are absolutely required for the constitution of this earth, and that from them, through the heat of the sun, vapors may be raised in sufficient abundance, which, either gathered into clouds, fall in rains and irrigate and nourish the entire earth for the production of vegetables <note>original: "vegetabilium" — Newton uses this to refer to all plant life</note>; or, condensed on the cold peaks of mountains (as some philosophize with reason), run down into springs and rivers: so for the preservation of the seas and fluids on the planets, comets seem to be required, from whose condensed exhalations and vapors whatever liquid is consumed by vegetation <note>the growth process of plants</note> and putrefaction <note>decomposition</note> and converted into dry earth, can be continually supplied and refreshed. For all vegetables grow entirely from liquids, then for the most part pass into dry earth through putrefaction, and mud perpetually settles from putrefied liquids. Hence the mass of dry earth increases daily, and the liquids, unless they received an increase from elsewhere, would have to decrease perpetually and finally fail.

Furthermore, I suspect that that spirit <note>In 17th-century natural philosophy, "spirit" referred to a highly subtle, active substance thought to be the source of life or chemical activity in the air</note>, which is the smallest but most subtle and...

<summary>Newton argues that comet tails move in tandem with their heads due to gravity and eventually disperse into space to replenish the water and "vital spirits" of planets. He views comets as essential to a self-sustaining cosmic cycle, preventing the Earth and other planets from drying out as liquids are converted into solid matter.</summary>
<keywords>comet tails, perihelion, gravity, planetary atmospheres, water cycle, vegetation, putrefaction, cosmic replenishment, natural philosophy</keywords>

## OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>ON THE SYSTEM OF THE WORLD</margin> ...the best <note>original: *optima*; referring to the most refined or essential part of the atmosphere</note>, and required for the life of all things, comes primarily from comets.

The atmospheres of comets, as they descend toward the sun, are drawn out into tails and diminished, becoming narrower (at least on the side facing the sun); conversely, during their retreat from the sun, when they no longer flow out so extensively into tails, they are broadened—provided that *Hevelius* <note>Johannes Hevelius (1611–1687), a prominent Polish astronomer known for his detailed lunar maps and observations of comets</note> correctly noted their phenomena. However, the heads appear smallest when they have just been heated by the sun and have broken out into the largest and most brilliant tails, and the nuclei are perhaps surrounded by a thicker and darker smoke in the lowest parts of their atmospheres. For all smoke excited by intense heat tends to be thicker and darker. Thus, the head of the comet we have been discussing appeared dimmer at equal distances from the sun and the earth after its perihelion <note>the point in an orbit closest to the sun</note> than before. In the month of December, it was usually compared with stars of the third magnitude, but in the month of November, with stars of the first and second magnitude. And those who had seen both describe the earlier comet as the greater one. For to a certain *young man from Cambridge* <note>original: *Cantabrigiensi*; likely a reference to one of Newton’s students or colleagues at the University of Cambridge</note>, on *November* 19, this comet, though its light was somewhat leaden and dull, equaled Spica <note>original: *Spicam Virginis*; the brightest star in the constellation Virgo</note> and sparkled more brightly than it did later. And to *Montenaro* <note>Geminiano Montanari (1633–1687), an Italian astronomer</note> on *Nov.* 20, Old Style <note>original: *st. vet.*; the Julian calendar used in England until 1752</note>, the comet appeared larger than stars of the first magnitude, with a tail two degrees in length. And *Mr. Storer* <note>Arthur Storer (c. 1645–1686), an early American astronomer and associate of Newton</note>, in letters that fell into our hands, wrote that its head in the month of *December*, when it was emitting a massive and most brilliant tail, was small and far inferior in visible size to the comet that had appeared in the month of *November* before sunrise. The reason for this was conjectured to be that the matter of the head was more abundant at the beginning and was gradually consumed.

It seems to point to the same conclusion that the heads of other comets, which emitted the largest and most brilliant tails, appeared somewhat dim and tiny. For in the year 1668, on *March* 5, New Style <note>original: *st. nov.*; the Gregorian calendar used in Catholic Europe</note>, at seven o'clock in the evening, *Father Valentin Estancel* <note>original: *Valentinus Estancius*; a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer</note>, living in *Brazil*, saw a comet very near the horizon at the winter sunset, with a head so small it was barely visible, but with a tail so exceedingly bright that those standing on the shore could easily see its image reflected from the sea. Indeed, it had the appearance of a glowing beam 23 degrees in length, slanting from the west toward the south and nearly parallel to the horizon. Such great brilliance lasted only three days, thereafter decreasing noticeably; and meanwhile, as the brilliance decreased, the tail increased in size. Whence also in

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK THREE.

In Portugal <note>original: *Lusitania*</note>, the comet is said to have occupied nearly a fourth part of the sky (that is, 45 degrees), stretching from west to east with remarkable splendor; yet it did not appear in its entirety, with its head always remaining hidden below the horizon in these regions. From the growth of the tail and the decrease in its brilliance, it is clear that the head was moving away from the sun, having been very close to it at the beginning, just like the behavior of the comet of the year 1680. 

In the *Saxon Chronicle* <note>a collection of annals in Old English chronicling the history of the Anglo-Saxons</note>, a similar comet of the year 1106 is recorded, whose star was small and dim (like that of 1680), but the splendor that radiated from it was very bright and like a "huge beam" <note>original: *trabs*; a term used by early astronomers to describe long, rectangular-shaped comets</note> stretching toward the east and north, as *Hevelius* also notes from *Simeon of Durham, the monk*. It appeared at the beginning of the month of *February*, and thereafter around evening, toward the winter sunset. From this, and from the position of the tail, it is inferred that the head was close to the sun. *The comet,* says Matthew Paris <note>a Benedictine monk and English chronicler</note>, *was distant from the sun by about one cubit <note>an informal unit of measurement used here to describe the angular distance in the sky, roughly 2 degrees</note>, emitting a long ray from itself from the third hour [more correctly the sixth] until the ninth hour.* 

Such also was 그 most fiery comet described by *Aristotle* in Book 1 of his *Meteorology*, chapter 6, *whose head was not seen on the first day because it had set before the sun, or at least was hidden under the solar rays; but on the following day it was seen as much as possible. For it left the sun at the smallest possible distance, and soon set. Because of the excessive heat [of the tail, specifically], the scattered fire of the head did not yet appear; but as time passed (says Aristotle), when the tail was burning less intensely, the comet's own face was restored [to the head]. And it extended its brilliance even to a third part of the sky [that is, to 60 degrees]. It appeared, however, in the winter time [in the 4th year of the 101st Olympiad <note>approximately 373–372 BCE</note>] and, ascending as far as the belt of Orion, it vanished there.* 

That comet of the year 1618, which emerged from the solar rays with an immense tail, seemed to equal or slightly exceed stars of the first magnitude; yet not a few larger comets have appeared which had shorter tails. Some of these are reported to have equaled Jupiter, others Venus, or even the moon.

We have said that comets are a kind of planet revolving around the sun in highly eccentric <note>non-circular or elongated</note> orbits. And just as among the planets without tails, those that revolve in smaller orbits and closer to the sun tend to be smaller, so also it seems consistent with reason that comets which approach closer to the sun at their perihelia <note>the point in an orbit closest to the sun</note> are for the most part smaller, lest they disturb the sun too much by their gravitational attraction. However, the transverse diameters of the orbits and the periodic times of their revolutions [must be determined] from the comparison of comets returning in the same orbits after long intervals of time,

## PROPOSITION 42. PROBLEM 22.

### *To correct the trajectory of a comet that has been found.*

**Operation 1.** Let the position of the plane of the trajectory be assumed, as found through the preceding proposition; and let three locations of the comet be selected that are defined by the most accurate observations and are as far apart from each other as possible. Let **A** be the time between the first and second observation, and **B** the time between the second and third. It is appropriate for the comet to be positioned at perigee <term>the point in an orbit where the object is closest to the sun</term> in one of these observations, or at least not be far distant from perigee. From these apparent locations, through trigonometric operations, let the three true locations of the comet be found within that assumed plane of the trajectory. Then, through those three found locations, around the center of the sun as a focus <note>original: *umbilicus*; literally "navel," the geometric center point for a conic section</note>, let a conic section <note>the shape of the orbit, such as an ellipse or parabola</note> be described by mathematical operations established by the help of Proposition 21, Book 1. Let the areas of this section, bounded by the radii drawn from the sun to the found locations, be **D** and **E**; namely, **D** is the area between the first and second observation, and **E** is the area between the second and third. And let **T** be the total time in which the entire area **D + E** ought to be described by the velocity of the comet, as found through Proposition 16, Book 1.

**Oper. 2.** Let the longitude of the nodes <term>the points where the comet's path crosses the Earth's orbital plane</term> of the trajectory plane be increased, by adding 20' or 30' to that longitude, which shall be called **P**; and let the inclination of that plane to the plane of the ecliptic <note>the plane of the Earth's orbit around the sun</note> be maintained. Then, from the three previously mentioned observed locations of the comet, let the three true locations be found in this new plane, as above; then also find the orbit passing through those locations, and the two areas of the same described between the observations, which shall be **d** and **e**, as well as the total time **t** in which the entire area **d + e** ought to be described.

**Oper. 3.** Let the longitude of the nodes from the first operation be maintained, and let the inclination of the trajectory plane to the plane of the ecliptic be increased, by adding 20' or 30' to that inclination, which shall be called **Q**. Then, from the three previously mentioned apparent locations of the comet, let the three true locations be found in this new plane, along with the orbit passing through those locations, as well as the two areas of the same described between the observations, which shall be **δ** and **ε**, and the total time **τ** in which the entire area **δ + ε** ought to be described.

will be the true transverse axis of the trajectory which the comet describes. Once the transverse axis is given, the periodic time <note>the time it takes to complete one full orbit</note> of the comet is also given. Which was to be found.

Furthermore, the periodic times of revolving comets, and the transverse axes of their orbits, will not be determined accurately enough except by comparing comets with one another that appear at different times. If several comets, after equal intervals of time, are found to have described the same orbit, it must be concluded that all these are one and the same comet, revolving in the same orbit. And then finally from the times of the revolutions, the transverse axes of the orbits will be given, and from these axes, the elliptical orbits will be determined.

To this end, therefore, the trajectories of several comets are to be computed under the hypothesis that they are parabolic <note>Newton assumes a parabola as a baseline because it is the simplest curve for a non-returning or long-period visitor</note>. For trajectories of this kind will always agree very closely with the phenomena. This is clear, not only from the parabolic trajectory of the comet of the year 1680, which I compared above with observations, but also from that notable comet which appeared in the years 1664 and 1665, and was observed by Hevelius <note>Johannes Hevelius (1611–1687), a prominent Polish astronomer</note>. In the month of February at the start of the year 1665, the first star of Aries, which I will call $\gamma$ in the following, was at 28° 30' 15'' of Aries ♈ with a northern latitude of 7° 8' 58''. The second star of Aries was at 29° 17' 18'' of Aries ♈ with a northern latitude of 8° 28' 16''. And a certain other star of the seventh magnitude, which I will call *A*, was at 28° 24' 45'' of Aries ♈ with a northern latitude of 8° 28' 33''. Now the Comet, on *February 7th at 7:30 PM in Paris* (that is, *February 7th at 8:37 PM in Danzig* <note>original: "Gedani," the Latin name for Danzig, modern-day Gdańsk</note>) according to the Old Style <note>the Julian calendar, which was then 10 days behind the Gregorian calendar used in much of Europe</note>, formed a right-angled triangle with those stars $\gamma$ and *A*, with the right angle at $\gamma$. And the distance of the comet from star $\gamma$ was equal to the distance between stars $\gamma$ and *A*, that is 1° 19' 46'' on a great circle <term>the shortest distance between two points on a sphere</term>; and therefore that distance was 1° 20' 26'' on the parallel of latitude of star $\gamma$. Wherefore, if the longitude of 1° 20' 26'' is subtracted from the longitude of star $\gamma$, there remains the longitude of the comet as 27° 9' 49'' of Aries ♈. *Auzout* <note>Adrien Auzout, a French astronomer</note>, from this observation of his, placed the comet at approximately 27° 0' of Aries ♈. And from the diagram with which *Hooke* <note>Robert Hooke, Newton’s contemporary and often rival</note> delineated its motion, it was then at 26° 59' 24'' of Aries ♈. By taking a middle value <note>original: "Ratione mediocri," meaning a weighted average or mean</note>, I placed the same at 27° 4' 46'' of Aries ♈. From the same observation, *Auzout* placed the latitude of the comet then at 7° 4' or 5' toward the north. It would have been more correctly placed at 7° 3' 29'', since the difference in the latitudes of the comet and star $\gamma$ was equal to the difference in the longitudes of stars $\gamma$ and *A*.

*February 22nd at 7:30 PM in London*, that is, *February 22nd at 8:46 PM in Danzig*, the distance of the comet from star *A*, according to *Hooke's* observation as drawn by himself in a diagram, as well as according to *Auzout’s* observations as drawn by *Petit* <note>Pierre Petit, a French mathematician and astronomer</note> in a diagram, was a fifth part of the distance between star *A* and the first star of Aries, or 15' 57''. And the distance of the comet from the line joining star *A* and the first star of Aries was a fourth part of that same fifth part, that is, 4'. And therefore the comet was at 28° 29' 46'' of Aries ♈, with a northern latitude of 8° 12' 36''.

*March 1st at 7:00 PM in London*, that is, *March 1st at 8:16 PM in Danzig*, the comet was observed near the second star of Aries; the distance between them compared to the distance between the first and second stars of Aries (that is, to 1° 33') was as 4 to 45 according to *Hooke*, or as 2 to 23 according to *Gottignies* <note>Gilles-François de Gottignies, a Jesuit scientist in Rome</note>. From this, the distance of the comet from the second star of Aries was 8' 16'' according to *Hooke*, or 8' 5'' according to *Gottignies*, or 8' 10'' by a middle value. Now the comet, according to *Gottignies*, had just now passed the second star of Aries by a space of about a fourth or fifth part of the path completed in one day, which is about 1' 35'' (with which *Auzout* sufficiently agrees), or a little less according to *Hooke*, say 1'. Therefore, if 1' is added to the longitude of the first star of Aries, and to...

*March 7, at 7:30 PM in Paris* (that is, *March 7, at 8:37 PM in Danzig* <note>original: "Gedani"</note>) from the observations of *Auzout* <note>Adrien Auzout, a French astronomer and founding member of the Academy of Sciences</note>, the distance of the comet from the second star of Aries was equal to the distance of the second star of Aries from star *A*, which is 52' 29''. And the difference of the longitudes of the comet and the second star of Aries was 45' or 46', or by a mean value 45' 30''. And therefore the comet was in 0° 2' 48'' of Taurus ♉. From the diagram of *Auzout’s* observations, which *Petit* <note>Pierre Petit, a French mathematician and physicist</note> constructed, *Hevelius* <note>Johannes Hevelius, a leading astronomer in Danzig known for his detailed celestial atlases</note> deduced the latitude of the comet to be 8° 54'. But the engraver <note>original: "sculptor"</note> irregularly curved the path of the comet toward the end of its motion, and *Hevelius*, in the diagram of *Auzout’s* observations which he himself constructed, corrected that irregular curvature, and thus made the latitude of the comet to be 8° 55' 30''. And by correcting the irregularity a little further, the latitude may come out to be 8° 56' or 8° 57'.

This comet was also seen on the 9th day of *March*, and then it ought to have been located in 0° 18' of Taurus ♉, with a northern latitude of about 9° 3' ½.

This comet appeared for three months, and described almost six zodiac signs, and in one day it completed nearly twenty degrees. Its course deflected greatly from a great circle, being curved toward the north; and its motion toward the end changed from retrograde <term>moving backward relative to the stars</term> to direct <term>moving forward in the usual order of the zodiac</term>. And notwithstanding so unusual a course, the theory from beginning to end agrees no less accurately with the observations than the theories of the planets are accustomed to agree with their observations, as will be evident to anyone inspecting the table. However, about two minutes should be subtracted where the comet was swiftest; which will be done by taking away twelve seconds from the angle between the ascending node <term>the point where the orbit crosses the ecliptic moving north</term> and the perihelion <term>the point in the orbit closest to the sun</term>, or by setting that angle at 49° 27' 18''. The annual parallax <note>the apparent shift of a star or comet caused by the Earth's orbit around the sun</note> of both comets (both this one and the previous one) was notable, and from this is demonstrated the annual motion of the earth in its great orbit <term>the "orbis magnus," or Earth's path around the sun</term>.

The theory is also confirmed by the motion of the comet which appeared in the year 1683. This was retrograde in its orbit, the plane of which contained an almost right angle with the plane of the ecliptic <term>the apparent path of the sun, which defines the plane of Earth's orbit</term>. Its ascending node (according to the calculation of *Halley* <note>Edmond Halley, Newton's close friend and the benefactor who funded the publication of the Principia</note>) was in 23° 23' of Virgo ♍; the inclination of the orbit to the ecliptic was 83° 11'; the perihelion was in 25° 29' 30'' of Gemini ♊. The perihelion distance from the sun was 56,020, where the radius of the great orbit is 100,000, and the time of perihelion was *July 2, at 3:50 AM*. From these examples it is abundantly clear that the motions of comets are shown no less accurately by the theory we have set forth than the motions of the planets are usually shown by their own theories. And therefore, the orbits of comets can be calculated through this theory, and the periodic time of a comet revolving in any orbit can finally be known; then at last the transverse sides <note>the semi-major axes</note> of the elliptical orbits and the heights of their aphelions <term>the point furthest from the Sun</term> will become known.

The retrograde comet <note>a comet that appears to move in the opposite direction to the planets</note> which appeared in the year 1607, described an orbit whose ascending node <term>the point where the orbit crosses the ecliptic from south to north</term> (according to Halley’s calculation) was in Leo 20° 21'; the inclination of the orbital plane to the plane of the ecliptic was 17° 2'; the perihelion was in Aquarius 2° 16'; and the perihelion distance from the sun was 58,680, where the radius of the Earth's orbit is 100,000. And the comet was at its perihelion on October 16 at 3:50 AM. This orbit matches very closely with the orbit of the comet that appeared in the year 1682. If these two comets were one and the same, this comet would revolve in a span of 75 years, and the major axis of its orbit will be to the major axis of the Earth's orbit as the cube root of $75 \times 75$ is to 1, or approximately 1778 to 100. And the aphelion distance of this comet from the sun will be to the distance...

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES ###

<margin>BOOK THREE</margin>

...even the average distance <note>original: "distantiam"</note> of the Earth from the Sun, as approximately 35 to 1. Once these things are known, it will not be difficult to determine the elliptical orbit of this comet. And these things will be so if the comet, in a space of seventy-five years, should return hereafter in this orbit <note>Newton is here predicting the return of what we now call Halley's Comet, which Edmond Halley had calculated to have a 75-76 year period</note>. Other comets seem to revolve over a longer time and to ascend higher.

Furthermore, comets, on account of their great number, and the great distance of their aphelia <term>the point in an orbit furthest from the Sun</term> from the Sun, and their long delay in those aphelia, ought to be somewhat disturbed by their mutual gravities upon one another; thus their eccentricities and their times of revolution should be now increased a little, now diminished. Accordingly, it is not to be expected that the same comet should return accurately in the same orbit and with the same periodic times. It is enough if no greater changes occur than those which may arise from the causes mentioned above.

And from this, the reason is given why comets are not confined to the zodiac in the manner of planets, but instead wander from there and are carried by various motions into all regions of the heavens. Namely, for this end: that in their aphelia, where they move most slowly, they may be as far distant as possible from each other, and may attract one another as little as possible. For this reason, comets which descend from a greater height, and therefore move most slowly in their aphelia, ought to ascend higher.

The comet which appeared in the year 1680 was less distant from the Sun at its perihelion <term>the point in an orbit closest to the Sun</term> than by a sixth part of the Sun's diameter; and on account of its extreme velocity in that vicinity, and the relative density of the Sun’s atmosphere, it must have felt some resistance and been somewhat retarded, and thus approached closer to the Sun. By approaching the Sun in each revolution, it will at length fall into the body of the Sun. But even in the aphelion, where it moves most slowly, it can sometimes be retarded by the attraction of other comets, and subsequently fall into the Sun. Thus also fixed stars, which gradually expire into light and vapors, can be replenished by comets falling into them, and, being kindled by new nourishment, may be regarded as new stars. Of this kind are the fixed stars that appear suddenly, and shine most brightly at the beginning, and then gradually vanish. Such was the star in the Chair of Cassiopeia <note>the constellation Cassiopeia</note> which *Cornelius Gemma*, while surveying that part of the heavens on a clear night on the eighth of November 1572, did not see at all; but on the next night (*Nov. 9*), he saw it brighter than all the fixed stars, and scarcely yielding to Venus in its light. *Tycho Brahe* saw this on the eleventh of the same month when it shone most brightly; and from that time, little by little...

...observed it gradually decreasing and vanishing over the space of sixteen months. In the month of *November*, when it first appeared, it equaled Venus in its brightness. In the month of *December*, having diminished somewhat, it seemed to equal Jupiter. In the *year 1573*, in the month of *January*, it was smaller than Jupiter and larger than *Sirius*, to which it became equal at the end of *February* and the beginning of *March*. In the months of *April* and *May*, it equaled stars of the second magnitude; in *June*, *July*, and *August*, stars of the third magnitude; in *September*, *October*, and *November*, stars of the fourth magnitude; in *December* and *January of 1574*, stars of the fifth magnitude; and in the month of *February*, stars of the sixth magnitude; and in the month of *March*, it vanished from sight. Its color was clear, whitish, and splendid from the beginning, later yellow, and in *March of 1573*, reddish like *Mars* or the star *Aldebaran*; in *May*, however, it took on a leaden whiteness, such as we see in *Saturn*, which color it preserved until the end, always becoming dimmer. Such also was the star in the right foot of the <note>original: "serpentarii"</note> Serpent-bearer <note>The constellation Ophiuchus</note>, which *Kepler’s* disciples observed to begin appearing on the 30th day of *September*, <term>Old Style</term> <note>The Julian calendar, which was still in use in England during Newton's time</note> in the year 1604, and which surpassed the light of the planet Jupiter, though it had not appeared at all the previous night. From that time, it truly decreased little by little, and in the space of fifteen or sixteen months, it vanished from sight. It is said that *Hipparchus* was also moved to observe the fixed stars and record them in a catalog because of such a new star shining beyond measure. But the fixed stars, which appear and vanish by turns, and which grow gradually and hardly ever surpass the light of fixed stars of the third magnitude, seem to be of another kind, and by revolving, show a bright side and a dark side by turns. Moreover, the vapors which arise from the sun and the fixed stars and the tails of comets can fall by their own gravity into the atmospheres of the planets and there be condensed and converted into water and humid spirits, and thereafter, through a slow heat, gradually migrate into salts, and sulfurs, and tinctures, and slime, and mud, and clay, and sand, and stones, and corals, and other terrestrial substances.

## GENERAL SCHOLIUM.

The hypothesis of <term>vortices</term> <note>The theory proposed by René Descartes that planets are carried around the sun by "whirlpools" of subtle matter</note> is beset by many difficulties. In order for each planet, by a radius drawn to the sun, to describe areas proportional to the time, the periodic times of the parts of the vortex ought to be in the duplicate ratio <note>The square</note> of the distances from the sun. In order for the periodic times of the planets to be in a <term>sesquialteral</term> <note>original: "sesquiduplicata" — the 3/2 power or the ratio where the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the distance</note> proportion of the distances from the sun, the periodic times...

# MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES

<header>MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES</header>

<margin>BOOK THREE</margin>
...the periodic times of the parts of the <term>vortex</term> <note>The "vortex" theory, championed by René Descartes, suggested that planets were carried around the Sun by a swirling whirlpool of invisible fluid. Newton spent much of Book 2 and 3 proving this was mathematically impossible.</note> would have to be in the <term>sesquiplicate proportion</term> <note>original: "sesquiplicata proportione"; this refers to a ratio of 3:2, or the 1.5 power. In modern terms, Newton is referring to Kepler's Third Law, where the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its distance from the Sun.</note> of the distances. In order for smaller vortices—revolving around Saturn, Jupiter, and other planets—to be maintained and float calmly within the Sun's vortex, the periodic times of the parts of the solar vortex would have to be equal. The rotations of the Sun and the planets around their own axes, which ought to correspond with the motions of the vortices, differ from all these proportions. The motions of comets are highly regular and observe the same laws as the motions of the planets, yet they cannot be explained by vortices. Comets are carried in very eccentric motions into all parts of the heavens, which could not happen unless vortices were removed.

Projectiles in our air feel only the resistance of the air. When the air is removed, as it is in <term>Boyle's vacuum</term> <note>original: "vacuo Boyliano"; named after Robert Boyle, who used an air pump to demonstrate that in a vacuum, objects like feathers and gold coins fall at the same speed because there is no air resistance.</note>, resistance ceases; indeed, a thin feather and solid gold fall with equal velocity in this vacuum. The same logic applies to the celestial spaces which are above the atmosphere of the Earth. All bodies in those spaces ought to move most freely; and therefore planets and comets should revolve perpetually in orbits of a given shape and position according to the laws explained above. They will indeed persist in their orbits by the laws of gravity, yet they could by no means have first acquired the regular position of the orbits through these laws alone.

The six primary planets revolve around the Sun in circles concentric to the Sun, in the same direction of motion, and nearly in the same plane. Ten moons revolve around the Earth, Jupiter, and Saturn in concentric circles, in the same direction of motion, and nearly in the planes of the planets' orbits. And all these regular motions do not have their origin from mechanical causes; since comets are carried freely in very eccentric orbits and into all parts of the heavens. By this kind of motion, comets pass through the orbits of the planets very quickly and easily, and in their <term>aphelia</term> <note>The point in an orbit where a body is furthest from the Sun and moves at its slowest speed.</note>, where they are slower and stay longer, they are at the greatest possible distance from each other, so that they attract each other as little as possible. This most elegant arrangement of the sun, planets, and comets could not have arisen except by the plan and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being. And if the fixed stars are the centers of similar systems, all these, constructed by a similar plan, will be subject to the dominion of *One*: especially since the light of the fixed stars is of the same nature as the light of the sun, and all systems transmit light into one another. And lest the systems of the fixed stars should fall into each other by their gravity, He has placed them at immense distances from one another.

# OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

<margin>ON THE SYSTEM OF THE WORLD</margin>

<margin>
a That is, universal Emperor.
</margin>
This Being governs all things, not as the soul of the world <note>The "soul of the world" (anima mundi) was an ancient idea that the universe itself is a living animal; Newton rejects this, arguing God is a separate ruler.</note>, but as Lord over all. And because of his dominion, the Lord God is usually called <sup>a</sup> *Pantokrator* <note>original Greek: Παντοκράτωρ; a title meaning "Almighty" or "Ruler of All."</note>. For "God" is a relative word and refers to servants: and deity is the dominion of God, not over his own body (as those imagine for whom God is the soul of the world), but over servants. The supreme God is a being eternal, infinite, and absolutely perfect: but however perfect a being may be, without dominion he is not Lord God. For we say "my God," "your God," "the God of *Israel*," "the God of gods," and "Lord of lords": but we do not say "my eternal," "your eternal," "the eternal of *Israel*," or "the eternal of gods"; we do not say "my infinite," or "my perfect." These titles have no relation to servants.

<margin>
b Our [Edward] Pococke <note>An English Orientalist and theologian (1604–1691) whom Newton respected.</note> derives the word "God" from the Arabic word *du* (and in the oblique case *di*), which signifies "Lord." And in this sense, princes are called gods in *Psalm* 84:6 and *John* 10:45. And *Moses* is said to be a god to his brother *Aaron*, and a god to King *Pharaoh* (*Exodus* 4:16 and 7:1). And in the same sense, the souls of dead princes were once called gods by the heathens, but falsely, because they lacked dominion.
</margin>
The word "God" everywhere <sup>b</sup> signifies "Lord": but every lord is not God. It is the dominion of a spiritual being that constitutes a God: a true dominion constitutes a true God, a supreme dominion a supreme God, and a feigned dominion a false God. And from his true dominion it follows that the true God is living, intelligent, and powerful; and from his other perfections, it follows that he is supreme, or supremely perfect. He is eternal and infinite, omnipotent and omniscient; that is, he endures from eternity to eternity, and is present from infinity to infinity: he governs all things; and he knows all things that happen or can happen. He is not eternity and infinity, but eternal and infinite; he is not duration and space, but he endures and is present. He endures always, and is present everywhere, and by existing always and everywhere, he constitutes duration and space. Since every particle of space is *always*, and every indivisible moment of duration is *everywhere*, certainly the maker and lord of all things cannot be *never* or *nowhere*. Every sentient soul is the same indivisible person at different times and in different organs of sense and motion. There are successive parts in duration, and coexisting parts in space, but neither are found in the person of a human or in his thinking principle; and much less in the thinking substance of God. Every human, insofar as he is a sentient thing, is one and the same human throughout his life in each and every organ of sense. God is one and the same God always and everywhere. He is omnipresent not by *power* <note>original: "virtutem"; in this context, it refers to God's ability to act at a distance.</note> alone, but also by *substance*: for power cannot exist without substance.

<meta>Catchword: test. (The original Latin "test." likely leads to "testis" or "testimonium," continuing the discussion of God's presence.)</meta>

<summary>In this opening of the General Scholium, Newton defines God not as a metaphysical abstraction or a "world soul," but as a literal "Lord" whose dominion over the universe is proven by its order. He argues that God’s existence is the very foundation of space and time themselves.</summary>
<keywords>Pantokrator, dominion, soul of the world, omnipresence, duration and space, Isaac Newton, natural theology, Pococke, Moses</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "General Scholium" from page 528. Newton is concluding his masterpiece by arguing that the intricate order of the planetary system proves the existence of an intelligent and powerful Being. Having just defined God as a "Universal Ruler," he now addresses God's omnipresence and the limits of human understanding regarding the divine substance.</meta>

### MATHEMATICAL PRINCIPLES. BOOK THREE.

[...can] be. <margin>c This was the opinion of the ancients, such as Pythagoras in Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 1; Thales, Anaxagoras, and Virgil in the *Georgics*, book 4, line 220, and the *Aeneid*, book 6, line 721; Philo in *Allegories*, book 1, near the beginning; and Aratus in *Phaenomena*, near the beginning. So also the sacred writers, such as Paul in Acts 17:27, 28; John in the Gospel 14:2; Moses in Deuteronomy 4:39 and 10:14; David in Psalm 139:7, 8, 9; Solomon in 1 Kings 8:27; Job 22:12, 13, 14; and Jeremiah 23:23, 24. However, the idolaters imagined the sun, moon, stars, the souls of men, and other parts of the world to be parts of the supreme god, and therefore to be worshipped, but falsely.</margin> In him <sup>c</sup> all things are contained and moved, yet without mutual effect <note>original: *sine mutua passione*. Newton means that while God acts upon the world, the world’s physical movements do not affect or "act back" on God’s nature.</note>. God suffers nothing from the motions of bodies; they feel no resistance from the omnipresence of God. It is universally confessed that the supreme God exists necessarily; and by the same necessity, he exists always and everywhere. Hence also he is entirely similar to himself, all eye, all ear, all brain, all arm, all power of sensing, understanding, and acting, but in a way not at all human, not at all corporeal, in a way utterly unknown to us. Just as a blind man has no idea of colors, so we have no idea of the ways in which the most wise God senses and understands all things. He is entirely devoid of all body and bodily shape, and therefore cannot be seen, nor heard, nor touched, nor ought he be worshipped under the representation of any bodily thing. We have ideas of his attributes, but what the substance of any thing might be, we do not know at all. We see only the shapes and colors of bodies, we hear only sounds, we touch only external surfaces, we smell only odors, and taste flavors: we know the inward substances by no sense, by no reflexive action; and much less do we have an idea of the substance of God. We know him only by his properties and attributes, and by the most wise and excellent structures of things and final causes <note>A "final cause" is the purpose or "end" for which something is created. Newton argues that the design of the universe proves a Designer.</note>, and we admire him for his perfections; but we revere and worship him for his dominion. For we worship as servants, and a God without dominion, providence, and final causes is nothing else but fate and nature. From blind metaphysical necessity, which is surely the same always and everywhere, no variation of things arises. All the diversity of created things according to places and times could only have arisen from the ideas and will of a Being existing necessarily. Moreover, God is said by allegory to see, hear, speak, laugh, love, hate, desire, give, receive, rejoice, be angry, fight, manufacture, found, and build. For all discourse about God is taken from human affairs by some likeness, not a perfect one indeed, but of some sort nonetheless. And this much concerning God, about whom it surely belongs to natural philosophy <note>In Newton's era, "natural philosophy" was the study of the physical world, encompassing what we now call physics, astronomy, and biology.</note> to discourse from phenomena.

<meta>catchword: Hitherto</meta>

<summary>In this passage from the General Scholium, Newton argues that God is an omnipresent, non-corporeal ruler whose existence is proven by the purposeful design of the universe. He asserts that while we cannot know God's "substance," we can understand Him through His "dominion" and the observable phenomena of nature, making the study of God a legitimate part of natural philosophy.</summary>
