<meta>This page concludes the "General Scholium," the famous concluding essay Newton added to the second and third editions of the *Principia*. Following the theological discussion on the previous page, Newton now returns to the scientific methodology that defines his work, famously declaring his refusal to invent "hypotheses" for things he cannot prove through observation.</meta>

# THE PRINCIPLES OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY, etc.

<margin>ON THE SYSTEM OF THE WORLD</margin>
Hitherto I have explained the phenomena of the heavens and of our sea by the force of gravity, but I have not yet assigned the cause of gravity. This force certainly arises from some cause that penetrates even to the centers of the sun and planets, without any weight or power being lost; it acts not according to the quantity of the surfaces of the particles upon which it acts (as mechanical causes usually do), but according to the quantity of solid matter; and its action is extended everywhere to immense distances, always decreasing in the **duplicate ratio** <term>duplicate ratio: the "inverse-square law," meaning if the distance doubles, the force becomes four times weaker (2 squared)</term> of the distances. Gravity toward the sun is composed of the gravities toward each individual particle of the sun, and as one moves away from the sun, it decreases accurately in the duplicate ratio of the distances as far as the orbit of Saturn—as is manifest from the stillness of the **aphelia** <term>aphelia: the points in a planet's orbit furthest from the sun</term> of the planets—and even to the farthest aphelia of the comets, provided that those aphelia are stationary. I have not yet been able to deduce the reason for these properties of gravity from the phenomena, and **I frame no hypotheses** <note>original: *hypotheses non fingo*. This is perhaps Newton's most famous quote. He is stating that he will not "make up" or "invent" underlying causes for gravity that he cannot prove through mathematical induction or observation.</note>. For whatever is not deduced from the phenomena is to be called a *hypothesis*; and hypotheses—whether metaphysical or physical, whether based on occult qualities or mechanical ones—have no place in *experimental philosophy*. In this philosophy, propositions are deduced from the phenomena and are made general by induction. This is how the impenetrability, mobility, and impetus of bodies, and the laws of motion and of gravity, became known to us. And it is enough that gravity really exists, and acts according to the laws we have set forth, and suffices for all the motions of the celestial bodies and of our sea.

It would now be appropriate to add something concerning a certain **most subtle spirit** <note>Newton's "subtle spirit" or "aether" was his theoretical way of explaining how light, electricity, and even human thought (nerve impulses) travel through space and the body. At the time, he lacked the experimental data to prove its existence.</note> that pervades gross bodies and lies hidden within them; by the force and actions of which the particles of bodies mutually attract one another at very small distances and cohere when they become contiguous; and by which electrical bodies act at greater distances, both by repelling and attracting neighboring corpuscles; and by which light is emitted, reflected, refracted, inflected, and heats bodies; and by which all sensation is excited, and the limbs of animals are moved at the command of the will—namely, by the vibrations of this spirit propagated through the solid filaments of the nerves from the external organs of the senses to the brain, and from the brain into the muscles. But these things cannot be explained in few words; nor is there a sufficient abundance of experiments by which the laws of the actions of this spirit must be accurately determined and demonstrated.

4. An Hypothesis and Explanation of the Cause of Gravity or Gravitation, Magnetism, *etc.*
5. Discourses of Earthquakes, their Causes and Effects, and Histories of several: To which are annexed Physical Explanations of several of the Fables in *Ovid*'s *Metamorphoses* <note>A famous Roman narrative poem; Hooke attempted to provide scientific explanations for the mythological transformations described by Ovid</note>, very different from other Mythological Interpreters.
6. Lectures for improving Navigation and Astronomy, with the Descriptions of several new and useful Instruments, illustrated with Engravings <note>original: "Sculptures"</note>. To these Discourses is prefixed the Author's Life. By *Richard Waller*, Secretary of the Royal Society. Folio <note>The largest standard book size, made from sheets folded only once</note>.

21. **A Treatise of Architecture**, with Remarks and Observations by that excellent Master thereof *Sebastian le Clerc*, Knight of the Empire, Designer and Engraver to the Cabinet of the late *French King*, and Member of the Academy of Arts and Sciences; necessary for young People who would apply to that noble Art. Engraved in 181 Copper Plates by *John Sturt*. Translated by Mr. *Chambers*. In 2 Volumes. Octavo. 1725.

22. **Philosophical Letters** between the late Learned Mr. *Ray*, and several of his ingenious Correspondents, Natives and Foreigners. To which are added those of *Francis Willoughby*, Esquire; the whole consisting of many curious Discoveries and Improvements in the History of Four-legged animals <note>original: "Quadrupeds"</note>, Birds, Fishes, Insects, Plants, Fossils, Fountains, *etc.* Published by *W. Derham*, Master of Arts and Fellow of the Royal Society. 1718.

23. **The Wisdom of God** manifested in the Works of the Creation. In two Parts. To which are added Answers to some Objections. By *John Ray*, late Fellow of the Royal Society. The Eighth Edition. Octavo. 1722.

24. **Three Physico-Theological Discourses**, concerning I. The primitive Chaos, and Creation of the World. II. The general Flood <note>original: "Deluge"</note>, its Causes and Effects. III. The Dissolution of the World, and future Great Fire <note>original: "Conflagration"</note>; wherein are largely discussed the Production and Use of Mountains; the Original of Fountains, of fossils <note>original: "formed Stones"</note>, and Sea Fishes, Bones and Shells found in the Earth; the Effects of particular Floods and Inundations of the Sea; the Eruptions of Volcanoes; the Nature and Causes of Earthquakes; also an Historical Account of the two late remarkable ones in *Jamaica* and *England*: With practical Inferences, illustrated with Copper Plates. By *John Ray*, late Fellow of the Royal Society. The Fourth Edition. Octavo. 1721.

25. **New Memoirs of Literature**, containing an Account of new Books printed both at home and abroad; with Dissertations upon several Subjects, Miscellaneous Observations, *etc.* For *February*, 1726. being the Fourteenth Number. To be continued Monthly. Octavo.

26. **A Treatise of Five Orders of Columns** in Architecture, namely <note>original: "viz."</note> *Tuscan*, *Doric*, *Ionic*, *Corinthian* and *Composite*, wherein the Proportions and Characters of the Members of their several Pedestals, Columns and Entablatures <note>The horizontal structure supported by columns</note>, are distinctly considered, with Respect to the Practice of the Ancients and Moderns. Also a most natural, easy and practical Method laid down for determining the most minute Part in all the Orders without a Fraction. To which is annexed a Discourse concerning Pilasters <note>Rectangular columns attached to a wall</note>, and of several Abuses introduced into Architecture. Engraved on Six Folio Plates of the several Orders, adorned with twenty-four Borders, as many initial Letters, and a like Number of Tail-Pieces <note>Decorative ornaments at the end of chapters</note>, by *John Sturt*. Written in French by *Claude Perrault*, of the Royal Academy of Paris, Author of the celebrated Comment on *Vitruvius* <note>The ancient Roman author of the definitive treatise on architecture</note>. Made English by *John James* of *Greenwich*. 1722.

27. **Rules and Examples of Perspective**, proper for Painters and Architects, with 150 Plates. By *Andrea Pozzo*. Translated into English by *John James* of *Greenwich*, Folio.
